docs.title: Appendix B: Careers in Neuroscience and Medicine
Appendix B: Careers in Neuroscience and Medicine
docs.text:
So, what do you want to be?

I'm a sea slug, so my career options are limited to "helping scientists win Nobel Prizes." Yours are much wider! This appendix maps out the many jobs that use what you learned in this book, and how people actually get there.

docs.title: B.1 One Brain, Many Careers
docs.text:
Think about a single patient who has a stroke. A neurologist (a doctor who treats diseases of the brain and nerves) figures out where the damage is. A neuroradiologist reads the brain scans. A neurosurgeon may operate. A neuroscience nurse watches the patient around the clock. Then a physical therapist, an occupational therapist, and a speech-language pathologist help the patient walk, get dressed, and talk again. Behind them, neuroscientists, engineers, and data scientists built and tested the drugs, scanners, and tools everyone uses.

That is the big idea of this appendix: neuroscience is not one job. It is a field that connects to medicine, research, rehabilitation, engineering, computing, and teaching. Some take more than a decade of training after high school, and others take far less. Patients need all of them.

A quick note before we start. The training paths below describe the United States and are typical, not guaranteed. Rules change, and many people take detours. Always check the official sources linked in each section and in the Sources list.

docs.title: B.2 Careers at a Glance
docs.text:
Here is a quick key for the table. A residency is paid, supervised on-the-job training that every new doctor completes after medical school. A fellowship is optional extra training in a narrower area after residency. A license is legal permission from a state to practice.

Career What they do Typical U.S. education and training path Neurologist Diagnoses and treats disorders of the brain, spinal cord, nerves, and muscles, such as stroke, epilepsy, migraine, multiple sclerosis, and Parkinson's disease. Does not usually operate. 4-year college degree → 4 years of medical school (MD or DO) → 4-year neurology residency, which includes a first year of general internal medicine → optional fellowship (for example, stroke or epilepsy). Neurosurgeon Operates on the brain, spine, and nerves, for example to remove tumors, relieve pressure after injuries, or fix problems in the spine. College → medical school → 7-year neurosurgery residency (one of the longest in medicine) → optional fellowship. Psychiatrist A medical doctor who diagnoses and treats mental health conditions such as depression, anxiety, schizophrenia, and addiction. Can prescribe medicine and provide therapy. College → medical school → 4-year psychiatry residency → optional fellowship (for example, child and adolescent psychiatry). Child neurologist A neurologist for infants, children, and teens. Treats conditions such as childhood epilepsy, cerebral palsy, and genetic disorders of the nervous system. College → medical school → typically 2 years of pediatrics (or an approved mix of pediatrics plus another year) → 3 years of child neurology, about 5 years in all. Neuroradiologist A doctor who specializes in reading images of the brain, spine, head, and neck, such as MRI and CT scans. Some also do image-guided procedures. College → medical school → diagnostic radiology residency (4 years of radiology, usually after a 1-year clinical year, so typically 5 years) → neuroradiology fellowship, which lasts 1 year (12 months) in ACGME-accredited programs. Neuroscientist (PhD researcher) Designs and runs experiments to discover how the nervous system works, in labs at universities, government agencies, or companies. Bachelor's degree (often biology, psychology, neuroscience, chemistry, or engineering) → PhD, which averages about 6 years for biomedical fields → usually 1 or more years of postdoctoral research training. Physician-scientist (MD/PhD) Sees patients and runs a research lab, often turning lab discoveries into new treatments. College → combined MD-PhD program, most often 7 to 8 years → residency → often a research-focused fellowship. Clinical psychologist / neuropsychologist Clinical psychologists assess and treat mental and behavioral health using therapy and testing (they usually do not prescribe medicine). Neuropsychologists study and test how brain damage or disease affects memory, attention, language, and behavior. Bachelor's degree → doctoral degree in psychology (PhD or PsyD), including a 1-year internship → supervised experience for a state license. Neuropsychologists typically add a 2-year postdoctoral residency in clinical neuropsychology, and many then seek board certification. Neuroscience nurse A registered nurse (RN) who cares for patients with stroke, brain injury, spinal cord injury, seizures, and other neurological conditions, often in intensive care units or stroke units. Nursing diploma, associate's degree, or bachelor's degree in nursing (BSN; many hospitals prefer a BSN) → pass the NCLEX licensing exam → work as an RN. After at least 1 year (2,080 hours) of neuroscience nursing, nurses can seek the CNRN (Certified Neuroscience Registered Nurse) credential. Physical therapist (PT) Helps people regain movement, strength, and balance after strokes, spinal cord injuries, or other conditions. Bachelor's degree with science prerequisites → Doctor of Physical Therapy (DPT), typically about 3 years → state licensing exam. Optional residency later. Occupational therapist (OT) Helps people do everyday activities (dressing, cooking, writing, working) after injury or illness, often by retraining skills or adapting tools and spaces. Bachelor's degree → entry-level master's or doctoral degree in occupational therapy (master's programs typically take 2 to 3 years) with supervised fieldwork → NBCOT certification exam → state license. Speech-language pathologist (SLP) Assesses and treats problems with speech, language, voice, fluency (such as stuttering), and swallowing. Many work with stroke survivors or with children in schools. Bachelor's degree → master's degree in speech-language pathology (usually about 2 years) → supervised clinical fellowship (at least 36 weeks and 1,260 hours for ASHA certification) and a national exam → state license and the CCC-SLP certificate. Neural / biomedical engineer Designs medical devices and technology, such as brain-computer interfaces, deep brain stimulators, cochlear implants, prosthetic limbs, and imaging machines. Bachelor's degree in biomedical engineering or a related engineering field. Some jobs require a graduate degree, and leading a research team usually does. Data scientist in neuroscience Uses statistics, programming, and machine learning to find patterns in large data sets, such as brain scans, recordings from neurons, or clinical trial results. At least a bachelor's degree (often math, statistics, computer science, or engineering). Some jobs require a master's or doctoral degree, and research roles in neuroscience often do. Science teacher / science communicator Teachers bring neuroscience into classrooms. Communicators explain science to the public as writers, journalists, video makers, museum educators, or podcasters. Teacher: bachelor's degree → state teaching license, which includes student teaching and exams (every state also offers alternative routes). Communicator: no single path. Many have a science degree plus strong writing or media experience.

What about salaries?

This appendix does not list salaries. Pay changes every year and varies a lot by location and setting. If you want current numbers, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics Occupational Outlook Handbook lists median pay for most of these jobs, with the year of the data.

docs.title: B.3 The Path to Becoming a Doctor (MD or DO)
docs.text:
In the U.S., there are two kinds of fully licensed physicians:

  • MD (Doctor of Medicine), the more common degree.
  • DO (Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine). DO schools teach the same core medicine plus required training in osteopathic manipulative medicine (OMM), which uses the hands to treat problems in the bones, joints, and muscles.

Both MDs and DOs can become neurologists, neurosurgeons, psychiatrists, or any other specialist. Since 2020, residencies for both MD and DO graduates have been accredited by one organization, the Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education (ACGME). Here are the steps in plain language.

flowchart TD
    A["High school<br/>(strong science, math, writing)"] --> B["College, about 4 years<br/>(any major + pre-med courses)"]
    B --> C["MCAT exam"]
    C --> D["Medical school, 4 years<br/>(MD or DO)"]
    D --> E["Residency, about 3 to 7+ years<br/>(depends on specialty)"]
    E --> F["Optional fellowship<br/>(length varies)"]
    E --> G["State license +<br/>board certification"]
    F --> G

Step 1: High school. Take the strongest science and math classes you can, and learn to write clearly. Explore what you enjoy (see Section B.5).

Step 2: College, with pre-med courses. You do not have to major in biology. The Association of American Medical Colleges (AAMC) says most medical schools have no preference about your major. You do need to take the courses that medical schools require and that the MCAT covers. At a minimum, the AAMC recommends a year each of biology, general chemistry, organic chemistry, and biochemistry. Many schools also want physics, math or statistics, English, and psychology or sociology. Requirements differ, so check each school.

Step 3: The MCAT. The Medical College Admission Test is a long, computer-based exam with four sections: chemistry and physics in living systems; biology and biochemistry; psychology, sociology, and biology of behavior; and critical reading and reasoning.

Step 4: Medical school (4 years). The first part is mostly classroom and lab science. The later part is mostly clinical rotations, where students work in hospitals and clinics in many specialties. Along the way, students take national licensing exams: the USMLE for MD students, and the COMLEX-USA for DO students (DO students may also take the USMLE).

Step 5: Residency (length depends on specialty). Most residencies last from about 3 to 7 years, depending on the specialty. For brain-related fields:

Specialty Typical residency length (ACGME) Neurology 4 years (48 months), including a first year of internal medicine (sometimes done as a separate preliminary year) Psychiatry 4 years (48 months) Child neurology about 5 years (2 years of pediatrics or an approved alternative + 3 years of child neurology) Diagnostic radiology typically 5 years (1 clinical year + 4 years of radiology), then a 1-year neuroradiology fellowship Neurosurgery 7 years (84 months)

Step 6: Optional fellowship. Many doctors add a fellowship to specialize further, for example in stroke, epilepsy, movement disorders, or neurocritical care. Fellowship length varies by field.

Step 7: Licensing and board certification. Every state requires physicians to be licensed. Most specialists also earn board certification, which the American Board of Medical Specialties describes as a higher standard than a license alone. It requires passing specialty exams and keeping skills current over a whole career.

Add it up and a neurologist typically trains for about 12 years after high school (4 + 4 + 4). A neurosurgeon trains for about 15 years, often more with a fellowship. That is a long road, but residents earn a salary (called a stipend), and every year you are learning by caring for real patients.

docs.title: B.4 The Research Path: PhD and MD/PhD
docs.text:
Some people love the question "Why?" more than anything else. For them, a research career may be the best fit.

The PhD path. A PhD (Doctor of Philosophy) is a research degree. In neuroscience, PhD students take a year or two of advanced classes and then spend most of their time doing original experiments in a lab. They finish by writing and defending a dissertation, a long report on their new discoveries. The AAMC notes that the average biomedical PhD in the U.S. takes about six years. Many biomedical PhD students receive a stipend (a living allowance) and help with tuition, for example through NIH training grants that cover stipends, tuition, and fees. Funding differs from program to program, so ask each one how it supports students.

After the PhD, most researchers do one or more postdoctoral positions ("postdocs"). These are temporary research jobs where they build skills and publish their work before applying to lead their own lab, work in industry, teach, or move into science policy or communication.

The MD/PhD path. A physician-scientist earns both an MD (or DO) and a PhD. Most MD-PhD students finish both degrees in 7 to 8 years, according to the AAMC. A common pattern is two years of medical school, then several years of PhD research, then a return to clinical rotations. After that comes residency, just like any other doctor.

Many MD-PhD programs are supported by the National Institutes of Health through the Medical Scientist Training Program (MSTP), run by the National Institute of General Medical Sciences (NIGMS). MSTP training grants help pay trainees' tuition, fees, and stipends. Trainees must be U.S. citizens, noncitizen nationals, or permanent residents, and each institution can have only one MSTP. MD-PhD admission is very competitive, and applicants usually need significant research experience in college.

Research is for doctors, too

You don't need a PhD to do research. Many MDs, nurses, therapists, and engineers help run clinical trials or study better ways to care for patients. If you like both people and puzzles, you can have both.

docs.title: B.5 What You Can Do in High School, Starting Now
docs.text:
You do not need to pick a career in ninth grade. The goal right now is to explore, build strong skills, and find out what you enjoy. Here are some concrete steps.

1. Take strong classes.

  • Biology and chemistry are the base for almost every career in this appendix. Take physics too if you can.
  • AP Psychology (if your school offers it) introduces brain and behavior topics, many of which also show up on the MCAT.
  • Statistics matters more than most students expect. Doctors read studies, scientists analyze data, and data scientists live in it.
  • Math and computer science help with engineering, data science, and research.
  • English and writing matter for everyone. Doctors write notes, scientists write papers, and teachers explain ideas.

2. Join or start a neuroscience club. A club can read articles, invite local scientists or doctors to speak, and study for competitions together. If your school has no club, a teacher sponsor and a few friends are often all you need to start one.

3. Compete in the Brain Bee. The International Brain Bee is a neuroscience competition for students generally aged 13 to 19. Students compete in a local Brain Bee, and local winners advance to their national competition. National champions can then compete in the IBB World Championship. Formats, dates, and extra rules (such as grade or school requirements) differ by chapter, so check your chapter's rules. You can find chapters on the Brain Bee website. This textbook was built to help you prepare.

4. Take part in Brain Awareness Week. Every March, the Dana Foundation runs Brain Awareness Week, a global campaign to get the public excited about brain science. Schools, universities, hospitals, and labs host events. Your club could run a booth, a brain-themed lesson for younger students, or a display for your school.

5. Look for research experiences, carefully. Many universities and hospitals run summer research programs for high school students. One well-known federal option is the NIH Summer Internship Program (SIP), where interns work full time in NIH research labs. It is not open to most high school students. In recent years, applicants have had to be U.S. citizens or permanent residents and 18 by September 30 of the internship year. High school applicants must be seniors who will graduate before the internship starts, and a senior who is only 17 on June 1 of that year must live within 40 miles of an NIH campus. Interns should also plan ahead for housing near the lab. Rules can change each year, so always read the current SIP page.

Be careful with pay-to-play programs

Some summer programs charge high fees and promise "research experience" or an edge in admissions. A high price does not mean a program is better. Many strong opportunities are free or even pay you. Before applying, ask a teacher or school counselor, find out who runs the program, and look for clear information about what you would actually do.

6. Read widely. Read science news, books about the brain, and articles from trustworthy sites. BrainFacts.org, from the Society for Neuroscience, is a good place to start.

7. Volunteer in healthcare settings. Hospitals, nursing homes, hospice programs, and clinics often have volunteer programs for teens. Most set a minimum age, so check with each one. Volunteering shows you what healthcare is really like: the waiting, the kindness, and the hard moments. It also helps you learn whether you enjoy working with patients.

8. Shadow professionals. Shadowing means following a doctor, nurse, therapist, or scientist for a day or more to watch what they do. Ask family friends, your own doctor, or a teacher if they know someone. Shadowing different jobs is one of the best ways to compare them.

9. Take care of yourself. Sleep, friendships, hobbies, and sports matter. A long career is a marathon, not a sprint.

docs.title: B.6 Ply's Advice
docs.text:
There is no single right path

Some of the best brain doctors and scientists started out as music majors, engineers, nurses, or late bloomers who found neuroscience in their twenties or thirties. Your path can bend and still get you somewhere great. Every big idea starts at a single synapse, and every big career starts with one small, curious step!

Here are a few last thoughts:

  • Many paths, one goal. Doctors, nurses, therapists, engineers, scientists, data experts, and teachers all help people with brain conditions. Pick the work that fits you: how much time you want to spend with patients, in a lab, at a computer, or in a classroom.
  • Detours are normal. People switch majors, take gap years, work before graduate school, or change careers. Admissions committees often value real-world experience.
  • Ask for help. Counselors, teachers, college pre-health advisors, and professionals in the field are usually happy to answer questions.
  • Check the facts yourself. Training rules and program details change. Use the official sources below to confirm anything before you make big decisions.

docs.title: List of Chapters
docs.text:
Chapters 1 to 4 build the foundation. After that, you can read in order or follow your interests. Each chapter lists its prerequisites at the top.

  1. Neurons, Glia, and the Nervous System: What neurons and glia are, how the nervous system is organized, and why myelin matters (case: multiple sclerosis).
  2. The Action Potential: How ion gradients and voltage-gated channels create the electrical signal of the nervous system (case: local anesthetics).
  3. Synapses and Neurotransmitters: How neurons talk chemically, the major neurotransmitters, and how drugs act at synapses (case: myasthenia gravis).
  4. A Tour of the Brain: Neuroanatomy: The lobes, deep structures, brainstem, cerebellum, spinal cord, and cranial nerves (case: Phineas Gage).
  5. Vision: From photoreceptors to the visual cortex, and how lesions cause specific visual field losses (case: pituitary tumor).
  6. Hearing, Touch, Taste, Smell, and Pain: The other senses, body maps in the cortex, and how pain works (case: phantom limb pain).
  7. Movement: Muscles, Reflexes, and Motor Control: Reflexes, motor cortex, basal ganglia, and cerebellum (case: Parkinson's disease).
  8. The Developing and Teenage Brain: How the brain builds itself, prunes connections, and changes through adolescence (case: fetal alcohol spectrum disorder).
  9. Learning, Memory, and Neuroplasticity: Memory systems, the hippocampus, and how synapses change with learning (case: Patient H.M.).
  10. Sleep and Brain States: Circadian rhythms, sleep stages, EEG, and why teens need more sleep (case: narcolepsy).
  11. Emotion, Stress, and the Body: The amygdala, the stress response, and the HPA axis (case: post-traumatic stress disorder).
  12. Language, Attention, and Decision-Making: Language networks, attention, and how the brain makes choices (case: aphasia).
  13. The Aging Brain and Neurodegeneration: Normal aging vs disease, and new treatments for Alzheimer's and ALS (cases: Alzheimer's disease, ALS).
  14. Brain Injury, Stroke, and Epilepsy: Concussion, stroke warning signs, and seizure first aid (cases: concussion, stroke, first seizure).
  15. Psychiatric Disorders, Developmental Disorders, and Addiction: Depression, anxiety, schizophrenia, autism, ADHD, and how addiction changes the brain (case: opioid overdose).
  16. How Doctors Examine the Brain: The neurological exam, lesion localization, and brain imaging: the capstone (case: a full neurological workup).

docs.title: Chapter 1: Neurons, Glia, and the Nervous System
Chapter 1: Neurons, Glia, and the Nervous System
Summary
docs.text: Your nervous system is built from two families of cells. Neurons carry messages as electrical and chemical signals, and glial cells keep those neurons fed, insulated, protected, and clean. This chapter tours the parts of a neuron, the three jobs neurons do, the glial cells that support them, and the blood-brain barrier that guards the brain. It ends at the bedside with multiple sclerosis, a disease in which the immune system attacks myelin, the insulation that lets signals travel fast.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• None beyond one year of high school biology.

Hi, I'm Ply!

I'm Ply, a California sea slug (Aplysia californica), and scientists learned how memories form by studying nerve cells just like mine. I only have about 20,000 neurons and you have billions, so I'm counting on you to put yours to good use! In this chapter you'll meet the cells that make every thought possible, and by the end you'll be able to explain why one patient's blurry vision traces back to a missing layer of fat. Every big idea starts at a single synapse!

Here's how I'll show up in every chapter:

  1. Welcome: I tell you why the chapter matters.
  2. Thinking: I flag a big idea worth pausing on.
  3. Tip: I share a shortcut for remembering or checking something.
  4. Warning: I point out a common mistake and how to avoid it.
  5. Encourage: I cheer you through the hard parts.
  6. Celebrate: I sum up what you just mastered.

If I'm not doing one of those six things, I'm not in the chapter.

docs.title: 1.1 Maya's Alarm Clock
docs.text:
It's 6:30 on a Tuesday morning. Maya, a 16-year-old soccer player who is studying for the Brain Bee, is fast asleep when her phone alarm starts to buzz. Before she is even fully awake, a chain of events has already begun. Tiny sensors in her ears turn the sound into electrical signals. Those signals race along nerve fibers into her brain. Her brain recognizes the sound ("ugh, the alarm"), decides what to do ("snooze it"), and sends a command down her spinal cord and out to the muscles of her arm. Her hand slaps the phone. All of this happens in well under a second, and Maya barely notices.

How can a lump of soft tissue do something so fast and so precise? The answer lives in its cells. Your brain contains about 86 billion neurons, the cells that carry messages, plus a roughly equal number of other cells, mostly helper cells called glia (Azevedo et al., 2009). In this chapter you'll learn what these cells look like, what each part does, and what goes wrong when one small part, a fatty wrapping called myelin, is damaged.

docs.title: 1.2 A Quick Chemistry Refresher
docs.text:
Before we meet neurons, we need four ideas from basic biology and chemistry. Neurons use all four, all the time.

Think about a crowded school hallway between classes, with a classroom door. If the hallway is packed and the classroom is nearly empty, people naturally drift into the classroom when the door opens. Nobody has to push them. They spread out because there's more room on the other side. Hold on to that picture.

The cell membrane. Every cell, including a neuron, is wrapped in a cell membrane: a thin, flexible barrier made mostly of fat molecules (lipids). It acts like the wall of the hallway. It keeps the inside of the cell separate from the outside, and most charged particles can't slip through it on their own.

Ions. An ion is an atom (or small molecule) that carries an electric charge because it has gained or lost electrons. Your body fluids are full of ions. The ones neurons care most about are sodium (Na⁺), potassium (K⁺), chloride (Cl⁻), and calcium (Ca²⁺). Because ions are charged, moving them around moves electric charge. That is the key to how neurons make electrical signals.

Proteins. A protein is a large molecule built from a chain of amino acids that folds into a specific shape. The shape decides the job. Some proteins in the cell membrane act as doors (channels) that let only certain ions through. Others act as pumps that use energy to push ions across the membrane.

Concentration gradients. A concentration gradient is a difference in how crowded a substance is in two places, like the packed hallway next to the empty classroom. Substances tend to move "down" their gradient, from crowded to less crowded, whenever a path opens. Neurons keep a steady gradient across their membranes. There is much more sodium outside the cell than inside, and much more potassium inside than outside.

The table below pulls these four ideas together and shows why each one matters for a neuron.

Idea Everyday picture Why neurons need it Cell membrane The wall of a hallway Keeps ions separated, so charge can build up Ion A charged particle Moving ions moves charge, which creates electrical signals Protein Doors and pumps in the wall Channels let specific ions through; pumps rebuild the gradients Concentration gradient A crowded hallway next to an empty room Stored "push" that drives ions through open channels

Chapter 2 shows how a neuron opens and closes its ion channels to fire a signal. For now, remember the big idea: a neuron controls the flow of charged particles across its membrane, and that flow is the language of the nervous system.

docs.title: 1.3 The Big Picture: Your Nervous System
docs.text:
Imagine a city. It has a downtown headquarters where decisions are made, and a huge web of roads and cables that reach every house. Messages travel in from the houses ("there's a fire on Elm Street") and out from headquarters ("send a fire truck"). Your body works the same way.

The nervous system is the body's communication network. It is the set of all the cells, tissues, and organs that sense the world, process information, and control the body. It has two main divisions:

  • The central nervous system (CNS) is the headquarters. It is made of the brain and the spinal cord. The CNS receives information, makes sense of it, and decides what to do.
  • The peripheral nervous system (PNS) is the road network. It includes all the nerves that branch out from the brain and spinal cord to the rest of the body: your skin, muscles, eyes, ears, heart, and gut. The PNS carries information into the CNS and carries commands back out.

A nerve is a bundle of many axons (long fibers from neurons, which you'll meet in the next section) wrapped together like wires in a cable. There are twelve pairs of cranial nerves that connect directly to the brain, and many more spinal nerves that branch from the spinal cord.

Here is how the two divisions compare.

Central nervous system (CNS) Peripheral nervous system (PNS) What it includes Brain and spinal cord Nerves outside the brain and spinal cord, and clusters of nerve cells along them City analogy Headquarters Roads and cables to every house Main job Process information and make decisions Carry information in and commands out Protected by Skull, spine, and the blood-brain barrier Mostly by surrounding tissue Glial cell that makes myelin Oligodendrocyte Schwann cell

In Maya's alarm story, the sound sensors in her ears and the nerves to her arm belong to the PNS. Recognizing the alarm and deciding to hit snooze happen in the CNS. Keep the last row of the table in mind; it matters later.

docs.title: 1.4 The Neuron: A Cell Built to Send Messages
docs.text:
Picture an uprooted tree lying on its side: spreading branches at one end, a thick base, a long trunk, and a tangle of roots at the far end. Now imagine messages flowing through it one way: in through the branches, down the trunk, and out through the roots to touch the next tree. That is a surprisingly good picture of a neuron.

A neuron (nerve cell) is a cell specialized to receive, process, and send information using electrical and chemical signals. Neurons come in many shapes, but most have four main parts.

  1. Dendrites are the "branches." A dendrite is a short, branching extension that receives messages from other neurons and passes them toward the cell body. A single neuron can have many dendrites, which lets it listen to many other neurons at once.
  2. The cell body, or soma, is the "base of the trunk." The cell body (soma) contains the nucleus (with the cell's DNA) and the machinery that builds most of the neuron's proteins. It also adds up all the incoming messages from the dendrites.
  3. The axon is the "trunk." An axon is a single long, thin fiber that carries the neuron's own signal away from the cell body. A neuron usually has just one axon, though it may branch near its end. Axons can be extremely long. Some, such as those that run from the lower end of the spinal cord to the muscles of the foot, are about a meter long. The spot where the axon leaves the cell body is a cone-shaped region called the axon hillock. Here and at the start of the axon, the neuron "decides" whether the incoming messages add up to enough to fire.
  4. Axon terminals are the "roots." An axon terminal is one of the small, swollen tips at the end of the axon's branches. This is where the neuron hands its message to the next cell, usually by releasing chemical messengers across a tiny gap. That gap, the synapse, is the star of Chapter 3.

Information in a typical neuron flows one way, in this order:

  1. Dendrites receive messages from other cells.
  2. The cell body adds up those messages.
  3. If the total is strong enough at the axon hillock and the start of the axon, the neuron fires a signal.
  4. The signal travels down the axon.
  5. The axon terminals pass the message on to the next neuron, a muscle, or a gland.

Don't mix up neuron and nerve

A common trap is using "neuron" and "nerve" as if they mean the same thing. A neuron is one single cell, while a nerve is a cable made of the axons of hundreds or thousands of neurons bundled together. If you can picture one wire versus a whole power cord, you'll never mix them up again.

docs.title: Where the "neuron" idea came from
docs.text:
It wasn't always obvious that the brain is made of separate cells. In the late 1800s, scientists argued about whether the nervous system was one giant connected web or a collection of individual cells. The Spanish scientist Santiago Ramón y Cajal stained brain tissue, studied it under the microscope, and drew detailed pictures of neurons by hand. His work showed that neurons are separate cells that communicate at contact points. He shared the 1906 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with the Italian scientist Camillo Golgi, whose staining method Cajal used and improved (Nobel Prize, 1906). Ironically, Golgi himself favored the "one giant web" idea (Wikipedia: Neuron doctrine).

Scientists also learn from animals with simpler nervous systems. The sea slug Aplysia (Ply's species) has relatively few neurons, and many are large and easy to identify. Eric Kandel used Aplysia to show how connections between neurons change during learning, work that earned him a share of the 2000 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine (Nobel Prize, 2000). You'll come back to Ply's neurons in Chapter 9.

docs.title: 1.5 Three Jobs for Neurons
docs.text:
It's afternoon, and Maya is at soccer practice. A ball flies toward her, she sees it, and she traps it with her foot. Three kinds of neurons make that happen, each defined by the direction its messages travel.

  • A sensory neuron carries information from the body and the outside world toward the CNS. Sensory neurons start at receptors that detect light, sound, touch, temperature, stretch, or chemicals. When light from the ball hits Maya's eyes, sensory neurons carry the news inward. (Sensory neurons are also called afferent neurons. "Afferent" means "carrying toward.")
  • A motor neuron carries commands from the CNS out to muscles (and glands). Motor neurons in Maya's spinal cord send long axons down her leg to the muscles that move her foot. (Motor neurons are also called efferent neurons. "Efferent" means "carrying away.")
  • An interneuron connects other neurons to each other inside the CNS. Interneurons sit between sensory input and motor output. They compare, combine, and route information. Much of the work of judging where the ball will land and choosing how to move happens in circuits of interneurons in Maya's brain and spinal cord.

Here is a side-by-side comparison of the three types you just met.

Neuron type Direction of message Where the cell body usually sits Maya example Sensory neuron Body → CNS Outside the spinal cord, in clusters along nerves, or in sense organs Light from the ball reaches her eyes Interneuron Neuron → neuron, within the CNS Brain and spinal cord Her brain predicts where the ball will land Motor neuron CNS → muscle or gland Brainstem and spinal cord (taking orders from motor areas of the brain) Her leg muscles contract to trap the ball

A memory trick for direction

Here's a shortcut: Sensory starts at the Surface and heads in; Motor moves Muscles and heads out. Interneurons are the "in-between" cells that link the two.

docs.title: 1.6 Myelin and Nodes of Ranvier: Insulation for Speed
docs.text:
Think about your phone's charging cable. Inside is a copper wire, and around it is a plastic coating that keeps the electricity from leaking out. Now imagine sending a signal down a wire that leaks along its whole length. The signal would fade and slow down.

Axons face the same problem. An axon's membrane is a little "leaky": as a signal travels, some electric charge escapes. Many axons solve this problem with insulation.

The myelin sheath is a fatty, insulating layer wrapped many times around an axon. It is made of lipids and proteins, and it isn't made by the neuron itself. Glial cells (Section 1.7) wrap it around the axon, like electrical tape wound around a wire. Myelin is what makes the brain's "white matter" look white.

Myelin is not one continuous tube. It comes in segments, with tiny gaps between them. Each bare gap is called a node of Ranvier, named after the French scientist Louis-Antoine Ranvier, who described them in the 1800s. Nodes are packed with ion channels. This is where the speed comes from: the signal is renewed at full strength at each node, and the insulated stretches in between let it race ahead without leaking. The signal seems to jump from node to node. (Chapter 2 gives this jumping its official name and explains the ion channels behind it.)

Myelin makes a big difference in speed.

Kind of axon Typical speed Comparison Thin, unmyelinated (for example, some pain and temperature fibers) About 1 meter per second Walking speed Thick, myelinated (for example, many motor neurons) More than 100 meters per second Race car speed

These figures come from an open university textbook on sensation and perception (University of Minnesota, Introduction to Sensation and Perception). The fastest myelinated axons carry signals more than a hundred times faster than the slowest bare ones. That's why the axons that control Maya's leg muscles are myelinated.

Why insulation means speed

Notice the shortcut: the neuron only has to renew its signal at the nodes, not at every point along the axon. Think of it like a relay race where runners only need to stand at a few checkpoints instead of every few steps. If the insulation between two checkpoints is lost, the baton has to be carried slowly the whole way, and it might be dropped.

This hints at what happens when myelin is damaged. Charge leaks out of the bare stretch, so the signal slows and weakens. If the damaged stretch is long enough, the signal fades out before it reaches the next healthy node, and the message is never delivered. That idea is the key to the disease at the end of this chapter.

docs.title: 1.7 Glia: The Nervous System's Support Crew
docs.text:
A soccer team isn't only the players on the field. Coaches, trainers, medical staff, and groundskeepers never score a goal, but without them the team falls apart. Your nervous system has a support crew too.

A glial cell (or glia) is any cell of the nervous system that is not a neuron. Glia don't send fast electrical signals the way neurons do. Instead, they build myelin, support and protect neurons, clean up, and fight infection. The German scientist Rudolf Virchow described them in 1856 while looking for the brain's "connective tissue," and the name glia comes from the Greek word for "glue." For a long time, glia were treated as packing material. We now know they are active partners.

How many glia are there? You may have read that glia outnumber neurons ten to one. A careful review of 150 years of cell counting found that the real ratio in the whole human brain is about one to one or a little less, with fewer than 100 billion glia in total (von Bartheld, Bahney, and Herculano-Houzel, 2016). The ratio varies by brain region, but "ten to one" was never backed by good data.

This chapter covers four kinds of glia.

Astrocytes. An astrocyte is a star-shaped glial cell of the CNS. ("Astro" means star.) Astrocytes are multitaskers. They give neurons structural and metabolic support, and recycle chemical messengers around synapses so signals stay crisp (OpenStax). Their long arms end in "end-feet" that wrap around the brain's tiny blood vessels. Those end-feet come up again in Section 1.9.

Oligodendrocytes. An oligodendrocyte is a glial cell of the CNS that makes myelin. ("Oligo" means few and "dendro" means branch.) Each oligodendrocyte sends out several arms, and each arm wraps one segment of myelin around a nearby axon. One oligodendrocyte can myelinate segments of many different axons, by some counts up to about 40.

Schwann cells. A Schwann cell is a glial cell of the PNS that makes myelin. Unlike an oligodendrocyte, each Schwann cell wraps just one segment of one axon. So a long peripheral axon needs a whole row of Schwann cells along its length. Schwann cells are named after the German scientist Theodor Schwann.

Microglia. Microglia are small immune cells that live in the CNS. Microglia constantly patrol the brain, find and swallow invaders and dead or damaged cells, and help trim away unneeded connections between neurons as the brain develops. You can think of them as the brain's security guards and cleanup crew rolled into one.

So many new words!

If the glia names feel like a vocabulary avalanche, that's normal; most people need a couple of passes. Try sorting them by just two questions: "Brain and spinal cord, or body?" and "What's its one main job?" The table below does exactly that, so use it as your cheat sheet.

Here are the four glial cells, sorted by where they live and what they do.

Glial cell Where it lives Main job Easy picture Astrocyte CNS Supports and feeds neurons, cleans up around synapses, wraps blood vessels Star-shaped caretaker Oligodendrocyte CNS Makes myelin for segments of many axons One octopus wrapping many wires Schwann cell PNS Makes myelin for one segment of one axon One roll of tape per segment Microglia CNS Immune defense and cleanup Security guard and janitor

Next, check Remove myelin (MS) and send the signal again with 2 damaged segments. The signal crawls through the bare stretch, weakens, and arrives late. Now slide to 3 or 4 damaged segments. This time the signal fades out before it reaches a healthy node, and the message never arrives. If this axon carried information from the eye, what would the person notice in each case?

docs.title: 1.9 The Blood-Brain Barrier: The Brain's Security Checkpoint
docs.text:
Think about airport security: travelers with tickets get through to the gates, and many other things are stopped. The brain has its own security checkpoint, built into the walls of its blood vessels.

In most of the body, the walls of the smallest blood vessels (capillaries) have small gaps, so many substances leak out of the blood into the tissue. The brain and spinal cord are different. The blood-brain barrier is a protective filter between the blood and the fluid around the brain's cells. It is formed mainly by the cells lining the brain's capillaries, which are sealed tightly together, with support from astrocyte end-feet wrapped around the vessels and other support cells embedded in the vessel walls (Wikipedia: Blood-brain barrier).

The blood-brain barrier does two jobs at once:

  • It lets in what the brain needs. Oxygen and some other small molecules pass through easily. Special transport proteins carry in glucose (the brain's main fuel) and amino acids.
  • It keeps out what could cause harm. Most germs, many large molecules, and many substances that dissolve easily in water are blocked.

This protection matters, because the brain is a very hungry organ. It makes up only about 2 to 3 percent of body weight but uses roughly 20 to 25 percent of the body's energy (OpenStax, Introduction to Behavioral Neuroscience; Scientific American, 2008). It needs a steady, carefully controlled supply.

The barrier has a downside for medicine: because it blocks so much, many drugs that might help brain diseases can't get in. And as you'll see next, in multiple sclerosis, immune cells that are normally kept out manage to cross into the brain and spinal cord, where they cause damage.

docs.title: At the Bedside: Blurry Vision and Tingling Legs
docs.text:
Meet the patient

Jordan is a 28-year-old graphic designer. Over three days, the vision in her right eye has become blurry and "washed out," as if she's looking through frosted glass. It hurts a little when she moves that eye. When she mentions it to her doctor, she adds something she had brushed off: a year ago, both of her legs tingled and felt numb for about two weeks, and then the feeling went away on its own. She also says her symptoms seem worse after a hot shower.

What the doctor checks: The doctor tests Jordan's vision and finds that her right eye sees less sharply and that colors look faded in that eye. A full neurological exam checks strength, sensation, reflexes, coordination, and walking. The doctor orders an MRI scan of the brain and spinal cord, which shows several small spots of damage (lesions) in the white matter, in more than one place. Other tests that doctors may use include a lumbar puncture (a sample of the fluid around the spinal cord, to look for signs of inflammation) and evoked potential tests, which measure how quickly the nervous system responds to stimulation such as a flashing pattern (NINDS, Multiple Sclerosis).

Where is the problem? (localization): Painful, blurry vision in one eye points to the optic nerve, the cable of axons that carries signals from the eye to the brain. This is called optic neuritis (inflammation of the optic nerve). Despite its name, the optic nerve is technically a tract of the CNS, and its myelin is made by oligodendrocytes, not Schwann cells (Wikipedia: Optic nerve). The earlier tingling in both legs points somewhere else: the spinal cord, where sensory pathways from both legs travel close together. So Jordan has had problems in at least two parts of the CNS, at two different times, and both are made of myelinated axons wrapped by oligodendrocytes. "Different places, different times, white matter" is a classic pattern that makes doctors think of one disease.

Diagnosis: Multiple sclerosis (MS), relapsing-remitting type. Multiple sclerosis is a long-lasting autoimmune disease in which the immune system mistakenly attacks myelin in the central nervous system. It also damages the axons and nerve cell bodies themselves over time. "Sclerosis" refers to the scar-like patches (plaques or lesions) that form where myelin has been attacked, which are visible on MRI. Symptoms usually begin between ages 20 and 40, and women are affected more often than men (NINDS). One large study of health insurance records estimated that about 727,000 U.S. adults were living with MS in 2010, with women affected about 2.8 times as often as men. Extending their numbers forward, the same researchers estimated roughly 850,000 to 914,000 by 2017, and they warned that this extension should be read with caution (Wallin et al., 2019). A 2023 study using a similar method found about 745,000 U.S. adults with MS (Hittle et al., 2023), but its records also date from 2008 to 2010, so these remain the most detailed national counts this book could find as of 2026. Most people with MS are first diagnosed with the relapsing-remitting form, in which attacks are followed by full or partial recovery.

Why it happens: This is the Neuron Explorer in real life. In MS, immune cells cross into the CNS and attack myelin and the oligodendrocytes that make it. Where myelin is stripped away, charge leaks out of the bare axon, and signals slow, weaken, or fail, just as in the sim. Slowed or blocked signals in the optic nerve cause blurry, washed-out vision. Blocked signals in the spinal cord's sensory pathways cause tingling and numbness. Symptoms can improve after an attack as inflammation calms down and the nervous system partly recovers. Many people with MS notice that heat temporarily makes symptoms worse (NINDS). Notice that the attack happens in the CNS, which is why the oligodendrocyte, not the Schwann cell, is the glial cell in trouble.

Treatment today: There is no cure yet, but treatment has improved a lot. For a sudden attack, doctors may give corticosteroids (strong anti-inflammatory medicines) for a few days to speed recovery, although these don't change the long-term course. To prevent future attacks and slow the disease, neurologists prescribe disease-modifying therapies, which calm or redirect the immune system. Some are pills, some are injections, and some are infusions. Physical and occupational therapy, treatment of symptoms like fatigue and stiffness, and staying active also help (NINDS). Most people with MS have a normal life expectancy.

What's new in research: One of the biggest advances has been B-cell depletion. B cells are a type of white blood cell, and drugs that remove many of them from the blood reduce MS attacks. In March 2017, the FDA approved ocrelizumab, a B-cell-depleting antibody, for relapsing MS and for primary progressive MS, making it the first approved disease-modifying therapy for the primary progressive form (Genentech, 2017). Other B-cell-depleting drugs have followed for relapsing MS, including ofatumumab (FDA approval, August 2020; Novartis, 2020) and ublituximab (FDA approval, December 2022; Pharmacy Times, 2023).

A newer kind of pill, called a BTK inhibitor (it blocks BTK, an enzyme that some immune cells use to pass signals inside the cell), crosses the blood-brain barrier and calms immune signaling inside the CNS, including in microglia. Its approval status differs by country, so dates matter. In December 2025, the FDA declined to approve tolebrutinib for secondary progressive MS without relapses (Pharmacy Times, 2025). In 2026 the European Union approved it for that form of MS, with liver injury listed as a known risk that needs close monitoring (NeurologyLive, 2026). As of 2026, it is not approved in the United States.

Researchers are also asking what triggers MS. A 2022 study that followed more than 10 million young adults in the U.S. military found that the risk of MS rose 32-fold after infection with Epstein-Barr virus (the virus that causes mononucleosis), but not after other viruses. That makes the virus a leading suspected cause (Bjornevik et al., 2022, Science). Most people who catch the virus never get MS, so other factors, such as genes and vitamin D, are also involved.

Your turn: diagnose a variation

A 45-year-old man had a stomach bug two weeks ago. Now, over a few days, his feet and hands tingle and his legs have become weak, climbing up toward his arms. His reflexes are gone. An MRI of his brain and spinal cord is normal, but tests of the nerves in his arms and legs show that signals travel very slowly along them. Like MS, this is an immune attack on myelin. Which part of the nervous system is affected, and which glial cell's myelin is under attack?

Answer: The peripheral nervous system. The normal brain and spinal cord MRI and the slowed signals in the limb nerves point to the PNS, so the myelin under attack is made by Schwann cells. This pattern fits Guillain-Barré syndrome, a rare disorder in which the immune system attacks the peripheral nerves, most commonly their myelin (NINDS, Guillain-Barré Syndrome). It is a medical emergency because weakness can spread to the breathing muscles. MS and Guillain-Barré both strip myelin, but they strike opposite sides of the CNS/PNS border.

This is a fictional teaching case. It is not medical advice. If you or someone you know has symptoms like these, talk to a doctor.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
Myth: The brain is made only of neurons. Reality: The brain contains about as many non-neuron cells as neurons. Most of these are glia, and the rest include the cells that make up blood vessels (Azevedo et al., 2009). A brain made only of neurons would have no myelin, no immune defense, and no blood-brain barrier.

Myth: Glia are just "glue" that holds neurons in place. Reality: The name is a leftover from the 1800s. Glia make myelin, feed neurons, clean up chemical messengers at synapses, help form the blood-brain barrier, and fight infection. When glia fail, as oligodendrocytes do in MS, the nervous system stops working properly.

Myth: Glia outnumber neurons ten to one. Reality: A review of 150 years of cell counting found that the ratio of glia to neurons in the whole human brain is about one to one or a little less, and the "ten to one" claim was never supported by solid data (von Bartheld et al., 2016).

Myth: We only use 10 percent of our brain. Reality: Brain imaging shows that over the course of a day, most regions of the brain are active, and some stay active even during sleep. The brain is only about 3 percent of body weight but uses about 20 percent of the body's energy, and an organ that expensive would not be mostly idle (Scientific American, 2008).

docs.title: Brain Bee Practice
docs.text:
1. Name the four main parts of a typical neuron, in the order a message travels through them.

Dendrites, cell body (soma), axon, and axon terminals. Messages come in through the dendrites, are added up in the cell body, travel down the axon, and leave through the axon terminals.

2. Which glial cell makes myelin in the central nervous system, and which makes it in the peripheral nervous system?

Oligodendrocytes make myelin in the CNS, and one oligodendrocyte can myelinate segments of many axons. Schwann cells make myelin in the PNS, and each Schwann cell wraps one segment of one axon.

3. What are nodes of Ranvier, and why do they matter?

They are the small, bare gaps between segments of myelin along an axon. They are packed with ion channels, so the signal is renewed at each node, which lets it seem to jump from node to node and travel much faster than along an unmyelinated axon.

4. A patient has optic neuritis now and had numbness in both legs a year ago. MRI shows white matter lesions in the brain and spinal cord. What disease is most likely, and what is being attacked?

Multiple sclerosis. The immune system is attacking myelin (and the oligodendrocytes that make it) in the central nervous system, causing lesions in different places at different times.

5. What is the blood-brain barrier, and which glial cell helps support it?

It is a protective filter formed mainly by tightly sealed cells lining the brain's capillaries, which lets in needed substances like glucose and oxygen but blocks most germs and many other molecules. Astrocytes support it by wrapping their end-feet around these blood vessels.

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
1. Define cell membrane, ion, and concentration gradient in your own words.
  2. List the four kinds of glial cells from this chapter and state where each one lives (CNS or PNS).
Answer
  1. The cell membrane is the thin, fatty barrier that wraps a cell and separates inside from outside. An ion is an atom or small molecule with an electric charge. A concentration gradient is a difference in how crowded a substance is in two places; substances tend to move from crowded to less crowded.
  2. Astrocytes (CNS), oligodendrocytes (CNS), microglia (CNS), and Schwann cells (PNS).

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
1. Explain the difference between the central nervous system and the peripheral nervous system, using the "city" analogy from Section 1.3.
  2. Explain why a myelinated axon carries signals faster than an unmyelinated axon of similar size.
Answer
  1. The CNS (brain and spinal cord) is like a city's headquarters, where information is processed and decisions are made. The PNS (nerves throughout the body) is like the road and cable network that carries messages in from the houses and commands back out.
  2. Myelin insulates the axon so that electric charge does not leak out along the way. The signal only has to be renewed at the nodes of Ranvier, so it seems to jump from node to node instead of being rebuilt at every point along the axon.

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
1. Maya touches a hot pan and pulls her hand away. For each step, name the type of neuron involved (sensory, interneuron, or motor): (a) heat detected in the skin of her fingertip; (b) signal relayed inside her spinal cord; (c) her arm muscles contract.
  2. A new medicine works well on brain cells in a lab dish but has no effect when given to patients as a pill. Using what you know about the blood-brain barrier, suggest one reason why, and one property the medicine would need to work better.

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
1. In the Neuron Explorer, removing myelin from 2 segments slows the signal, but removing it from 3 segments blocks it. Analyze why the length of a damaged stretch matters, using the ideas of leaking charge and renewal at nodes.
  2. A patient has muscle weakness. Compare how you would expect the problem to look if it came from damaged motor neurons in the spinal cord versus damaged Schwann cells along the nerves to the legs. What test results might help tell them apart?

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
1. A website claims that "glia are just filler cells, so brain health is all about neurons." Evaluate this claim using at least three pieces of evidence from this chapter.
  2. Which do you think is the most important job of glia: making myelin, supporting the blood-brain barrier, or immune defense? Defend your choice using an example of what goes wrong when that job fails.

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
1. Design a one-page infographic for middle school students explaining what myelin is and why MS affects signals. Use an analogy other than this chapter's phone cable.
  2. Write a short fictional case (5 to 7 sentences) of a patient whose symptoms come from a problem in the PNS rather than the CNS. Include the symptoms, one exam finding, and the clue that lets a doctor localize the problem to the PNS.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The nervous system has two divisions: the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) processes information, and the peripheral nervous system (nerves throughout the body) carries information in and commands out.
  • Neurons send messages by controlling the flow of ions across their cell membrane, using membrane proteins and concentration gradients.
  • A typical neuron receives messages through dendrites, adds them up in the cell body (soma), sends its signal down the axon, and passes it on at the axon terminals.
  • Sensory neurons carry information toward the CNS, motor neurons carry commands out to muscles, and interneurons connect neurons within the CNS.
  • The myelin sheath insulates axons, and the signal is renewed at nodes of Ranvier, so myelinated axons can carry signals more than a hundred times faster than thin unmyelinated ones.
  • Glial cells are roughly as numerous as neurons (about one to one, or a little fewer): astrocytes support neurons and the blood-brain barrier, oligodendrocytes (CNS) and Schwann cells (PNS) make myelin, and microglia defend and clean the brain.
  • In multiple sclerosis, the immune system attacks CNS myelin, so signals slow or fail, causing symptoms such as blurry vision and tingling that depend on where the damage is.

You've met the whole crew!

You can now name every part of a neuron, sort the glial cells by job and location, and explain why a patch of missing myelin can blur someone's vision. Next, in Chapter 2, we'll zoom in on the axon and watch ions rush through their channels to create the electrical spike every neuron uses to talk!

docs.title: Quiz: Neurons, Glia, and the Nervous System
Quiz: Neurons, Glia, and the Nervous System
docs.text: Test your understanding of Chapter 1. Choose the best answer, then click Show Answer to check.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
Which part of a neuron receives incoming messages from other neurons and passes them toward the cell body?

  1. Axon
  2. Dendrite
  3. Axon terminal
  4. Myelin sheath
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Dendrites are the short, branching "receivers" of a neuron, and they pass incoming messages toward the cell body. The axon (A) is a tempting choice because it is also a long extension, but it carries the neuron's own signal away from the cell body.

Concept Tested: Dendrite Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
Which pair of structures makes up the central nervous system?

  1. The brain and the cranial nerves
  2. The spinal cord and the spinal nerves
  3. The brain and all the nerves in the body
  4. The brain and the spinal cord
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The central nervous system (CNS) is made of the brain and the spinal cord, the "headquarters" that processes information. Options A and B mix in nerves, which carry messages to and from the CNS and belong to the peripheral nervous system.

Concept Tested: Central Nervous System Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
Which glial cell makes myelin in the peripheral nervous system?

  1. Schwann cell
  2. Oligodendrocyte
  3. Astrocyte
  4. Microglia
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Schwann cells make myelin in the PNS, and each one wraps a single segment of a single axon. Oligodendrocytes (B) also make myelin, but only in the CNS, where one cell can wrap segments of many different axons.

Concept Tested: Schwann Cell Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 4
docs.text:
Why does a myelinated axon carry signals faster than a thin unmyelinated axon?

  1. Myelin produces extra electrical charge that pushes the signal along.
  2. Myelin makes the axon shorter, so the signal has less distance to travel.
  3. Myelin insulates the axon so charge doesn't leak out, and the signal is renewed only at the nodes of Ranvier.
  4. Myelin carries the signal itself, so the axon no longer needs to.
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Myelin is insulation: it keeps charge from leaking out, so the signal only needs to be renewed at the bare nodes of Ranvier and seems to jump from node to node. Option D is a common mix-up; myelin is a wrapping made by glial cells and does not carry the signal itself.

Concept Tested: Myelin Sheath Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 5
docs.text:
What is a concentration gradient, and why does it matter to a neuron?

  1. A difference in electric charge only, which lets the membrane block all ions
  2. A difference in how crowded a substance is in two places, which gives ions a "push" through open channels
  3. A protein pump in the membrane that moves ions one at a time
  4. A layer of fat around the axon that keeps ions from moving
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A concentration gradient is a difference in how crowded a substance is in two places, and substances tend to move from crowded to less crowded when a path opens. That stored "push" is what drives ions through open channels. Option C describes a membrane protein (a pump), which helps rebuild gradients but is not the gradient itself.

Concept Tested: Concentration Gradient Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 6
docs.text:
Which statement best describes the job of the blood-brain barrier?

  1. It stops all substances, including glucose, from reaching brain cells.
  2. It is a layer of myelin that surrounds the whole brain.
  3. It is made by microglia that eat everything entering the brain.
  4. It lets in what the brain needs, such as glucose and oxygen, while blocking most germs and many other molecules.
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The blood-brain barrier, formed mainly by tightly sealed cells lining the brain's capillaries and supported by astrocyte end-feet, is a selective filter. Option A is a common misunderstanding: the barrier is not a solid wall, and transport proteins actively carry glucose, the brain's main fuel, across it.

Concept Tested: Blood-Brain Barrier Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 7
docs.text:
A 30-year-old woman develops blurry vision and pain in one eye. Her MRI shows several white matter lesions in her brain and spinal cord, and her doctor diagnoses multiple sclerosis. Which cell's product is the main target of the immune attack in her disease?

  1. Myelin made by oligodendrocytes
  2. Myelin made by Schwann cells
  3. The cell bodies of sensory neurons in the skin
  4. The blood vessels that supply the eye
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. MS is an autoimmune attack on myelin in the central nervous system, and CNS myelin, including the optic nerve's, is made by oligodendrocytes. Option B is the most tempting distractor, but Schwann cells make myelin in the peripheral nervous system, which is the target in a different disease, Guillain-Barré syndrome.

Concept Tested: Multiple Sclerosis Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 8
docs.text:
Maya touches a hot pan and jerks her hand away. Which neuron type carries the command from her spinal cord to her arm muscles?

  1. Sensory neuron
  2. Interneuron
  3. Motor neuron
  4. Microglia
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Motor neurons carry commands from the CNS out to muscles. Sensory neurons (A) handle the first step, carrying the "hot!" message from the skin into the spinal cord, and interneurons (B) connect neurons inside the CNS, but neither one sends commands to muscles.

Concept Tested: Motor Neuron Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 9
docs.text:
Two patients both have an immune attack on myelin. Patient 1 has blurry vision in one eye and lesions on a brain MRI. Patient 2 has weakness that climbs from the feet up the legs, a normal brain and spinal cord MRI, and slowed signals in the nerves of the arms and legs. What best explains the difference?

  1. Patient 1 has damaged axon terminals, while Patient 2 has damaged dendrites.
  2. Patient 1's disease affects CNS myelin made by oligodendrocytes, while Patient 2's affects PNS myelin made by Schwann cells.
  3. Both patients have the same disease, but Patient 2's is milder.
  4. Patient 1's disease affects microglia, while Patient 2's affects astrocytes.
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Brain lesions point to the CNS (as in multiple sclerosis), while a normal brain and spinal cord MRI with slowed limb nerves points to the PNS (as in Guillain-Barré syndrome). Option C is tempting, but the two patterns come from different locations and different myelin-making cells, not from a difference in severity.

Concept Tested: Peripheral Nervous System Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: Question 10
docs.text:
In the Neuron Explorer, removing myelin from 2 segments makes the signal arrive late, but removing it from 3 segments blocks it completely. What does this pattern show?

  1. Any loss of myelin always stops a signal.
  2. Myelin loss has no effect until the axon terminals are damaged.
  3. The nodes of Ranvier inside the damaged stretch keep the signal at full strength.
  4. A longer bare stretch lets more charge leak out, so the signal can fade below the level needed to be renewed at the next healthy node.
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. In a bare stretch, charge leaks out and the signal weakens as it goes. A short stretch only slows it, but a longer one lets it fade so much that the next healthy node cannot renew it. Option A ignores the fact that small patches of damage can slow a signal without stopping it, which helps explain why MS symptoms vary.

Concept Tested: Node of Ranvier Bloom's Level: Analyze

References: Neurons, Glia, and the Nervous System
docs.text:
1. Brain Basics: The Life and Death of a Neuron - National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NIH) - A plain-language tour of the parts of a neuron, the three kinds of neurons (sensory, motor, interneuron), and glial support cells. It is a great first read if this chapter is your first look at brain cells.

  2. 1.1 Building a Nervous System - OpenStax, Introduction to Behavioral Neuroscience (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) - A free, open college textbook section covering neurons, dendrites and axons, the main types of glia, myelin, and the blood-brain barrier. It goes one step deeper than this chapter, so it suits students who want more detail.

  3. Multiple Sclerosis (MS) - National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NIH) - The government's overview of MS: how the immune system attacks myelin, the types of MS, early symptoms such as optic neuritis, how doctors diagnose it with MRI and other tests, and current treatments. It is the main source for this chapter's Bedside case.

  4. Guillain-Barré Syndrome - National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NIH) - Explains a rare disorder in which the immune system attacks the peripheral nerves, often their myelin. Reading it next to the MS page shows how the same kind of damage looks different in the PNS than in the CNS.

  5. The Search for True Numbers of Neurons and Glial Cells in the Human Brain: A Review of 150 Years of Cell Counting - von Bartheld, Bahney, and Herculano-Houzel, Journal of Comparative Neurology (2016), free on PubMed Central - A review that traces where the "ten glia for every neuron" claim came from and shows that the real ratio is about one to one or a little less. It is a good example of how science corrects a "fact" that textbooks repeated for decades.

  6. The Prevalence of MS in the United States: A Population-Based Estimate Using Health Claims Data - Wallin et al., Neurology (2019), free on PubMed Central - The study behind this chapter's estimate that about 727,000 U.S. adults were living with MS in 2010 (extended, with a caution from the authors, to roughly 850,000 to 914,000 by 2017), with women affected about 2.8 times as often as men. The abstract shows how researchers count a disease across a whole country.

  7. Epstein-Barr Virus May Be Leading Cause of Multiple Sclerosis - Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health (2022) - A readable news summary of the Science study that followed more than 10 million young adults in the U.S. military and found that MS risk rose 32-fold after Epstein-Barr virus infection. It shows how a long-term study can point toward the cause of a disease.

  8. Conduction Velocity and Myelin - Introduction to Sensation and Perception, University of Minnesota open textbook - A short, clear page on why thick, myelinated axons carry signals much faster than thin, bare ones, with speeds compared to walking and race cars. It also briefly discusses diseases that strip myelin.

  9. Do People Only Use 10 Percent of Their Brains? - Scientific American (2008) - Two neurologists explain why the "10 percent" claim is a myth, using evidence from brain imaging and brain injury. It is useful practice in checking a popular brain claim against evidence.

  10. Glia - Wikipedia - An overview of all the major kinds of glial cells, their jobs, and the history of their discovery by Rudolf Virchow. Use it as a starting point and follow its cited sources for details.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Neurons send messages as brief electrical pulses called action potentials. The chapter starts with the tiny voltage that every resting neuron keeps across its membrane, then shows how sodium and potassium channels open and close in a set order to make a spike that is always the same size. You will see why a neuron needs a short rest after each spike, how the strength of a stimulus is coded as a firing rate, and why myelin makes signals travel faster. The chapter ends at the dentist's chair, where a local anesthetic called lidocaine blocks sodium channels, switches off pain, and leaves a numb lip.
