docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 1: Neurons, Glia, and the Nervous System
  • Chapter 2: The Action Potential
  • Chapter 3: Synapses and Neurotransmitters
  • Chapter 4: A Tour of the Brain: Neuroanatomy (especially the occipital, temporal, and parietal lobes, the thalamus, and the cranial nerves)

Welcome to the Brain's Biggest Sense

I'm Ply, a sea slug, and yes, I have two tiny eyes! Yours are far fancier, and the wiring behind them is one of the best maps in all of neuroscience. Learn this one pathway well, and you'll be able to look at a patient's vision test and say where in the brain the problem is.

docs.title: 5.1 Maya's Blind Side
docs.text:
Maya is at Tuesday soccer practice. She's dribbling up the right wing with her eyes locked on the ball. Her teammate Jordan sends a pass in from the left. Maya doesn't react until the ball is almost at her feet, and it bounces off her shin. "Didn't you see that?" Jordan yells. Maya honestly isn't sure. She saw something move, but it was a blur.

That night, studying for the Brain Bee, she starts to worry. Is something wrong with her eyes, or with her brain? The eyes catch light, but the brain builds the picture, and a problem anywhere along that route can steal part of your vision. By the end of this chapter, you'll know how to tell the difference, and whether Maya needs to worry.

docs.title: 5.2 Turning Light into Language: Sensory Transduction
docs.text:
Think about a solar panel. Sunlight hits it, and out comes electricity that wires can carry. Your senses do the same job. The world sends you light, sound, pressure, heat, and chemicals, but neurons speak only one language: electrical signals, like the action potentials from Chapter 2. Sensory transduction is the process of converting a physical or chemical stimulus into an electrical signal in a nerve cell. The cells that do this are called sensory receptors.

Every sense has its own receptor type: light-sensitive cells for vision, and hair cells, nerve endings, and chemical-sensing cells for the senses in Chapter 6. Vision is a great place to start, because scientists know its transduction steps in fine detail.

docs.title: The front of the eye: a focusing system
docs.text:
People often say the eye is "like a camera," and the front half really is. Light passes through the cornea (the clear dome at the front), the pupil, and the lens. The cornea and lens bend the light into a sharp image on the back of the eye, and tiny muscles reshape the lens to focus near or far.

Because a lens flips images, the picture on the back of your eye is upside down and reversed left to right. Your brain doesn't "flip it back." It simply learns what each spot on the retina means. Keep this flip in mind. It matters a lot for vision loss.

docs.title: The back of the eye: a thin sheet of brain
docs.text:
The retina is the thin layer of nerve tissue that lines the back of the eye and turns light into nerve signals. Surprisingly, the retina grows out of the brain in the embryo. When an eye doctor shines a light into your eye, they're looking at a piece of your central nervous system.

The retina has layers of five main kinds of neurons. The first three pass the signal forward, in this order, and the last two link cells side to side:

  1. Photoreceptors catch light (the next section is all about them).
  2. Bipolar cells pass the signal forward.
  3. Ganglion cells collect the signal and send it out of the eye. Their axons form the optic nerve.
  4. Horizontal cells connect photoreceptors and bipolar cells side to side.
  5. Amacrine cells connect bipolar and ganglion cells side to side.

The side-to-side cells let neighbors compare notes, which is how the retina starts finding edges (Section 5.6).

Oddly, the retina is built "inside out." Light passes through the ganglion and bipolar cell layers before reaching the photoreceptors at the back. In one small spot, those layers are pushed aside. That spot is the fovea, a tiny pit in the center of the retina packed with cones. It gives you your sharpest vision. When you "look at" something, you're aiming your foveas at it.

docs.title: The blind spot
docs.text:
The ganglion cell axons leave the eye at the optic disc, where blood vessels also enter. The optic disc has no photoreceptors, so each eye has a blind spot. You don't notice it because the other eye covers that spot and your brain fills in the gap.

Find Your Own Blind Spot

Draw an X and, a few finger-widths to its right, a dot. Close your left eye, stare at the X with your right eye, and slowly move the page toward your face: at one distance the dot vanishes, because its image has landed on your optic disc.

docs.title: Two cameras in one eye
docs.text:
Imagine owning two cameras. One is a night-vision camera that works in near darkness but takes grainy, black-and-white pictures. The other takes sharp color photos, but only in plenty of light. Your retina carries both.

A photoreceptor is a neuron in the retina that is specialized to detect light. Humans have two kinds, called rods and cones:

  • Rods work in dim light. The human retina has about 120 million of them. They are extremely sensitive: a fully dark-adapted rod can respond to a single particle of light, called a photon. But rods don't tell colors apart, and they give blurry, low-detail vision. In bright daylight they are "maxed out" and stop signaling changes. Rods are spread across the retina but are missing from the fovea.
  • Cones work in bright light and give us sharp detail and color. There are about 6 million cones. They are packed most tightly in the fovea, with a thinner scattering in the rest of the retina.

(Numbers from the OpenStax textbook Introduction to Behavioral Neuroscience.) Rods outnumber cones about 20 to 1, yet your sharpest vision depends on the smaller cone team.

Feature Rods Cones Number per retina About 120 million About 6 million Best light level Dim (night) Bright (day) Color? No Yes (three types) Detail Low High Where most dense Outside the fovea In the fovea

Now you can solve part of Maya's mystery. Jordan's pass came from far to her left, so its image landed far from her fovea. That part of the retina has few cones, and each of its ganglion cells collects signals from a wide area. So her side vision was blurry but good at noticing motion. That's why she saw "something move." This isn't a disease. To see details, you have to bring the image onto your fovea.

docs.title: How a photoreceptor catches light
docs.text:
Here is where sensory transduction happens. Each rod is stuffed with a light-catching molecule called rhodopsin. Rhodopsin has two parts: a protein called opsin and a small molecule called retinal, which your body makes from vitamin A.

In the dark, retinal has a bent shape. When it absorbs a photon, it snaps straight. That shape change switches on the opsin protein, which starts a chain reaction inside the cell. The end result is that sodium channels in the cell membrane close.

This part surprises most people. Most neurons get more active when stimulated. Photoreceptors do the opposite:

  • In the dark, sodium channels are open. Positive sodium ions flow in, so the photoreceptor sits at about −40 mV. That is less negative than the −70 mV resting potential you learned for a typical neuron. In this state, the photoreceptor releases its neurotransmitter, glutamate, all the time.
  • In the light, sodium channels close. The cell becomes more negative (it hyperpolarizes), and it releases less glutamate.

So a photoreceptor's message is "less glutamate means light," and brighter light closes more channels. A nerve signal doesn't always mean "fire more." What matters is the change, and the bipolar cells downstream know how to read it.

docs.title: Three cone types
docs.text:
Color vision is the ability to tell apart lights by their wavelength, which we experience as different colors. Light comes in a range of wavelengths. Shorter visible wavelengths look blue to us, and longer ones look red.

A single cone cannot tell color by itself. A cone just counts the photons it catches. A few photons at its favorite wavelength and many photons at a wavelength it barely absorbs can produce the same response. With one cone type, you'd see only shades of gray.

The fix is to compare. Humans have three types of cones, each with a slightly different opsin protein that is best at catching a different part of the spectrum:

Cone type Nickname Peak sensitivity S (short wavelength) "Blue" cone About 420 nm M (medium wavelength) "Green" cone About 534 nm L (long wavelength) "Red" cone About 564 nm

For comparison, rod rhodopsin peaks near 498 nm. (A nanometer, nm, is one billionth of a meter.) These values are from OpenStax.

Your brain works out color by comparing how strongly the three cone types respond to the same patch of light. If S cones respond strongly and L cones barely respond, the light is toward the blue end. A TV screen uses this trick: mixing just red, green, and blue pixels can make a wide range of colors. Most mammals, including dogs and cats, have only two cone types, so your pet doesn't see colors the way you do.

docs.title: Opponent colors
docs.text: The three cones are only the first step. Neurons in the retina and thalamus then compare the cones in "opponent" pairs. Some cells take the difference between L and M cones, a red versus green signal. Others compare S cones against L and M cones added together, a blue versus yellow signal. In the 1800s, these were rival theories: Hermann von Helmholtz argued for three color receptors (trichromacy), and Ewald Hering argued for opposing color pairs. Both turned out to capture part of the truth, at different stages: three cone types at the start, opponent comparisons after that (Shevell and Martin, Journal of the Optical Society of America A, 2017). Opponent pairs help explain afterimages. Stare at a red square and then at a white wall, and you see a greenish afterimage. The parts of the system that signal red have adapted (tired out), so the green side of the pair "wins" for a moment.

docs.title: Color blindness
docs.text:
Some people are born with only two working cone types, or with one cone pigment that is slightly off. They can't tell apart some colors that most people see as different. The most common type makes red and green hard to tell apart.

The National Eye Institute reports that about 1 in 12 men have a color vision deficiency. OpenStax gives about 8% of males and 0.4% of females for the red-green type. Why the big difference? The genes for the red and green cone pigments sit on the X chromosome. Males have only one X, so one faulty copy is enough to cause color blindness. Females have two X chromosomes, so a working copy on the other X usually covers for a faulty one.

docs.title: 5.6 Receptive Fields: The Retina Finds Edges
A retina that edits
docs.text:
The retina doesn't send every "pixel" to the brain. Each eye has over 100 million photoreceptors but only one to two million ganglion cells, so the retina has to summarize. What it sends is mostly news about edges, places where light changes to dark.

To see how, we need one idea. A receptive field is the specific area of the sensory world that can change a particular neuron's activity. For a ganglion cell, that's a small patch of the visual scene. (The idea started with touch: a nerve fiber in your skin responds only to touch on its own small patch of skin.)

docs.title: Center and surround
docs.text:
In 1953, Stephen Kuffler recorded from single ganglion cells in the cat retina. He found that their receptive fields are circles with two zones: a center and a surround ring. The two zones have opposite effects:

  • An on-center cell fires a burst when light hits its center, and is quieted by light on its surround.
  • An off-center cell is the reverse. It fires most to a dark spot surrounded by light.

When the whole receptive field is lit evenly, the center says "fire!" and the surround says "stop!" They mostly cancel, and the cell barely responds. But when an edge puts light on the center and darkness on part of the surround, the cell responds strongly. Horizontal cells help build the surround. That's why a cartoon of a few lines is easy to recognize: your visual system cares more about edges than overall brightness.

docs.title: Out of the eye: the optic nerve
docs.text:
Bipolar cells are so short that they signal with graded voltage changes, not action potentials. Ganglion cells must send signals a long way, so they are the first retinal cells to fire action potentials.

The optic nerve is the bundle of ganglion cell axons that carries visual signals from one eye to the brain. You met it in Chapter 4 as cranial nerve II. Most of its fibers head toward the thalamus for conscious vision. Some go to the midbrain to help steer the eyes. A small group, fewer than 1 in 100 ganglion cells in the human retina, sense light themselves and report brightness to the brain's body clock.

docs.title: 5.7 The Visual Field: What You Can See Right Now
docs.text:
Hold your gaze on one spot straight ahead. Everything you can see without moving your eyes, from the center out to the edges, is your visual field. Doctors split it into halves using a vertical line through the point you're looking at:

  • the left visual field (everything to the left of that line)
  • the right visual field (everything to the right)

Each eye has its own visual field, and the two overlap a lot. Cover your right eye: your left eye still sees things on both your left and your right. Each eye's field has an inner part, toward the nose (the nasal field), and an outer part, toward the temple (the temporal field).

Now combine this with the upside-down, reversed image from Section 5.3. Light from your left visual field lands on the right half of each retina. For the left eye, that's the half closest to the nose, the nasal retina. For the right eye, it's the outer half, the temporal retina.

Read that twice. It's the most important idea in this chapter for understanding vision loss:

  • Temporal visual field → nasal retina
  • Nasal visual field → temporal retina

Retina Halves and Field Halves Are Opposites

A classic mistake on lesion questions is mixing up "temporal retina" with "temporal field." Because the lens flips the image, the temporal (outer) field always lands on the nasal (inner) retina, and the nasal field lands on the temporal retina.

docs.title: The crossing rule
docs.text:
The visual pathway is the chain of nerve fibers and brain areas that carries signals from the retina to the visual cortex. First, an analogy.

Picture two delivery trucks, one from each eye, heading to a city with a Left Warehouse and a Right Warehouse. The rule: packages about the left side of the world go to the Right Warehouse, and packages about the right side go to the Left Warehouse. Each truck carries both kinds, so at a big intersection the trucks swap half their loads.

That intersection is the optic chiasm, the X-shaped spot at the base of the brain where the two optic nerves meet and some of their fibers cross to the other side. The rule is:

  • Fibers from the nasal half of each retina cross to the other side.
  • Fibers from the temporal half of each retina stay on the same side.

Since the nasal retina of the left eye and the temporal retina of the right eye both see the left visual field, this rule sends all left-field information to the right side of the brain. Roughly half the fibers cross. The result: each side of the brain sees the opposite half of the world, using input from both eyes.

One Rule Explains Almost Everything

Nasal fibers cross, temporal fibers stay. If you remember that one line, plus the fact that the retina sees the world flipped, you can figure out every lesion pattern in this chapter instead of memorizing them.

docs.title: After the chiasm
docs.text:
After the chiasm, the bundle on each side is called an optic tract. Each tract holds fibers from both eyes, all about the opposite visual field. It ends in the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN), a six-layered part of the thalamus, the sensory relay station from Chapter 4. The two eyes' fibers go to separate LGN layers, so their signals are still kept apart here.

From the LGN, a broad fan of axons called the optic radiation sweeps back to the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe. It has two main parts:

  • The upper fibers travel under the parietal lobe. They carry the lower part of the opposite visual field.
  • The lower fibers take a detour. They loop forward into the temporal lobe before turning back. This detour is called Meyer's loop, and it carries the upper part of the opposite visual field. (The image on the retina is upside down, so lower retina means upper field.)

The flowchart below traces the path for information about the left visual field.

flowchart TD
    A["Left visual field"] --> B["Nasal retina of LEFT eye"]
    A --> C["Temporal retina of RIGHT eye"]
    B --> D["Left optic nerve"]
    C --> E["Right optic nerve"]
    D -- "crosses at" --> F["Optic chiasm"]
    E -- "stays on same side" --> F
    F --> G["Right optic tract"]
    G --> H["Right LGN (thalamus)"]
    H --> I["Right optic radiation<br/>(Meyer's loop + parietal fibers)"]
    I --> J["Right primary visual cortex (V1)"]

docs.title: Where seeing becomes shapes
docs.text:
The primary visual cortex, also called V1, is the first area of the cerebral cortex to receive visual signals from the thalamus. It lies in the occipital lobe, mostly along the inner surface between the two hemispheres. You may also see it called "striate cortex" because it looks striped under a microscope.

V1 keeps a map of the visual field, called a retinotopic map: neighboring points in the world are handled by neighboring patches of V1. The map is stretched in the middle. Because so many ganglion cells serve the fovea, it gets a huge share of V1. Your center of gaze gets the most brainpower.

docs.title: Hubel and Wiesel's lines and edges
docs.text:
In 1958, David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel began recording from single neurons in the visual cortex of cats, and later monkeys. Small spots of light, which work well for retinal cells, often did little. Then, as Hubel told the story, they slid a glass slide out of their projector. Its faint straight edge swept across the screen, and the neuron suddenly fired rapidly.

They had found that many V1 neurons respond best to lines or edges at a particular angle. One cell might love vertical edges, and its neighbor might prefer edges tilted slightly. They described "simple cells," which need the edge in an exact spot, and "complex cells," which respond to a correctly tilted edge anywhere in their receptive field. Many complex cells also care about the direction the edge moves.

Their explanation shows receptive fields building on each other. Wire several center-surround cells lined up in a row to one V1 cell, and that cell fires most when a bar at just the right angle covers the whole row. In 1981, Hubel and Wiesel shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their discoveries about how the visual system processes information. (Roger Sperry received the other half of that year's prize for his work on the two brain hemispheres.)

Cell type Receptive field shape Best stimulus Retinal ganglion cell Circle with center and surround Spot of light or dark (an edge on the center) V1 simple cell Long, narrow zones Bar or edge at one angle, in one exact spot V1 complex cell Larger area Bar or edge at one angle, anywhere in the field, often moving

docs.title: 5.10 Ventral and Dorsal Streams: What and Where
docs.text:
V1 is only the start. Visual information then flows into many other areas, organized into two main routes called the ventral and dorsal streams.

  • The ventral stream runs from the occipital lobe down into the lower temporal lobe. It answers "What is it?" It recognizes objects, colors, and faces. Deep in this stream, some neurons respond best to faces, and an area in the human temporal lobe called the fusiform face area becomes active when we look at faces.
  • The dorsal stream runs from the occipital lobe up into the parietal lobe. It answers "Where is it, and how do I act on it?" It tracks position and movement. One area in this stream, called MT, is packed with neurons tuned to the direction of motion.

A memory trick: ventral is "vhat" (what), and dorsal is "where/do."

In 1982, Leslie Ungerleider and Mortimer Mishkin proposed this "what versus where" split, based partly on monkeys with damage to one stream. In 1992, Melvyn Goodale and David Milner argued that the dorsal stream is really about guiding action, or "how." A key patient, known as D.F., had brain damage from carbon monoxide poisoning. She couldn't say how a slot was tilted, yet she could post a card through it at the correct angle. Her "what" system was damaged, but her "how" system still worked.

Maya uses both streams every time she plays. Her ventral stream recognizes Jordan's face and jersey. Her dorsal stream tracks the ball's path and guides her foot to meet it.

docs.title: 5.11 Visual Field Defects: Reading the Map Backward
docs.text:
A visual field defect is a missing area in a person's visual field caused by damage somewhere along the visual pathway, from the retina to the cortex. Because the pathway is so orderly, the shape of the missing area tells a doctor where the damage is. This is called localization, and it's one of the most satisfying skills in neurology.

Doctors test the visual field one eye at a time. At the bedside, the doctor may wiggle fingers in each part of the field ("confrontation testing"). A machine called a perimeter is more precise: the patient stares at a center dot and presses a button whenever a faint light flashes.

Visual field maps are always drawn as the patient sees them: the left eye's map on the left, with the patient's left side on the left of each circle.

Two words will help you name the patterns:

  • Hemianopia means loss of half of the visual field (the half on one side of the vertical line).
  • Homonymous means the same side is lost in both eyes (for example, the left half in each eye).

Now apply the crossing rule:

  • In front of the chiasm (optic nerve), only fibers from one eye are present, so the damage affects only that eye.
  • At the chiasm, the damage hits the crossing fibers, which come from both nasal retinas. Nasal retinas see the temporal fields, so both eyes lose their outer halves. This is bitemporal hemianopia.
  • Behind the chiasm (optic tract, radiation, or cortex), each side carries the opposite field from both eyes, so damage causes a homonymous loss on the opposite side.
Lesion site Field defect Typical description Left optic nerve Left eye blind; right eye normal Monocular vision loss Center of optic chiasm Outer half lost in each eye Bitemporal hemianopia Right optic tract Left half lost in both eyes, often uneven between eyes Left homonymous hemianopia Left Meyer's loop (temporal lobe) Upper-right quarter lost in both eyes Right superior homonymous quadrantanopia ("pie in the sky") Left parietal optic radiation Lower-right quarter lost in both eyes Right inferior homonymous quadrantanopia ("pie on the floor") Right occipital cortex (V1) Left half lost in both eyes, center often spared Left homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing

Two details are worth knowing. Meyer's loop damage often comes from surgery in the front of the temporal lobe, and people often don't notice the "pie in the sky" loss at first. Damage to the occipital cortex is usually from a stroke. In many of those patients, the very center of vision, served by the macula (the area around the fovea), is spared. One common explanation is that the tip of the occipital lobe, where central vision is mapped, can get blood from a second artery. But scientists still debate the reason, and sparing doesn't happen in every patient.

Localization Takes Practice

If this feels like a lot, that's normal: doctors in training practice these maps over and over. Use the simulator below, predict before you peek, and the patterns will start to feel obvious.

docs.title: Diagram: Visual Pathway Lesion Simulator
docs.text:
Open the Visual Pathway Lesion Simulator fullscreen

MicroSim specification: Visual Pathway Lesion Simulator

Type: microsim sim-id: ch05-visual-pathway Library: p5.js Status: Implemented Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: differentiate Learning Objective: The learner will differentiate the visual field defects caused by lesions at five sites (left optic nerve, optic chiasm, right optic tract, left Meyer's loop, right occipital cortex) and predict the defect in each eye before revealing it.

Canvas: responsive width; 620 px drawing area plus 85 px control area.

Controls: "Lesion site" menu (None plus the five sites); clickable red dots for the same sites; "Hide result" checkbox for predict-first use.

Behavior: Top-down schematic with retina halves color-coded (blue = left visual field, orange = right visual field). A lesion turns cut fibers gray and dashed, and two field maps (drawn as the patient sees them) shade lost areas. Results: optic nerve = monocular blindness; chiasm = bitemporal hemianopia; optic tract = left homonymous hemianopia; Meyer's loop = right superior homonymous quadrantanopia; occipital cortex = left homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. Maps are idealized.

What to try. Start with "None" and trace the blue fibers: they come from the inner half of the left eye and the outer half of the right eye, and both end in the right side of the brain. Then check Hide result, pick a lesion, and sketch what each eye will lose before you uncheck the box.

What to notice. Only the optic nerve lesion affects just one eye. Every lesion behind the chiasm takes away the same side in both eyes, opposite the damaged side of the brain. Try it in reverse: if both eyes lose the upper-right quarter, which red dot did you click?

docs.title: Back to Maya
docs.text: So, does Maya have a field defect? Her optometrist checks each eye separately and finds a full visual field in both. Maya's "blind side" was ordinary peripheral vision. Jordan's pass landed on a part of her retina built for catching motion, not for detail. Her coach's advice, to scan the field with quick glances instead of staring at the ball, is good neuroscience: each glance points her foveas at something new.

docs.title: At the Bedside: The Driver Who Kept Bumping Door Frames
docs.text:
Meet the patient

Mr. Alvarez is a 47-year-old delivery driver. Over the past year, he keeps bumping his shoulders on door frames and clipping his van's side mirror on gateposts. Twice a car seemed to "come out of nowhere" in the next lane. He also has dull headaches. He can still read signs and his phone, so he figures he's just tired and clumsy. His wife insists he see a doctor.

What the doctor checks: His sharpness of vision (visual acuity) is normal in each eye. During confrontation testing, with one eye covered, he can't see the doctor's fingers wiggling in the outer half of his field, and the same thing happens with the other eye. Formal perimetry confirms it: the left eye has lost the left (temporal) half of its field, and the right eye has lost the right (temporal) half. The rest of his eye exam is normal.

Where is the problem? (localization): Only one place holds the fibers for both temporal fields: the crossing fibers in the middle of the optic chiasm. An optic nerve lesion would affect only one eye, and a lesion behind the chiasm would take the same side from both eyes. The pituitary gland sits just below the chiasm, so a mass growing up from there is the prime suspect.

Diagnosis: An MRI with contrast shows a large pituitary tumor pushing up out of its bony pocket and pressing on the optic chiasm. A pituitary tumor is an abnormal growth in the pituitary gland, the small hormone-control gland at the base of the brain. Most are pituitary adenomas, which are noncancerous, grow slowly, and don't spread. Since 2022, the World Health Organization's tumor classification has recommended a new name, pituitary neuroendocrine tumor (PitNET), but many doctors and patient guides still say "adenoma" (Tsukamoto and Miki, Japanese Journal of Radiology, 2023). Blood tests show that his tumor isn't making extra hormones, so it's called a "nonfunctioning" adenoma. Final diagnosis: bitemporal hemianopia caused by a nonfunctioning pituitary adenoma compressing the optic chiasm.

Why it happens: The tumor presses on the crossing fibers in the center of the chiasm. Those fibers come from the nasal half of each retina, which sees the temporal (outer) visual field. So he loses the outer side of each eye's view and bumps into things on both sides. His central vision still works, which is why he could read signs and didn't notice the problem for so long.

Treatment today: Because the tumor is pressing on the visual pathway, the standard approach is surgery to remove it. Most pituitary tumors can be removed through the nose and sinuses, called transsphenoidal surgery, so no opening in the skull is needed. After surgery, doctors repeat visual field tests and check his hormone levels, because the pituitary may need support. Radiation is an option if the tumor can't be fully removed or grows back. One important exception: tumors that make the hormone prolactin (prolactinomas) are usually treated first with medicines called dopamine agonists, which can shrink the tumor.

What's new in research: Doctors want to predict how much vision will come back after surgery. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) is a quick, painless light scan that measures the thickness of the retina's nerve fiber layer (the ganglion cell axons). In a 2015 study of 107 patients, eyes with a normal-thickness layer before surgery usually recovered near-normal visual fields (81%), compared with 37% of eyes where the layer had already thinned (Danesh-Meyer et al., Journal of Clinical Neuroscience, 2015). A 2024 study also linked a thicker layer before surgery to better results (Han et al., PLoS ONE, 2024). The idea is simple: if the axons are still there, they have a better chance of working again once the pressure is removed.

Your turn: diagnose a variation

A different patient with a pituitary tumor has lost only the upper outer quarter of each eye's visual field. Where is the tumor pressing, and why the upper field?

Answer: The tumor is pushing on the chiasm from below, so it squeezes the lower crossing fibers first. Those fibers come from the lower nasal retina. Because the image on the retina is upside down, the lower nasal retina sees the upper temporal field. Doctors often see this pattern early, and it can grow into a full bitemporal hemianopia if the tumor keeps growing.

This is a fictional teaching case. It is not medical advice. If you or someone you know has symptoms like these, talk to a doctor.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
Myth: The eye works like a camera, and the brain just records the picture. Reality: Only the front of the eye works like a camera. The retina is part of the brain and edits the image, mostly reporting edges. Then many brain areas build what you "see": shape, color, motion, and faces. Seeing is constructed by the brain.

Myth: The left eye sends its signals to the right brain, and the right eye to the left brain. Reality: Each half of the visual world goes to the opposite hemisphere. Only the nasal half of each retina crosses at the chiasm. Each hemisphere gets input from both eyes about the opposite side of space.

Myth: Damage to the right side of the brain makes you blind in the right eye. Reality: Damage behind the chiasm on the right takes away the left half of the visual field in both eyes. Only damage in front of the chiasm (to the eye or optic nerve) causes blindness in one eye.

Myth: Color-blind people see only in black and white. Reality: Almost all color-blind people see many colors. Most have trouble telling apart certain reds and greens because one cone type is missing or works differently. Seeing no color at all is very rare.

docs.title: Brain Bee Practice
docs.text:
1. What is the name of the light-absorbing pigment in rods, and what vitamin is part of it made from?

Rhodopsin. Its light-catching part, retinal, is made from vitamin A.

2. Which retinal cells are the first to fire action potentials, and what do their axons form?

Retinal ganglion cells. Their axons bundle together to form the optic nerve (cranial nerve II).

3. A patient has lost the outer half of the visual field in both eyes. Name the defect and the most likely site of the lesion.

Bitemporal hemianopia. The lesion is at the center of the optic chiasm, often from a pituitary tumor pressing on it.

4. Damage to Meyer's loop in the right temporal lobe causes what visual field defect?

A left superior homonymous quadrantanopia, the "pie in the sky" defect: the upper-left quarter is lost in both eyes.

5. Which visual processing stream would be most important for recognizing a friend's face, and which lobe does it travel into?

The ventral ("what") stream, which travels from the occipital lobe into the lower temporal lobe.

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
1. List, in order, the structures a visual signal passes through from the retina to the primary visual cortex.
  2. Name the two types of photoreceptors and state which one is responsible for color vision.
Answer
  1. Photoreceptors → bipolar cells → ganglion cells → optic nerve → optic chiasm → optic tract → lateral geniculate nucleus (thalamus) → optic radiation → primary visual cortex (V1).
  2. Rods and cones. Cones are responsible for color vision.

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
1. Explain why a photoreceptor releases more glutamate in the dark than in the light.
  2. Explain why an on-center ganglion cell responds weakly when its whole receptive field is lit evenly.
Answer
  1. In the dark, sodium channels in the photoreceptor stay open, so the cell is depolarized (about −40 mV) and keeps releasing glutamate. Light triggers a chain reaction that closes those channels, so the cell hyperpolarizes and releases less glutamate.
  2. Light on the center excites the cell, but light on the surround inhibits it. When both are lit, the two effects largely cancel, so the cell signals contrast (edges), not overall brightness.

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
1. A person has a stroke in the left occipital lobe. Use the crossing rule to predict which part of the visual field is lost in each eye.
  2. A highway warning light must catch a driver's side vision at night. Based on rods and cones, should it rely on color or on flashing? Justify your answer.

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
1. Two patients both say they have trouble seeing on their left. Patient A has lost all vision in the left eye. Patient B has lost the left half of the visual field in both eyes. Compare where each lesion is likely to be, and explain how the visual field test tells them apart.
  2. Mr. Alvarez had normal visual acuity but a serious visual field defect. Analyze why acuity testing alone missed his problem, using what you know about the fovea and the crossing fibers.

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
1. A website claims, "Your eyes see the world, and your brain just receives the image." Evaluate this claim using at least two pieces of evidence from this chapter.
  2. Imagine a driver's license office that checks only visual acuity (the eye chart). Judge whether it should also test the visual field. Consider safety, cost, and people like Mr. Alvarez.

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
1. Write a short fictional case of a patient with a "pie in the sky" visual field defect. Include their symptoms, the exam finding, and a localization that a classmate could solve.
  2. Design a one-page poster that teaches middle school students the rule "nasal fibers cross, temporal fibers stay," using an analogy of your own.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Sensory transduction turns light into electrical signals. Photoreceptors do this in an unusual way: light hyperpolarizes them and reduces their glutamate release.
  • Rods (about 120 million) handle dim light with low detail. Cones (about 6 million) handle bright light, fine detail, and color vision, which comes from comparing three cone types.
  • The retina is part of the brain. Its receptive fields have a center and a surround, so it sends mostly news about edges and contrast through the optic nerve.
  • At the optic chiasm, fibers from the nasal half of each retina cross and temporal fibers stay. As a result, each hemisphere sees the opposite half of the visual field using both eyes.
  • The visual pathway runs through the optic tract, the LGN of the thalamus, and the optic radiation (including Meyer's loop) to the primary visual cortex (V1), where neurons respond to lines and edges at specific angles.
  • Beyond V1, the ventral stream identifies "what" and the dorsal stream handles "where" and "how."
  • The shape of a visual field defect reveals the lesion site. A pituitary tumor pressing on the chiasm classically causes bitemporal hemianopia.

You Can Read the Map Now!

You just learned to look at a vision test and point to a spot in the brain, which is real clinical reasoning! Next, in Chapter 6, we'll see how the other senses perform their own transductions, from hair cells that "hear" to the strange case of pain in a missing limb.

docs.title: Quiz: Vision
docs.text: Test your understanding of Chapter 5. Choose the best answer, then click Show Answer to check.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
Which type of photoreceptor is far more numerous in the human retina and works best in dim light?

  1. Cones
  2. Rods
  3. Retinal ganglion cells
  4. Bipolar cells
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The retina has about 120 million rods and only about 6 million cones. Rods are very sensitive and handle dim light, but they give low detail and no color. Cones (A) handle bright light, detail, and color. Ganglion and bipolar cells are retinal neurons, but they are not photoreceptors.

Concept Tested: Rods and Cones Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
At the optic chiasm, which nerve fibers cross to the opposite side of the brain?

  1. Fibers from the temporal half of each retina
  2. All fibers from the left eye
  3. Only fibers from the fovea
  4. Fibers from the nasal half of each retina
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Fibers from the nasal (inner) half of each retina cross at the chiasm, and fibers from the temporal half stay on the same side. A common mistake is thinking a whole eye crosses (B), but each hemisphere gets input from both eyes about the opposite visual field.

Concept Tested: Optic Chiasm Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
In which lobe of the brain is the primary visual cortex (V1) found?

  1. Occipital lobe
  2. Temporal lobe
  3. Parietal lobe
  4. Frontal lobe
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. V1 lies in the occipital lobe at the back of the brain. The temporal (B) and parietal (C) lobes receive visual information later, through the ventral and dorsal streams, but they are not where it first reaches the cortex.

Concept Tested: Primary Visual Cortex Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 4
docs.text:
What happens inside a rod when it absorbs light?

  1. Sodium channels open, and the rod fires an action potential
  2. The rod depolarizes and releases more glutamate
  3. Sodium channels close, the rod hyperpolarizes, and it releases less glutamate
  4. The rod releases dopamine onto the optic nerve
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. In the dark, sodium channels in the rod are open, so it is depolarized and releases glutamate steadily. Light changes the shape of retinal in rhodopsin, which triggers a chain reaction that closes those channels. Options A and B describe how most neurons respond to a stimulus. Photoreceptors do the opposite, which is why they surprise people.

Concept Tested: Sensory Transduction Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 5
docs.text:
Why does an on-center retinal ganglion cell respond only weakly when its entire receptive field is lit evenly?

  1. Excitation from light on the center is largely canceled by inhibition from light on the surround
  2. Ganglion cells respond only to colored light, not white light
  3. Even light saturates the cell so it cannot fire
  4. The surround is made of rods, which do not work in light
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Center-surround receptive fields have opposite zones. Light on the center excites an on-center cell, while light on the surround inhibits it, so even light mostly cancels out. This is why the retina mainly signals edges and contrast. Option C confuses ganglion cells with rods, which do saturate in bright light.

Concept Tested: Receptive Field Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 6
docs.text:
Why is red-green color blindness much more common in males than in females?

  1. Males have fewer cones in the fovea
  2. Testosterone damages the green cone pigment
  3. Males are missing rods in the center of the retina
  4. The genes for the red and green cone pigments are on the X chromosome
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Males have one X chromosome, so a single faulty red or green pigment gene causes color blindness. Females have two X chromosomes, and a working copy usually makes up for a faulty one. Option C is true of everyone (rods are absent from the fovea), so it can't explain a difference between the sexes.

Concept Tested: Color Vision Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 7
docs.text:
A 70-year-old woman has a stroke in her right occipital lobe. Which visual field defect is she most likely to have?

  1. Blindness in the right eye only
  2. Loss of the left half of the visual field in both eyes, often with the center spared
  3. Loss of the outer half of the visual field in each eye
  4. Loss of the right half of the visual field in both eyes
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Behind the chiasm, the right side of the brain handles the left visual field from both eyes, so damage there causes a left homonymous hemianopia. Occipital strokes often spare central (macular) vision. Option A is a common misconception: brain damage behind the chiasm does not blind one eye.

Concept Tested: Visual Field Defect Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 8
docs.text:
After brain damage, a patient cannot name or describe common objects by sight, or say how a slot is tilted. Yet she reaches for objects accurately and turns a card to fit through the slot. Which part of the visual system is most likely damaged?

  1. The dorsal stream
  2. The optic chiasm
  3. The ventral stream
  4. The rods of the retina
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The ventral ("what") stream, running into the lower temporal lobe, is needed to recognize objects. Her accurate reaching shows that the dorsal ("where/how") stream to the parietal lobe still works. This matches the famous patient D.F. Damage to the dorsal stream (A) would impair reaching, the opposite of what she shows.

Concept Tested: Ventral and Dorsal Streams Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 9
docs.text:
A 47-year-old driver keeps bumping into door frames on both sides. He can read an eye chart normally. Testing each eye separately shows that the left eye has lost the left half of its field and the right eye has lost the right half. What is the most likely cause?

  1. A stroke in the left occipital lobe
  2. Damage to the left optic nerve
  3. Damage to Meyer's loop in the temporal lobe
  4. A pituitary tumor pressing on the optic chiasm
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Losing the outer (temporal) half of each eye's field is bitemporal hemianopia. The only place where both nasal retinas' crossing fibers meet is the middle of the optic chiasm, which sits just above the pituitary gland. A left occipital stroke (A) would remove the right half of the field in both eyes, not the outer halves.

Concept Tested: Pituitary Tumor Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: Question 10
docs.text:
A patient has completely lost vision in the left eye, but the right eye's visual field is normal. Where along the visual pathway is the lesion most likely to be?

  1. Left optic nerve
  2. Optic chiasm
  3. Right optic tract
  4. Left occipital cortex
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Only structures in front of the chiasm carry fibers from just one eye, so a one-eye loss points to the eye or its optic nerve. Lesions at or behind the chiasm (B, C, D) affect fibers from both eyes and change the visual field of both eyes.

Concept Tested: Optic Nerve Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.text:
1. 6.2 The Retina - OpenStax, Introduction to Behavioral Neuroscience (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) - Explains the retina's cell layers, rods versus cones, phototransduction, and color blindness in clear steps. It is the main source for this chapter's photoreceptor numbers and cone sensitivity peaks.
  2. 6.4 The Thalamus and Primary Visual Cortex - OpenStax, Introduction to Behavioral Neuroscience - Covers the crossing at the optic chiasm, the layered LGN, and Hubel and Wiesel's discovery of edge-detecting cells in V1. Great for readers who want more detail on simple and complex cells.
  3. 6.5 Extrastriate Cortex - OpenStax, Introduction to Behavioral Neuroscience - Describes the dorsal and ventral streams, the motion area MT, and face-selective neurons. A good next step after Section 5.10.
  4. Color Blindness - National Eye Institute (NIH) - A plain-language overview of color vision deficiency, who gets it, and how people adapt. Useful for checking facts about how common it is.
  5. Pituitary Tumors - National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NIH) - Explains what pituitary tumors are, their symptoms (including vision changes), and how they are diagnosed and treated. Good background for the Bedside case.
  6. Pituitary tumor - MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia (U.S. National Library of Medicine) - A short patient-friendly page on symptoms, tests such as visual field testing and MRI, and transsphenoidal surgery through the nose.
  7. Localizing the Lesion (Visual Fields) - Jonathan Trobe, NOVEL (Neuro-Ophthalmology Virtual Education Library), University of Utah - A neuro-ophthalmologist's guide matching each visual field pattern to a lesion site. Advanced, but excellent for Brain Bee competitors who want to check every pattern in the simulator.
  8. Optic radiation - Wikipedia - Describes the path of the optic radiation from the LGN to V1, including Meyer's loop and the "pie in the sky" defect. Use it as a starting point and check claims against the other sources here.
  9. One brain, two visual systems - Mel Goodale and David Milner, The Psychologist (British Psychological Society), 2006 - The scientists behind the "perception versus action" idea tell the story of patient D.F. in their own words. A readable look at how one patient changed a field.
  10. Clinical efficacy of optical coherence tomography parameters to predict the visual field outcome following pituitary adenoma surgery - Han et al., PLoS ONE, 2024 - An open-access study showing that a thicker retinal nerve fiber layer before surgery is linked to better visual field recovery. Shows how a retina scan can help predict a patient's outcome.

docs.title: Chapter 6: Hearing, Touch, Taste, Smell, and Pain
Chapter 6: Hearing, Touch, Taste, Smell, and Pain
Summary
docs.text: Every sense starts with a receptor cell that turns energy, such as a sound wave, a push on the skin, or a chemical, into electrical signals. This chapter follows those signals for hearing, balance, touch, body position, taste, smell, and pain. You will see how the somatosensory cortex keeps a distorted map of the body, and how doctors use skin "stripes" called dermatomes to find spinal problems. The chapter ends with a puzzle that has fascinated doctors for more than 150 years: pain in a limb that is no longer there.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 1: Neurons, Glia, and the Nervous System
  • Chapter 2: The Action Potential
  • Chapter 3: Synapses and Neurotransmitters
  • Chapter 4: A Tour of the Brain: Neuroanatomy
  • Chapter 5: Vision

Five senses? Try a lot more.

I'm a sea slug with no ears, so I rely on touch and chemical senses. You get ears that hear and balance you, skin that tells silk from sandpaper, and a nose and tongue that work as a team. In this chapter you'll learn how each sense reports to the brain, and how a doctor can touch your skin with a pin and figure out which part of your spinal cord is hurt.

docs.title: 6.1 A Paper Cut, a Bruise, and a Bland Slice of Pizza
docs.text:
Maya is 16, plays soccer, and is studying for the Brain Bee. On Tuesday she slices her fingertip on the edge of a flashcard. The cut is so tiny she can barely see it, yet it stings so sharply that she drops the cards. That afternoon a defender kicks her shin at practice, leaving a big purple bruise. It aches, but she can almost ignore it.

On Friday Maya has a cold. Her nose is stuffed up, and her favorite pizza tastes like warm cardboard. Nothing is wrong with her tongue. So why does a tiny cut hurt more than a big bruise? And why does a blocked nose ruin the taste of food? By the end of this chapter you will be able to answer both questions with real neuroscience.

docs.title: 6.2 How Any Sense Works: Translators at the Border
docs.text:
Imagine your brain as a control room sealed inside the skull. It never touches the outside world directly. All it receives are action potentials, which you met in Chapter 2. So each sense needs a translator at the border: a cell that turns outside energy into the brain's electrical language.

That translation step is called sensory transduction. The translator cell is a sensory receptor. Different senses use receptors tuned to different kinds of energy:

  • Push, stretch, or vibration (mechanical energy): hearing, balance, touch, body position
  • Chemicals: taste and smell
  • Heat and cold: temperature sense
  • Damaging or nearly damaging stimuli: pain

Action potentials all look alike. A signal from a touch receptor feels like touch because of where the wire goes: touch nerves connect to touch areas of the brain, and sound nerves connect to hearing areas. This is sometimes called the "labeled line" idea.

Same message, different wires

When someone touches my siphon, touch-sensing neurons fire and I pull my gill in to protect it. That simple reflex is what Eric Kandel studied in my species. Your brain uses the same trick I do: the meaning of a signal comes from which neurons carry it, not from the shape of the spike.

So how many senses do people have? Far more than five. The table lists the ones in this chapter, plus vision from Chapter 5.

Sense What it detects Receptor type Vision Light Photoreceptors (rods and cones) Hearing Sound waves Hair cells (mechanical) Balance Head turning, tilting, and speeding up Hair cells (mechanical) Touch Pressure, vibration, stretch, texture Mechanoreceptors Body position Where your limbs are Muscle spindles, tendon organs Temperature Warm and cold Temperature-sensitive nerve endings Pain Damage or threat of damage Nociceptors Taste Chemicals dissolved in saliva Taste receptor cells Smell Chemicals floating in air Olfactory sensory neurons

docs.title: 6.3 Hearing: The Cochlea and Hair Cells
docs.text:
Sound is a pressure wave in the air. Its frequency, measured in hertz (Hz), is how many waves pass each second, and we hear it as pitch. Humans hear from about 20 Hz (a deep rumble) to about 20,000 Hz (a high whine).

Before we name the parts, picture a piano keyboard rolled up like a snail shell, with low notes at one end and high notes at the other. When a sound comes in, the "key" for that pitch moves the most. Your inner ear works much like this.

Here is the path a sound takes:

  1. Sound waves make the eardrum vibrate.
  2. Three tiny middle-ear bones (malleus, incus, and stapes) pass the vibration along and amplify it.
  3. The last bone pushes on a window into the cochlea, a snail-shaped, fluid-filled tube in the inner ear.
  4. The fluid ripples, and a ribbon of tissue inside, the basilar membrane, moves in a traveling wave.
  5. Sensory cells on that membrane bend and start the electrical signal.

Those sensory cells are hair cells. Each has a bundle of tiny stiff projections on top called stereocilia. When the basilar membrane moves, the stereocilia tilt, ion channels at their tips open, positive ions rush in, and the hair cell releases neurotransmitter onto auditory nerve fibers. Together, the cochlea and hair cells are where sound becomes neural signals.

The basilar membrane is stiff and narrow at the base of the cochlea (near the middle ear) and floppy and wide at the apex (the tip of the spiral). So high sounds, around 20,000 Hz, vibrate the base most, and low sounds, around 20 Hz, travel to the apex. This map of pitch is called tonotopy, and it is kept at almost every station on the way to the cortex. Cochlear implants use it: electrodes near the base stimulate high-pitch nerve fibers, and deeper electrodes stimulate low-pitch fibers.

The human cochlea has about 3,500 inner hair cells, which do most of the job of sending sound information to the brain. Three more rows of outer hair cells act like tiny amplifiers. They change length very quickly and boost faint sounds at particular pitches.

Hair cells are delicate. According to the National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD), sounds at or below 70 A-weighted decibels (dBA) are unlikely to cause hearing loss even after long exposure, but long or repeated exposure to sounds at or above 85 dBA can cause hearing loss, mostly by killing hair cells. Birds and amphibians can regrow hair cells, but humans cannot. After loud noise, hearing can be dulled for 16 to 48 hours and then seem to recover, though some lasting damage may remain (NIDCD). An extremely loud burst, such as a gunshot or explosion, can cause permanent loss right away. Once hair cells die, that hearing loss is permanent. That is a real reason to turn your earbuds down.

docs.title: 6.4 The Auditory Pathway
docs.text:
Once hair cells fire, the signal travels along cranial nerve VIII (the vestibulocochlear nerve) into the brainstem. The route from the cochlea to the cortex is the auditory pathway, and it has several relay stations, each with a job.

One key job is finding where a sound comes from. A car honking on your left reaches your left ear a tiny bit sooner, and louder, than your right. The superior olivary complex in the brainstem, the first station that receives input from both ears, compares their timing and loudness.

The table lists the main stops in order.

Stop Location Main job Cochlear nuclei Brainstem, where the medulla meets the pons First stop for every auditory nerve fiber; keeps the pitch map Superior olivary complex Lower brainstem (pons) Compares the two ears to locate sounds Lateral lemniscus Bundle of axons in the brainstem Carries signals upward Inferior colliculus Midbrain Major relay; combines pitch, timing, and location Medial geniculate body Thalamus Gateway from the brainstem to the cortex Primary auditory cortex Temporal lobe Conscious hearing; pitch is still mapped in order

Because each ear's signals reach both sides of the brain, damage to one auditory cortex usually does not cause deafness in one ear. One-sided deafness usually points to the ear or the auditory nerve.

docs.title: 6.5 Balance: The Vestibular System
docs.text:
Try this. Look at a finger held at arm's length and shake your head side to side. The finger stays sharp. Now hold your head still and wave the finger at the same speed. It blurs. The difference is the vestibular system at work.

The vestibular system is the inner ear's balance sensor. It shares fluid, hair cells, and cranial nerve VIII with the cochlea. It has two kinds of parts:

  • Semicircular canals. Three fluid-filled loops at roughly right angles, like the corner of a box. When you turn your head, the fluid lags behind because of inertia, like coffee in a spinning mug, and bends a gel flap holding hair cells. The canals sense rotation.
  • Otolith organs. Two pouches, the utricle and saccule, whose hair cells sit under a gel topped with calcium carbonate grains called otoconia. Gravity and straight-line acceleration shift the grains, telling your brain which way is down and when you speed up.

The finger test shows the vestibulo-ocular reflex. When your head turns, signals from the semicircular canals reach your eye muscles through only a few synapses, so your eyes swing the opposite way fast enough to keep the world steady. This reflex is why Maya can read a defender's body while dribbling at full speed. It also explains why you feel dizzy after spinning and stopping: the fluid in your canals keeps sloshing, so your ears say "turning" while your eyes say "still."

In a common balance problem called benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, loose otoconia tumble into a semicircular canal and send false "spinning" signals, causing brief, intense vertigo with certain head movements, such as rolling over in bed.

docs.title: 6.6 Touch and Body Sense: The Somatosensory System
docs.text: "Soma" means body. The somatosensory system is the set of receptors, nerves, and brain areas that handle touch, pressure, vibration, temperature, pain, and body position. Its receptors are spread over the whole body, not packed into one organ like the eye or ear.

docs.title: Mechanoreceptors
docs.text:
A mechanoreceptor is a receptor that responds to mechanical force, such as pressure, stretch, or vibration. In the skin, many are nerve endings wrapped in capsules or attached to special cells. Force opens ion channels in the nerve ending, including a family called Piezo channels.

Two features make each mechanoreceptor good at a different job:

  • Depth. Receptors near the surface have small, sharp receptive fields, the patch of skin that can activate them. Deeper receptors have large, blurry receptive fields.
  • Adaptation. Slowly adapting receptors keep firing as long as pressure lasts, like a doorbell held down. Rapidly adapting receptors fire when something changes and then go quiet, like a motion-sensor light.

The table compares the four classic touch receptors.

Receptor Depth in skin Adaptation Good at sensing Merkel disk Shallow Slow Steady pressure, edges, and shapes, like the dots of Braille Meissner corpuscle Shallow Rapid Light touch and slipping, like a cup sliding in your grip Ruffini ending Deep Slow Skin stretch, like bending a finger Pacinian corpuscle Deep Rapid Vibration, like a phone buzzing in your pocket

Rapid adaptation is why you stop noticing your socks soon after putting them on.

In 2021, David Julius and Ardem Patapoutian shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discovering receptors for temperature and touch, including the Piezo channels.

docs.title: Proprioception
docs.text: Close your eyes and touch your nose. You can do it because of proprioception, the sense of where your body parts are and how they move. Its receptors sit in muscles, tendons, and joints. The two most important are muscle spindles, which sense how much a muscle is stretched, and Golgi tendon organs, which sense how hard a muscle is pulling on its tendon. You will meet muscle spindles again in Chapter 7, because they drive the knee-jerk reflex.

docs.title: Nerve fibers: fast lanes and slow lanes
docs.text:
Each receptor connects to a sensory neuron whose cell body sits in a dorsal root ganglion, a cluster of cell bodies just outside the spinal cord. As you learned in Chapter 2, thicker axons with more myelin conduct faster. Sensory fibers come in several sizes.

Fiber type Myelin Approximate speed Main signals Aβ (A-beta) Thick 36 to 72 m/s Touch, vibration, pressure Aδ (A-delta) Thin 4 to 36 m/s Sharp, fast pain; temperature C None 0.4 to 2 m/s Slow, burning or aching pain; temperature; itch

docs.title: From skin to cortex: the touch pathway
docs.text:
Touch and body-position signals take the dorsal column pathway. The sensory axon climbs the spinal cord on the same side to the medulla. There it synapses, and the next neuron crosses to the opposite side and rises to the thalamus, which relays the signal to the cortex. Because of that crossing, the left side of your brain feels the right side of your body.

Keep your eye on the crossing

Sensory pathways can feel like a maze of names. For each one, ask just two questions: where does it cross the midline, and where does it end? Those two answers solve most lesion puzzles.

docs.title: 6.7 Maps of the Body: Dermatomes, Cortex, and the Homunculus
Dermatomes: stripes on the skin
docs.text:
The spinal cord has 31 segments: 8 cervical (neck), 12 thoracic (chest), 5 lumbar (lower back), 5 sacral, and 1 coccygeal. Each segment has a pair of dorsal roots that bring in sensory information. A dermatome is the strip of skin whose sensation is carried by one spinal nerve root.

Picture a person on hands and knees. The dermatomes run in roughly horizontal bands, like zebra stripes, and get stretched out along the arms and legs.

Doctors use dermatomes like an address book. Numbness in one stripe points to a problem at that spinal level or nerve root, such as a herniated disc pressing on one root in the neck. Doctors test standard "key points," listed below.

Spinal level Key test spot on the skin C4 Top of the shoulder C6 Thumb C7 Middle finger C8 Little finger T4 Chest at the nipple line T10 Belly button (umbilicus) L3 Inner knee L4 Inner ankle L5 Top of the foot S1 Outer heel

Two warnings come with this table. First, dermatome maps disagree between textbooks, and borders vary from person to person because neighboring dermatomes overlap. Treat these as standard test spots, not perfect borders. Second, the face has no spinal dermatome. Facial skin is supplied mainly by the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V).

docs.title: The somatosensory cortex and the homunculus
docs.text:
Touch signals from the thalamus arrive at the somatosensory cortex. The first stop, the primary somatosensory cortex (S1), is a strip of cortex on the postcentral gyrus, the ridge just behind the central sulcus at the front of the parietal lobe (see Chapter 4).

S1 holds an orderly map of the opposite side of the body, with neighboring body parts mostly in neighboring patches. The leg and foot are near the top of the brain and on the inner (medial) wall between the hemispheres. Moving down the side of the brain, you pass the trunk, arm, hand, and fingers, then the face, lips, tongue, and throat.

The map is not to scale. Body parts with densely packed receptors, like the hands, lips, and face, get huge areas, while the trunk gets a small one. Draw a little person with each part sized by its share of cortex and you get the famous homunculus ("little man"), with giant hands and lips.

Neurosurgeon Wilder Penfield built this map in Montreal by stimulating the exposed cortex of awake patients during epilepsy surgery and asking what they felt. He and Edwin Boldrey published the first homunculus in the journal Brain in 1937, using data from 126 patients. That first drawing combined sensory and motor results in one figure. The real map is messier than the cartoon, and in 1950 Penfield himself warned against reading too much into the drawing's shapes and sizes. Still, the main idea holds: more receptors means more cortex and finer touch.

Whose left is it?

In a front view of a person, their right side is on your left. Then touch crosses to the opposite hemisphere. Students often flip one of these and get the wrong side, so say both steps out loud: "patient's right hand, so left hemisphere."

In the MicroSim below, click a spot on the body to see its S1 segment on the opposite hemisphere and its dermatome level.

Then click the lips: the readout names the trigeminal nerve, not a spinal level. Finally, press Quiz me and try to place five regions in a row on the first try.

docs.title: 6.8 Taste: Gustation
docs.text:
Gustation is the sense of taste. It detects chemicals dissolved in saliva. Taste receptor cells are grouped into taste buds, each a cluster of about 50 to 150 cells shaped a bit like a garlic bulb. Most sit in the bumps on your tongue, called papillae, but some are on the roof of the mouth and in the throat. A newborn has about 10,000 taste buds, and people may start to lose some after age 50.

Taste receptors respond to at least five basic taste qualities:

Taste What it usually signals Example Sweet Sugars, which mean energy Fruit Salty Sodium and other minerals Chips Sour Acids, which can mean spoiled or unripe food Lemon Bitter Many plant toxins Coffee, kale Umami Savory amino acids such as glutamate Parmesan, broth

Taste travels on three cranial nerves: the facial nerve (VII) for the front two-thirds of the tongue, the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) for the back third, and the vagus nerve (X) for the throat. All three reach the nucleus of the solitary tract in the medulla. Signals then pass through the thalamus to the gustatory cortex in the insula, tucked inside the lateral sulcus.

Different types of taste cells are scattered all over the tongue, so every part with taste buds can detect all five tastes. The famous "tongue map," with sweet at the tip and bitter at the back, is a myth. It grew out of a 1901 German study that found only small differences in sensitivity, which later textbook drawings turned into separate "zones."

docs.title: 6.9 Smell: Olfaction
docs.text:
Olfaction is the sense of smell. It detects chemicals called odorants that float in the air. The receptors are olfactory sensory neurons, real neurons that sit in a small patch of tissue high in the nasal cavity. Their axons pass through tiny holes in a thin bone called the cribriform plate and reach the olfactory bulb on the underside of the brain.

Each olfactory sensory neuron makes just one type of odorant receptor protein. Humans have about 400 working odorant receptor genes, while mice and dogs have roughly two to three times as many. Richard Axel and Linda Buck shared the 2004 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discovering these odorant receptors and how the olfactory system is organized.

How can a few hundred receptor types tell apart thousands of smells? Think of an alphabet. Neurons with the same receptor all send axons to the same knot in the olfactory bulb, called a glomerulus. Each odor activates a combination of glomeruli, the way a word combines letters, and hundreds of "letters" make an enormous number of "words."

Smell has two unusual features:

  • A shortcut to the cortex. Vision, hearing, touch, and taste pass through the thalamus before reaching the cortex. Smell does not. The olfactory bulb sends signals straight to the olfactory (piriform) cortex and has direct links to the amygdala, an emotion center. (Some smell information does reach the thalamus later, but only after the olfactory cortex.) This direct route may help explain why a smell can bring back a memory or feeling so suddenly.
  • Self-repair. Olfactory sensory neurons are constantly replaced from stem cells in the nasal lining, which is rare for neurons. This ability declines with age.

Now for the rest of Maya's puzzle. When you chew, aromas drift from the back of your throat up into your nose. This retronasal smell combines with taste to create flavor, and much of the "taste" of pizza is really smell. A cold blocks that channel, so food tastes bland even though the tongue works fine.

docs.title: 6.10 Pain: Nociception and the Pain Pathway
docs.text:
The International Association for the Study of Pain, a worldwide group of pain researchers, updated its definition in 2020 (Raja et al., Pain, 2020). It defines pain as an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience linked to actual or possible tissue damage, or resembling such an experience. That definition separates two things that are easy to mix up:

  • Nociception is the nervous system's detection of damaging or potentially damaging stimuli: the signal.
  • Pain is what the brain makes of that signal, shaped by attention, mood, and context.

You can have nociception without much pain, or pain with no new tissue damage at all, as you will see with phantom limbs.

docs.title: Nociceptors
docs.text:
The receptors for nociception are nociceptors: free nerve endings, bare branches of sensory axons with no capsule, found in skin, muscles, joints, and many organs. They respond to intense pressure, extreme temperatures, or chemicals from damaged tissue. Many use TRP ion channels. One TRP channel opens with dangerous heat and also with capsaicin, which is why chili peppers feel hot. Its discovery was part of David Julius's 2021 Nobel Prize work.

Nociceptors use two fiber types from Section 6.6. Thin myelinated Aδ fibers carry a fast, sharp "first pain." Unmyelinated C fibers carry a slower, aching "second pain." Stub your toe and you feel both: a sharp jolt, then a spreading ache.

A rare genetic condition shows why nociception matters. People with congenital insensitivity to pain, which can be caused by changes in a sodium channel (Nav1.7) that pain fibers rely on, feel touch but not pain, so they can be badly injured without noticing.

docs.title: The pain pathway
docs.text:
The main route for pain and temperature is the spinothalamic tract. It differs from the touch pathway in where it crosses.

  1. A nociceptor fiber enters the dorsal horn of the spinal cord and synapses there.
  2. The second neuron crosses to the opposite side within the spinal cord, close to the level where it entered.
  3. It climbs the spinal cord and brainstem to the thalamus.
  4. Thalamic neurons send the signal to S1, which tells you where it hurts and how much.
  5. Other branches reach the insula, the anterior cingulate cortex, and limbic areas involved in emotion, which help make pain feel unpleasant and motivating.

The flowchart summarizes the pain pathway, including the brain's own volume control, which comes next.

flowchart TD
    A["Nociceptor in skin<br/>(free nerve ending)"] -->|"Aδ fiber: fast, sharp<br/>C fiber: slow, aching"| B["Dorsal horn of spinal cord<br/>(first synapse)"]
    B -->|"crosses to opposite side<br/>inside the spinal cord"| C["Spinothalamic tract"]
    C --> D["Thalamus"]
    D --> E["Somatosensory cortex (S1):<br/>where and how strong"]
    D --> F["Insula and anterior cingulate:<br/>how unpleasant"]
    G["Periaqueductal gray (midbrain)"] -->|"descending control:<br/>endorphins, serotonin,<br/>norepinephrine"| B

The bottom arrow in the chart is the descending pain control system. Starting in a midbrain region called the periaqueductal gray, it sends signals down to the dorsal horn that can turn pain transmission down. It works through the body's own opioid chemicals, called endorphins, and through serotonin and norepinephrine from Chapter 3. It helps explain why soldiers and athletes sometimes feel little pain from serious injuries during intense action.

Because touch crosses in the medulla but pain crosses in the spinal cord, damage to one half of the spinal cord causes loss of fine touch and position sense on the same side below the injury, but loss of pain and temperature on the opposite side. This classic pattern is called Brown-Séquard syndrome.

Now we can partly answer Maya's paper cut question. Her fingertip is packed with sensory endings and owns a large territory on the somatosensory map, so her brain gets a detailed, sharply located signal, and she keeps using the finger. Her shin bruise is deeper damage in a region with a smaller cortical map, felt mostly as a dull C-fiber ache that is harder to pin down. Pain is not a simple measure of damage.

docs.title: 6.11 Gate Control Theory: Why Rubbing Helps
docs.text:
When Maya gets kicked in the shin, she rubs it, and it really does help a little. Why?

In 1965, Ronald Melzack and Patrick Wall proposed the gate control theory of pain in the journal Science. Their idea was that the dorsal horn of the spinal cord acts like a gate that controls how much pain information gets sent up to the brain. Here is a simple version of the circuit:

  • Pain fibers (C and Aδ) excite the projection neuron that sends pain signals to the brain. They also quiet a small inhibitory interneuron in the dorsal horn. Both effects open the gate.
  • Large touch fibers (Aβ) weakly excite the projection neuron but strongly excite the inhibitory interneuron, which releases inhibitory transmitters such as GABA to quiet the pain pathway. That helps close the gate.

So rubbing a bump fires many touch fibers, which boosts the inhibitory interneuron and partly closes the gate. Signals from the brain can also open or close the gate, which helps explain why distraction, stress, and expectations change how much something hurts. Some details of the 1965 model have since been revised, but its central idea, that pain signals are filtered in the spinal cord and by the brain, changed pain science.

docs.title: 6.12 Phantom Limbs: When the Map Outlives the Body
docs.text:
During the U.S. Civil War, physician Silas Weir Mitchell treated many soldiers who had lost limbs and still felt them, sometimes painfully. He is usually credited with coining the term "phantom limb" in 1871, though earlier doctors had described the experience.

Doctors now separate three related experiences after an amputation:

  • Phantom sensation: feeling that the missing limb is still there, sometimes with a position or tingling, but without pain.
  • Residual limb pain: pain in the remaining part of the limb, often from an irritated nerve end at the cut.
  • Phantom limb pain: pain that feels like it comes from the missing part, such as a clenched fist, burning, or cramping fingers.

Phantom limb pain is common. A 2020 review that combined many studies estimated that about 64% of people with amputations experience it. A larger 2026 review of 51 studies and about 13,000 people found a similar figure, about 61% (Zhang et al., BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders, 2026). Both reviews saw a wide range between studies.

How can a missing limb hurt? Part of the answer is the cortical map. After an arm amputation, the hand area of S1 loses its usual input, and on the homunculus the face area sits right next to it. In the 1990s, V. S. Ramachandran and colleagues reported that touching the face of some arm amputees made them feel touch on the missing hand, suggesting face inputs had spread into the silent hand territory. A 1995 brain-imaging study by Herta Flor and colleagues linked more phantom limb pain to more reorganization of the S1 map.

The story is not settled. A 2013 study found that people with more phantom pain actually kept more of their original hand map. Then, in 2025, a team scanned three adults before and for months to years after an arm amputation. The hand and lip maps in S1 stayed almost the same, with no sign of the lip area spreading into the hand area (Schone et al., Nature Neuroscience, 2025). Three people is a small study, but it challenges the classic "remapping" story. Today most scientists think phantom limb pain comes from several sources together: injured nerve endings in the residual limb, changes in the dorsal horn, and changes in the brain's representation of the missing limb.

The map is part of you

Phantom limbs show that what you feel is built by the brain's map of your body, not by the body part alone. Remove the hand, and the map can still produce a hand, sometimes a painful one.

docs.title: At the Bedside: Pain in a Hand That Is No Longer There
docs.text:
Meet the patient

Daniel is a 32-year-old Army veteran whose right arm was amputated below the elbow eight months ago after a vehicle crash during his service. The wound has healed well. But most nights he feels his missing right hand clenched into a tight fist, fingernails "digging into" his palm, with cramping and burning pain. It is worse when he is stressed or tired, and it ruins his sleep.

What the doctor checks: The doctor examines the residual limb for infection or skin breakdown and checks the prosthetic socket fit. She taps along the nerves of the residual limb to look for a neuroma, a tangled, oversensitive bundle of regrowing nerve fibers that can fire a shooting pain when touched. She asks Daniel to describe three things separately: pain in the residual limb, painless feelings in the missing hand, and pain that seems to come from the missing hand. When she lightly touches his face, he feels some touches on his "missing" fingers.

Where is the problem? (localization): There is no tissue where Daniel feels the pain, so the problem must lie along the nervous system that used to serve the hand: cut nerve endings in the residual limb, pain neurons in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord segments that served the hand (about C6 to T1), and the hand area of his left primary somatosensory cortex, because the right side of the body is mapped on the left hemisphere. Face touches felt in the phantom hand were long explained by the neighboring face area spreading into the hand's territory, though newer brain scans (Section 6.12) question how much the map really changes.

Diagnosis: Phantom limb pain, with phantom sensations.

Why it happens: The brain's map of the right hand loses its input but does not disappear. Injured nerve endings can fire on their own and send noisy signals, dorsal horn neurons can become more excitable, and the brain's hand map, which largely stays in place, reads those signals as coming from the missing hand. With no feedback that the hand has relaxed, the brain may produce a painful, stuck posture, and stress can open the spinal "gate" further.

Treatment today: No single treatment works for everyone. Care usually combines medicines for nerve pain, physical therapy, a well-fitted prosthesis, support for sleep and stress, and sometimes surgery for a painful neuroma.

Many clinics also try mirror therapy: a mirror between Daniel's arms shows his left hand's reflection where his right hand used to be, so when he opens his real left hand, his brain "sees" the missing hand open too. V. S. Ramachandran and colleagues introduced the idea in the 1990s, and a small 2007 trial in people with leg amputations reported less pain with a mirror than with a covered mirror or mental imagery. The overall evidence is mixed. A 2022 combined analysis of randomized trials found a short-term benefit, but a 2023 review of only placebo-controlled trials could not conclude that it works, mainly because the trials were small and of low quality. Mirror therapy is low-risk and helps some patients, but it is not a proven cure.

What's new in research: In targeted muscle reinnervation (TMR), surgeons give cut nerves a new "job" by connecting them to motor nerves of nearby muscles, which may make painful neuromas less likely. In a randomized trial of 28 people with chronic pain after major limb amputation, TMR reduced phantom limb pain more than standard neuroma surgery over a year of follow-up, although one simpler comparison just missed statistical significance (Dumanian and colleagues, Annals of Surgery, 2019). Larger studies are still needed.

Your turn: diagnose a variation

A patient with a below-knee amputation feels a sharp, electric jolt in his residual limb whenever his prosthetic socket presses one spot, and tapping that spot reproduces it. He also feels his missing foot, but it does not hurt. What is the likely source of his pain, and is it phantom limb pain?
