Answer: This sounds like residual limb pain from a neuroma at a cut nerve end. The pain is triggered at one spot and felt in the residual limb, so the main problem is the peripheral nerve, not the brain's map. His painless feeling of the missing foot is a phantom sensation, not phantom limb pain. Care would focus on the socket fit and the neuroma.

This is a fictional teaching case. It is not medical advice. If you or someone you know has symptoms like these, talk to a doctor.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
Myth: Humans have exactly five senses. Reality: You also sense balance (vestibular system), body position (proprioception), temperature, and pain, each with its own receptors and pathways.

Myth: The tongue has separate zones for sweet, salty, sour, and bitter. Reality: Every area of the tongue with taste buds can detect all five basic tastes. The "tongue map" came from textbook redrawings that exaggerated small differences in sensitivity found in a 1901 study.

Myth: How much something hurts tells you how much damage there is. Reality: Pain depends on which receptors fire, how densely packed they are, how the spinal "gate" filters the signal, and what the brain attends to. A paper cut can hurt more than a large bruise.

Myth: Phantom limb pain is imaginary or "all in the patient's head." Reality: Phantom limb pain is real, with causes in the nerves, spinal cord, and the brain's body map. Calling it imaginary can keep people from getting help.

docs.title: Brain Bee Practice
docs.text:
1. Which part of the cochlea responds best to high-pitched sounds, and what is this pitch map called?

The base of the cochlea (near the middle ear); the apex responds to low pitches. The pitch map is called tonotopy.

2. Name the two kinds of vestibular sense organs and what each detects.

The semicircular canals detect head rotation. The otolith organs (utricle and saccule) detect gravity, head tilt, and straight-line acceleration.

3. A patient has numbness on the back of the middle finger but nowhere else. Which spinal nerve root is most likely affected?

C7. The middle finger is the standard key test spot for the C7 dermatome.

4. Why does smell differ from all other senses in how it reaches the cortex?

Olfactory signals go from the olfactory bulb straight to the olfactory (piriform) cortex without first relaying through the thalamus. Other senses pass through the thalamus first.

5. According to gate control theory, why does rubbing an injury reduce pain?

Rubbing activates large Aβ touch fibers, which excite inhibitory interneurons in the dorsal horn. These quiet the projection neurons that carry pain to the brain, partly "closing the gate."

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
1. List the four classic skin mechanoreceptors and state whether each adapts slowly or rapidly.
  2. Name the three cranial nerves that carry taste and the brainstem nucleus where taste signals first arrive.
Answer
  1. Merkel disk (slow), Meissner corpuscle (rapid), Ruffini ending (slow), Pacinian corpuscle (rapid).
  2. Facial (VII), glossopharyngeal (IX), and vagus (X); they deliver taste to the nucleus of the solitary tract in the medulla.

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
1. Explain why a signal from a touch receptor feels like touch rather than sound, even though all action potentials look alike.
  2. Explain why food tastes bland when you have a stuffed-up nose.
Answer
  1. A signal's meaning depends on where its pathway ends. Touch receptors connect to pathways ending in the somatosensory cortex, so their signals are felt as touch (the "labeled line" idea).
  2. Much of flavor is retronasal smell, aromas rising from the mouth into the nose. A cold blocks that channel, so the brain gets taste but little smell.

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
1. A patient's left hand is touched with a cotton swab, and an fMRI scan (a brain scan that shows which areas are active) is recorded. Predict which hemisphere and which gyrus will show the strongest early response, and roughly where along that gyrus.
  2. A construction worker uses a loud jackhammer all day without ear protection. Predict what will happen to his hearing over the years and explain why it cannot be reversed.

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
1. After an injury that damaged the left half of the spinal cord at a mid-chest level, a patient cannot feel a pin prick on his right leg but can feel it on his left leg. He also cannot tell which way his left big toe is being moved. Use the crossing points of the two sensory pathways to explain this pattern.
  2. Compare the touch pathway and the smell pathway. Identify two ways their routes to the cortex differ and one way they are similar.

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
1. A website calls mirror therapy "a proven cure for phantom limb pain." Evaluate this claim using the evidence in this chapter, and rewrite it as one accurate sentence.
  2. Dermatome maps differ between textbooks. Should doctors still use dermatome key points in exams? Defend your answer with two reasons.

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
1. Design a safe experiment, using household materials, to test whether the fingertip can tell two nearby points apart better than the back of the hand. State your hypothesis, procedure, and how you will record results.
  2. Write a short fictional case of a patient whose symptoms point to damage in one part of the auditory or vestibular system. Include the key symptom, one exam finding, and the location a classmate should identify.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Every sense uses receptors that transduce energy into electrical signals, and the brain reads each signal by where its pathway ends. Humans have far more than five senses.
  • Cochlear hair cells turn sound into neural signals, with pitch mapped from high (base) to low (apex). Lost human hair cells do not grow back.
  • The vestibular system senses rotation (semicircular canals) and gravity and linear acceleration (otolith organs).
  • Skin mechanoreceptors detect touch, muscle spindles and tendon organs detect body position, and nociceptors detect damage, carried by Aδ and C fibers.
  • Touch crosses in the medulla and pain crosses in the spinal cord; both reach the opposite somatosensory cortex, a distorted body map called the homunculus. Dermatomes link skin areas to spinal levels, though maps vary.
  • Taste detects five basic qualities across the tongue. Smell uses combinations of hundreds of receptor types, skips the thalamus, and supplies most of flavor.
  • Pain is built by the brain. It can be turned down by the spinal gate and descending control, and it can even come from a missing limb.

You can map a body now!

You followed signals from ears, skin, tongue, and nose all the way to the cortex, and you can now turn a numb finger into a spinal level. In Chapter 7, we flip the direction: instead of signals coming in, you'll see how the brain sends commands out to move your muscles.

docs.title: Quiz: Hearing, Touch, Taste, Smell, and Pain
Quiz: Hearing, Touch, Taste, Smell, and Pain
docs.text: Test your understanding of Chapter 6. Choose the best answer, then click Show Answer to check.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
Which part of the cochlea vibrates most in response to a high-pitched sound of about 20,000 Hz?

  1. The apex, at the tip of the spiral
  2. The base, near the middle ear
  3. The middle of the spiral, for every sound
  4. The semicircular canals
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The basilar membrane is stiff and narrow at the base, so it resonates with high frequencies, while the floppy, wide apex responds to low frequencies around 20 Hz. The apex (A) is a common mix-up because it is the "end" of the spiral. The semicircular canals (D) sense head rotation, not sound.

Concept Tested: Cochlea and Hair Cells Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
Which sense sends its signals to the cortex without first relaying through the thalamus?

  1. Hearing
  2. Taste
  3. Touch
  4. Smell
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The olfactory bulb sends signals directly to the olfactory (piriform) cortex and has direct links to the amygdala. Taste (B) is a tempting choice because taste and smell work together, but taste signals pass through the thalamus before reaching the gustatory cortex in the insula.

Concept Tested: Olfaction Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
Which skin receptor sits deep in the skin, adapts rapidly, and is best at detecting vibration?

  1. Pacinian corpuscle
  2. Merkel disk
  3. Meissner corpuscle
  4. Ruffini ending
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Pacinian corpuscles are deep, rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors that respond to vibration, like a phone buzzing in your pocket. Meissner corpuscles (C) also adapt rapidly, but they sit near the surface and detect light touch and slipping. Merkel disks and Ruffini endings adapt slowly.

Concept Tested: Mechanoreceptor Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 4
docs.text:
On the sensory homunculus, the lips and hands are drawn much larger than the back. What is the best explanation?

  1. The lips and hands have more skin surface area than the back.
  2. The lips and hands are used for movement, so they share space with the motor cortex.
  3. The lips and hands have densely packed receptors, so they need more cortex to process their input.
  4. The lips and hands are closer to the brain, so their nerves are shorter.
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The size of each area on the somatosensory map reflects how densely the body part is supplied with receptors, not its physical size. The back actually has far more skin than the lips, so choice A is backward. Movement (B) is handled by a separate map in the motor cortex.

Concept Tested: Homunculus Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 5
docs.text:
Maya has a stuffed-up nose from a cold, and her favorite pizza tastes bland. Which explanation is most accurate?

  1. The cold virus has temporarily destroyed most of her taste buds.
  2. Aromas from the food cannot reach her olfactory neurons through the back of the nose, and much of flavor comes from smell.
  3. The sweet and salty zones at the tip of her tongue are swollen.
  4. Her facial nerve has stopped carrying taste signals from the front of her tongue.
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Flavor combines taste with retronasal smell, the aromas that rise from the mouth into the nose while chewing. A blocked nose stops those aromas from reaching the olfactory sensory neurons. Choice C relies on the tongue-map myth: every part of the tongue with taste buds can detect all five tastes.

Concept Tested: Gustation Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 6
docs.text:
According to gate control theory, why does rubbing a bumped elbow reduce the pain?

  1. Rubbing activates large touch fibers that excite inhibitory interneurons in the dorsal horn, which reduce pain signals sent to the brain.
  2. Rubbing releases endorphins directly from the skin onto the nociceptors.
  3. Rubbing physically pushes nociceptors away from the injured tissue.
  4. Rubbing speeds up C fibers so the pain signal finishes sooner.
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. In the model proposed by Melzack and Wall in 1965, large Aβ touch fibers strongly excite inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord's dorsal horn, which "close the gate" on projection neurons carrying pain. Endorphins (B) are real pain-reducing chemicals, but they act in the descending control system from the brain, not by release from rubbed skin.

Concept Tested: Gate Control Theory Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 7
docs.text:
After a fall, a patient reports numbness in a band of skin that wraps around her body at the level of her belly button. Which spinal level is most likely involved?

  1. C6
  2. T4
  3. L5
  4. T10
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The umbilicus (belly button) is the standard key test spot for the T10 dermatome. T4 (B) is the nipple line, higher on the chest, and is a common mix-up. C6 is the thumb and L5 is the top of the foot. Remember that dermatome borders vary somewhat between people and maps.

Concept Tested: Dermatome Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 8
docs.text:
During brain surgery, a doctor lightly touches the patient's left thumb while recording from the cortex. Where would the strongest early response most likely appear?

  1. The left postcentral gyrus, near the top of the brain
  2. The right precentral gyrus, in front of the central sulcus
  3. The right postcentral gyrus, partway down the side of the brain between the arm and face areas
  4. The right postcentral gyrus, on the inner (medial) wall between the hemispheres
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Touch crosses the midline, so the left thumb is mapped on the right primary somatosensory cortex in the postcentral gyrus. On the homunculus, the hand and thumb sit partway down the lateral surface, just above the face area. The medial wall (D) holds the leg and foot, and the precentral gyrus (B) is the primary motor cortex.

Concept Tested: Somatosensory Cortex Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 9
docs.text:
A patient has a knife wound that damaged only the right half of the spinal cord at chest level. Which finding below the injury fits the way the touch and pain pathways cross?

  1. Loss of pain and temperature on the left leg, with loss of fine touch and position sense on the right leg
  2. Loss of pain and temperature on the right leg, with loss of fine touch and position sense on the left leg
  3. Loss of all sensation on both legs
  4. Loss of all sensation on the right leg only
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Pain fibers cross to the opposite side within the spinal cord near where they enter, so a right-sided injury interrupts pain and temperature from the left leg. Touch and position fibers climb on the same side until they cross in the medulla, so their loss is on the right. Choice B reverses the two pathways, which is the most common error. This pattern is called Brown-Séquard syndrome.

Concept Tested: Pain Pathway Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: Question 10
docs.text:
A man whose right hand was amputated reports that when his right cheek is lightly touched, he also feels touch on his missing right thumb. Which explanation best fits the evidence in this chapter?

  1. Nerves from the face have physically grown down the arm into the residual limb.
  2. The thumb was never truly represented in the cortex, so any touch can be felt there.
  3. The man is imagining the sensation because he misses his hand.
  4. The face area of the somatosensory cortex sits next to the hand area, and face input may now activate the hand's territory.
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. On the homunculus, the face area borders the hand area. After amputation, the hand area loses its input, and research by V. S. Ramachandran and others suggested that face inputs can activate it, so face touch is felt in the phantom hand. Choice C reflects the myth that phantom sensations are imaginary. Scientists still debate this explanation: a 2025 study that scanned people before and after arm amputation found that the hand map stayed largely stable. How much remapping contributes to phantom limb pain, which likely has several sources, is also debated.

Concept Tested: Phantom Limb Pain Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: References: Hearing, Touch, Taste, Smell, and Pain
References: Hearing, Touch, Taste, Smell, and Pain
docs.text:
1. How Do We Hear? - National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIH) - A short, clearly illustrated walk from the eardrum to the auditory nerve, including how hair cells near the wide end of the cochlea (the base of the spiral, near the middle ear) detect high pitches. A good first read before Section 6.3.

  2. Noise-Induced Hearing Loss - National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIH) - Explains which sound levels are risky (85 dBA and above with long or repeated exposure), why human hair cells do not grow back, and how to protect your hearing. Directly useful for anyone who wears earbuds.

  3. Smell Disorders - National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIH) - Describes olfactory sensory neurons, the "second channel" from the throat to the nose, and why food tastes bland with a cold. It answers the pizza half of this chapter's hook.

  4. Taste Disorders - National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIH) - Covers the five basic tastes, how many taste buds people have, and how taste combines with smell to make flavor. It also notes that taste cell types are scattered across the tongue, which debunks the tongue map.

  5. 7.2 How Does Acoustic Information Enter the Brain? - OpenStax, Introduction to Behavioral Neuroscience (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) - A free college-level textbook section on the cochlea, inner and outer hair cells, tonotopy, and the first auditory relays in the brainstem. Read it when you want more depth than this chapter gives.

  6. 9.2 Somatosensation in the Central Nervous System - OpenStax, Introduction to Behavioral Neuroscience (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) - Covers dermatomes, gate control theory, the touch and pain pathways and where they cross, descending pain control, and the sensory homunculus. It is the best single open source for Sections 6.6 through 6.11.

  7. Dermatome (anatomy) - Wikipedia - Lists the standard key test points for each spinal level (for example, C6 thumb, T10 umbilicus, S1 outer heel) and notes that each person's exact dermatome pattern is unique. Useful for checking the levels used in the MicroSim.

  8. Cortical homunculus - Wikipedia - Explains the sensory and motor homunculi, their history with Wilder Penfield and colleagues, and newer research that refines the classic map. Good background for Section 6.7.

  9. The prevalence and risk factors for phantom limb pain in people with amputations: A systematic review and meta-analysis - Limakatso K, Bedwell GJ, Madden VJ, Parker R. PLOS ONE, 2020 (open access) - Pools many studies and estimates that about 64% of people with amputations have phantom limb pain, with large differences between studies. A good model of how researchers combine evidence.

  10. Effect of mirror therapy in the treatment of phantom limb pain in amputees: A systematic review of randomized placebo-controlled trials does not find any evidence of efficacy - Guémann M, Olié E, Raquin L, Courtet P, Risch N. European Journal of Pain, 2023 (open access) - A careful review showing that the best-controlled trials of mirror therapy are too small and too low in quality to prove it works. Read it alongside the Bedside case to see why scientists describe this treatment cautiously.

docs.title: Chapter 7: Movement: Muscles, Reflexes, and Motor Control
Chapter 7: Movement: Muscles, Reflexes, and Motor Control
Summary
docs.text: Every movement you make, from a blink to a penalty kick, ends with muscle fibers pulling. This chapter follows a movement from the bottom up: how a muscle fiber contracts, how motor units set force, and how spinal reflexes act without waiting for the brain. Then it climbs to the top: the motor cortex and corticospinal tract send commands, the basal ganglia act as a gas pedal and brake, and the cerebellum corrects errors and helps you learn skills. It ends at the bedside with Parkinson's disease, where losing dopamine neurons makes movement slow and hard to start.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
1. Skeletal Muscle Contraction
  2. Motor Unit
  3. Reflex Arc
  4. Stretch Reflex
  5. Primary Motor Cortex
  6. Corticospinal Tract
  7. Upper vs Lower Motor Neuron
  8. Basal Ganglia
  9. Substantia Nigra
  10. Direct and Indirect Pathways
  11. Cerebellar Coordination
  12. Motor Learning
  13. Parkinson's Disease
  14. Levodopa
  15. Deep Brain Stimulation

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 1: Neurons, Glia, and the Nervous System
  • Chapter 2: The Action Potential
  • Chapter 3: Synapses and Neurotransmitters
  • Chapter 4: A Tour of the Brain: Neuroanatomy

Let's get moving!

I'm a sea slug, so my top speed is not very impressive. But my slow crawl and your fastest sprint follow the same plan: decide, command, adjust, and pull. In this chapter you'll learn how a decision becomes motion, and why a doctor can often tell where a problem is just by watching someone move.

docs.title: 7.1 One Kick, Many Brain Areas
docs.text:
It's the last minute of a tied soccer game. Maya, a 16-year-old midfielder who is also studying for the Brain Bee, steps up to take a penalty kick. She glances at the goalkeeper, picks the bottom-left corner, takes three steps, plants her left foot, and swings her right leg through the ball. The whole thing takes about two seconds.

Those two seconds use a surprising amount of brain. Something had to decide to aim left. Something had to turn that plan into muscle commands, keep her balanced on one leg, and adjust the swing when the grass was slippery. At the very end, thousands of muscle fibers in her thigh had to pull at the right moment with the right force. Why does one kick need so many parts of the nervous system?

docs.title: An everyday analogy: a film crew
docs.text:
Before naming any brain structures, picture a film crew shooting a stunt. A director decides what the scene should be. A camera operator turns the plan into specific actions. A safety officer keeps a hand on the brake, letting only the planned action start. A stunt coordinator compares each take to the plan and calls out corrections. The stunt performers do the physical work. And some actions, like flinching when something flies at your face, happen so fast that nobody waits for the director.

Your motor system has all of these roles. The performers are your muscles, the instant flinches are reflexes run by the spinal cord, the camera operator is the primary motor cortex, the safety officer is the basal ganglia, and the stunt coordinator is the cerebellum. The director's job is spread across planning areas in the front of the brain.

The flowchart below shows how these pieces connect. Planning areas decide, the motor cortex sends commands down the spinal cord, and two "advisor" loops (basal ganglia and cerebellum) shape the command.

flowchart TD
    A["Planning areas in the frontal lobe<br/>(decide the goal)"] --> B["Primary motor cortex<br/>(sends the command)"]
    B --> C["Corticospinal tract<br/>(upper motor neurons)"]
    C --> D["Spinal cord<br/>(lower motor neurons and reflex circuits)"]
    D --> E["Skeletal muscle<br/>(contracts)"]
    E -->|"sensory feedback"| D
    E -->|"sensory feedback"| F["Cerebellum<br/>(compares plan to result)"]
    F -->|"corrections via thalamus"| B
    A --> G["Basal ganglia<br/>(gas pedal and brake)"]
    G -->|"via thalamus"| B

We'll start at the bottom of this chart, with the muscle, and work our way up.

docs.title: 7.2 How a Muscle Pulls
docs.text: Muscles can only pull. They never push. When you straighten your knee, muscles on the front of your thigh pull. When you bend it, muscles on the back pull. Muscles that pull in opposite directions around a joint work in pairs, so every movement is a tug-of-war that the nervous system referees.

docs.title: The analogy: hands on a rope
docs.text: Imagine a team hauling a boat to shore with a rope. Each person grabs the rope, pulls, lets go, reaches forward, and grabs again. No single grab moves the boat far, but thousands of quick grabs haul it in. Inside each muscle fiber, tiny protein "hands" do almost exactly this.

docs.title: The real steps
docs.text:
Skeletal muscle contraction is the process in which an electrical signal from a motor neuron makes a muscle fiber shorten and pull on a bone. A skeletal muscle is made of long cells called muscle fibers. Inside each fiber are two kinds of protein filaments. Actin filaments are the "rope." Myosin filaments have little heads that act as the "hands." Here is the sequence, building on Chapter 2 and Chapter 3:

  1. An action potential travels down a motor neuron to the neuromuscular junction, the synapse between a motor neuron and a muscle fiber.
  2. The axon terminal releases acetylcholine, which binds to receptors on the muscle fiber and depolarizes it.
  3. The muscle fiber fires its own action potential, which spreads across its membrane.
  4. That electrical wave makes an internal storage compartment, the sarcoplasmic reticulum, release calcium inside the fiber.
  5. Calcium moves a blocking protein (tropomyosin) aside, uncovering grip sites on actin.
  6. Myosin heads grab actin, bend, and pull it toward the center. This is the "power stroke."
  7. ATP, the cell's energy molecule, lets each myosin head let go and reset to grab again. When nerve signals stop, calcium is pumped back into storage and the muscle relaxes.

One surprise: ATP is needed to release the grip. After death, ATP runs out, myosin stays locked onto actin, and muscles stiffen. This is rigor mortis (OpenStax, Section 10.1).

The table below sums up who does what in the steps you just read.

Player Job in contraction Acetylcholine Carries the signal across the neuromuscular junction Calcium The "on switch" that uncovers grip sites on actin Actin The "rope" that gets pulled Myosin The "hands" that grab and pull ATP Lets myosin let go and reset

docs.title: 7.3 Motor Units: How the Brain Sets the Force
docs.text:
Maya uses the same thigh muscle to tap a short pass and to blast a shot at the goal. How does one muscle produce both?

Each muscle fiber gets input from just one motor neuron, but one motor neuron branches to many muscle fibers. A motor unit is one motor neuron plus all of the muscle fibers it controls. When that neuron fires, all of its fibers contract together. A muscle contains many motor units (OpenStax, Section 10.1).

The nervous system turns up force in two ways:

  1. Fire faster. A higher rate of action potentials releases calcium again before the fibers relax, so their pulls add up.
  2. Recruit more motor units to pull at the same time.

Recruitment follows the size principle. Small motor neurons, which control few fibers, are easier to excite, so they fire first. Large motor neurons, which control many fibers, need stronger input and join only when more force is needed (OpenStax, Section 10.2). That's how you can hold an egg gently, then lift a heavy backpack with the same hand.

Small motor units Large motor units Fibers per motor neuron Few Many Input needed to fire Small Large When recruited First, for light tasks Later, for more force Example in Maya's game A soft pass A full-power shot

Muscles don't decide on their own

A muscle fiber has no idea how hard it "should" pull. The nervous system decides, by choosing how many motor units to recruit and how fast each one fires.

docs.title: 7.4 Reflexes: Shortcuts in the Spinal Cord
docs.text:
Remember touching a hot pan in Chapter 2? Your hand jerked away before you felt the pain. That was a reflex, handled mostly by your spinal cord.

Think of an automatic door at a grocery store. It doesn't call the manager when you walk up. A sensor detects you, a small local circuit decides "open," and a motor slides the door. Reflexes work the same way: a fast local circuit handles a predictable situation, and the brain hears about it afterward.

docs.title: The reflex arc
docs.text:
A reflex arc is the nerve pathway that produces a reflex, an automatic and rapid response to a stimulus. It has five parts:

  1. A sensory receptor detects the stimulus.
  2. A sensory neuron carries the signal into the spinal cord.
  3. An integration center in the spinal cord links input to output, either by a direct synapse or through interneurons.
  4. A motor neuron carries the command out.
  5. An effector, usually a muscle, responds.

Because the signal makes a short trip, a reflex is faster than a movement that goes up to the brain and back.

docs.title: The stretch reflex and the knee-jerk test
docs.text:
The stretch reflex is the automatic contraction of a muscle when it is suddenly stretched. The sensors are muscle spindles, tiny stretch detectors inside the muscle. They are part of proprioception, your sense of body position, from Chapter 6.

When a doctor taps the tendon below your kneecap:

  1. The tap stretches the quadriceps, the big muscle on the front of the thigh.
  2. Muscle spindles in the quadriceps fire.
  3. Their sensory neurons enter the spinal cord and synapse directly on quadriceps motor neurons. With only one synapse, this is a monosynaptic reflex.
  4. The quadriceps contracts, and the lower leg kicks forward.
  5. A branch of the sensory neuron also excites an inhibitory interneuron that relaxes the hamstrings on the back of the thigh, so they don't fight the kick. This is reciprocal inhibition.

The knee-jerk (patellar) reflex tests spinal cord segments L2 to L4 (Wikipedia: Patellar reflex). A missing reflex can point to damage in that loop. A much-too-strong reflex can point to a problem above the loop, as Section 7.6 explains. In daily life, the stretch reflex helps keep a buckling knee from collapsing when Maya lands awkwardly.

Reflexes are not fully separate from the brain. Signals from the brain constantly turn them up or down. When that control is cut off, for example after a spinal cord injury, reflexes below the injury often become exaggerated (OpenStax, Section 10.2).

Reflexes can even learn. Eric Kandel studied a protective reflex in the sea slug Aplysia, which has only about 20,000 nerve cells: touch it, and it pulls in its gill. He showed that this reflex could be strengthened for days or weeks by changes at the synapse between sensory and motor neurons, work that earned a share of the 2000 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine (Nobel Prize press release, 2000). You'll see more in Chapter 9.

docs.title: 7.5 From Command to Muscle: The Motor Cortex and the Corticospinal Tract
docs.text: Reflexes are automatic. Maya's penalty kick is not. A voluntary movement starts in the brain.

docs.title: The primary motor cortex
docs.text:
The primary motor cortex is a strip of the frontal lobe, on the precentral gyrus just in front of the central sulcus, that sends the main commands for voluntary movement. It lies right in front of the somatosensory cortex from Chapter 6.

The motor cortex holds a body map, the motor homunculus. Neighboring body parts are controlled by neighboring strips of cortex, and parts that need fine control, like the hands, lips, and tongue, get far more cortex than the trunk or legs (OpenStax, Section 10.3). That's why you can thread a needle with your fingers but not your toes.

The real map is less tidy than the classic drawing of a little person stretched along the cortex. A 2023 brain-imaging study in humans found that the foot, hand, and mouth areas are not one continuous strip. They alternate with zones that don't control any single body part. Those zones are wired to a brain network involved in planning actions and in body control such as arousal, and they became active when people planned coordinated hand and foot movements or moved the trunk or face. The researchers named this system the somato-cognitive action network (SCAN): the motor strip mixes areas for fine control of one body part with areas for whole-body action planning (Gordon and colleagues, 2023, Nature). The homunculus is still a useful first picture, as long as you remember it is a simplification.

Control of the limbs is contralateral: each side of the motor cortex controls the opposite side of the body. Maya's right-legged kick came mainly from her left motor cortex.

docs.title: The corticospinal tract
docs.text: A command reaches motor neurons in the spinal cord through the corticospinal tract, a long bundle of axons running from the cortex (cortico) to the spinal cord (spinal). The axons start in the motor cortex and nearby areas, descend through the deep white matter and the brainstem, and most of them cross to the other side in the lowest part of the brainstem, the medulla. That crossing is why the left brain controls the right body. The crossed fibers form the lateral corticospinal tract, which mainly controls the limbs, especially fine finger movements. A smaller set controls trunk muscles (OpenStax, Section 10.3; Wikipedia: Corticospinal tract). In the spinal cord, these axons connect to motor neurons and to the reflex circuits you just learned about.

docs.title: 7.6 Upper vs. Lower Motor Neurons: A Doctor's Shortcut
docs.text:
The command chain uses two kinds of neurons, and doctors care a lot about which one is damaged.

  • An upper motor neuron starts in the brain, such as in the motor cortex, and carries commands down to the brainstem or spinal cord. It never touches a muscle.
  • A lower motor neuron has its cell body in the brainstem or the front (ventral) part of the spinal cord, and its axon runs out to a muscle. Every command, from the brain or from a reflex, must pass through lower motor neurons.

Upper motor neurons don't just say "go." They also hold spinal reflex circuits in check. So the two kinds of damage look different:

  • Lower motor neuron damage cuts the muscle's only connection. The muscle becomes weak and floppy, its reflexes shrink or vanish, it wastes away over time, and it may show small twitches called fasciculations (Wikipedia: Lower motor neuron lesion).
  • Upper motor neuron damage leaves the reflex loops working but unsupervised. The muscle is weak, reflexes are exaggerated, and muscles become stiff in a way that increases with fast stretching, called spasticity. Stroking the sole makes the big toe point up instead of curling down: the Babinski sign, which is abnormal after about 12 months of age (Wikipedia: Upper motor neuron lesion).

The table below organizes the comparison you just read.

Finding Upper motor neuron damage Lower motor neuron damage Muscle tone Increased (spastic) Decreased (floppy) Reflexes Exaggerated Reduced or absent Babinski sign Present (toe goes up) Absent Muscle wasting Little Marked Fasciculations No Yes Example Stroke in the motor cortex Injury to a nerve

Some diseases damage both. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), covered in Chapter 13, attacks upper and lower motor neurons, so patients can show both sets of signs.

A quick way to remember

Think "Upper = Up." With upper motor neuron damage, tone goes up, reflexes go up, and the big toe goes up.

docs.title: 7.7 The Basal Ganglia: Gas Pedal and Brake
docs.text: We have a commander and a delivery route. But how does the brain choose which movement to send, and keep the others from slipping out? When Maya kicks, she must swing her right leg and hold back every competing movement.

docs.title: The analogy: a car with the parking brake on
docs.text:
Picture a car parked on a hill with the parking brake pulled tight. To drive, you release the brake for the movement you want and keep it on for everything else. Your brain works this way. At rest, a set of nuclei holds a steady brake on movement. To move, the brain releases that brake for one chosen action. Releasing a brake is a "double negative": you create movement by stopping something that was stopping you.

This part has a lot of names

The basal ganglia circuit is famous for being confusing, so it's fine if it takes two reads. Keep the car in mind: one pathway releases the brake, one presses it, and dopamine tips the balance.

docs.title: Meet the players
docs.text:
The basal ganglia are a group of nuclei deep in the brain that help select wanted movements, suppress unwanted ones, and form habits. They work in a loop with the cortex and thalamus. The main motor parts are:

  • The striatum (the caudate and putamen), the input station. It receives excitatory input from the cortex, and its output neurons are inhibitory (they use GABA).
  • The globus pallidus, with an external part (GPe) and an internal part (GPi).
  • The subthalamic nucleus (STN), the only basal ganglia nucleus whose output is excitatory (glutamate).
  • The substantia nigra, a midbrain nucleus named "black substance" for its dark color. Its pars compacta (SNc) contains dopamine-making neurons that send dopamine to the striatum. Its pars reticulata (SNr) works with the GPi as an output station.

GPi and SNr are the brake. Their inhibitory neurons fire at a high rate all the time, holding back the thalamus, which would otherwise excite the motor cortex (Wikipedia: Basal ganglia).

docs.title: The direct and indirect pathways
docs.text:
From the striatum, signals reach the brake by two routes, called the direct and indirect pathways.

Direct pathway ("GO"): Cortex excites striatal neurons that carry D1 dopamine receptors. These neurons inhibit GPi/SNr. Inhibiting the brake releases the thalamus, which excites the motor cortex, and the chosen movement goes ahead.

Indirect pathway ("NO-GO"): Cortex excites a different set of striatal neurons that carry D2 receptors. These inhibit GPe. Because GPe normally inhibits the STN, quieting GPe releases the STN. The STN then excites GPi/SNr, pressing the brake harder, and competing movements are held back.

The table lists every connection in this classic model and its sign. If you keep track of the signs, the rest of the circuit makes sense.

Connection Transmitter Effect Cortex → striatum Glutamate Excites (+) Striatum (D1) → GPi/SNr GABA Inhibits (−) Striatum (D2) → GPe GABA Inhibits (−) GPe → STN GABA Inhibits (−) STN → GPi/SNr Glutamate Excites (+) GPi/SNr → thalamus GABA Inhibits (−) Thalamus → cortex Glutamate Excites (+) SNc → striatal D1 neurons Dopamine Excites (+) SNc → striatal D2 neurons Dopamine Inhibits (−)

docs.title: Dopamine tips the balance
docs.text:
Look at the last two rows. Dopamine excites the D1 (GO) neurons and inhibits the D2 (NO-GO) neurons (Wikipedia: Basal ganglia; OpenStax, Section 10.3). Both effects push the same way: more dopamine means a weaker brake and more movement.

This two-pathway picture is the classic model of the basal ganglia, laid out in the late 1980s, including in a widely cited 1989 review by Albin, Young, and Penney (Trends in Neurosciences, 1989). It explains movement disorders as two opposite kinds of imbalance:

  • Hypokinetic disorders ("too little movement") happen when the brake is too strong. Parkinson's disease is the main example.
  • Hyperkinetic disorders ("too much movement") happen when the brake is too weak. Examples include the dance-like movements called chorea in Huntington's disease, in which striatal neurons break down and die (NINDS: Huntington's Disease), and the extra movements (dyskinesia) some people with Parkinson's develop after years of dopamine-boosting medicine.

A useful model, not the whole brain

The two-pathway model is a simplified map. Real basal ganglia have extra routes, such as a "hyperdirect" pathway from cortex straight to the STN, and scientists still debate how cleanly the two pathways separate. In mice, for example, neurons of both pathways become active together just as a movement starts, which challenges the simple idea that one pathway only means "go" and the other only means "stop" (Cui and colleagues, 2013).

Now try the circuit yourself. Every label in the simulation (striatum, GPe, GPi/SNr, STN, SNc, thalamus, direct and indirect pathways) was defined above.

docs.title: Diagram: Basal Ganglia Gas and Brake
docs.text:
Open the Basal Ganglia Gas and Brake fullscreen

MicroSim specification: Basal Ganglia Gas and Brake

Type: microsim sim-id: ch07-basal-ganglia Library: p5.js Status: Implemented Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: explain Learning Objective: The learner will explain how lowering or raising dopamine shifts the balance between the direct and indirect pathways, and predict whether movement output will be too little, normal, or too much.

Canvas: width-responsive; 550 px drawing area plus 50 px control area (iframe 602 px).

Controls: dopamine slider, 0% to 200% of normal (step 10%, default 100%); Reset button.

Behavior: nodes and connection signs match the table in Section 7.7 (arrows with + are excitatory, flat bars with − are inhibitory, dashed lines are dopamine). Line thickness scales with the sending node's activity. Illustrative model with dopamine d (1 = normal): D1 = 0.5 + 0.35(d − 1); D2 = 0.5 − 0.35(d − 1); GPe = 1 − D2; STN = 1 − GPe; GPi/SNr = 0.5 − 0.5(D1 − 0.5) + 0.5(STN − 0.5); movement output = thalamus = 1 − GPi/SNr. The meter reads "Too little" when output < 0.35 (dopamine 50% or less), "Normal" from 0.35 to 0.65, and "Too much" when output > 0.65 (dopamine 150% or more). The sim is labeled as a simplified model with illustrative values.

Start at 100% dopamine, where every pathway is medium thickness and the meter reads "Normal." Before you touch the slider, predict: if dopamine drops, which pathway gets thinner and which gets thicker? Then drag the slider to 30%. The direct pathway fades, the indirect pathway thickens, the GPi/SNr brake strengthens, the thalamus goes quiet, and the meter slides into "Too little." That is the basal ganglia in Parkinson's disease.

Now drag the slider to 170%. The direct pathway dominates, the brake weakens, and the meter moves into "Too much," like the extra movements that can appear when dopamine signaling is pushed too high. Find the settings where the meter changes zones, and notice that "normal" is a balance, not a maximum.

docs.title: 7.8 The Cerebellum: The Coordination Coach
docs.text:
The basal ganglia help choose which movement happens. The cerebellum helps make it smooth and accurate.

A navigation app constantly compares where you are with where you should be, and recalculates when you drift. The cerebellum, the wrinkled structure under the back of the brain, does this for movement.

Cerebellar coordination is the cerebellum's job of timing and smoothing movements by comparing the intended movement with the actual one and sending corrections. It receives a copy of the plan from the cortex (through the brainstem) and feedback about the actual movement, mostly from muscle spindles and other proprioceptors. When the two don't match, it sends corrections through the thalamus to the motor cortex (OpenStax, Section 10.3). If Maya's planted foot slips, her cerebellum helps adjust the swing.

The cerebellum is small but packed. It is only about 10% of the brain's mass, yet it holds about 69 billion of the brain's roughly 86 billion neurons, about four out of five (Herculano-Houzel, 2009).

Cerebellar damage doesn't paralyze anyone. Instead, movements become clumsy and poorly timed, a condition called ataxia. Signs include dysmetria (overshooting or undershooting a target), an intention tremor that gets worse as the hand nears a target, and a wide, unsteady walk. Damage to one side of the cerebellum affects the same side of the body (Wikipedia: Cerebellum), unlike the motor cortex. Doctors use this difference to locate a problem.

Question Basal ganglia Cerebellum Main job Select and start wanted movements; suppress others Coordinate, time, and correct movements Analogy Gas pedal and brake Navigation app that recalculates Damage causes Too little movement (Parkinson's) or too much (chorea) Clumsy, inaccurate movement (ataxia) Typical tremor At rest (in Parkinson's disease) During movement, worse near the target

docs.title: 7.9 Motor Learning: Practice Makes Automatic
docs.text:
The first time Maya tried to curve a ball around a wall of defenders, she had to think about every detail. Now she does it without thinking. What changed?

Motor learning is the process by which practice turns a clumsy, effortful movement into a smooth, accurate, and largely automatic skill. It leans on two structures you just met (OpenStax, Section 10.3):

  • The cerebellum uses the errors from each attempt to fine-tune the next. Slow, careful practice gives it time to notice and fix errors.
  • The basal ganglia, working with the cortex, help "package" a sequence of movements into a habit that runs with little conscious attention.

As a skill moves from early (slow, many errors) to late (fast, automatic), attention is freed for the game, like watching the goalkeeper instead of your own foot. OpenStax also notes that imagined practice, rehearsing a movement in your mind, can improve performance because it uses some of the same circuits. It adds to real practice but doesn't replace it.

docs.title: 7.10 When the Brake Is Stuck: Parkinson's Disease, Levodopa, and DBS
docs.text: Now we can put the chapter together to understand one of the most common movement disorders.

docs.title: What goes wrong
docs.text:
Parkinson's disease is a nervous system disorder that affects movement and gets worse over time. It happens mainly because dopamine-making neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta weaken and die. By the time symptoms appear, most people have lost about 60 to 80% or more of these cells (NINDS: Parkinson's Disease). Damaged cells in most people with Parkinson's contain Lewy bodies, clumps of a protein called alpha-synuclein.

The average age when symptoms start is in the early to mid-60s. In most people the cause is unknown, and both genes and environment are thought to contribute (NINDS). Because the risk rises with age, the number of people living with Parkinson's is growing as populations get older. A 2025 study based on Global Burden of Disease data projected that the number of people with Parkinson's worldwide will more than double between 2021 and 2050, to about 25 million, with population aging as the main driver (Su and colleagues, 2025, BMJ).

Your simulation shows why losing dopamine slows movement. The direct pathway weakens, the indirect pathway strengthens, and both changes tighten the brake on the thalamus. NINDS lists four common motor signs:

  • Tremor most obvious when the hand is at rest, often a "pill-rolling" rub of thumb and finger. Some people never develop a tremor.
  • Rigidity, stiffness a doctor feels when moving the person's arm, sometimes with small catches ("cogwheel" rigidity).
  • Bradykinesia, slowness of movement, including fewer facial expressions.
  • Postural instability, balance problems that raise the risk of falls, often with a stooped, shuffling walk.

Many people also have sleep problems, constipation, or loss of smell before movement symptoms begin (NIA: Parkinson's Disease).

docs.title: Levodopa: refilling the tank
docs.text:
Why not just give dopamine? Because dopamine in the blood can't easily cross the blood-brain barrier, the tightly sealed lining of the brain's blood vessels. Its precursor can. Levodopa (L-dopa) is a medicine that the brain converts into dopamine, and it is the main treatment for Parkinson's disease. Levodopa is almost always combined with carbidopa, which blocks levodopa's breakdown in the rest of the body so more reaches the brain (NINDS).

The story connects back to Ply. Arvid Carlsson showed that dopamine is a neurotransmitter that matters for movement: animals given a drug that depleted their transmitter stores stopped moving on their own, and recovered after receiving L-dopa. His work led to the realization that Parkinson's is caused by too little dopamine and could be treated with L-dopa. Carlsson shared the 2000 Nobel Prize with Paul Greengard and with Eric Kandel, the Aplysia scientist (Nobel Prize press release, 2000).

Levodopa eases symptoms, but it does not replace lost neurons or stop the disease from progressing. After years of treatment, its effect may wear off between doses ("off" periods), and some people develop dyskinesia, extra twisting or writhing movements (NINDS). In the simulation, that is like overshooting from "Too little" into "Too much."

docs.title: Deep brain stimulation
docs.text:
Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is a treatment in which a neurosurgeon implants a thin wire electrode deep in the brain, connected to a battery-powered pulse generator under the skin of the chest, like a heart pacemaker. The electrical pulses change abnormal activity in the circuit. DBS does not cure Parkinson's and does not help every symptom (NINDS).

The targets come straight from the basal ganglia circuit: the subthalamic nucleus (STN) or the internal globus pallidus (GPi). The FDA approved DBS at these targets for Parkinson's disease in 2002, after approving DBS in the thalamus for essential tremor and Parkinson's tremor in 1997 (NINDS: DBS history). A newer version, adaptive DBS, senses brain signals and adjusts stimulation automatically. The FDA approved the first adaptive DBS system for Parkinson's disease in February 2025 (Medtronic press release, February 24, 2025).

docs.title: At the Bedside: The Slowing Teacher
docs.text:
Meet the patient

Mr. Alvarez is a 62-year-old retired history teacher. For about a year, his right hand has shaken while it rests in his lap. The shaking fades when he reaches for his coffee. His wife says he walks more slowly, with short shuffling steps, and his right arm no longer swings. His handwriting has become small and cramped, and his voice is softer. Looking back, he lost much of his sense of smell several years ago, and his wife says he sometimes seems to act out his dreams.

What the doctor checks: The neurologist watches him sit, stand, and walk. His right hand shows a pill-rolling tremor at rest that lessens when he moves on purpose. Moving his right wrist, she feels stiffness with small catches (cogwheel rigidity). When he taps finger and thumb quickly, the taps get smaller and slower (bradykinesia). He takes several small steps to turn. Just as important, his strength is normal, his reflexes are normal, there is no Babinski sign, and his finger-to-nose test is accurate.

Where is the problem? (localization): Normal strength, normal reflexes, and no Babinski sign argue against upper or lower motor neuron damage. An accurate finger-to-nose test with no intention tremor argues against the cerebellum. A resting tremor, rigidity, and slowness that began on one side point to the basal ganglia, specifically to lost dopamine input from the substantia nigra pars compacta. The early loss of smell and dream-enacting behavior fit the same disease.

Diagnosis: Parkinson's disease. No single test proves it. Doctors diagnose it mainly from the history and exam. Blood tests and MRI help rule out other conditions, and a dopamine transporter (DaT) scan can help, though it can't tell Parkinson's apart from some related disorders (NINDS).

Why it happens: Most of his dopamine neurons in the SNc have been lost. With less dopamine in the striatum, the direct (GO) pathway weakens and the indirect (NO-GO) pathway strengthens. The GPi/SNr brake on the thalamus becomes too strong, so the motor cortex gets too little "go" signal: the "Too little" zone in the simulation.

Treatment today: Standard care starts with medicine that raises dopamine signaling, most often carbidopa-levodopa. Other options include dopamine agonists, which act like dopamine, and MAO-B inhibitors, which slow dopamine breakdown. Exercise, physical therapy, and speech therapy help with movement, balance, and voice. If medicines later stop working smoothly, his neurologist may discuss DBS of the STN or GPi (NINDS). Newer options, as of 2026, include a small pump that delivers a levodopa-based medicine under the skin around the clock, which the FDA approved in October 2024 for advanced Parkinson's with "off" periods (AbbVie, 2024). In September 2026 the FDA approved tavapadon, the first approved dopamine agonist designed to act selectively on D1-type receptors (D1 and D5), the kind found on direct (GO) pathway neurons (NeurologyLive, 2026). Like levodopa, these treat symptoms. None has been shown to slow the disease.

What's new in research: The alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay (SAA) is a lab test that checks spinal fluid for misfolded alpha-synuclein "seeds" that can make normal alpha-synuclein misfold and clump. In a study of 1,123 people, it was positive in 87.7% of people with Parkinson's disease and negative in 96.3% of healthy controls, and it was also positive in many people who had early warning signs like loss of smell or dream-enacting behavior but no movement symptoms yet (Siderowf et al., 2023, Lancet Neurology). In 2024 the FDA issued a Letter of Support encouraging its use in research and clinical trials (Michael J. Fox Foundation, 2024). That is not FDA approval of a diagnostic test.

A version is offered by a commercial lab, and NINDS notes that such tests can help diagnose Parkinson's but cannot tell it apart from some similar disorders, such as multiple system atrophy and Lewy body dementia (NINDS). Researchers hope it will help find people early enough to test treatments that might slow the disease.

Your turn: diagnose a variation

Eight years later, Mr. Alvarez still takes carbidopa-levodopa. About an hour after each dose, he develops twisting, writhing movements of his arms and trunk that he can't control. Before his next dose, he becomes slow and stiff again. What is happening, and how does the basal ganglia model explain it?

Answer: These are levodopa-induced dyskinesias plus "off" periods. At the dose's peak, dopamine signaling overshoots: the direct pathway dominates, the indirect pathway is suppressed, and the GPi/SNr brake becomes too weak, so unwanted movements slip through (the "Too much" zone). As the dose wears off, he slides back into "Too little." Swings like this are one reason doctors may adjust medicines or consider DBS.

This is a fictional teaching case. It is not medical advice. If you or someone you know has symptoms like these, talk to a doctor.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
Myth: Muscles decide for themselves how hard to contract. Reality: A muscle fiber contracts only when its motor neuron fires. The nervous system sets force by choosing how many motor units to recruit and how fast each one fires.

Myth: Parkinson's disease is just shaking. Reality: Slowness (bradykinesia) and rigidity are core features, and some people with Parkinson's never develop a tremor. Many also have non-movement symptoms, like loss of smell or sleep problems, sometimes years before movement symptoms.

Myth: Every reflex goes up to the brain before you react. Reality: Reflexes like the knee-jerk are handled by spinal cord circuits. The brain finds out afterward, though it does adjust how strong reflexes are.

Myth: Levodopa is dopamine, and it cures Parkinson's. Reality: Levodopa is the raw material the brain turns into dopamine, used because dopamine can't easily cross the blood-brain barrier. It eases symptoms but doesn't restore lost neurons or stop progression.

docs.title: Brain Bee Practice
docs.text:
1. What is a motor unit?

A single motor neuron together with all of the muscle fibers it controls. When the neuron fires, all of those fibers contract together.

2. Name the parts of a reflex arc in order.

Sensory receptor, sensory neuron, integration center in the spinal cord, motor neuron, and effector (usually a muscle).

3. A patient has weakness in one arm, exaggerated reflexes, and an upgoing big toe when the sole is stroked. Upper or lower motor neuron damage?

Upper motor neuron damage. Brisk reflexes, spasticity, and a Babinski sign mean the lower motor neurons and reflex loops work but have lost control from above.

4. Which neurons die in Parkinson's disease, and which neurotransmitter do they make?

Neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, in the midbrain. They make dopamine and send it to the striatum.

5. Damage to the right side of the cerebellum causes clumsiness on which side of the body?

The right side. Cerebellar damage affects the same side of the body, unlike motor cortex damage, which affects the opposite side.

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
1. List the two ways the nervous system increases the force of a muscle contraction.
  2. Name the two pathways from the striatum to GPi/SNr, and say which is "GO" and which is "NO-GO."
Answer
  1. Firing motor neurons faster, and recruiting more motor units.
  2. The direct pathway is "GO"; the indirect pathway is "NO-GO."

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
1. Explain why ATP is needed for a muscle to relax, not just to contract.
  2. Explain why dopamine, which excites D1 neurons but inhibits D2 neurons, pushes both pathways toward more movement.
Answer
  1. ATP lets each myosin head release actin and reset. Without ATP, myosin stays locked on, which is why muscles stiffen after death (rigor mortis).
  2. Exciting the direct pathway inhibits the GPi/SNr brake. Inhibiting the indirect pathway weakens a route that would press the brake harder. Both weaken the brake and favor movement.

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
1. A doctor taps a patient's patellar tendon and gets no response on either side. Using the reflex arc, list three different places where the problem could be.
  2. In the Basal Ganglia Gas and Brake simulation, find the lowest dopamine setting that still reads "Normal." Describe how the direct pathway, indirect pathway, and GPi/SNr compare with 100%.

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
1. Compare a patient with a stroke in the left motor cortex to a patient with damage to the left side of the cerebellum. Which side of the body is affected in each, and how would the movement problems look different?
  2. Huntington's disease damages striatal neurons. The classic model proposes that chorea comes from early loss of the striatal neurons that form the indirect pathway. Use the circuit signs to explain why losing a NO-GO pathway would cause extra movement.

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
1. A website claims, "Parkinson's is caused by low dopamine, so the best treatment is the highest possible dose of levodopa." Evaluate this claim using the direct and indirect pathways and dyskinesia.
  2. The alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay has an FDA Letter of Support for clinical trials but is not an FDA-approved diagnostic. Weigh the benefits and risks of using it to tell people without symptoms that they may develop Parkinson's disease.

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
1. Design a classroom demonstration (no animals or medicines) that shows the difference between small and large motor units, or between a reflex and a voluntary movement. Describe materials, steps, and what students should observe.
  2. Write a short fictional case of a patient with a cerebellar problem. Include at least three findings and a localization paragraph explaining why the cerebellum, not the basal ganglia or motor neurons, is the likely site.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Muscles only pull. A motor neuron's signal releases calcium in a muscle fiber, letting myosin pull on actin; ATP lets myosin let go and reset.
  • A motor unit is one motor neuron and all its fibers. The brain sets force by recruiting small motor units first, then larger ones, and by firing them faster.
  • Reflex arcs, like the monosynaptic stretch reflex tested by the knee-jerk, run through the spinal cord, though the brain sets their strength.
  • The primary motor cortex sends commands down the corticospinal tract, which mostly crosses in the medulla, so each side of the brain controls the opposite side of the body.
  • Upper motor neuron damage causes spasticity, brisk reflexes, and a Babinski sign. Lower motor neuron damage causes floppy weakness, weak reflexes, wasting, and fasciculations.
  • The basal ganglia act as a gas pedal and brake. Dopamine from the substantia nigra strengthens the direct (GO) pathway and weakens the indirect (NO-GO) pathway. The cerebellum corrects errors, and both help motor learning.
  • In Parkinson's disease, lost dopamine neurons make the brake too strong. Levodopa, other medicines, exercise, and DBS of the STN or GPi treat symptoms but don't cure the disease.

You followed a movement from neuron to bedside!

You can now trace a kick from a decision in the cortex to myosin pulling on actin, and explain why a missing brain chemical can freeze a person in place. Next, in Chapter 8, we'll see how these circuits are built, and why the teenage brain is still under construction.

docs.title: Quiz: Movement: Muscles, Reflexes, and Motor Control
Quiz: Movement: Muscles, Reflexes, and Motor Control
docs.text: Test your understanding of Chapter 7. Choose the best answer, then click Show Answer to check.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
What is a motor unit?

  1. A whole muscle together with all of the nerves that reach it
  2. One motor neuron together with all of the muscle fibers it controls
  3. A single muscle fiber together with its actin and myosin filaments
  4. A sensory neuron and a motor neuron that form a reflex loop
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A motor unit is one motor neuron plus every muscle fiber it connects to; when the neuron fires, all of those fibers contract together. Option A describes a whole muscle, which contains many motor units, not one.

Concept Tested: Motor Unit Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
Where is the primary motor cortex?

  1. On the postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe
  2. In the occipital lobe at the back of the brain
  3. In the cerebellum, under the back of the brain
  4. On the precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The primary motor cortex is a strip of the frontal lobe on the precentral gyrus, just in front of the central sulcus. The postcentral gyrus (option A) sits just behind the central sulcus and holds the somatosensory cortex, which is why the two are easy to mix up.

Concept Tested: Primary Motor Cortex Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
In Parkinson's disease, which neurons are mainly lost?

  1. Dopamine-making neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta
  2. Acetylcholine-releasing motor neurons in the spinal cord
  3. Neurons of the cerebellum that correct movement errors
  4. Upper motor neurons in the primary motor cortex
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Parkinson's disease mainly results from the loss of dopamine-making neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, which send dopamine to the striatum. Option B describes lower motor neurons, whose loss causes floppy weakness and wasting, not the slowness and rigidity of Parkinson's.

Concept Tested: Substantia Nigra Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 4
docs.text:
During skeletal muscle contraction, what is the main job of calcium released inside the muscle fiber?

  1. It supplies the energy that powers each myosin power stroke
  2. It carries the nerve signal across the neuromuscular junction
  3. It moves tropomyosin aside so myosin can grab actin
  4. It makes each myosin head let go of actin and reset
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Calcium acts as the "on switch": it shifts the blocking protein tropomyosin and uncovers grip sites on actin so myosin heads can bind and pull. Options A and D describe jobs of ATP, and option B describes acetylcholine.

Concept Tested: Skeletal Muscle Contraction Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 5
docs.text:
Why does activity in the direct pathway of the basal ganglia lead to more movement?

  1. It sends commands straight to the muscles through the spinal cord
  2. It inhibits GPi/SNr, which releases the thalamus from inhibition
  3. It excites the subthalamic nucleus, which then excites the cortex
  4. It releases extra dopamine directly onto the motor cortex
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. GPi/SNr normally act as a brake on the thalamus. The direct pathway inhibits that brake, so the thalamus is released and can excite the motor cortex. This "double negative" is called disinhibition. Option C is wrong because exciting the subthalamic nucleus is part of the indirect pathway, which presses the brake harder.

Concept Tested: Direct and Indirect Pathways Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 6
docs.text:
Why is the knee-jerk (patellar) reflex so fast?

  1. The signal crosses only one synapse in the spinal cord and never has to reach the brain first
  2. The signal travels to the motor cortex at nearly the speed of light
  3. The quadriceps senses the tap and contracts without any nerves involved
  4. The cerebellum predicts the tap and starts the kick ahead of time
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The stretch reflex is monosynaptic: muscle spindle sensory neurons synapse directly on quadriceps motor neurons in the spinal cord, so the loop is very short. Option C reflects the misconception that muscles act on their own; the muscle contracts only because its motor neuron fires.

Concept Tested: Stretch Reflex Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 7
docs.text:
A 45-year-old man injured a nerve in his right leg. His right thigh muscle is now weak, floppy, and visibly thinner, with small twitches under the skin. His right knee-jerk reflex is absent, and his toes curl down when the sole is stroked. Where is the damage most likely?

  1. Upper motor neurons in the left primary motor cortex
  2. The right side of the cerebellum
  3. The basal ganglia on the left side
  4. Lower motor neurons supplying the right thigh
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Floppy weakness, muscle wasting, fasciculations, an absent reflex, and no Babinski sign are classic lower motor neuron signs. Damage in the left motor cortex (option A) would also weaken the right leg, but it would cause spasticity, brisk reflexes, and an upgoing toe instead.

Concept Tested: Upper vs Lower Motor Neuron Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 8
docs.text:
A woman with early Parkinson's disease begins taking carbidopa-levodopa, and her movements improve. According to the basal ganglia model in this chapter, what most likely changed in her brain?

  1. GPi/SNr became more active, putting a stronger brake on the thalamus
  2. Dopamine from the medicine crossed into the brain directly from the blood
  3. Her brain made more dopamine, strengthening the direct pathway and weakening the indirect pathway
  4. Her lost substantia nigra neurons grew back and began firing again
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The brain converts levodopa into dopamine, which excites the direct (GO) pathway and inhibits the indirect (NO-GO) pathway, weakening the brake on the thalamus. Option B is wrong because dopamine itself can't easily cross the blood-brain barrier, which is why levodopa is used. Option D is wrong because levodopa does not replace lost neurons.

Concept Tested: Levodopa Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 9
docs.text:
A 58-year-old woman has trouble buttoning her shirt with her left hand. When she reaches for her nose, her left hand overshoots and shakes more as it gets close. She walks with a wide, unsteady gait. Her strength and reflexes are normal. Where is the problem most likely?

  1. The left side of the cerebellum
  2. The right side of the cerebellum
  3. The basal ganglia on the left side
  4. The right primary motor cortex
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Overshooting (dysmetria), a tremor that worsens near the target (intention tremor), and a wide unsteady gait point to the cerebellum, and cerebellar damage affects the same side of the body. Option B is the common mistake of applying the motor cortex's opposite-side rule to the cerebellum.

Concept Tested: Cerebellar Coordination Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: Question 10
docs.text:
For Parkinson's disease, deep brain stimulation electrodes are placed in the subthalamic nucleus (STN) or the internal globus pallidus (GPi). Which reasoning best explains why these targets make sense?

  1. The STN and GPi are where dopamine is made, so stimulating them refills dopamine
  2. In the classic model, the STN and GPi help create the too-strong brake on the thalamus, so changing their activity can ease it
  3. The STN and GPi are in the spinal cord, where they connect directly to leg muscles
  4. The STN and GPi are where the corticospinal tract crosses to the other side
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. With too little dopamine, the indirect pathway releases the STN, which excites GPi, and the GPi/SNr brake on the thalamus becomes too strong. DBS at these nodes changes that abnormal activity. Option A is wrong because dopamine is made in the substantia nigra pars compacta, not the STN or GPi.

Concept Tested: Deep Brain Stimulation Bloom's Level: Analyze

References: Movement: Muscles, Reflexes, and Motor Control
docs.text:
1. Parkinson's Disease - National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS) - The government's plain-language guide to Parkinson's symptoms, causes, diagnosis, and treatments, including carbidopa-levodopa and deep brain stimulation. It is the main source for this chapter's Bedside case and a good place to check facts.
  2. Parkinson's Disease: Causes, Symptoms, and Treatments - National Institute on Aging (NIA) - A short, readable overview that explains early, easy-to-miss signs like small handwriting, a soft voice, and loss of smell. Helpful for seeing Parkinson's as more than a tremor.
  3. Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) for the Treatment of Parkinson's Disease and Other Movement Disorders - NINDS - Explains where DBS electrodes go (STN, GPi, and thalamus), when the FDA approved each use, and how basic research on basal ganglia circuits led to the therapy. Shows how circuit diagrams turn into treatments.
  4. 10.1 The Physiological Actions Implementing Movement: Contraction of Muscles - OpenStax, Introduction to Behavioral Neuroscience (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) - A free textbook section on how actin, myosin, calcium, and ATP produce contraction, with clear figures of the sarcomere and motor units. Good next step after Sections 7.2 and 7.3.
  5. 10.2 Eliciting Contractions from Lower Levels: Lower Motoneurons and Reflex Arcs - OpenStax, Introduction to Behavioral Neuroscience - Covers lower motor neurons, the size principle, muscle spindles, and the knee-jerk reflex, using a soccer-kick example. Matches Sections 7.3 and 7.4.
  6. 10.3 Our Brain Gets Involved: Responsibilities of Upper Motor Systems - OpenStax, Introduction to Behavioral Neuroscience - Explains the motor cortex, corticospinal tracts, the direct and indirect basal ganglia pathways, the cerebellum's error correction, and motor learning. The best single free reading for Sections 7.5 to 7.9.
  7. Basal ganglia - Wikipedia - A detailed overview of basal ganglia anatomy, the direct, indirect, and hyperdirect pathways, and how dopamine acts on D1 and D2 neurons. Useful for checking the signs in this chapter's circuit table; verify details against primary sources.
  8. Assessment of heterogeneity among participants in the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative cohort using α-synuclein seed amplification: a cross-sectional study - Siderowf et al., Lancet Neurology (2023) - The large study behind this chapter's "What's new" section, reporting how well the spinal-fluid alpha-synuclein test separated people with Parkinson's from healthy controls. A challenging but real example of biomarker research.
  9. FDA Encourages Use of Parkinson's Biomarker for Future Clinical Trials - Michael J. Fox Foundation (September 2024) - Explains the FDA's 2024 Letter of Support for the alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay in research and trials. A good lesson in the difference between regulatory "support" and "approval."
  10. The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2000: Press Release - NobelPrize.org - Describes how Arvid Carlsson linked dopamine to movement and L-dopa to Parkinson's treatment, and how Eric Kandel used the Aplysia gill-withdrawal reflex to study learning. Connects this chapter to Ply's story.

docs.title: Chapter 8: The Developing and Teenage Brain
Chapter 8: The Developing and Teenage Brain
Summary
docs.text: Your brain was not built all at once. It started as a tiny folded tube, filled with new neurons that crawled to their places, and made far more connections than it would keep. During childhood and the teen years, the brain prunes the connections it doesn't use and insulates the ones it does, with the prefrontal cortex finishing last. This chapter follows that journey to the mid-twenties, explains why teens are drawn to rewards and peers, and shows what happens when alcohol interferes before birth.

docs.text:
1. Neural Tube
