docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 1: Neurons, Glia, and the Nervous System (neurons, glia, myelin)
  • Chapter 2: The Action Potential (how signals travel along axons)
  • Chapter 3: Synapses and Neurotransmitters (synapses, dopamine, glutamate, GABA)
  • Chapter 4: A Tour of the Brain: Neuroanatomy (cerebral cortex, frontal lobe, prefrontal cortex)

A Brain Under Construction

I'm Ply, a sea slug with only about 20,000 neurons, so I got built pretty fast. Your brain took much longer, and parts of it are still being remodeled as you read this. This chapter is about you: how your brain got built, why the teen years are a special construction phase, and what can go wrong before birth.

docs.title: 8.1 Why Do Teenagers Take More Risks?
docs.text:
Maya is 16. After a Saturday soccer game, a teammate with a brand-new license offers her a ride home. Three other friends pile in. Someone turns the music up and dares the driver to "see what this car can do." Maya knows the road curves ahead. She aced a reaction-time quiz last week while studying for the Brain Bee. Yet with friends cheering in the back seat, the dare doesn't sound as dumb as it would if she were alone.

That night, Maya scrolls past a headline: "Teen brains aren't finished until 25!" Is her brain "half-built"? And if she knew the risk, why did the dare feel so tempting? This chapter answers with what scientists have actually measured. The short answer: the teenage brain isn't broken. It is in a very active phase of construction, and the timing of that construction helps explain both the risks teens take and how quickly they learn.

docs.title: 8.2 Building a Brain: The Big Picture
docs.text:
Before we name any structures, picture how a new city might be built.

First, builders lay down the outline. Next, factories make lots of workers, who travel along scaffolding to their job sites. Then they build roads between every building they can reach, far more than the city needs. For years, the city watches traffic. Busy roads are kept and paved into highways. Unused roads are closed. The city ends up with fewer roads, but a much more efficient network.

Your brain was built in almost exactly that order:

  1. A flat sheet of cells folds into a tube that sets the basic outline (the neural tube).
  2. Stem cells divide to make enormous numbers of new neurons (neurogenesis).
  3. The new neurons travel to their final positions (neuronal migration).
  4. Neurons connect to each other by forming synapses, overshooting what an adult brain keeps (synaptogenesis).
  5. Unused synapses are removed (synaptic pruning), and busy pathways are insulated with myelin (myelination).

The first three steps happen mostly before birth. The last two continue into the twenties. The flowchart below summarizes the sequence.

flowchart TD
    A["Neural tube forms<br/>(weeks 3-4 after conception)"] --> B["Neurogenesis:<br/>stem cells make neurons<br/>(mostly before birth)"]
    B --> C["Neuronal migration:<br/>neurons travel to their layers"]
    C --> D["Synaptogenesis:<br/>synapses form and overshoot<br/>(before birth into early childhood)"]
    D --> E["Synaptic pruning:<br/>unused synapses removed<br/>(childhood into the 20s)"]
    D --> F["Myelination:<br/>busy axons insulated<br/>(before birth into the late 20s)"]
    E --> G["Mature, efficient circuits<br/>that keep adapting for life"]
    F --> G

docs.title: 8.3 The Neural Tube: Where It All Starts
docs.text:
Early in pregnancy, part of the embryo's outer cell layer (the ectoderm) forms a flat strip called the neural plate. Its edges rise like two walls, curl toward each other, and zip together into a hollow tube. This is the neural tube, which becomes the entire central nervous system. The upper end becomes the brain and the rest becomes the spinal cord. The hollow inside remains as the brain's fluid-filled ventricles and the spinal cord's central canal (OpenStax, Section 5.1; NINDS).

According to the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS), the neural tube typically folds and closes during the third and fourth weeks of development, about a month after conception, often before a person knows they are pregnant.

When the tube does not close properly, the result is a neural tube defect. If the back end fails to close, part of the spinal cord can be left exposed, a condition called spina bifida. If the front end fails to close, the forebrain does not develop, a condition called anencephaly (NINDS).

The CDC reports that folic acid, a B vitamin, is the only form of folate shown to help prevent neural tube defects. Because the tube closes so early, the CDC recommends folic acid every day for anyone who could become pregnant, not just after a positive test (CDC). Keep this example in mind for Section 8.13.

docs.title: 8.4 Making Neurons and Moving Them Into Place
Neurogenesis
docs.text:
Cells lining the inner wall of the neural tube divide very fast. These are neural stem cells, which can copy themselves and also produce specialized cells. Neurogenesis is the creation of new neurons from stem cells. Later, stem cells switch to producing glia, the support cells from Chapter 1 (OpenStax, Section 5.2).

NINDS states that most of the brain's neurons have already been created by the time we're born. Whether adults make many new neurons is still debated. NINDS notes that neuroscientists disagree about how many and how often (NINDS, Brain Basics). The big neuron-building phase happens before birth.

docs.title: Neuronal migration
docs.text:
New neurons usually aren't born where they will work. Neuronal migration is the movement of new neurons from their birthplace to their final home. Many climb along long glial fibers called radial glia, which stretch like ropes from the inner wall of the neural tube to the outer surface (NINDS, Brain Basics). Radial glia are also neural stem cells, so they help make neurons and then guide them. The cortex is built "inside-out": the earliest-born neurons settle in the deepest layers, and later-born neurons crawl past them toward the surface (OpenStax, Section 5.2).

If migration goes wrong, neurons end up in the wrong place. In a rare condition called lissencephaly ("smooth brain"), the cortex develops without its normal folds. NINDS lists neuronal migration problems as the cause (NINDS).

Surprisingly, the developing brain also makes extra neurons, and large numbers die along the way. This is part of the plan. Neurons compete for survival signals called neurotrophins, and those that don't get enough self-destruct in an orderly process called apoptosis (OpenStax, Section 5.3).

docs.title: 8.5 Wiring Up: Synaptogenesis and Synaptic Pruning
Synaptogenesis: making too many connections
docs.text:
Once a neuron arrives, it grows dendrites and an axon and connects with other neurons. Recall from Chapter 3 that a synapse is the junction where one neuron passes a chemical message to another. Synaptogenesis is the formation of new synapses.

In a classic study, Peter Huttenlocher and Arun Dabholkar measured synapse density in human cortex at different ages, comparing an auditory (hearing) area with a prefrontal (planning) area. Synapse formation began in both before birth. But auditory cortex peaked around 3 months after birth, while the prefrontal area didn't peak until after 15 months (Huttenlocher and Dabholkar, 1997).

At their peaks, young brains are crowded with synapses. A later study of the human prefrontal cortex found that dendritic spines, the tiny bumps where most excitatory synapses sit, are two to three times more dense in childhood than in adults (Petanjek and colleagues, 2011).

docs.title: Synaptic pruning: use it or lose it
docs.text:
Why build extra connections? Your genes can't predict which language you'll hear or whether you'll play soccer or piano. So the brain overbuilds, then lets experience decide.

Synaptic pruning is the removal of weak or unused synapses during development. The rule is often summarized as "use it or lose it." Synapses that are active often get strengthened and kept. Synapses that are rarely used get removed (OpenStax, Section 5.3). Like closing unused roads, this makes traffic flow better.

Pruning, like synapse formation, follows a regional schedule. In Huttenlocher's data, net synapse loss in the auditory cortex was over by about age 12, while in the prefrontal cortex it extended to mid-adolescence (Huttenlocher and Dabholkar, 1997). Petanjek's team found that substantial pruning of prefrontal spines continues through the twenties before settling at adult levels (Petanjek and colleagues, 2011).

Who does the pruning? Partly microglia, the brain's resident immune cells. In young mice, microglia were caught "eating" synaptic inputs in the visual system during peak pruning, and this depended on how active those inputs were (Schafer and colleagues, 2012).

Less Can Be More

A mature brain has fewer synapses than a toddler's brain, and that's a good thing. Pruning turns a tangled thicket into tuned circuits shaped by what you actually do. Every big idea starts at a single synapse, but a good brain also knows which ones to let go!

docs.title: 8.6 Myelination Over Time
docs.text:
Pruning is half of the remodeling story. The other half is insulation. Recall from Chapters 1 and 2 that myelin is a fatty wrapping made by glial cells, and it lets action potentials jump from node to node, so signals travel much faster.

Myelin starts being laid down before birth. It appears first in peripheral nerves, then the spinal cord, then the brain. The busiest period is the first year after birth, and it continues in the front of the brain through childhood and adolescence (OpenStax, Section 5.3). We call this gradual, region-by-region process myelination over time.

How long does it continue? MRI can track white matter, the parts of the brain made mostly of myelinated axons. One team scanned 103 people aged 5 to 32, each at least twice. Many pathways finished maturing by late adolescence, but the long "association" pathways linking distant parts of the cortex kept maturing after adolescence (Lebel and Beaulieu, 2011).

A huge study combined 123,984 MRI scans from 101,457 people, from before birth to age 100. Total white matter volume rose quickly in early childhood, then kept rising slowly, peaking at about 29 years. Gray matter volume (cell bodies and synapses), by contrast, peaked at about 6 years and then slowly declined (Bethlehem and colleagues, 2022). Both changes are part of normal maturation.

The MicroSim below puts this together. Its curves follow the findings above: sensory cortex peaks and prunes early, prefrontal cortex peaks later and keeps pruning into the twenties, and white matter keeps rising for years.

docs.title: 8.7 Critical Periods: Windows for Experience
docs.text:
What happens if a young brain doesn't get the experience it expects? David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel answered this in kittens. They closed one eyelid for a time, then recorded from neurons in the visual cortex. If the eye was closed during a window in the first few months of life, the cortex rewired so that far fewer neurons responded to the closed eye. During the most sensitive weeks (the fourth and fifth weeks of life), closing an eye for as little as 3 to 4 days caused a sharp change. Closing an adult cat's eye for over a year produced no detectable effect (Hubel and Wiesel, 1970).

Hubel and Wiesel shared the 1981 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their discoveries about how the visual system processes information (NobelPrize.org).

A critical period is a window in development when a particular experience (or a harmful exposure) has an especially large and lasting effect on the brain.

This matters in the clinic. In amblyopia ("lazy eye"), the brain and one eye don't work together well, so the brain relies on the stronger eye and vision in the weaker eye worsens. Doctors cover the stronger eye with a patch, or blur it with eye drops, to force the brain to use the weaker eye. The National Eye Institute says early treatment works well, and treatment is usually less effective in adults than in children (NEI).

Critical periods don't mean the brain stops changing afterward. Plasticity, the brain's ability to change with experience, is highest early in life and declines with age, but it doesn't disappear (OpenStax, Section 5.4). Chapter 9 explores lifelong plasticity.

docs.title: 8.8 The Adolescent Brain: Remodeling, Not Broken
docs.text:
Adolescence is the phase of life between childhood and adulthood. The World Health Organization defines it as ages 10 to 19 (WHO). The adolescent brain is the brain during this phase. Surprisingly, the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) explains that the brain stops growing in size by early adolescence. The teen years are about fine-tuning how the brain works (NIMH), through the pruning and myelination you just explored. NIMH lists several features of the teen brain:

  • It is highly adaptable. Challenging classes, exercise, and creative activities like music or art can help strengthen brain circuits.
  • Sleep timing shifts. The sleep hormone melatonin stays high later at night and drops later in the morning, which may explain why teens stay up late and struggle to wake early.
  • It may respond to stress differently, which may raise the risk of anxiety and depression.
  • Many mental illnesses first appear in adolescence, including anxiety, depression, bipolar disorder, eating disorders, and schizophrenia (see Chapters 11 and 15).
  • Most teens become healthy adults, and some adolescent brain changes may support long-term resilience.

None of these points says the teen brain is "defective." It is specialized for a stage of life where learning fast, exploring, and building social connections really matter.

docs.title: 8.9 Prefrontal Maturation: The Last Region to Finish
docs.text:
Recall from Chapter 4 that the prefrontal cortex, at the front of the frontal lobe, handles executive functions: planning, prioritizing, resisting impulses, and weighing long-term consequences. NIMH describes it as one of the last brain regions to mature (NIMH).

Prefrontal maturation is the slow refinement of this region and its connections. It includes pruning of extra synapses, myelination of the long pathways linking the prefrontal cortex to the rest of the brain, and strengthening of the circuits that get used.

A well-known study scanned 13 healthy children every two years for 8 to 10 years (ages 4 to 21). Time-lapse "movies" of gray matter showed that higher-order association areas, which combine information, matured only after the sensory and motor areas that feed them (Gogtay and colleagues, 2004). A 2021 review calls this a "sensorimotor-to-association axis" of development (Sydnor and colleagues, 2021). It's the same pattern you saw in the MicroSim: sensory first, prefrontal last.

docs.title: So is the brain "finished" at 25?
docs.text:
You have probably heard that "the brain isn't done developing until 25." Here is what the research shows:

  • Development continues into the twenties. NIMH states that the brain finishes developing and maturing in the mid-to-late 20s (NIMH). Prefrontal pruning continues through the twenties (Petanjek and colleagues, 2011), and total white matter volume peaks at about 29 (Bethlehem and colleagues, 2022).
  • There is no single finish line. Different measures level off at different ages. Gray matter volume peaks in childhood, while white matter keeps growing into the late twenties. Neuroscientists themselves have urged the field to work out how "brain maturity" should even be defined and measured (Somerville, 2016).
  • People vary a lot. The brain-chart study found large differences between individuals of the same age (Bethlehem and colleagues, 2022). No one's brain flips a switch on their 25th birthday.
  • Different abilities mature at different ages. A study of 5,227 people aged 10 to 30 in 11 countries found that cognitive capacity, the ability to reason logically in calm conditions, reached adult levels around age 16. Psychosocial maturity, the ability to restrain yourself in emotional, exciting, or risky moments, didn't reach adult levels until after 18 (Icenogle and colleagues, 2019).

So "25" is rough shorthand, not a hard cutoff. Brain development continues gradually into the mid-to-late twenties, with large individual differences, and the brain keeps changing with experience for life.

Careful With the Number 25

Don't say "the brain is finished at 25" on a Brain Bee answer or anywhere else. Say "brain development, especially in the prefrontal cortex, continues into the mid-to-late twenties, and the timing varies from person to person." That's accurate, and it shows you know the science behind the slogan.

docs.title: 8.10 Reward Sensitivity in Teens
docs.text:
Back to Maya in the car: she understood the danger, so why did the dare feel tempting? The answer involves two brain systems that mature on different schedules.

The first is the reward system. Dopamine neurons (Chapter 3) signal to a deep region called the ventral striatum, which includes the nucleus accumbens. This circuit becomes active when we expect something good, like praise or the thrill of winning. The second is the control system centered on the prefrontal cortex, which can put the brakes on impulses.

Psychologist Laurence Steinberg proposed that around puberty, the brain's reward-related and social-emotional system is remodeled, driven mainly by big changes in the dopamine system. This increases reward sensitivity, the tendency to be strongly motivated by possible rewards, especially in the presence of peers. Meanwhile, the control system matures gradually through adolescence and young adulthood. The gap between the two makes mid-adolescence a time of heightened vulnerability to risky choices (Steinberg, 2008).

In one fMRI study of 37 people aged 7 to 29, teens showed exaggerated activity in the nucleus accumbens when they received rewards, compared with both children and adults. Meanwhile, a prefrontal area involved in evaluating rewards looked more like a child's than an adult's (Galvan and colleagues, 2006).

docs.title: The peer effect
docs.text:
In one experiment, 306 adolescents (13 to 16), young adults (18 to 22), and adults (24 and older) completed questionnaires and a risk-taking task, either alone or with two same-age peers present. Everyone took more risks with friends, but the peer effect was much stronger for adolescents and young adults than for adults (Gardner and Steinberg, 2005).

A later study put teens, young adults, and adults in an fMRI scanner during a simulated driving task. When teens knew peers were watching, reward-related regions, including the ventral striatum, became more active, and that activity predicted their risky choices. Adults didn't show this peer boost (Chein and colleagues, 2011). So friends do more than "pressure" teens. Just having them around seems to make the reward of a risky choice feel bigger.

According to the CDC (in a fact page updated in 2025), drivers aged 16 to 19 have a fatal crash rate almost three times as high as drivers aged 20 and older per mile driven, and the presence of teen or young adult passengers increases the crash risk of unsupervised teen drivers (CDC). That is one reason the graduated driver licensing systems recommended by the CDC limit teen passengers and nighttime driving while new drivers gain experience (CDC).

Reward sensitivity isn't all bad. The same drive also pushes teens to try new things, make friends, and learn skills, which are important jobs of adolescence. The goal is to point that energy toward healthy challenges.

Use Your Brain's Schedule

Knowing about the peer effect is a tool. Decide on your rules (like "I don't ride with a driver who's showing off") when you're calm and alone, because your in-the-moment judgment will be under the most pressure exactly when friends are cheering.

docs.title: 8.11 Teratogens: When the Environment Interferes
docs.text:
A teratogen is something in the environment that can cause, or raise the risk of, a birth defect by interfering with an embryo's or fetus's development. Examples include some medicines, street drugs, alcohol, tobacco and nicotine, toxic chemicals, and some viruses and bacteria (Nationwide Children's Hospital). Because the brain and spinal cord keep developing throughout pregnancy, they stay sensitive to teratogens the whole time.

Timing matters. Critical periods work in both directions: the brain's sensitivity during these windows can be beneficial or damaging (OpenStax, Section 5.4). An exposure while the neural tube is closing can affect different structures than the same exposure while synapses are forming.

Alcohol in a pregnant person's blood passes to the developing baby through the umbilical cord (CDC). In a widely cited study in young rats, alcohol triggered the death of large numbers of developing neurons by blocking a type of glutamate receptor and over-activating a type of GABA receptor (Chapter 3). The researchers found that the most vulnerable period lined up with the period of rapid synapse formation, which in humans runs from about the sixth month of pregnancy to several years after birth (Ikonomidou and colleagues, 2000). Animal studies can't tell us everything about people, but they help explain why prenatal alcohol exposure is linked to a smaller brain.

docs.title: 8.12 Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders
docs.text:
Fetal alcohol spectrum disorders (FASDs) are a group of conditions that can occur in a person who was exposed to alcohol before birth. The word "spectrum" means the effects range from mild to severe and differ from person to person. FASDs can affect behavior, learning, and physical health for life (CDC).

FASD is an umbrella term, not a single diagnosis. The CDC describes several diagnoses under it:

Diagnosis What it involves (simplified) Fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS) The most involved end of the spectrum: central nervous system problems, specific facial features, and growth problems Partial fetal alcohol syndrome (pFAS) Prenatal alcohol exposure, some of the facial features, and either growth problems or central nervous system problems Alcohol-related neurodevelopmental disorder (ARND) Problems with learning and behavior, and sometimes intellectual disability, without the full set of physical features Alcohol-related birth defects (ARBD) Problems with organs such as the heart, kidneys, bones, or hearing Neurobehavioral disorder associated with prenatal alcohol exposure (ND-PAE) Problems with thinking and memory, behavior, and daily living skills

Source: CDC, About FASDs.

docs.title: Signs and how common it is
docs.text:
Common signs include trouble paying attention, hyperactivity, poor memory, learning disabilities (especially in math), poor judgment, poor coordination, small head size, and short height or low weight. Some people also have distinctive facial features, such as a smooth ridge between the nose and upper lip, called a smooth philtrum (CDC). But many people with an FASD, such as those with ARND, don't have these features, and NIAAA notes that FASDs are often undiagnosed or misdiagnosed (NIAAA).

FASDs are more common than many people think. A study that examined first graders in four U.S. communities between 2010 and 2016 estimated that 1.1% to 5.0% had an FASD (May and colleagues, 2018). The authors note that four communities may not represent every part of the country, but this study is still the source of the "1% to 5% of U.S. first graders" estimate in NIAAA's fact sheet, updated in December 2025 (NIAAA). NIAAA calls prenatal alcohol exposure a leading preventable cause of birth defects and neurodevelopmental disorders in the United States (NIAAA).

docs.title: What happens in the brain
docs.text: Brain scans of people exposed to alcohol before birth most often show a smaller overall brain volume and abnormalities of the corpus callosum, the thick bundle of axons connecting the two hemispheres. A review of imaging studies concluded that alcohol's effects appear widespread, affecting almost the entire brain (Lebel, Roussotte, and Sowell, 2011). That fits this chapter: alcohol can disrupt several steps of the building plan.

docs.title: Prevention
docs.text: The CDC is clear: there is no known safe amount of alcohol during pregnancy or while trying to get pregnant, no safe time, and no safe type (wine and beer included). It's also never too late to stop, because the baby's brain keeps growing throughout pregnancy (CDC). FASDs are completely preventable if a developing baby is not exposed to alcohol.

docs.title: 8.13 Nature and Nurture: Both, Always
docs.text:
Is the brain shaped by nature (genes) or nurture (environment and experience)? This chapter's honest answer: both, working together.

  • Genes set up the plan. Genes guide the folding of the neural tube, the birth of neurons, and the paths they migrate along. OpenStax estimates that about 70% of neural tube defects are due to genetic factors.
  • The environment can change the outcome. Yet many of those same defects can be prevented when the mother gets enough folic acid (OpenStax, Section 5.1). A genetic risk plus a nutritional factor together determine what happens.
  • Experience tunes the wiring. Hubel and Wiesel's kittens had normal genes for vision, but without visual experience in one eye during the critical period, their visual cortex wired up differently.
  • Harmful exposures and supportive environments both matter. Alcohol before birth can alter brain development. After birth, the CDC lists early diagnosis, special education and social services, and a stable, loving home free of violence as protective factors that can reduce later problems for people with FASDs (CDC, FASD Treatment).

So nature and nurture don't compete. They work together: genes build a brain designed to be shaped by experience, and experience works on the brain genes have built. The teen years are one of the most important stages of that back-and-forth.

docs.title: At the Bedside: A Second Grader Who Can't Keep Up
docs.text:
Meet the patient

Jordan is 7 and in second grade. His teacher reports that he has trouble sitting still, loses track of directions halfway through, and is falling behind in math even with extra help. His foster mother adds that he forgets things he learned the week before, gets frustrated easily, and is the shortest child in his class. His records note that his birth mother drank alcohol regularly during her pregnancy.

What the doctor checks: The pediatrician measures Jordan's height, weight, and head circumference and plots them on growth charts. All three are below the 10th percentile for his age. She examines his face closely and notes short eye openings, a thin upper lip, and a smooth philtrum (the ridge between the nose and upper lip). His neurological exam shows mild clumsiness but no weakness. A team evaluation, including a psychologist, finds below-average memory and executive function (attention, planning, and impulse control). There is no blood test for FASDs. The diagnosis is made from history, physical findings, growth, and neurodevelopmental testing (CDC; Hoyme and colleagues, 2016).

Where is the problem? (localization): Unlike a stroke, which damages one spot, Jordan's symptoms point to many systems at once: attention and impulse problems suggest prefrontal circuits, memory problems suggest circuits including the hippocampus, clumsiness suggests motor networks, and a small head suggests the brain grew less than expected. Imaging studies of people with prenatal alcohol exposure fit this picture: reduced overall brain volume, frequent abnormalities of the corpus callosum, and widespread changes in many regions (Lebel, Roussotte, and Sowell, 2011). This is a diffuse developmental problem, not a focal lesion.

Diagnosis: Fetal alcohol syndrome, the most involved condition on the fetal alcohol spectrum. Jordan has all four key elements: characteristic facial features, growth problems, signs of reduced brain growth (small head size), and neurobehavioral impairment, along with documented prenatal alcohol exposure (Hoyme and colleagues, 2016).

Why it happens: Alcohol reached Jordan through the umbilical cord while his brain was being built. It acted as a teratogen during critical windows. Animal research suggests it can kill large numbers of developing neurons during the period of rapid synapse formation, partly by disrupting glutamate and GABA signaling (Ikonomidou and colleagues, 2000). Fewer neurons, altered wiring, and a smaller brain help explain his trouble with attention, memory, and learning.

Treatment today: There is no cure for FASDs, but early help makes a real difference. Care includes special education matched to the child's needs, behavioral support, social services for the family, medicines for some symptoms, and case management (CDC, FASD Treatment; NIAAA). A stable, loving home, early diagnosis, and freedom from violence are protective factors that reduce later problems.

What's new in research: Researchers are testing whether the nutrient choline helps young children with FASDs. A combined report of three small randomized, placebo-controlled trials in children aged 2.5 to 5.9 found a modest benefit of choline on a memory task compared with placebo (partly only a trend, and larger in the youngest children), but no effect on IQ or executive functioning (Wozniak and colleagues, 2025). Choline is still being studied for FASDs. It is not an established standard treatment, and families should not start supplements without talking to a doctor.

Your turn: diagnose a variation

Suppose a different second grader, Sam, has the same attention and impulse-control problems as Jordan. But Sam's height, weight, and head size are all normal, his face has none of the features listed above, and his birth mother is known not to have drunk alcohol during pregnancy. What condition should the doctor think about first, and why can't the doctor diagnose an FASD?

Answer: Without prenatal alcohol exposure, an FASD isn't the right diagnosis. Attention and impulse problems with normal growth and features could instead suggest attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), which the CDC notes shares some symptoms with FAS (CDC). This shows why the history (including prenatal exposures) and the physical exam matter: similar behaviors can come from different causes.

Part 2: Not a disease, a developmental stage

Nothing is medically wrong with Maya. Her brain is doing what a typical 16-year-old brain does. Her reward system is highly responsive, especially with friends watching (Chein and colleagues, 2011), and her prefrontal control circuits are still being refined (Steinberg, 2008). Her logical knowledge of the danger is adult-level, but her self-control in an exciting, emotional moment may not be yet (Icenogle and colleagues, 2019).

What helps: Planning ahead when calm, graduated licensing rules that limit teen passengers and night driving, and a parent-teen driving agreement (CDC) work with the teen brain. Next time, Maya rides home with a teammate's parent.

This is a fictional teaching case. It is not medical advice. If you or someone you know has symptoms like these, talk to a doctor.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
Myth: "The teenage brain is just a broken or unfinished adult brain." Reality: The teen brain is in a normal, active remodeling phase. It is highly adaptable, and NIMH notes that most teens become healthy adults.

Myth: "Brain development is over by 18." Reality: Prefrontal pruning continues through the twenties, long association pathways keep maturing after adolescence, and white matter volume peaks at about 29. Development continues into the mid-to-late twenties.

Myth: "The brain is finished at exactly 25." Reality: "25" is rough shorthand. Different measures level off at different ages, people vary widely, and scientists are still working out how to define and measure "brain maturity."

Myth: "More synapses always means a smarter brain." Reality: Toddlers have far more synapses than adults. Pruning away unused synapses makes circuits more efficient. Mature brains are tuned, not crowded.

Myth: "A little alcohol late in pregnancy is safe for the baby." Reality: The CDC states there is no known safe amount, time, or type of alcohol during pregnancy. The baby's brain grows throughout pregnancy.

docs.title: Brain Bee Practice
docs.text:
1. What embryonic structure gives rise to the brain and spinal cord, and when does it normally close?

The neural tube. According to NINDS, it typically folds and closes in the third to fourth week after conception, often before a person knows they are pregnant.

2. What type of glial cell acts as a guide rope for migrating neurons in the developing cortex?

Radial glia. New neurons climb along their long fibers from the inner wall of the neural tube toward the brain's surface. Radial glia also act as neural stem cells.

3. Define synaptic pruning, and name a region that finishes pruning early and one that finishes late.

Synaptic pruning is the removal of weak or unused synapses during development ("use it or lose it"). Sensory cortex, such as auditory cortex, finishes early (by about age 12), while prefrontal cortex continues pruning through adolescence and into the twenties.

4. What did Hubel and Wiesel's kitten experiments show about critical periods?

Closing one eye during a window early in life caused far fewer visual cortex neurons to respond to the closed eye, and the effect lasted, while closing an adult cat's eye had no detectable effect. This showed a critical period for visual cortex wiring. Hubel and Wiesel shared the 1981 Nobel Prize.

5. Name the umbrella term for conditions caused by prenatal alcohol exposure, and name its most involved diagnosis.

Fetal alcohol spectrum disorders (FASDs). The most involved diagnosis is fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS), which includes central nervous system problems, characteristic facial features, and growth problems.

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
1. List the five main steps of brain construction in order, starting with the neural tube.
  2. What is a teratogen? Give one example from this chapter.
Answer
  1. Neural tube formation, neurogenesis, neuronal migration, synaptogenesis, then synaptic pruning together with myelination.
  2. A teratogen is something in the environment that can interfere with development before birth and cause a birth defect. Alcohol is the main example in this chapter.

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
1. Explain, using the "city roads" analogy, why the brain makes more synapses than it keeps.
  2. Explain why the CDC recommends folic acid for anyone who could become pregnant, not just people who already know they are pregnant.
Answer
  1. The brain can't know in advance which connections will be useful, just as a city can't predict which roads will carry traffic. It builds extra connections, then keeps and strengthens the busy ones and removes the unused ones, which makes the remaining circuits more efficient.
  2. The neural tube closes about three to four weeks after conception, often before someone knows they are pregnant. Folic acid has to already be in the body during that window to help prevent neural tube defects.

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
1. A 9-year-old has amblyopia in her left eye. Using the idea of a critical period, explain why her eye doctor wants to start patching her right eye now rather than waiting until she is an adult.
  2. Maya's younger brother is about to get his driver's license. Using what you learned about reward sensitivity and peers, design two rules for his first six months of driving and explain the brain science behind each.

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
1. In the MicroSim, compare the sensory and prefrontal synapse curves at ages 2, 12, and 22. What pattern do you see, and how does it match Gogtay's finding about the order of cortical maturation?
  2. Jordan (the Bedside case) and a child with a stroke might both have trouble with attention. Analyze why the doctor localizes Jordan's problem as "diffuse" but a stroke as "focal."

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
1. A news headline says: "Science proves teens can't make good decisions until 25." Evaluate this claim using at least three pieces of evidence from Section 8.9. What would a more accurate headline say?
  2. Some say a developing brain means teens have no responsibility for their choices; others say the brain science is irrelevant. Evaluate both views using the "maturity gap" study.

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
1. Design a one-page poster explaining synaptic pruning and myelination to 9th graders, with an analogy, a sketch graph labeled as schematic, and one healthy-habit takeaway.
  2. Write a short public-awareness message (about 100 words) about preventing fetal alcohol spectrum disorders. It must be accurate, non-blaming, and include at least two facts from the CDC.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The nervous system starts as a neural tube that closes about three to four weeks after conception. Folic acid helps prevent neural tube defects.
  • Most neurons are made before birth (neurogenesis) and then travel to their places, often along radial glia (neuronal migration).
  • The brain overproduces synapses (synaptogenesis) and then removes unused ones (synaptic pruning). Sensory cortex peaks and prunes early, while prefrontal cortex peaks later and keeps pruning into the twenties.
  • Myelination continues for decades, and total white matter volume peaks at about age 29. Experience during critical periods has an especially strong effect on wiring.
  • The adolescent brain is remodeling, not broken. Development continues into the mid-to-late twenties with large individual variation. "25" is shorthand, not a finish line.
  • Teens show heightened reward sensitivity, especially around peers, while prefrontal control circuits are still maturing. This helps explain risk-taking, and it can be managed with smart planning.
  • Alcohol is a teratogen. Prenatal exposure can cause fetal alcohol spectrum disorders, which are lifelong but completely preventable. Brain development always reflects nature and nurture working together.

You Followed a Brain From Tube to Twenties!

You just traced how a brain builds, trims, and insulates itself, and why your own brain is in one of its most exciting construction phases right now. Next up, in Chapter 9, we'll see how all those carefully kept synapses store memories, and meet the famous patient H.M., who taught scientists where memories are made.

docs.title: Quiz: The Developing and Teenage Brain
Quiz: The Developing and Teenage Brain
docs.text: Test your understanding of Chapter 8. Choose the best answer, then click Show Answer to check.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
According to NINDS, when does the neural tube typically fold and close?

  1. During the last month of pregnancy
  2. About three to four weeks after conception
  3. Right after birth, during the first week of life
  4. Around the middle of pregnancy, at about 20 weeks
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The neural tube typically closes during the third and fourth weeks after conception, often before a person knows they are pregnant. That is why folic acid is recommended for anyone who could become pregnant. It does not happen at mid-pregnancy or after birth. By then the brain is already far along.

Concept Tested: Neural Tube Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
Which cells act like guide ropes that many newborn neurons climb along to reach their place in the developing cortex?

  1. Microglia
  2. Oligodendrocytes
  3. Radial glia
  4. Schwann cells
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Radial glia stretch from the inner wall of the neural tube to the outer surface, and many migrating neurons crawl along them. Radial glia also act as neural stem cells. Microglia help prune synapses, and oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells make myelin, but none of them is the main migration guide.

Concept Tested: Neuronal Migration Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
What is a teratogen?

  1. Something in the environment that can cause or raise the risk of a birth defect
  2. A gene that controls when the neural tube closes
  3. A glial cell that removes unused synapses
  4. A hormone that rises during puberty and increases reward-seeking
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A teratogen is an environmental factor, such as alcohol, some medicines, street drugs, or some infections, that can interfere with development before birth. It is not a gene, a cell, or a puberty hormone. Alcohol is the best-studied teratogen affecting the brain.

Concept Tested: Teratogen Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 4
docs.text:
Why can synaptic pruning make the brain work better, even though it removes connections?

  1. Pruning removes neurons that have stopped firing, freeing space for new neurons to be born
  2. Pruning removes the myelin from slow axons so they can be rebuilt thicker
  3. Pruning happens only in sensory cortex, which leaves the prefrontal cortex free to grow
  4. Pruning removes weak or unused synapses and keeps the active ones, leaving more efficient circuits
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Synaptic pruning follows "use it or lose it": active synapses are strengthened and kept, while unused ones are removed, like closing roads nobody drives on so traffic flows better. Pruning removes synapses, not myelin, and it isn't about making room for new neurons. It also happens in the prefrontal cortex, just later than in sensory cortex.

Concept Tested: Synaptic Pruning Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 5
docs.text:
Why does the CDC recommend daily folic acid for anyone who could become pregnant, rather than only after pregnancy is confirmed?

  1. Folic acid is needed mainly during the teen years, when the prefrontal cortex is pruning
  2. Neural tube defects form in the first few weeks of pregnancy, often before a person knows they are pregnant
  3. Folic acid speeds up myelination, which begins in the first week after conception
  4. Folic acid prevents all birth defects, so it should be taken as early as possible
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The neural tube closes so early that waiting for a positive pregnancy test can miss the window when folic acid helps. Folic acid helps prevent neural tube defects, not all birth defects. Myelination begins months later, starting in the spinal cord, and peaks in the first year after birth.

Concept Tested: Neural Tube Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 6
docs.text:
Which statement best describes what research shows about when the brain "finishes" developing?

  1. The brain is fully mature at exactly age 25, when the prefrontal cortex switches on
  2. Brain development is essentially complete by age 18
  3. Development, especially of the prefrontal cortex and white matter, continues gradually into the mid-to-late twenties, with large differences between people
  4. The brain reaches its adult size and maturity at the same time, in early adolescence
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. NIMH says the brain finishes maturing in the mid-to-late twenties, prefrontal pruning continues through the twenties, and white matter volume peaks at about 29. There is no single finish line, and people vary. "Exactly 25" is a slogan, not a cutoff. The brain reaches adult size in early adolescence, but it keeps fine-tuning long after.

Concept Tested: Prefrontal Maturation Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 7
docs.text:
A 5-year-old is diagnosed with amblyopia ("lazy eye"). Her uncle had the same problem but was not treated until age 30. Based on critical periods, what outcome is most likely?

  1. The 5-year-old is likely to respond better to patching, because the visual system is more changeable in childhood
  2. Both will respond equally well, because the visual cortex never loses plasticity
  3. The uncle will respond better, because an adult brain has more myelin to support learning
  4. Neither can improve, because amblyopia is caused by damage to the eye itself
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The visual system has a critical period early in life. The National Eye Institute says early treatment works well and treatment is usually less effective in adults. Plasticity declines with age (it doesn't vanish), and amblyopia is a problem of how the brain and eye work together, not eye damage.

Concept Tested: Critical Period Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 8
docs.text:
A 7-year-old has attention and memory problems, is below the 10th percentile for height, weight, and head size, and has a smooth philtrum and a thin upper lip. Records show his birth mother drank alcohol during pregnancy. Which diagnosis best fits?

  1. Lissencephaly caused by a neuronal migration error
  2. A neural tube defect such as spina bifida
  3. Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) alone
  4. Fetal alcohol syndrome, a condition on the fetal alcohol spectrum
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Prenatal alcohol exposure plus characteristic facial features, growth problems, small head size, and neurobehavioral problems fits fetal alcohol syndrome. ADHD can share attention symptoms, but it doesn't explain the growth problems, facial features, and exposure history. Spina bifida and lissencephaly have different causes and signs.

Concept Tested: Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 9
docs.text:
In the Synaptic Pruning Over a Lifetime MicroSim, you set the age to 16. Which comparison matches what the research-based curves show?

  1. Both regions are still adding synapses, and white matter has already peaked
  2. Sensory cortex is pruning heavily, while prefrontal cortex has finished pruning
  3. Sensory cortex pruning is mostly done, while prefrontal cortex is still pruning and white matter is still rising
  4. Both regions finished pruning at the same age, around 12
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Net synapse loss in auditory cortex ends by about age 12, but prefrontal pruning continues through adolescence and into the twenties, and white matter volume keeps rising to a peak near 29. The two regions follow different schedules, sensory first and prefrontal last.

Concept Tested: Synaptic Pruning Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: Question 10
docs.text:
In one experiment, adolescents, young adults, and adults did a risk-taking task either alone or with two peers present. Everyone took more risks with peers, but the effect was much stronger in adolescents and young adults. What is the best conclusion?

  1. Teens take risks because they don't understand danger as well as adults do
  2. The presence of peers has a bigger effect on risky decisions in younger people than in adults
  3. Peers make adults safer drivers but make teens more dangerous
  4. Risk-taking is caused entirely by peer pressure and has nothing to do with the brain
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The study found a peer effect in every age group, but it was stronger for younger participants. Brain imaging later showed peers boost activity in teens' reward regions. Option A is a common myth. Other research shows teens' logical reasoning reaches adult levels around 16, while self-control in emotional moments matures later.

Concept Tested: Reward Sensitivity in Teens Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: References: The Developing and Teenage Brain
References: The Developing and Teenage Brain
docs.text:
1. The Teen Brain: 7 Things to Know - National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) - A short, reliable fact sheet on how the teen brain changes, including prefrontal maturation, sleep timing, stress, and mental health. A good first read for any student who wants the official science behind the "teen brain" headlines.

  2. About Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders (FASDs) - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) - Explains the types of FASDs, their signs, how they are diagnosed, and why there is no known safe amount of alcohol during pregnancy. It is the main public health source for this chapter's Bedside case.

  3. Understanding Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders - National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) - Covers how common FASDs are, why they are often missed, and the range of treatments and supports. Useful for seeing how researchers and clinicians think about FASD as a lifelong condition.

  4. Brain Basics: The Life and Death of a Neuron - National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS) - A readable overview of how neurons are born, migrate along radial glia, connect, and die. It pairs well with Sections 8.4 and 8.5.

  5. 5.2 Growth and Development of the Early Brain - OpenStax, Introduction to Behavioral Neuroscience (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) - A free college-level textbook section on neural stem cells, neurogenesis, radial glia, and the inside-out layering of the cortex. Good for readers who want more detail than this chapter gives.

  6. 5.4 Experience Dependent Plasticity - OpenStax, Introduction to Behavioral Neuroscience (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) - Covers critical periods, Hubel and Wiesel's kitten experiments, fetal alcohol syndrome, and the adolescent brain in one section. Helpful for connecting the "windows" idea to both learning and harm.

  7. Dynamic mapping of human cortical development during childhood through early adulthood - Gogtay and colleagues, PNAS (2004) - The well-known study that followed children with repeated MRI scans and showed sensory areas maturing before higher-order areas like the prefrontal cortex. Its time-lapse brain "movies" are famous and worth a look.

  8. Extraordinary neoteny of synaptic spines in the human prefrontal cortex - Petanjek and colleagues, PNAS (2011) - Found that prefrontal synaptic spines are two to three times more dense in childhood than in adulthood and that pruning continues through the twenties. This is one of the main pieces of evidence behind "development continues into the twenties."

  9. A Social Neuroscience Perspective on Adolescent Risk-Taking - Steinberg, Developmental Review (2008) - An influential review explaining why risk-taking rises in adolescence and falls in adulthood, based on a reward system and a control system that mature on different schedules. Readable for motivated high school students.

  10. Synaptic pruning - Wikipedia - A general overview of synaptic pruning, its timing, and the cells involved, with links to the original research. Use it as a starting point, then check its claims against the primary sources above.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Every time you learn something, your brain physically changes. This chapter explains what memory is, how short-term, working, and long-term memory differ, and why the hippocampus is needed to form new memories of facts and events but not new skills. You will see how synapses grow stronger through Hebbian learning and long-term potentiation, and how Eric Kandel used the sea slug Aplysia to watch learning happen at a single synapse. The chapter ends with Patient H.M., the man whose surgery in 1953 taught science that memory is not one thing.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 1: Neurons, Glia, and the Nervous System
  • Chapter 2: The Action Potential
  • Chapter 3: Synapses and Neurotransmitters
  • Chapter 4: A Tour of the Brain: Neuroanatomy

Welcome to my favorite chapter

This is the chapter where my family gets famous! Scientists used sea slugs like me to discover how a memory is stored at a synapse. By the end, you'll know why your brain is never quite the same after you learn something, and you'll have better ways to study for your next test.

docs.title: 9.1 Maya's Two-Week Problem
docs.text:
Maya's Brain Bee competition is two weeks away. She has a thick stack of flashcards on neuroanatomy, and soccer practice takes up most of her afternoons. Her plan is simple: relax for twelve days, then cram everything into the last two nights. Her older cousin, a nursing student, shakes her head. "Do twenty minutes a day instead," she says. "Same total time. You'll remember way more."

Maya isn't convinced. The total hours are the same, so why would the schedule matter?

Her cousin is right, and the reasons go all the way down to the synapse. In the 1880s, Hermann Ebbinghaus memorized lists of nonsense syllables and tested himself after different delays. He found that forgetting is fast at first and then slows down, a pattern now called the forgetting curve. A 2015 study repeated his experiment and got similar results (Murre & Dros, 2015).

Ebbinghaus also noticed that spreading repetitions out in time works better than bunching them together. A large 2006 review pooled 839 tests of this idea from 317 experiments and confirmed the spacing effect: spaced study usually beats cramming for long-term recall (Cepeda et al., 2006).

By the end of this chapter, you'll be able to explain a leading idea about why spacing works, using what happens inside neurons. First, though, we need to pin down what learning and memory are.

docs.title: 9.2 Intuition First: Paths Through a Field
docs.text:
Imagine a grassy field between your school and a bus stop. The first person who walks across leaves almost no mark. But if people keep taking the same route, the grass gets trampled, and a path appears. Soon the path is the easiest way across, and people follow it without thinking. If everyone stops using it, the grass slowly grows back.

Your brain works in a similar way. Your neurons are linked by an enormous number of synapses. When a pattern of activity runs through the same connections again and again, those connections change so the pattern is easier to repeat. That's the core idea of this whole chapter.

Now for the scientific words.

  • Learning is the process by which experience changes the nervous system, and therefore changes later behavior. It includes studying vocabulary, getting used to a noisy room, and practicing a soccer move.
  • Memory is the information that learning leaves behind, along with the brain's ability to store it and get it back later. Learning is the walking; memory is the path.

Memory has three basic steps. First, encoding turns an experience into a pattern of neural activity. Second, storage keeps that information over time. Third, retrieval brings it back when you need it. A failure at any step feels like "forgetting," but the cause can be very different.

docs.title: 9.3 Memory Comes in Stages
docs.text:
Not all memories last the same amount of time. Psychologists and neuroscientists sort them by how long they last.

Short-term memory holds a small amount of information for seconds to a few minutes. When a friend tells you a phone code and you repeat it until you type it in, you are using short-term memory. If you get distracted, it's usually gone.

Working memory is a special kind of short-term memory that you actively use, not just hold. Think of it as the brain's mental whiteboard. When Maya does a math problem in her head, she keeps the numbers on the whiteboard, works with them, and erases them when she's done. Working memory depends on networks in the cerebral cortex, including the frontal and parietal lobes (OpenStax, Section 18.1). What sets it apart is that information is thrown away once it's no longer needed. You don't need to remember where you parked last Tuesday, only where you parked today.

Long-term memory stores information for hours, days, or a lifetime. Your first day of high school, the rules of soccer, and how to ride a bike are all long-term memories.

How does a fragile short-term memory become a lasting long-term one? Through memory consolidation: the gradual process that turns new, easily disrupted memories into stable, long-lasting ones. Consolidation takes time. Right after learning, a memory can be weakened or lost. As consolidation goes on, the memory becomes much harder to disrupt. Emotion matters too. Stress hormones released right after an event can strengthen consolidation, which is one reason emotional moments are often remembered vividly (OpenStax, Section 18.1).

The flowchart below shows how information moves through these stages. Every term in it has already been defined above.

flowchart LR
    A["Experience<br/>(sights, sounds, practice)"] --> B["Short-term memory<br/>seconds to minutes"]
    B --> C["Working memory<br/>hold and use"]
    C -->|"not needed: discarded"| X["Forgotten"]
    B -->|"consolidation<br/>(takes time)"| D["Long-term memory<br/>hours to a lifetime"]
    D -->|"retrieval"| C

Notice the arrow from long-term memory back to working memory. When you remember something, you pull it out of storage and into your mental whiteboard so you can use it.

docs.title: 9.4 Two Big Families of Long-Term Memory
docs.text:
Long-term memory is not one single system. It splits into two big families that depend on different brain regions.

Declarative memory is memory you can consciously bring to mind and declare, or put into words. It answers "what" questions. It has two types:

  • Episodic memory holds personal events tied to a time and place, like Maya's last birthday party.
  • Semantic memory holds facts and general knowledge, like "the hippocampus is in the temporal lobe."

Procedural memory is memory for skills and habits. It answers "how" questions: how to dribble a ball, type on a keyboard, or tie your shoes. It builds up slowly with practice, and it's hard to explain in words. Try describing exactly how you keep your balance on a bike. You can do it, but you can't easily say it.

Procedural memory is the best-known member of a wider family that scientists call nondeclarative memory: memory that shows up in what you do rather than in what you can report. Besides skills and habits, this family includes simple conditioning, emotional learning, and priming, where seeing something once makes it easier to recognize later even if you don't remember seeing it (Squire, 2009). This chapter focuses on procedural memory because it gives the clearest contrast with declarative memory.

The table below summarizes the two families you just met.

Feature Declarative memory Procedural memory Question it answers "What?" (facts and events) "How?" (skills and habits) Can you put it into words? Yes Not easily How it's learned Can form after a single experience Usually needs repeated practice Example Remembering that dopamine is a neurotransmitter Getting faster at a video game Key brain regions Hippocampus and nearby medial temporal lobe, plus cortex for long-term storage Basal ganglia and cerebellum, among others

The brain-region row comes from decades of patient and animal studies, summarized in Squire (2009). You'll see where that evidence came from in Section 9.6.

docs.title: 9.5 The Hippocampus: Memory's Librarian
docs.text:
The hippocampus is a curved structure tucked inside the medial (inner) part of each temporal lobe. You have two, one on each side of the brain. Its name comes from the Greek word for "seahorse," because of its curled shape. It was one of the deep structures on the brain tour in Chapter 4.

The hippocampus is essential for forming new declarative memories. Think of it as a librarian who receives a new book (an experience), catalogs it, and links it to related books on shelves all over the library (the cortex). Over months and years, those links in the cortex become strong enough to stand on their own. That's why damage to the hippocampus mostly harms new memories while many old memories survive. This slow handoff from the hippocampus to the cortex is one form of memory consolidation.

The hippocampus also helps with spatial memory, meaning memory for places and routes. A famous study used MRI to compare licensed London taxi drivers, who must learn the city's tangled streets, with people who didn't drive taxis. The back (posterior) part of the hippocampus was larger in the taxi drivers, and its size was related to how long they had been driving (Maguire et al., 2000). At the same time, a front part of the hippocampus was smaller in the drivers. The study suggests that adult brains can change their structure in response to what we ask them to do. Because it compares groups at one point in time, though, it can't prove by itself that driving caused the change.

The hippocampus is not a hard drive

A common mistake is saying "memories are stored in the hippocampus." The hippocampus is needed to form new memories of facts and events, but long-term declarative memories end up spread across the cortex. Skills rely mostly on other regions, like the basal ganglia and cerebellum.

docs.title: 9.6 Amnesia and the Lessons of Patient H.M.
docs.text:
Amnesia is a serious loss of memory caused by brain injury, disease, or (rarely) psychological trauma. Doctors describe two main kinds, based on time:

  • Anterograde amnesia is trouble forming new memories after the injury. ("Antero" means forward.)
  • Retrograde amnesia is loss of memories from before the injury. ("Retro" means backward.)

Many people with amnesia have some of both. Unlike in movies, a person with amnesia usually still knows who they are and can hold a conversation.

The most famous case of amnesia in history is Patient H.M., whose real name, Henry Molaison, was made public after he died in 2008. In 1953, at age 27, Henry had severe epilepsy that high doses of medication could not control. His seizures made it impossible for him to work. A neurosurgeon named William Scoville, in Hartford, Connecticut, removed the medial part of the temporal lobe on both sides of his brain. This is called a bilateral medial temporal lobe resection. By the surgeon's description, it included much of the hippocampus, the amygdala, and nearby cortex (Squire, 2009).

The operation helped control his seizures, but it left him with severe anterograde amnesia. The psychologist Brenda Milner traveled from Montreal to test him. She and Scoville published the results in 1957 (Scoville & Milner, 1957). H.M. was studied by Milner, her student Suzanne Corkin, and many others for about five decades. What they found reshaped neuroscience:

  1. Memory is its own brain function. H.M.'s intelligence, personality, language, and perception seemed largely intact. Before his case, many scientists thought memory was spread evenly through the cortex and mixed in with other abilities. H.M. showed that forming new memories depends on specific structures.
  2. Short-term memory is separate from long-term memory. H.M. could repeat back a string of six or seven digits, a normal score. He could keep a number in mind for a while by rehearsing it over and over. But once his attention moved to something else, the information was gone (Squire, 2009).
  3. Old memories can survive. H.M. recognized famous people who were in the news before his surgery much better than those who became famous after it. Some memories from the years just before surgery were lost, so he also had some retrograde amnesia.
  4. Procedural memory is separate from declarative memory. This was the most surprising finding. Milner asked H.M. to trace a star while seeing his hand and the paper only in a mirror. That is hard for anyone at first, because the mirror flips every movement. Over three days of practice, H.M. got steadily better, just like healthy people do. Yet each day he had no memory of ever doing the task before (Squire, 2009).

That mirror-drawing result showed that a person can learn a skill without remembering the learning. The brain has more than one memory system.

One man, two memory systems

H.M. got better and better at mirror drawing but couldn't remember practicing it. His procedural memory worked while his declarative memory for new events did not. That's strong evidence that the brain uses separate systems for "knowing that" and "knowing how."

One more point keeps the story accurate. Because H.M.'s surgery removed several structures, his case alone could not show that the hippocampus by itself is the key. Later studies of patients and animals with smaller lesions showed that the hippocampus and the cortex around it form a medial temporal lobe memory system. Damage limited to the hippocampus causes real but milder memory loss than H.M. had (Squire, 2009). You'll see H.M. again at the bedside at the end of this chapter.

docs.title: 9.7 Neuroplasticity: The Brain That Changes
docs.text:
So far, we've talked about where memories form. Now we ask how. The answer is neuroplasticity.

Neuroplasticity (or just "plasticity") is the nervous system's ability to change its structure and function in response to experience. "Plastic" here means moldable, like clay, not the material water bottles are made of. Plasticity happens at several levels:

  • Synapses can become stronger or weaker.
  • Neurons can grow new branches and new synapses, or lose old ones.
  • Brain regions can change size or take on new jobs, as in the taxi-driver study.

Plasticity is strongest early in life (you read about synaptic pruning in Chapter 8), but it continues throughout adulthood. Every new memory is a small act of plasticity.

docs.title: 9.8 Hebbian Learning: Firing Together
docs.text:
In 1949, the psychologist Donald Hebb proposed an idea in his book The Organization of Behavior. If neuron A repeatedly helps make neuron B fire, he suggested, the connection from A to B should grow stronger. This rule is called Hebbian learning. It's often summed up as "neurons that fire together, wire together." That catchy phrase came later from other scientists, not from Hebb himself, but it captures his idea.

In the field analogy, each time two connected neurons are active together, the path between them gets a little more worn in. Hebbian learning explains how memories can link things together. If you always hear a song during summer road trips, the neurons that represent the song and the neurons that represent the trips are active at the same time. Their connections strengthen. Later, the song alone can bring back the memories of the trips.

Hebb's rule was a smart guess. For about 25 years, nobody had direct proof that real synapses behave this way.

docs.title: 9.9 Long-Term Potentiation: Hebb's Idea in a Real Brain
docs.text:
In 1973, Timothy Bliss and Terje Lømo reported the evidence. Working with anesthetized rabbits, they stimulated a bundle of axons, called the perforant path, that carries signals into a part of the hippocampus called the dentate gyrus. Then they gave a burst of high-frequency stimulation. Afterward, the same single test pulse produced a bigger response in the dentate gyrus than before. In most of their animals, the boost lasted from 30 minutes to 10 hours (Bliss & Lømo, 1973). Later experiments showed that it can last for weeks.

This lasting boost in synaptic strength after intense activity is called long-term potentiation (LTP). "Potentiation" just means "made stronger." The opposite process, a long-lasting weakening of a synapse, is called long-term depression (LTD). Both are needed: a brain that could only strengthen synapses would eventually fill up and lose flexibility (OpenStax, Section 18.4).

docs.title: How LTP works: a lock that needs two keys
docs.text:
To understand LTP, recall from Chapter 3 that glutamate is the brain's main excitatory neurotransmitter. At many synapses in the hippocampus, glutamate acts on two kinds of receptors on the receiving (postsynaptic) neuron:

  • AMPA receptors are channels that open when glutamate binds. They let in sodium ions and depolarize (excite) the cell. They do most of the everyday signaling.
  • NMDA receptors are channels that also bind glutamate, but at resting voltage their pore is plugged by a magnesium ion. The plug only pops out when the cell is already strongly depolarized. When NMDA receptors do open, they let in calcium ions as well as sodium.

That means an NMDA receptor is like a lock that needs two keys at the same time: glutamate from the sending neuron and strong depolarization of the receiving neuron. Scientists call this a coincidence detector. It's Hebb's rule built out of a protein: the synapse is strengthened only when the sending neuron fires and the receiving neuron is strongly active at the same time.

Here is the sequence, step by step:

  1. A strong burst of activity releases lots of glutamate.
  2. Many AMPA receptors open, and the postsynaptic neuron depolarizes strongly.
  3. The depolarization pops the magnesium plug out of the NMDA receptors.
  4. Calcium flows in through the NMDA receptors.
  5. Calcium switches on enzymes, including one called CaMKII. These enzymes make existing AMPA receptors work better and add new AMPA receptors to the membrane.
  6. With more and better AMPA receptors, the same amount of glutamate now produces a bigger response. The synapse has been potentiated.

This first stage is called early LTP. It lasts a few hours and uses proteins already present in the synapse. A longer-lasting stage, late LTP, needs the neuron to make new proteins, and it can involve growing new synaptic connections, such as new dendritic spines (OpenStax, Section 18.4). Hold on to that idea. You'll see it again in the sea slug.

This part is dense, and that's okay

If the NMDA receptor feels confusing, just remember the two-key lock: glutamate and a strongly excited receiving cell. Everything else in LTP follows from that one clever trick.

Does LTP really underlie memory? The evidence is strong but still being tested. In rats, drugs that block NMDA receptors interfere with some kinds of learning. In 2006, researchers also showed that a single learning experience (rats learning to avoid a mild shock) produced the same synaptic changes in the hippocampus as LTP made in the lab (Whitlock et al., 2006). Most neuroscientists think changes in synaptic strength like LTP and LTD are a central mechanism of memory, but the full link is still an active research question (OpenStax, Section 18.4).

docs.title: 9.10 The Aplysia Model: Learning in a Sea Slug
docs.text:
The human brain has billions of neurons, far too many to track the change behind a single memory. The neuroscientist Eric Kandel decided to study learning in a much simpler animal: the sea slug Aplysia. According to the Nobel committee, Aplysia has only around 20,000 nerve cells, many of them unusually large and easy to record from (Nobel Prize press release, 2000). (Some textbooks give a lower estimate, about 10,000.) Using a simple animal to discover rules that also apply to humans is called the Aplysia model, and it's a classic example of how basic research works.

Aplysia breathes through a delicate gill. Behind the gill is a fleshy spout called the siphon. If you gently touch the siphon, the slug quickly pulls its gill in for protection. This is the gill-withdrawal reflex. The circuit behind it is small enough to map neuron by neuron:

  • A sensory neuron in the siphon detects the touch.
  • It connects directly to a motor neuron that makes the gill muscle contract.
  • A shock to the tail activates other sensory neurons, which drive facilitating interneurons. The most important of these release the neurotransmitter serotonin (5-HT) onto the terminal of the siphon sensory neuron (Kandel, 2012).

docs.title: Two simple kinds of learning
docs.text:
With this reflex, Kandel's team studied two of the simplest forms of learning. Neither one links two different things together; both simply change how strongly an animal responds. Together they are called habituation and sensitization.

Habituation is a decrease in response to a harmless stimulus that is repeated over and over. You do this all the time. When you first sit near a loud air conditioner, you notice it. After a while, you stop hearing it. When the siphon is touched again and again, the slug's gill withdrawal gets smaller and smaller. Kandel's group showed that the cause is not a tired muscle or a worn-out sense organ. Instead, the siphon sensory neuron releases less neurotransmitter onto the motor neuron with each touch. The synapse itself weakens (Kandel, 2012). After a rest, a habituated response gradually comes back.

Sensitization is an increase in response to many stimuli after a strong or unpleasant one. After a scary movie, you might jump at the smallest creak in the house. In Aplysia, a shock to the tail makes the gill pull in harder when the siphon is touched later, even though the siphon touch hasn't changed. It works like this. The tail shock activates the facilitating interneurons, which release serotonin onto the siphon sensory neuron's terminal. Serotonin triggers a chain of chemical signals inside that terminal, using a messenger called cAMP and an enzyme called protein kinase A. The result is that the sensory neuron releases more transmitter with each action potential, so the motor neuron gets a bigger signal (Kandel, 2012). When sensitization restores a response that had been habituated, it's called dishabituation.

Notice that the same synapse can be weakened by one kind of experience and strengthened by another. The synapse is where the learning lives.

docs.title: Diagram: Aplysia Habituation and Sensitization
docs.text:
Open the Aplysia Habituation and Sensitization MicroSim fullscreen
