Behavior: Each siphon touch records a response bar equal to 100 times the current synaptic strength (arbitrary units) and then depresses the synapse (habituation). A tail shock raises a serotonin facilitation factor and partly restores a depressed synapse, so later touches give larger, orange bars (sensitization and dishabituation). Rest recovers half of the remaining habituation and removes half of the remaining facilitation. The side view shows the gill pulling in by an amount that matches the response. The circuit panel shows the siphon sensory neuron, motor neuron, tail sensory neuron, and serotonin interneuron, with a synaptic-strength meter. Labeled as a simplified, qualitative model.

Try this in the sim. Touch the siphon six or seven times and watch the bars shrink while the synapse-strength meter falls below 1.0. That's habituation. Now shock the tail and touch again. The next bar jumps up and turns orange, because serotonin has boosted transmitter release from the sensory neuron. Press Rest, test again, and see the partial recovery.

Then press Reset and shock the tail before any touches. The first response is bigger than the baseline of 100. In each case, ask yourself: did the siphon touch change, or did the synapse change? The numbers are arbitrary and show direction only.

docs.title: From short-term to long-term memory in a slug
docs.text:
Kandel's team found that Aplysia has both short-term and long-term memory, just like we do.

  • A single tail shock produces sensitization that lasts minutes. This short-term memory uses chemical changes to proteins that are already in the synapse.
  • Repeated, spaced shocks produce sensitization that lasts days to weeks. This long-term memory needs the neuron to switch on genes and build new proteins. If protein synthesis is blocked, the long-term change fails, but the short-term change still works (Kandel, 2012; Nobel press release, 2000).

Long-term memory also changes the structure of the synapse. After long-term habituation, sensory neurons had about 35 percent fewer connections onto their target cells than in untrained animals. After long-term sensitization, the number of sensory-neuron terminals more than doubled (Kandel, 2012). Learning literally rewires the circuit.

This should sound familiar. Short-term memory in the slug works like early LTP (modify existing proteins). Long-term memory in the slug works like late LTP (make new proteins, grow new connections). The same basic rules show up in sea slugs and in the mammalian hippocampus.

For this work, Eric Kandel shared the 2000 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Arvid Carlsson and Paul Greengard "for their discoveries concerning signal transduction in the nervous system." The Nobel committee credited Kandel with showing how the strength of synapses can be changed and which molecules are involved, using the sea slug's nervous system (Nobel Prize press release, 2000). Kandel's Nobel lecture was titled "The Molecular Biology of Memory Storage: A Dialog between Genes and Synapses" (Nobel lecture page).

docs.title: 9.11 Back to Maya: Why Spacing Beats Cramming
docs.text:
Now we can answer Maya's question. Remember the key finding from the sea slug: a single training session produces a short-term change, but repeated, spaced sessions switch on new protein synthesis and the growth of new connections. The same holds for many animals. A 2016 review found that spaced training produces stronger long-term memory than massed (crammed) training in Aplysia, fruit flies, bees, rodents, and monkeys, as well as people (Smolen, Zhang & Byrne, 2016). Researchers are still working out exactly why, but one idea is that the molecular steps that build long-term memory need time between sessions to finish and reset.

Cramming feels effective because the information is fresh the next morning, but much of it slides down the steep early part of the forgetting curve. Spaced study gives your synapses repeated chances to consolidate. Here's Maya's new plan:

Study habit What it does in the brain Maya's version Space it out Gives consolidation time between sessions 20 minutes of flashcards every day for two weeks Test yourself Practices retrieval. On tests given days later, it beat re-reading, even though re-reading looked better on a test given 5 minutes later (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006) Says answers out loud before flipping the card Mix in meaning Links new facts to existing memories (Hebbian connections) Connects "hippocampus" to H.M.'s story instead of just the word Practice skills often Builds procedural memory through repetition Uses short daily sessions to label brain diagrams

Study like a sea slug

Five short sessions spread over a week usually beat one five-hour marathon. In sea slugs like me, spacing gives synapses time to build the new proteins that long-term memory needs, and scientists think something similar may happen in you.

docs.title: At the Bedside: Patient H.M. and Anterograde Amnesia
docs.text:
This bedside case is different from the others in this book. It describes a real, well-documented historical patient. The clinical reasoning below is written for teaching. It shows how the case would be understood with today's knowledge.

Meet the patient

In 1953, Henry Molaison is 27 years old and lives in Connecticut. He has had seizures since childhood, and they have become so frequent and severe that he can't hold a job, even on high doses of anti-seizure medicine. After an experimental operation on both sides of his brain, his seizures are much better controlled. But his family and the hospital staff notice something alarming. He doesn't recognize hospital staff he has seen many times. He apologizes for forgetting the names of people he was introduced to minutes ago, and he forgets each day's events almost as fast as they happen. Yet he can chat normally, his personality seems unchanged, and he does well on intelligence tests.

What the doctor checks: A neurologist or neuropsychologist would test several kinds of memory separately. A digit-span test (repeating back a list of numbers) checks short-term memory; H.M. did normally. Delayed recall, such as remembering a short story or a list of words after 20 minutes of distraction, checks the formation of new declarative memories; H.M. failed. Questions about public events and famous faces from different decades check older memories. Skill-learning tasks like mirror drawing check procedural memory; H.M. improved normally. Today, an MRI scan would show exactly which structures were missing. Doctors evaluating memory loss also commonly use cognitive testing, blood tests, and brain imaging to look for causes (MedlinePlus).

Where is the problem? (localization): The pattern points to a specific system. Attention, language, and short-term memory work, so the cortex as a whole is functioning. Skill learning works, so the basal ganglia and cerebellum are fine. Older memories are mostly present, so long-term storage in the cortex is largely intact. What's broken is the step that turns new experiences into lasting declarative memories. That step depends on the hippocampus and the surrounding medial temporal lobe on both sides. The surgery removed exactly that region.

Diagnosis: Severe anterograde amnesia, with some retrograde amnesia for the years just before the operation, caused by bilateral medial temporal lobe resection.

Why it happens: Without the hippocampus and nearby cortex on both sides, new information can stay in short-term or working memory but can't be consolidated into long-term declarative memory. Because procedural memory relies on different circuits, H.M. could still learn new motor skills without remembering that he had practiced them.

Treatment today: There is no treatment that can regrow a removed hippocampus. Care for memory loss depends on the cause, and support focuses on daily life: written reminders for important tasks, familiar objects and photos, and help from family and caregivers (MedlinePlus).

H.M.'s case showed how much memory can be lost when the medial temporal lobes are removed on both sides, and epilepsy surgery is planned very differently today. According to the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS), surgery is usually considered only after at least two seizure medicines have failed, surgeons try to avoid brain areas needed for memory, speech, and movement, and less invasive options now include laser ablation and implanted responsive-stimulation devices (NINDS: Epilepsy and Seizures).

What's new in research: After Henry Molaison died on December 2, 2008, his brain was preserved and sliced into thin sections for study. In 2014, a team led by Jacopo Annese published a detailed 3D digital reconstruction built from 2,401 images collected during a 53-hour sectioning procedure. They found that a sizable piece of the back part of his hippocampus had actually survived the operation, while most of the entorhinal cortex, which feeds information into the hippocampus, had been removed. They also found a small lesion in the left orbitofrontal cortex and changes in the white matter (Annese et al., 2014). These details help scientists interpret five decades of testing.

Your turn: diagnose a variation

A 60-year-old woman has a stroke that damages her cerebellum. Months later, she can tell you what she had for breakfast and describe the details of her hospital stay. But in physical therapy, she improves much more slowly than expected at a new balance exercise, even after weeks of practice. Which memory system is most affected, and how is she the "opposite" of H.M.?

Answer: Her declarative memory (remembering events and facts) works, so her hippocampus is doing its job. Her trouble is learning a new motor skill, which is procedural memory. The cerebellum is one of the structures important for procedural learning. She is roughly the reverse of H.M., who could learn skills but couldn't remember new events. Comparing patients like this is how neuroscientists show that two brain systems are truly separate.

H.M. was a real, historical patient whose case is documented in the published scientific literature; the "Your turn" variation is a fictional teaching case. This is not medical advice. If you or someone you know has symptoms like these, talk to a doctor.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
Myth: Memory works like a video recording that plays back exactly what happened. Reality: Remembering is an active rebuilding process. Each time you recall a memory, it can be changed and then stored again, a process called reconsolidation (OpenStax, Section 18.1). That's why two people can honestly remember the same event differently, and why confident memories can still be wrong.

Myth: Everyone has a learning style (visual, auditory, or kinesthetic), and you learn best when teaching matches your style. Reality: People do have preferences, but a major 2008 review found virtually no evidence that matching teaching to a person's "style" improves learning (Pashler et al., 2008). Strategies like spacing and self-testing help nearly everyone.

Myth: Cramming works just as well as spacing if the total study time is the same. Reality: Cramming can get you through tomorrow's quiz, but spaced practice leads to much better long-term memory. The spacing effect holds across hundreds of experiments (Cepeda et al., 2006).

Myth: The adult brain is fixed, and only children's brains can change. Reality: Plasticity is strongest early in life, but it continues in adults. Every new long-term memory changes synapses, and adult brain structure can differ with experience, as in London taxi drivers (Maguire et al., 2000).

Myth: H.M. couldn't learn anything after his surgery. Reality: H.M. could not form new declarative memories, but he learned new motor skills such as mirror drawing at a normal rate. He just couldn't remember the practice sessions.

docs.title: Brain Bee Practice
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between anterograde and retrograde amnesia?

Anterograde amnesia is an inability to form new memories after a brain injury. Retrograde amnesia is the loss of memories formed before the injury. Patient H.M. had severe anterograde amnesia and some retrograde amnesia.

2. Which receptor acts as a coincidence detector during long-term potentiation, and why?

The NMDA glutamate receptor. It opens only when glutamate is bound and the postsynaptic cell is strongly depolarized, which removes the magnesium block from its pore. Calcium then enters and triggers the strengthening of the synapse.

3. In Aplysia, which neurotransmitter released by facilitating interneurons produces sensitization of the gill-withdrawal reflex?

Serotonin (5-HT). A tail shock activates interneurons that release serotonin onto the siphon sensory neuron's terminal. This increases transmitter release onto the gill motor neuron.

4. What task showed that Patient H.M. could still form procedural memories?

Mirror drawing. Brenda Milner had him trace a star while seeing only its reflection in a mirror. He improved over three days of practice but did not remember having done the task before.

5. Who shared the 2000 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Eric Kandel?

Arvid Carlsson and Paul Greengard. The prize recognized their discoveries about signal transduction in the nervous system. Kandel's part was showing how synapses change during learning and memory, using Aplysia.

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
1. Define memory consolidation in one sentence.
  2. Name the two main types of declarative memory and give an example of each.
Answer
  1. Memory consolidation is the gradual process that turns new, fragile memories into stable long-term memories.
  2. Episodic memory (a personal event, like your last birthday) and semantic memory (a fact, like "glutamate is excitatory").

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
1. Explain why habituation in Aplysia is considered learning and not just muscle fatigue.
  2. Explain, in your own words, how Hebbian learning could make a song remind you of a summer trip.
Answer
  1. Kandel's group showed the change happens at the synapse between the sensory neuron and the motor neuron, which releases less transmitter with each touch. The muscle and sense organ still work, and a tail shock can bring the response right back (dishabituation), which fatigue would not explain.
  2. During the trip, neurons representing the song and neurons representing the trip are active at the same time, so the connections between them strengthen. Later, activating the "song" neurons is enough to activate the "trip" neurons.

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
1. A new student moves next to a train track. At first, every train wakes her up. After two weeks, she sleeps through them. One night a smoke alarm goes off, and afterward she wakes up at the next train. Name the type of learning shown in each part of this story.
  2. Using what you learned about the spacing effect and late LTP, design a two-week study schedule for a 40-word vocabulary list. Explain why your schedule should work better than studying the night before.

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
1. Compare early LTP in the hippocampus with short-term sensitization in Aplysia. What is similar, and what is different?
  2. H.M. could not form new declarative memories, but many of his older memories survived. What does this tell you about where long-term declarative memories are stored, compared with where they are formed?

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
1. A company advertises an app that "identifies your learning style so you can study the way your brain prefers." Using evidence from this chapter, judge whether a student should pay for it.
  2. H.M.'s surgery was an experiment that caused permanent harm, yet it led to major discoveries. Today, surgeons would not do this operation. Evaluate how modern epilepsy surgery has changed because of what was learned.

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
1. Design a simple experiment, using classmates as volunteers, to test whether spaced study beats cramming. Name your two groups, what they study, how you will measure memory, and what result would support the spacing effect.
  2. Create a one-page comic strip in which a single synapse "narrates" what happens to it during habituation, sensitization, and long-term memory formation in Aplysia. Include serotonin, transmitter release, and new protein synthesis.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Learning changes the nervous system; memory is what that change stores. Memories move from short-term and working memory into long-term memory through consolidation.
  • Long-term memory has separate systems: declarative memory (facts and events) depends on the hippocampus and medial temporal lobe to form, while procedural memory (skills) relies on other circuits like the basal ganglia and cerebellum.
  • Patient H.M. lost the ability to form new declarative memories after both medial temporal lobes were removed in 1953, but he could still learn motor skills. His case showed that memory is a distinct brain function with several systems.
  • Neuroplasticity means the brain changes with experience at every age. Hebbian learning proposes that connections strengthen when neurons are active together.
  • Long-term potentiation is a lasting increase in synaptic strength. NMDA receptors act as coincidence detectors, letting in calcium that adds and boosts AMPA receptors.
  • In the Aplysia model, habituation weakens and sensitization strengthens the same sensory-to-motor synapse. Long-term memory there needs new proteins and new synaptic connections, work recognized with Kandel's 2000 Nobel Prize.
  • Spaced practice usually beats cramming for long-term memory. A leading explanation, best shown in animals like Aplysia, is that lasting synaptic changes need time and repeated activation to build.

You just rewired your brain!

Every big idea starts at a single synapse, and reading this chapter changed some of yours! Come back in a few days to make those changes last. Next, in Chapter 10, we'll look at sleep and how it connects to memory.

docs.title: Quiz: Learning, Memory, and Neuroplasticity
docs.text: Test your understanding of Chapter 9. Choose the best answer, then click Show Answer to check.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
Which type of memory lets you hold a few pieces of information in mind and work with them, such as numbers in a mental math problem, and then discard them?

  1. Procedural memory
  2. Working memory
  3. Episodic memory
  4. Semantic memory
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Working memory is the brain's "mental whiteboard": a short-term memory you actively use and then erase when you no longer need it. Episodic memory (C) is a long-term memory of personal events, not a temporary workspace.

Concept Tested: Working Memory Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
In 1953, which surgeon removed the medial temporal lobes on both sides of Henry Molaison's brain to treat his seizures?

  1. Wilder Penfield
  2. Eric Kandel
  3. Donald Hebb
  4. William Scoville
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. William Scoville, a neurosurgeon in Hartford, Connecticut, performed the bilateral medial temporal lobe resection. Brenda Milner then tested H.M. and reported the results with Scoville in 1957. Wilder Penfield (A) was a neurosurgeon whose own temporal lobe patients had memory problems, but he did not operate on H.M.

Concept Tested: Patient H.M. Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
In the Aplysia gill-withdrawal circuit, which neurotransmitter do facilitating interneurons release onto the siphon sensory neuron after a tail shock?

  1. Serotonin
  2. Dopamine
  3. GABA
  4. Acetylcholine
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A tail shock activates interneurons that release serotonin (5-HT) onto the sensory neuron's terminal, increasing transmitter release and producing sensitization. Dopamine (B) was the focus of Arvid Carlsson's Nobel work, not the transmitter in this circuit.

Concept Tested: Aplysia Model Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 4
docs.text:
Why is the NMDA receptor called a "coincidence detector" in long-term potentiation?

  1. It opens whenever glutamate binds, no matter what the postsynaptic cell is doing.
  2. It detects when two different neurotransmitters arrive at the same time.
  3. It opens only when glutamate is bound and the postsynaptic cell is already strongly depolarized.
  4. It fires an action potential only when two presynaptic neurons are active together.
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. At rest, a magnesium ion plugs the NMDA channel. Strong depolarization pops the plug out, so the channel passes current only when glutamate (from the sending cell) and depolarization (in the receiving cell) happen together. Option A describes AMPA receptors, which open with glutamate alone.

Concept Tested: Long-Term Potentiation Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 5
docs.text:
Kandel's group found that habituation of the gill-withdrawal reflex is caused mainly by which change?

  1. The gill muscle becomes tired after repeated contractions.
  2. The siphon sensory neuron releases less transmitter onto the motor neuron.
  3. The touch receptors in the siphon stop detecting touch.
  4. Serotonin is released onto the motor neuron.
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Habituation is learning at the synapse: with each repeated touch, the sensory neuron releases less transmitter, so the motor neuron gets a weaker signal. Muscle fatigue (A) is a common misconception; a tail shock can quickly restore the response (dishabituation), which fatigue would not explain.

Concept Tested: Habituation and Sensitization Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 6
docs.text:
Which statement best describes memory consolidation?

  1. The gradual process that turns new, fragile memories into stable long-term memories
  2. The instant copying of every experience into permanent storage
  3. The process of discarding information from working memory
  4. The loss of old memories that happens after a brain injury
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Consolidation takes time, and memories can be disrupted until it is complete. Option B reflects the "video recording" myth; memories are neither instant nor exact copies.

Concept Tested: Memory Consolidation Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 7
docs.text:
A 45-year-old man survives a brain infection that damaged both of his medial temporal lobes. He can repeat back a phone number right away and remembers his childhood clearly. But he cannot remember conversations from earlier in the day. Which problem best describes his memory loss?

  1. Retrograde amnesia only
  2. Loss of procedural memory
  3. Loss of working memory
  4. Anterograde amnesia
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. He can't form new long-term declarative memories, which is anterograde amnesia, like Patient H.M. His working memory (C) works, since he can repeat a number right away, and his old memories survive, so this isn't mainly retrograde amnesia (A).

Concept Tested: Amnesia Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 8
docs.text:
Maya has 100 minutes to study for a Brain Bee test that is two weeks away. Based on the spacing effect and what Kandel found about long-term memory in Aplysia, which plan should help her remember the most on test day?

  1. One 100-minute session the night before the test
  2. One 100-minute session today, then no review
  3. Five 20-minute sessions spread across the two weeks
  4. Two 50-minute sessions back to back the day before the test
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Spaced sessions usually produce better long-term memory than massed (crammed) sessions. In Aplysia, repeated spaced training is what triggers the new protein synthesis and synaptic growth needed for long-term memory. Option D is still massed practice, even though it is split into two parts.

Concept Tested: Learning Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 9
docs.text:
After a stroke, a patient clearly remembers her hospital stay and can describe new events in detail. However, she learns a new balance exercise much more slowly than expected, even after weeks of practice. Which comparison with Patient H.M. is most accurate?

  1. She has the same memory problem as H.M., only milder.
  2. Her problem is roughly the reverse of H.M.'s: her procedural memory is affected, while her declarative memory works.
  3. Like H.M., she has lost her working memory.
  4. Her problem shows that the hippocampus is needed for learning skills.
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. H.M. could learn motor skills such as mirror drawing but could not form new declarative memories. This patient shows the opposite pattern, which suggests damage to skill-learning circuits such as the cerebellum. Option D is wrong because H.M.'s case showed that skill learning does not depend on the hippocampus.

Concept Tested: Procedural Memory Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: Question 10
docs.text:
Short-term sensitization in Aplysia and early LTP in the hippocampus are similar to each other, and different from long-term memory, in which key way?

  1. Both change proteins already present at the synapse and do not need new protein synthesis.
  2. Both require the growth of new synaptic connections.
  3. Both happen only in the hippocampus.
  4. Both weaken the synapse instead of strengthening it.
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Short-term sensitization and early LTP both strengthen synapses by modifying existing proteins. Long-term sensitization and late LTP need new protein synthesis and can involve new synaptic connections, so option B describes the long-term forms instead.

Concept Tested: Neuroplasticity Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: References: Learning, Memory, and Neuroplasticity
docs.text:
1. The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2000: Press release - NobelPrize.org - The official announcement of the prize shared by Arvid Carlsson, Paul Greengard, and Eric Kandel. Its Kandel section explains, in plain language, how sea slug synapses store short-term and long-term memories.

  2. Eric R. Kandel: Nobel Lecture, "The Molecular Biology of Memory Storage: A Dialog between Genes and Synapses" - NobelPrize.org - Kandel's own account of the Aplysia experiments. It's challenging reading, but motivated students will see how a career-long research program unfolds.

  3. The molecular biology of memory: cAMP, PKA, CRE, CREB-1, CREB-2, and CPEB - Kandel, Molecular Brain (2012), PubMed Central - A free review of how habituation and sensitization change the sensory-to-motor synapse, and how long-term memory needs new proteins and new synapses. It's the source for the chapter's synapse-counting results.

  4. The Legacy of Patient H.M. for Neuroscience - Squire, Neuron (2009), PubMed Central - A clear, readable history of what five decades of testing H.M. taught scientists about memory systems, including the mirror-drawing experiment. It's the best single article on the case.

  5. Loss of Recent Memory After Bilateral Hippocampal Lesions - Scoville & Milner, Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery, and Psychiatry (1957), PubMed Central - The original 1957 report describing the memory loss that followed H.M.'s operation. Reading even the first pages shows what a landmark clinical paper looks like.

  6. Postmortem examination of patient H.M.'s brain based on histological sectioning and digital 3D reconstruction - Annese et al., Nature Communications (2014) - The open-access study that sliced and digitally rebuilt H.M.'s brain. It shows which parts of his hippocampus were actually removed and which survived.

  7. 18.1 Memory is Classified Based on Time Course and Type of Information Stored - OpenStax, Introduction to Behavioral Neuroscience (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) - A free textbook section on short-term, working, and long-term memory, consolidation, and reconsolidation. It's a good next step after this chapter.

  8. 18.4 Synaptic Mechanisms of Long-Term Memory - OpenStax, Introduction to Behavioral Neuroscience (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) - Explains LTP, LTD, NMDA and AMPA receptors, and the Bliss and Lømo experiment in more depth, with helpful diagrams.

  9. The right time to learn: mechanisms and optimization of spaced learning - Smolen, Zhang & Byrne, Nature Reviews Neuroscience (2016), PubMed Central - A review of why spaced training beats massed training, from sea slugs to people. It connects study habits directly to cell biology.

  10. Epilepsy and Seizures - National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS) - The NIH overview of epilepsy, including the hippocampus's role in temporal lobe epilepsy and how modern epilepsy surgery works. It shows how medicine changed after H.M.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Every night your brain moves through a predictable series of states, from relaxed waking to light sleep, deep slow-wave sleep, and dreaming REM sleep. This chapter explains how scientists read those states with the EEG, how a master clock in the hypothalamus times them, and why sleep matters for memory, mood, and safety. You'll see why teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep and why so few get it. Finally, you'll meet a teen with narcolepsy and learn how the loss of a small group of orexin neurons can make the boundary between waking and sleep fall apart.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 1: Neurons, Glia, and the Nervous System
  • Chapter 2: The Action Potential
  • Chapter 3: Synapses and Neurotransmitters
  • Chapter 4: A Tour of the Brain: Neuroanatomy
  • Chapter 9: Learning, Memory, and Neuroplasticity

Welcome to the night shift

I'm a sea slug, and even I have daily rhythms of rest and activity. You'll spend about a third of your life asleep, yet most people have no idea what their brain is doing during those hours. By the end of this chapter, you'll be able to read a night of sleep like a doctor reads a chart, and you'll know why your own sleep is worth protecting.

docs.title: 10.1 Maya's Six-Hour Nights
docs.text:
It's the middle of Brain Bee season, and Maya has a system. Soccer practice ends at 6, homework fills the evening, and after that she studies neuroanatomy flashcards until about 12:30 a.m. Her alarm goes off at 6:30. That's six hours of sleep on school nights. On Saturdays she sleeps until almost noon, and she figures that evens things out.

Lately, though, something is off. Facts she studied on Tuesday seem to have vanished by Thursday. She snapped at her younger brother over nothing. During a free period she put her head down "for a second" and woke up 20 minutes later. Maya is a smart, careful student, so she asks a fair question: Is six hours actually a problem, and if so, what exactly is her brain missing?

To answer her, we need to see what the brain does at night. Sleep is not one thing. It's a sequence of very different brain states, and the last hours before the alarm are not like the first.

docs.title: 10.2 Is the Brain Off When You Sleep? Consciousness and Brain States
docs.text:
Think about your school building at night. The halls are dark, but the custodians are cleaning and the computers are backing up. The building isn't off. It's in a different mode, doing work that can't happen during class. Your brain at night is a lot like that.

Consciousness is your state of awareness of yourself and your surroundings. In medicine, doctors often think about two parts: arousal (how awake you are) and awareness (what you are experiencing). In deep sleep, both drop. During dreaming (REM sleep), you are asleep and mostly cut off from the outside world, but you can still have vivid experiences inside your head.

A brain state is an overall pattern of activity across the brain that goes along with a certain level of consciousness. Waking, light sleep, deep sleep, and dreaming sleep are all different brain states. Each has its own electrical signature and chemistry.

The key idea for this chapter: the brain never shuts off during sleep. Neurons keep firing action potentials (you met these in Chapter 2). What changes is the pattern of firing, which neurons are active, and which neurotransmitters are being released.

docs.title: 10.3 Listening to the Brain: The EEG and Brain Waves
The stadium analogy
docs.text:
Imagine standing outside a packed football stadium with a microphone. If 70,000 fans are all chatting in small groups, your microphone picks up a low, fuzzy hum. You can't make out any single voice, and the sound is small. But if the whole crowd starts chanting together, slowly and in rhythm, your microphone picks up big, rolling waves of sound.

That is almost exactly how a brain recording works. Each neuron is one fan. When millions of cortical neurons are busy with different jobs, their electrical signals partly cancel out, and the recording looks small and fast. When large groups of neurons fire together in a slow rhythm, their signals add up into tall, slow waves.

docs.title: What an EEG measures
docs.text:
An electroencephalogram (EEG) is a recording of the brain's electrical activity made with small metal disks (electrodes) placed on the scalp. The electrodes don't record single action potentials. Instead, they pick up the combined, mostly synaptic electrical activity of huge numbers of cortical neurons lined up near the surface. (Those synaptic currents come from the receptor channels you studied in Chapter 3.)

The German psychiatrist Hans Berger recorded the first human EEG in 1924 and published his results in 1929. One of the first patterns he described was a rhythm of about 10 waves per second over the back of the head when a person relaxed with eyes closed. We now call it the alpha rhythm.

In a sleep study, the EEG is combined with sensors for eye movements, muscle tone, and breathing. That full overnight recording is called a polysomnogram.

docs.title: Brain waves
docs.text:
Brain waves are the repeating rhythms that show up in an EEG. Scientists describe them with two measurements:

  • Frequency: how many waves happen each second, measured in hertz (Hz). Ten waves per second is 10 Hz.
  • Amplitude: how tall the waves are, measured in microvolts (µV), or millionths of a volt.

Fast, small waves usually mean many neurons are doing different jobs. Slow, tall waves usually mean large groups of neurons are firing together in sync, like the chanting crowd. Now that both terms are defined, here is a summary of the main rhythms you'll meet in this chapter.

Brain wave Frequency (approx.) When you see it Beta faster than about 13 Hz Alert, eyes open, thinking hard Alpha about 8 to 13 Hz Awake and relaxed with eyes closed Theta about 4 to 7 Hz Drowsy; N1 sleep Delta (slow waves) below about 4 Hz; the slow waves that define N3 are 0.5 to 2 Hz and tall (over 75 µV) Deep N3 sleep

Slow and tall means in sync

Remember this one rule: tall, slow EEG waves mean lots of neurons are firing together. That's why deep sleep has the biggest waves of the night, even though you are the least aware you'll ever be.

docs.title: 10.4 The Clock Inside: Circadian Rhythms, the SCN, and Melatonin
A rhythm that keeps time on its own
docs.text:
Most people get sleepy around the same time each night, even without a bedtime rule. That's because your body runs on an internal clock.

A circadian rhythm is a cycle in the body or behavior that repeats about once every 24 hours. The word comes from Latin: circa ("about") and dies ("day"). Body temperature, hormone levels, alertness, and the timing of sleep all follow circadian rhythms.

The "about" matters. When people live in carefully controlled labs with no clues about the time of day, their clocks keep running, but not at exactly 24 hours. A well-known 1999 study found that the human circadian clock runs on an average cycle of about 24.18 hours (Czeisler and colleagues, Science, 1999). Each day, morning light nudges the clock back into step with the real day. Resetting a biological clock to match the outside world is called entrainment.

docs.title: The master clock: the suprachiasmatic nucleus
docs.text:
The brain's master clock is the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), a pair of tiny clusters of neurons in the hypothalamus. The name tells you where it sits: supra means "above," and the chiasm is the optic chiasm, where the two optic nerves cross. (You toured the hypothalamus in Chapter 4.)

That location is not an accident. The SCN needs to know when it's light outside. A special group of cells in the retina, called intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells, contain a light-sensitive pigment called melanopsin. These cells send signals straight to the SCN along a pathway called the retinohypothalamic tract. Melanopsin is most sensitive to blue light, at about 480 nanometers (OpenStax, Introduction to Behavioral Neuroscience, section 15.2).

Inside each SCN neuron, "clock genes" keep time with a feedback loop: the proteins CLOCK and BMAL1 turn on the Per and Cry genes, and the PER and CRY proteins slowly build up and switch CLOCK and BMAL1 back off. One full loop takes about a day.

docs.title: Melatonin: the darkness signal
docs.text:
The SCN controls many body rhythms, including the release of a hormone that signals "it's night." Melatonin is a hormone made by the pineal gland, a small gland deep in the brain. Melatonin levels are high at night and low during the day. Rising melatonin in the evening helps you feel sleepy as it gets dark (NINDS, Brain Basics: Understanding Sleep).

Bright light, especially at night, quickly lowers melatonin. That's one reason doctors and scientists talk so much about evening light from rooms and screens.

The flowchart below traces the pathway from light to melatonin that we just described.

flowchart LR
    A["Light enters the eye"] --> B["Melanopsin cells in the retina"]
    B -->|"retinohypothalamic tract"| C["SCN: master clock in the hypothalamus"]
    C --> D["Signals to the pineal gland"]
    D --> E["Melatonin: high at night, low by day"]
    A -. "light at night lowers melatonin" .-> E

docs.title: Two forces that time your sleep
docs.text:
The clock is only half the story. Scientists often describe sleep timing with a two-process model (OpenStax, section 15.3):

  • Process S (sleep pressure): the longer you stay awake, the stronger your need for sleep becomes. One chemical that builds up during waking is adenosine, which makes you feel sleepy. Caffeine works by blocking adenosine's effects, which is why coffee delays sleepiness without removing the need for sleep.
  • Process C (the circadian clock): the SCN pushes you toward alertness at some times of day and toward sleep at others, no matter how long you've been awake.

When both forces line up at night, falling asleep is easy. When they fight, as after flying across time zones, sleep gets harder.

docs.title: 10.5 A Night in Stages: NREM and REM Sleep
Sleep is a staircase, not a light switch
docs.text:
Falling asleep is less like flipping a switch and more like walking down a staircase into a basement, then climbing back up to a strange, busy attic, several times a night.

These steps are called sleep stages: distinct phases of sleep identified from the EEG, eye movements, and muscle tone. Under the scoring rules of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM), there are three stages of NREM sleep (N1, N2, and N3) and one stage of REM sleep. (Older books split deep sleep into "stage 3" and "stage 4." The current rules combine them into N3.)

docs.title: NREM sleep
docs.text:
NREM sleep (non-rapid eye movement sleep) is the part of sleep in which the eyes are mostly still and the EEG slows down step by step. It includes three stages.

  • N1 (falling asleep). This is the lightest stage and the doorway into sleep. It usually lasts only several minutes. The relaxed alpha rhythm fades and is replaced by slower theta waves of about 4 to 7 Hz.
  • N2 (light sleep). Two new EEG features appear. Sleep spindles are short bursts of fast waves, roughly 12 to 14 Hz, lasting at least half a second. K-complexes are single large waves: a sharp swing one way followed by a slower swing the other way. N2 takes up more of the night than any other stage (NINDS).
  • N3 (deep or slow-wave sleep). The EEG fills with tall, slow delta waves of about 0.5 to 2 Hz, over 75 µV in amplitude (Watson and colleagues, 2013). This is the deepest stage of sleep, and it's the hardest one to wake someone from. Most N3 happens in the first half of the night.

docs.title: REM sleep
docs.text:
REM sleep (rapid eye movement sleep) is the stage in which the eyes dart back and forth under closed lids, the EEG looks surprisingly like waking, and most of the body's muscles are temporarily paralyzed. It was first described by Eugene Aserinsky and Nathaniel Kleitman in a short 1953 paper in Science, after Aserinsky noticed bursts of rapid eye movements in sleeping people.

REM has three features worth remembering:

  1. An "awake-looking" EEG. The waves are low in amplitude and mixed in frequency. REM often includes runs of sawtooth waves (about 2 to 6 Hz), which look like the teeth of a saw.
  2. Rapid eye movements in bursts.
  3. Muscle atonia, a near-total loss of muscle tone in the arms and legs. The brainstem actively blocks movement signals so that you don't act out your dreams. Breathing muscles and eye muscles keep working.

Dreams are most vivid in REM, though people can dream in other stages too. Across a night, a person spends about two hours dreaming, even if they remember little of it (NINDS).

Four stages, one trick

That's a lot of vocabulary, so tie each stage to one picture: N1 is "drifting," N2 is "spindles," N3 is "big slow waves," and REM is "busy brain, frozen body." If you can sketch one wave for each, you're ready for the Brain Bee.

docs.title: Cycles across the night
docs.text:
A healthy sleeper goes N1 → N2 → N3 → back up to N2 → REM. That loop is one sleep cycle, and it takes about 90 minutes. The first REM period usually begins about 90 minutes after you fall asleep and lasts only about 10 minutes. Later REM periods get longer and can reach about an hour near morning (OpenStax, section 15.3).

So the night is lopsided:

  • Early night: mostly N2 and N3, with short REM periods.
  • Late night: little or no N3, with mostly N2 and long REM periods.

The table below sums up the four stages you just read about.

Stage Type EEG signature Body and experience N1 NREM Theta waves (about 4 to 7 Hz) Drifting off; easy to wake N2 NREM Sleep spindles and K-complexes Light sleep; largest share of the night N3 NREM Tall delta waves (about 0.5 to 2 Hz) Deep sleep; hard to wake; mostly early in the night REM REM Low-voltage, mixed, "awake-looking" Rapid eye movements, vivid dreams, limb muscles paralyzed; longer toward morning

docs.title: 10.6 Building a Hypnogram
docs.text:
A hypnogram is a graph of sleep stages across a night. Time runs left to right, and each stage gets its own row, with Wake at the top and N3 at the bottom. Sleep doctors make hypnograms from a polysomnogram.

The MicroSim below shows an illustrative hypnogram for a healthy teenager who sleeps 9 hours. With cycles of about 90 minutes, 9 hours holds roughly five or six cycles. The data are made up to show the typical pattern, not taken from a real person.

docs.title: Diagram: Hypnogram Builder
docs.text:
Open the Hypnogram Builder fullscreen

Content: Illustrative (not real) 540-minute teen night, six cycles of about 90 minutes. Totals: REM 135, N2 273, N3 113, N1 15, Wake 4 minutes. N3 only in the first four cycles; REM periods grow from 10 to 35 minutes. Schematic 3-second EEG per stage (alpha 8 to 13 Hz; theta 4 to 7 Hz; spindle about 12 to 14 Hz and K-complex; delta 0.5 to 2 Hz; low-voltage mixed waves with sawtooth waves), labeled "Schematic shape, not a real recording."

Controls: "Hours of sleep" slider (4 to 9 h, step 0.5, default 9). "Show EEG for" menu (default N3). "Reset to 9 h" button. Clicking a stage label or hovering over the night also selects a stage.

Chapter Anchors: cycles of about 90 minutes; most N3 in the first half of the night; REM periods longer toward morning; cutting 9 h to 6 h loses about half of REM and almost no N3.

Try this:

  1. Click each stage name on the left (or use the menu) and compare the EEG traces. Which stage has the tallest, slowest waves? Where do you see a spindle and a K-complex?
  2. Hover across the night from left to right. Notice where the N3 "valleys" are and how the red REM bars get longer as morning approaches.
  3. Now be Maya. Drag the Hours of sleep slider down to 6.0 h, which is like setting the alarm three hours early.

When you cut the night to 6 hours, almost all of the N3 survives, because deep sleep is packed into the early cycles. But you lose about half of the night's REM sleep (67 of 135 minutes in this example) and more than a third of N2. Short sleep doesn't shave a little off every stage evenly. It chops off the end of the night, where the longest REM periods live. Going to bed later with the same alarm has a similar effect.

docs.title: The librarian analogy
docs.text:
Picture a library. All day, returned books pile up on a small cart by the front desk. After closing, the librarian shelves each book where it belongs, next to related books. By morning the cart is empty and ready for a new day.

In Chapter 9, you learned that the hippocampus helps form new memories, while long-term storage depends heavily on the cortex. The hippocampus is like the cart, and the cortex is like the shelves. A lot of the sorting happens while you sleep.

docs.title: What sleep does for memory
docs.text:
Sleep and memory is the research area that studies how sleep strengthens and reorganizes what we learned while awake, a process called memory consolidation. Here's what researchers have found so far (Diekelmann and Born, Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 2010; Rasch and Born, Physiological Reviews, 2013):

  • During slow-wave (N3) sleep, slow oscillations in the cortex, sleep spindles, and fast bursts in the hippocampus appear to work together. They help replay new memories and move them from the hippocampus toward long-term storage in the cortex.
  • During REM sleep, brain activity and gene activity related to synaptic plasticity may help strengthen and stabilize those memories in cortical circuits.
  • Both kinds of sleep likely matter. The NINDS notes that memory consolidation most likely requires both NREM and REM sleep.

Sleep may also help the brain take out the trash. In a 2013 study in mice, the space between brain cells grew by about 60% during sleep, and a waste protein called beta-amyloid was cleared faster (Xie and colleagues, Science, 2013). This was a mouse study, and the idea is now debated. In 2024, a different team measured how fast a dye left the brains of mice and found that clearance was about 30% lower during sleep than during waking, and about 50% lower under anesthesia (Miao and colleagues, Nature Neuroscience, 2024; UK Dementia Research Institute summary). Other researchers have questioned that study's methods, and neither result has been settled in humans. As of 2026, "sleep washes waste out of the brain" is an exciting hypothesis, not an established fact.

docs.title: 10.8 Teen Sleep Needs and the Shifted Teen Clock
How much sleep do teens need?
docs.text:
Teen sleep needs refers to how much sleep adolescents require for good health, and it's more than most people think. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends that teenagers 13 to 18 years old sleep 8 to 10 hours per 24 hours on a regular basis (Paruthi and colleagues, Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine, 2016). The CDC uses the same range of 8 to 10 hours for teens (CDC, About Sleep). Adults 18 and older need 7 or more hours.

Very few teens reach that target. In the 2025 national Youth Risk Behavior Survey, only 24% of U.S. high school students (about 1 in 4) reported getting at least 8 hours of sleep on an average school night. That share did not change from 2023 to 2025, and it was lower in 2025 than in 2015 (CDC, YRBS: Sleep, 2026).

docs.title: The teen clock runs late
docs.text:
Part of the problem is biology. During puberty, circadian rhythms commonly shift later. Teens tend to feel sleepy later at night and need to sleep later in the morning (CDC, MMWR, 2015). This is not laziness. It's a real change in the timing of the clock.

Now add an early school bell. In 2014 the American Academy of Pediatrics recommended that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. But a CDC analysis of the 2011-12 school year found that the average start time for U.S. public middle and high schools was 8:03 a.m., and only 17.7% of these schools started at 8:30 or later (CDC, MMWR, 2015).

If your clock makes it hard to fall asleep before 11:30 p.m. and you must wake at 6:30 a.m., the most you can get is 7 hours.

Work with your clock, not against it

Your SCN listens to light. Bright light in the morning helps set your clock earlier, while bright light late at night pushes it later and lowers melatonin. A regular wake time, even on weekends, gives your clock a steady anchor.

docs.title: 10.9 Sleep Deprivation: What Short Sleep Costs
docs.text: Sleep deprivation means getting less sleep than your body needs. It can be acute (one all-nighter) or chronic (too little sleep night after night, like Maya's six-hour routine).

docs.title: The 6-hour experiment
docs.text:
One of the most important studies on chronic short sleep was done in a lab with 48 healthy adults (Van Dongen and colleagues, Sleep, 2003). Participants were assigned to spend 4, 6, or 8 hours in bed each night for 14 nights in a row (a fourth group stayed awake for three nights straight). The researchers tested their attention and thinking every day.

  • People limited to 6 hours or less got steadily worse over the two weeks.
  • By the end, their performance problems were as large as those seen after up to two full nights with no sleep at all.
  • The surprising part was that their ratings of their own sleepiness barely changed after the first few days. They didn't realize how impaired they had become.

That matters for Maya. She feels "used to" six hours, but her brain may be paying a price she can't feel.

docs.title: Effects across the body and mind
docs.text:
The National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute lists many effects of sleep deficiency (NHLBI), which we can group like this:

Area What short sleep can do Learning and attention Harder to learn, focus, and react quickly Mood and social life More frustration and worry; harder to read other people's emotions Safety Drowsy driving causes serious crashes, injuries, and deaths Long-term health Linked to high blood pressure, heart disease, diabetes, obesity, and depression

docs.title: Can you catch up on weekends?
docs.text:
Sleeping in on Saturday does help you feel better, and it partly pays back some sleep debt. But it doesn't fully undo a week of short nights. In a 2019 lab study of adults, a pattern of short weeknight sleep followed by weekend "recovery" sleep still disrupted the body's metabolism (Depner and colleagues, Current Biology, 2019). Big swings between weekday and weekend sleep times also create what scientists call social jet lag: returning to the weekday schedule on Monday is like adjusting to a new time zone (OpenStax, section 15.5).

So, back to Maya's question. Her six-hour nights cut off the REM-rich end of every night, they keep her in the zone where performance slips without her noticing, and her Saturday sleep-ins can't fully fix it. The forgotten facts, the short temper, and the accidental nap in study hall all fit.

docs.title: A light switch that needs a hand on it
docs.text:
Healthy people don't flicker in and out of sleep all day. Scientists describe this with a flip-flop switch model (OpenStax, section 15.3):

  • A sleep-promoting group of neurons in the hypothalamus releases the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA to quiet the wake centers.
  • Wake-promoting groups in the brainstem and hypothalamus release norepinephrine, serotonin, histamine, and acetylcholine, and they quiet the sleep center in return.

Because each side shuts down the other, the system tends to snap firmly into one state. But a switch like that can be wobbly. It works best when something holds it steady in the "awake" position during the day.

docs.title: Meet orexin
docs.text:
That stabilizer is orexin, also called hypocretin: a small signaling peptide made by a cluster of neurons in the lateral hypothalamus. It helps keep the brain awake and keeps the sleep-wake switch stable. Orexin neurons excite the wake-promoting centers, helping you stay awake through the day and preventing pieces of REM sleep from breaking into waking life.

Orexin has two names because two research teams discovered it at almost the same time in 1998. One team named the peptides "hypocretins" (de Lecea and colleagues, PNAS, 1998). The other named them "orexins," from the Greek word for appetite, because the team first studied their role in feeding (Sakurai and colleagues, Cell, 1998).

The link to sleep came from dogs. A research group had long studied a line of Doberman pinschers with inherited narcolepsy. In 1999 they showed that the dogs' disorder came from a mutation in the gene for orexin receptor 2 (Lin and colleagues, Cell, 1999). A year later, two groups studying human brains found that people with narcolepsy had lost most of their orexin. One reported an 85 to 95% reduction in the number of orexin neurons (Thannickal and colleagues, Neuron, 2000), and the other found a widespread absence of the orexin peptides themselves (Peyron and colleagues, Nature Medicine, 2000).

Missing orexin is not the same as being tired

Don't confuse narcolepsy with ordinary sleepiness from staying up late. A sleep-deprived teen has a working switch that's being pushed too hard. A person with narcolepsy type 1 has lost the hand that holds the switch steady, so even a full night's sleep doesn't fix the problem.

docs.title: At the Bedside: The Student Who Collapsed When She Laughed
docs.text:
Meet the patient

Alex is a 17-year-old high school senior. For about a year she has been falling asleep in class, sometimes in the middle of a test, even after 9 hours of sleep. She takes naps after school and wakes up feeling refreshed for a short while. Her friends have noticed something stranger: when she laughs hard at a joke, her head drops, her knees buckle, and once she slid to the floor. She stayed fully aware the whole time and could hear everyone, and it was over in less than a minute. She also reports waking up unable to move for a few seconds, sometimes while "seeing" a person standing in her room. Her parents first wondered if she was just staying up too late.

What the doctor checks: The doctor takes a careful history and asks Alex to keep a sleep diary for one to two weeks to make sure she isn't simply short on sleep. A neurological exam is normal. Next comes a sleep study in two parts (NINDS).

First, an overnight polysomnogram records her EEG, eye movements, muscle tone, and breathing. The next day, a multiple sleep latency test (MSLT) gives her several scheduled nap chances and measures how fast she falls asleep and whether she goes straight into REM. Under current diagnostic criteria, narcolepsy is supported by an average time to fall asleep of 8 minutes or less across the naps, plus REM sleep appearing soon after sleep onset at least twice (in the naps, or in the naps plus the night before) (Reiter and colleagues, Sleep, 2015). Alex falls asleep in about 3 minutes on average and enters REM in three of five naps. Doctors can also measure orexin (hypocretin-1) in spinal fluid from a lumbar puncture; very low levels confirm type 1.

Where is the problem? (localization): Two clues point to the hypothalamus. First, Alex is sleepy all day despite enough sleep, so the system that holds wakefulness is failing. Second, pieces of REM sleep are breaking into waking life: losing muscle tone while awake is REM atonia at the wrong time, and "seeing" a figure while paralyzed on waking is a dream overlapping with waking. The neurons that keep the wake switch stable and keep REM in its place are the orexin neurons of the lateral hypothalamus.

Diagnosis: Narcolepsy type 1 (narcolepsy with cataplexy). Narcolepsy is a chronic neurological disorder in which the brain can't properly control the sleep-wake cycle. Type 1 is defined by excessive daytime sleepiness plus either very low orexin in spinal fluid or cataplexy with a positive MSLT. Cataplexy is a sudden loss of muscle tone, often triggered by strong emotions like laughter, during which the person stays conscious. Narcolepsy type 1 affects an estimated 1 in 2,000 people in the U.S. (FDA, 2026), and symptoms usually begin between ages 7 and 25 (NINDS).

Why it happens: Nearly everyone with type 1 has extremely low orexin, mostly because the orexin-making neurons in the hypothalamus have been lost. Scientists think the most likely cause is an attack by the person's own immune system on these neurons, together with genetic and environmental factors. A gene variant called HLA-DQB1*06:02 raises the risk, and new cases have followed infections such as strep throat and the 2009 H1N1 flu (NINDS). Without orexin, the flip-flop switch from Section 10.10 becomes unstable, so Alex slips into sleep by day and REM features leak into wakefulness.

Treatment today: There's no cure, but treatment can control symptoms well, and it often takes time to find the right mix (NINDS). Care usually combines:

  • Healthy sleep habits: a regular sleep schedule and short planned naps during the day.
  • Wake-promoting medicines and stimulants for daytime sleepiness.
  • Sodium oxybate, which is FDA-approved for cataplexy and daytime sleepiness and is distributed under tight restrictions.
  • Pitolisant, a medicine that acts on histamine receptors and is approved for daytime sleepiness in adults and in children 6 and older.
  • Certain antidepressants, which can reduce cataplexy.
  • Support at school and safety planning, such as scheduled nap breaks during the day and talking with the doctor about when driving is safe.

What's new in research: On August 5, 2026, the FDA approved oveporexton (brand name Orzeyful), a twice-daily tablet that activates orexin receptor 2. According to the FDA, it directly activates the same brain receptor that the body's own orexin would normally stimulate, standing in for the missing signal rather than only treating individual symptoms (FDA press announcement, August 5, 2026). The approval is for adults with narcolepsy type 1. Its safety and effectiveness have not been established in people under 18, so for 17-year-old Alex it is not yet an approved option. The path to this drug ran straight from the orexin discoveries in Section 10.10.

Your turn: diagnose a variation

Jordan, 16, is also falling asleep in class. Jordan has never had sudden weakness when laughing or startled. A sleep diary shows Jordan sleeps about 5.5 hours on school nights (gaming until after 1 a.m., alarm at 6:45) and 11 hours on weekends. After two weeks of going to bed earlier and getting 9 hours a night, the daytime sleepiness mostly goes away. What is the most likely explanation, and why is it probably not narcolepsy type 1?

Answer: The most likely explanation is chronic insufficient sleep, or sleep deprivation. Jordan has no cataplexy, and the sleepiness improves once Jordan gets enough sleep. That points to a working sleep-wake switch that has simply been shortchanged, not lost orexin neurons. This is why doctors check a sleep diary before an MSLT: a person who is simply short on sleep can also fall asleep quickly during nap tests.

This is a fictional teaching case. It is not medical advice. If you or someone you know has symptoms like these, talk to a doctor.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
Myth: "The brain shuts off when you sleep." Reality: The brain stays active all night. It cycles through distinct states, and during REM sleep the EEG looks much like it does when you're awake. Sleep is a change in the pattern of activity, not an off switch.

Myth: "You can catch up on all your lost sleep on the weekend." Reality: Sleeping in helps you feel better, but it doesn't fully undo a week of short nights. A lab study found that weekday short sleep plus weekend catch-up sleep still disrupted metabolism, and big weekend schedule swings cause social jet lag.

Myth: "After a while, your body gets used to six hours of sleep." Reality: In the 14-day lab study, people on 6 hours a night kept getting worse at attention tasks, but they felt only a little sleepier. Feeling used to short sleep is not the same as performing well.

Myth: "Teens stay up late only because they're lazy or glued to their phones." Reality: Screens and habits can make it worse, but puberty itself commonly shifts the circadian clock later. That's a big reason the American Academy of Pediatrics and the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommend middle and high school start times of 8:30 a.m. or later (AASM position statement, 2017).

Myth: "People with narcolepsy are just very tired." Reality: Narcolepsy type 1 is a neurological disorder caused by the loss of orexin neurons. Its symptoms, like cataplexy and sleep paralysis, come from REM sleep breaking into waking. Ordinary sleep loss does not cause cataplexy.

docs.title: Brain Bee Practice
docs.text:
1. Which brain structure is the body's master circadian clock, and where is it located?

The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN). It's in the hypothalamus, just above the optic chiasm, where it receives light information from the retina.

2. Name two EEG features that mark stage N2 sleep.

Sleep spindles (brief bursts of fast waves, roughly 12 to 14 Hz) and K-complexes (single large waves with a sharp swing followed by a slower swing in the opposite direction).

3. Why is REM sleep sometimes called 'paradoxical sleep'?

During REM sleep the EEG looks much like waking, with low-voltage, mixed fast activity, yet the person is deeply asleep and most body muscles are paralyzed. An awake-looking brain inside a sleeping, motionless body is the paradox.

4. A patient has sudden loss of muscle tone when laughing but stays fully conscious. What is this symptom called, and which neurons are usually lost?

Cataplexy. It's the hallmark of narcolepsy type 1, which is caused by the loss of orexin (hypocretin) neurons in the lateral hypothalamus.

5. Which hormone does the pineal gland release at night, and what does light do to it?

Melatonin. Bright light, especially at night, quickly lowers melatonin levels.

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
1. List the four sleep stages used in current sleep scoring, and say which ones are NREM.
  2. What does the abbreviation EEG stand for, and what does it measure?
Answer
  1. N1, N2, N3, and REM. N1, N2, and N3 are NREM stages.
  2. Electroencephalogram. It records the combined electrical activity of large groups of cortical neurons using electrodes on the scalp.

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
1. Explain in your own words why deep N3 sleep produces taller EEG waves than waking does.
  2. Describe how light reaching the eye can change melatonin levels. Name the structures in the pathway.
Answer
  1. In N3, large groups of cortical neurons fire together in a slow rhythm, so their electrical signals add up into tall, slow waves. When you're awake, neurons are doing many different jobs at different times, so their signals partly cancel out and the EEG looks small and fast.
  2. Light activates melanopsin-containing retinal ganglion cells, which signal the SCN through the retinohypothalamic tract. The SCN controls the pineal gland, and light (especially at night) lowers the pineal gland's release of melatonin.

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
1. Using the Hypnogram Builder, set the slider to 7.5 hours. Record how many minutes of REM and N3 are kept, then explain why one stage loses more than the other.
  2. A friend says, "I'll just drink an energy drink, so I don't need sleep." Use the idea of adenosine and sleep pressure to explain what caffeine does and doesn't do.

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
1. Two hypnograms are shown to you. Night A has N3 in the first three cycles and REM periods that get longer through the night. Night B has REM appearing within a few minutes of falling asleep and several brief awakenings. Which night is more consistent with narcolepsy, and what evidence supports your answer?
  2. Compare sleep deprivation and narcolepsy type 1. How are their causes different, even though both cause daytime sleepiness?

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
1. Your school board is debating whether to move the high school start time from 7:30 a.m. to 8:30 a.m. Using evidence from this chapter, write a short argument for or against the change. Include at least one possible drawback.
  2. A sleep-tracking app claims it can tell you exactly how many minutes of REM you got last night using only your phone's motion sensor. Judge how trustworthy that number is, given how sleep stages are actually scored.

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
1. Design a two-week experiment to test whether getting 9 hours of sleep instead of 6 improves vocabulary recall in high school students. Describe your groups, what you would measure, and how you would make the comparison fair.
  2. Create a one-page poster for your school that explains teen sleep needs using accurate facts from this chapter and one hypnogram drawing.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The brain never shuts off during sleep. It moves through distinct brain states that the EEG can tell apart by frequency and amplitude.
  • Sleep has NREM stages (N1, N2, N3) and REM sleep. Cycles last about 90 minutes, with most deep N3 early in the night and the longest REM periods near morning.
  • The suprachiasmatic nucleus in the hypothalamus is the master circadian clock. Light reaches it from the retina, and it controls the pineal gland's release of melatonin.
  • Sleep helps consolidate memories, with slow-wave sleep and REM sleep likely playing complementary roles.
  • Teens need 8 to 10 hours of sleep, but puberty shifts the clock later, and only about 1 in 4 U.S. high school students got 8 hours on school nights in the 2025 CDC survey.
  • Cutting sleep short mostly removes late-night REM and N2, and chronic short sleep impairs performance even when people don't feel it.
  • Narcolepsy type 1 is caused by the loss of orexin (hypocretin) neurons, which destabilizes the sleep-wake switch and lets REM features like cataplexy intrude into waking.

You made it through the night!

You can now read a hypnogram, name every sleep stage by its brain waves, and explain why a missing peptide can make someone collapse with laughter. Next, in Chapter 11, we'll look at emotion and stress, and how the brain and body react when life gets intense.

docs.title: Quiz: Sleep and Brain States
docs.text: Test your understanding of Chapter 10. Choose the best answer, then click Show Answer to check.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
Which structure is the brain's master circadian clock?

  1. The pineal gland
  2. The hippocampus
  3. The suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus
  4. The thalamus
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), which sits just above the optic chiasm in the hypothalamus, is the master clock. The pineal gland is a common wrong answer because it releases melatonin, but it takes its timing orders from the SCN rather than keeping time itself.

Concept Tested: Suprachiasmatic Nucleus Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
Which EEG features are the signature of stage N2 sleep?

  1. Sleep spindles and K-complexes
  2. Alpha waves over the back of the head
  3. Sawtooth waves and rapid eye movements
  4. Tall delta waves filling most of the recording
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. N2 is marked by sleep spindles (short bursts of roughly 12 to 14 Hz waves) and K-complexes (single large waves). Tall delta waves are tempting because N2 is "real" sleep, but they define the deeper stage, N3.

Concept Tested: NREM Sleep Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
How much sleep does the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommend for teenagers ages 13 to 18?

  1. 6 to 7 hours per night
  2. 7 or more hours, the same as adults
  3. 10 to 12 hours per night
  4. 8 to 10 hours per 24 hours
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The AASM recommends 8 to 10 hours per 24 hours for teens, and the CDC uses the same range. "7 or more hours" is the recommendation for adults 18 and older, not for teens.

Concept Tested: Teen Sleep Needs Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 4
docs.text:
Why does an EEG during deep N3 sleep show taller waves than an EEG during alert waking?

  1. Neurons fire much stronger action potentials during deep sleep.
  2. Large groups of cortical neurons fire together in a slow rhythm, so their signals add up.
  3. The electrodes are pressed closer to the scalp when a person lies down.
  4. Fewer neurons are active, so the remaining ones are easier to record.
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Tall, slow waves appear when many neurons are synchronized, so their electrical signals add together instead of canceling out. Option A is a common mix-up: individual action potentials are all-or-none and don't get "bigger" in sleep; it's the synchrony that changes.

Concept Tested: Brain Waves Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 5
docs.text:
What is the main job of melatonin in the sleep-wake cycle?

  1. It is a nighttime hormone from the pineal gland that signals darkness and helps you feel sleepy.
  2. It builds up in the brain the longer you stay awake and is blocked by caffeine.
  3. It is made by neurons in the lateral hypothalamus and keeps you awake during the day.
  4. It is released in bright morning light to wake you up.
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Melatonin rises at night, is lowered by bright light, and helps you feel sleepy as it gets dark. Option B describes adenosine (sleep pressure), and option C describes orexin, which promotes wakefulness.

Concept Tested: Melatonin Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 6
docs.text:
Which statement best describes how REM sleep is distributed across a normal night?

  1. REM happens once, right after falling asleep.
  2. REM periods are about the same length all night.
  3. REM periods start short and get longer toward morning.
  4. REM is concentrated in the first half of the night, along with deep sleep.
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The first REM period begins about 90 minutes after sleep onset and is short, and later REM periods can last about an hour. Option D is a common mix-up: it's N3, not REM, that is packed into the first half of the night.

Concept Tested: REM Sleep Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 7
docs.text:
Maya usually sleeps 9 hours, but during exam week her alarm cuts her nights to 6 hours. Based on a typical hypnogram, which stage will she lose the most of, as a share of its usual total?

  1. N3 deep sleep
  2. REM sleep
  3. N1 sleep
  4. All stages equally
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Cutting the night short removes the last hours, which hold the longest REM periods, so about half of REM can be lost. N3 is the tempting answer because people think of it as "the important sleep," but it is concentrated early in the night and mostly survives a 6-hour night.

Concept Tested: Sleep Stages Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 8
docs.text:
A student says, "I've slept 6 hours a night for two weeks, and I feel totally used to it, so my brain must be fine." Based on the 14-day sleep-restriction study described in the chapter, what is the best response?

  1. You're right. After about a week, the brain fully adapts to 6 hours.
  2. Feeling fine means your performance is fine, because sleepiness is the best measure of impairment.
  3. Only people sleeping 4 hours or less showed any decline.
  4. People on 6 hours kept getting worse at attention tests while rating themselves only slightly sleepier.
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. In that study, people limited to 6 hours or less showed steadily growing deficits, eventually similar to up to two nights without sleep, yet their sleepiness ratings barely changed. Option C is wrong because the 6-hour group also declined.

Concept Tested: Sleep Deprivation Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 9
docs.text:
A 17-year-old falls asleep in class despite sleeping 9 hours, and her knees buckle when she laughs, though she stays fully aware. On an MSLT she falls asleep within minutes and enters REM in several naps. Which explanation best fits?

  1. Chronic insufficient sleep from staying up late
  2. Seizures starting in the temporal lobe
  3. Loss of orexin neurons, letting REM features intrude into waking
  4. Overproduction of melatonin by the pineal gland
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Sleepiness despite enough sleep plus emotion-triggered weakness with preserved awareness (cataplexy) points to narcolepsy type 1, caused by loss of orexin neurons in the lateral hypothalamus. Option A is the main distractor, but insufficient sleep doesn't cause cataplexy, and she is already sleeping 9 hours.

Concept Tested: Narcolepsy Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: Question 10
docs.text:
Researchers found that Doberman pinschers with inherited narcolepsy carry a mutation in the gene for orexin receptor 2, and that people with narcolepsy have lost most of their orexin neurons. What do these two findings together suggest?

  1. Narcolepsy in people is caused by the same receptor mutation found in the dogs.
  2. Orexin signaling is needed to keep the sleep-wake switch stable, whether the problem is the signal or its receptor.
  3. Orexin is mainly a feeding hormone with no real role in sleep.
  4. Narcolepsy is caused by too much orexin activity in the brain.
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Breaking the system at the receptor (dogs) or at the source of the signal (human orexin neurons) produces the same disorder, which shows that orexin signaling stabilizes wakefulness. Option A is tempting, but most human cases involve loss of orexin neurons, not receptor mutations.

Concept Tested: Orexin (Hypocretin) Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: References: Sleep and Brain States
docs.text:
1. Brain Basics: Understanding Sleep - National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NIH) - A clear overview of NREM and REM sleep, the brain structures and chemicals that control sleep (including the SCN, melatonin, adenosine, and orexin), and how sleep needs change with age. A great first stop for reviewing this whole chapter.

  2. Narcolepsy - National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NIH) - Explains the symptoms, types, causes, diagnostic tests, and current treatments for narcolepsy, including the 2026 approval of an orexin-based medicine. Useful background for the Bedside case.

  3. About Sleep - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention - Lists recommended hours of sleep for every age group, including 8 to 10 hours for teens, with links to the expert statements behind each number. Handy for checking your own sleep target.

  4. Recommended Amount of Sleep for Pediatric Populations: A Consensus Statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine - Paruthi and colleagues, Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine (2016) - The short, official expert statement that sets the recommendation of 8 to 10 hours for ages 13 to 18 and summarizes the health risks of regularly getting less. It's only two pages, so it's a good first research paper to read.

  5. School Start Times for Middle School and High School Students: United States, 2011-12 School Year - CDC, Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (2015) - Reports how early U.S. middle and high schools start and explains why the teen circadian clock shifts later during puberty. Useful evidence for any school start time debate.

  6. 15.3 Regulation of Sleep - OpenStax, Introduction to Behavioral Neuroscience (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) - A free college-level textbook section on the two-process model, sleep stages, sleep cycles, and the flip-flop switch. Read it when you want more depth than this chapter gives.

  7. 15.2 Where Are Rhythms in the Brain? - OpenStax, Introduction to Behavioral Neuroscience (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) - Covers the suprachiasmatic nucleus, light-sensing retinal cells and melanopsin, clock genes, and melatonin. Good for students who want to understand how a group of cells can keep time.

  8. What Are Sleep Deprivation and Deficiency? - National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NIH) - Describes how too little sleep affects learning, mood, safety, and long-term health. A clear, trustworthy source for health class projects on sleep.

  9. About Sleep's Role in Memory - Rasch and Born, Physiological Reviews (2013) - A detailed review of how slow-wave sleep, sleep spindles, and REM sleep may help consolidate memories. It's advanced, but the introduction and figures are readable for motivated high school students.

  10. Reduced Number of Hypocretin Neurons in Human Narcolepsy - Thannickal and colleagues, Neuron (2000) - The landmark study showing that people with narcolepsy have lost 85 to 95% of their orexin (hypocretin) neurons. A good example of how a careful look at brain tissue can reveal the cause of a disease.

docs.title: Chapter 11: Emotion, Stress, and the Body
Chapter 11: Emotion, Stress, and the Body
Summary
docs.text: Emotions are more than feelings. They are whole-body responses run by a network of brain regions, with the amygdala as one key hub. In this chapter you'll learn how the brain learns what to fear and how it triggers two stress systems: a fast, nerve-based "fight-or-flight" response and a slower hormone chain called the HPA axis, which releases cortisol. You'll see why a short burst of stress is healthy, why stress that never switches off wears the body and brain down, and how people regulate their emotions. The chapter ends at the bedside with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) after a car crash, and the treatments that help.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
1. Emotion
  2. Limbic System
  3. Amygdala
  4. Fear Conditioning
  5. Stress Response
  6. HPA Axis
  7. Cortisol
  8. Fight or Flight
  9. Chronic Stress Effects
  10. Emotion Regulation
  11. Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 1: Neurons, Glia, and the Nervous System
  • Chapter 2: The Action Potential
  • Chapter 3: Synapses and Neurotransmitters
  • Chapter 4: A Tour of the Brain: Neuroanatomy
  • Chapter 9: Learning, Memory, and Neuroplasticity

Why your heart pounds

Even I pull my gill in fast when something pokes my tail, and I only have about 20,000 neurons! You have billions, and some of them are wired to keep you alive when danger shows up. In this chapter we'll follow a scare from your eyes to your hormones and back again. Once you understand your stress system, it gets a lot less mysterious.

docs.title: 11.1 Maya's Racing Heart
docs.text:
It's 7:55 a.m., five minutes before Maya's chemistry test. She studied. She knows the material. But her heart is pounding, her palms are damp, her mouth is dry, and her stomach feels like it's doing laps. When the teacher hands out the papers, Maya's mind goes blank for a second, and then, slowly, the answers come back.
