Brains that struggle are still brains

Hi, I'm Ply, and this may be the most personal chapter in the book. Almost everyone knows someone with depression, anxiety, ADHD, autism, or a substance use problem. Here, everything you learned about synapses and learning explains these conditions with science instead of blame, and knowing how to spot an overdose could let you save a life.

docs.title: 15.1 Maya's Friend and the Vape
docs.text:
Maya is 16, plays soccer, and is studying for the Brain Bee. After practice, her friend Jordan pulls out a small, colorful vape. "It's not like smoking," Jordan says. "It just helps me relax before a test." Lately Jordan vapes before first period, between classes, and on the bus. On a weekend trip without the vape, Jordan was irritable, couldn't focus, and talked about little else.

Maya has a Brain Bee question of her own: what is nicotine doing to Jordan's brain? To answer it, we need to know how the brain decides what is worth repeating (the reward pathway), how synapses adjust to a drug that keeps flooding them (tolerance), and why stopping feels so bad (withdrawal). First, though, we'll survey the conditions psychiatrists treat, because many involve the same circuits.

If you need help now

If you or someone you know is struggling, call or text 988 (the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline in the U.S.). It is free, confidential, and available 24/7. You can also chat at 988lifeline.org.

For substance use or mental health treatment referrals, call SAMHSA's National Helpline at 1-800-662-4357 (1-800-662-HELP). It is free, confidential, open 24/7, 365 days a year, and available in English and Spanish.

If someone may be overdosing, call 911.

docs.title: 15.2 What Is a Mental Illness?
docs.text:
Start with an everyday picture. Think of the brain as a sound mixing board with thousands of sliders: how alert you feel, how much you worry, how much you enjoy things. Everyone's board is set a little differently, and the settings shift with sleep, stress, and life events. Usually the board adjusts itself. Sometimes a group of sliders gets stuck far out of range for weeks or months, and studying, sleeping, or connecting with others suffers. That is closer to what a mental illness is. The picture has a limit, though: the real brain has no single slider for worry or joy. Each "setting" comes from many circuits, genes, and experiences working together.

A mental illness is a condition that affects a person's thinking, emotions, or behavior in a lasting way and causes real distress or makes daily life harder. The National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) separates "any mental illness" (mild to severe) from "serious mental illness," which seriously limits major life activities. These conditions involve the brain, genes, the body, relationships, and environment. None are character flaws.

Mental illness is common. In 2025, an estimated 54.6 million U.S. adults, or 20.6%, had a mental illness in the past year, according to the National Survey on Drug Use and Health (NSDUH). Teens are affected too. In the same survey, about 15.1% of U.S. adolescents aged 12 to 17 (3.7 million) had a major depressive episode in the past year, down from 20.8% in 2021 (SAMHSA, 2025 NSDUH). The survey changed how it estimates adult mental illness in 2025, so these adult numbers can't be compared directly with older published figures, such as the 23.1% for 2022 that NIMH still lists (NIMH).

How do doctors tell a disorder from a hard week? They look at:

  • How long the symptoms last (for example, at least two weeks for depression)
  • How much the symptoms disrupt school, work, relationships, or self-care
  • Whether something else explains the symptoms better, such as a thyroid problem, a medication, or a drug

Clinicians use criteria from the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders to make these calls consistently. The current version is the DSM-5-TR, a text revision of the fifth edition released in 2022 (American Psychiatric Association). No single blood test or brain scan diagnoses these conditions today. Diagnosis comes from a careful interview and observation, plus tests to rule out other medical causes.

docs.title: Depression
docs.text:
Everyone feels sad sometimes. Depression (also called major depressive disorder or clinical depression) is different. It is a mood disorder in which a person has a low or "empty" mood, or loses interest and pleasure in most activities, for most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks (NIMH). Other common symptoms include:

  • Hopelessness, guilt, or feeling worthless
  • Fatigue, trouble concentrating, and changes in sleep and appetite
  • Aches and pains without a clear physical cause
  • Thoughts of death or suicide

Notice how many symptoms involve the body, not just mood. Sleep, appetite, and energy depend partly on the hypothalamus and the stress system from Chapter 11. NIMH describes the causes of depression as a mix of genetic, biological, environmental, and psychological factors.

Depression is treatable. Evidence-based talk therapies include cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), which helps people change unhelpful thoughts and behaviors. Antidepressant medicines usually take about 4 to 8 weeks to work. When other treatments haven't helped, doctors may use brain stimulation, such as electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) or repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) (NIMH).

docs.title: Is depression a "chemical imbalance"?
docs.text:
You may have heard that depression is caused by "low serotonin." This idea, the monoamine hypothesis, guided drug development for decades because many antidepressants raise serotonin or norepinephrine at synapses. The full story is more complicated.

  • If low serotonin were the whole cause, antidepressants should work within hours, because they raise serotonin at synapses quickly. Instead, they take weeks.
  • Not everyone responds to medicines that target serotonin.
  • A 2022 umbrella review in Molecular Psychiatry looked across many kinds of serotonin research and found no consistent evidence that depression is caused by lowered serotonin (Moncrieff et al., 2022). Other scientists debated some of its methods and conclusions. Most experts now describe depression as having many interacting causes rather than one missing chemical.

Still, "not caused by low serotonin" does not mean "antidepressants don't work" or "depression isn't real." Antidepressants help many people, possibly by changing how brain circuits adapt over weeks. One idea links long-term stress to lower levels of brain growth factors, and antidepressants to higher levels (OpenStax, 14.2). Current views treat depression as the result of many interacting biological, psychological, and social factors.

A traffic jam, not an empty tank

I like to picture depression less like a car with an empty gas tank and more like a city with a long-lasting traffic jam. Many roads, signals, and drivers are involved, so there is more than one way to help traffic flow again: medicine, therapy, sleep, exercise, and support can each open a different road.

docs.title: Anxiety disorders
docs.text:
Anxiety is a normal alarm. Before Maya's Brain Bee competition, her heart races, a response driven by the amygdala and stress hormones from Chapter 11. Anxiety disorders are conditions in which fear or worry is too strong, lasts too long, shows up across many situations, and interferes with daily life. They are among the most common mental health conditions: based on large national surveys done in the early 2000s, NIMH reports that about a third of U.S. adolescents and adults experience an anxiety disorder at some point (NIMH).

The table below compares the main types.

Anxiety disorder Core experience Example Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) Hard-to-control worry on most days for at least 6 months, plus symptoms like restlessness, fatigue, muscle tension, or poor sleep Constant worry about grades, family, and health, even when things are going fine Panic disorder Repeated, unexpected surges of intense fear with a pounding heart, shortness of breath, or dizziness Sudden fear in class that feels like a heart attack Social anxiety disorder Intense fear of being judged or embarrassed in social situations Avoiding raising a hand or eating in the cafeteria Specific phobias Strong fear of a specific object or situation Fear of needles that makes a person skip doctor visits

For GAD, NIMH calls CBT the "gold standard" talk therapy. Medicines such as SSRIs and SNRIs (two antidepressant classes) can also help, though they take several weeks. Benzodiazepines act quickly, but people can develop tolerance and dependence, so doctors use them with caution and usually only briefly (NIMH).

docs.title: 15.4 Schizophrenia
docs.text:
Schizophrenia is a serious mental illness that affects how a person thinks, feels, and behaves. People are usually first diagnosed between ages 16 and 30, after a first episode of psychosis, a state in which a person loses some contact with reality (NIMH). Doctors group the symptoms into three families (NIMH):

  • Psychotic (positive) symptoms are experiences added to normal life: hallucinations (hearing or seeing things others don't, often voices), delusions (firm beliefs that are not true, such as being watched), and disorganized thinking or speech.
  • Negative symptoms are abilities that are reduced: less motivation, less emotional expression, less speech, and pulling away from friends. They are sometimes mistaken for depression.
  • Cognitive symptoms are problems with attention, concentration, and memory that make school or work harder.

Schizophrenia runs in families, but no single gene causes it. Many genes each add a little risk, which may combine with life experiences such as stressful surroundings or exposures before birth. Imaging studies find subtle differences in the size of some brain areas and in their connections.

The best-known chemical clue involves dopamine. Most older antipsychotic medicines block dopamine D2 receptors, and they reduce hallucinations and delusions. This led to the "dopamine hypothesis": too much dopamine signaling in certain pathways may drive psychotic symptoms. Like the serotonin story for depression, this is only part of the picture. Antipsychotics help negative and cognitive symptoms much less, and newer medicines act on several receptor types (OpenStax, 14.2). In September 2024, the FDA approved xanomeline and trospium chloride (Cobenfy) for adults with schizophrenia. It is the first antipsychotic that targets acetylcholine (cholinergic) receptors instead of dopamine receptors, more evidence that dopamine is not the whole story (FDA).

Treatment works best as a team effort: antipsychotic medicine reduces psychotic symptoms, and psychosocial treatments help with daily skills, school, and work. For first-episode psychosis, coordinated specialty care, a team-based, recovery-focused approach that includes the person and their family, is more effective at reducing symptoms than typical care (NIMH).

Two facts fight stigma. Schizophrenia is not "split personality," which is a different condition (dissociative identity disorder). And most people with schizophrenia are not violent. In fact, they are more likely than people without the illness to be harmed by others (NIMH).

docs.title: 15.5 Developmental Differences: Autism and ADHD
docs.text:
Neurodevelopmental conditions begin in early brain development and shape how a person experiences the world from childhood on. The neurodiversity perspective points out that human brains naturally vary, and that some differences bring real strengths as well as real challenges. Supports should help people thrive, not force everyone into one mold.

A note on language: many autistic people prefer identity-first language ("autistic person"), while others prefer person-first language ("person with autism"). This chapter uses both. When you're unsure how someone describes themselves, ask, and use what they prefer.

docs.title: Autism spectrum disorder
docs.text:
Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurological and developmental condition that affects how people communicate, interact with others, learn, and behave. It has two core features (NIMH):

  1. Differences in social communication and interaction, such as reading facial expressions, taking turns in conversation, or understanding unwritten social rules.
  2. Restricted interests and repetitive behaviors, such as deep focus on favorite topics, strong preference for routines, repeated movements, or being over- or under-sensitive to sounds, lights, or textures.

It is called a spectrum because autistic people have a wide range of characteristics, needs, strengths, and challenges. One person may speak little and need daily support; another may excel at programming but find crowded hallways exhausting. Signs usually appear in the first two years of life.

The CDC's monitoring network estimated that about 1 in 31 (3.2%) 8-year-old children had been identified with autism in 2022 (the latest estimate as of 2026, published in 2025), and boys were identified more than three times as often as girls (CDC).

The primary causes are not fully known. Genes play a large role, and risk factors include having an autistic sibling, older parents, certain genetic conditions, and very low birth weight. Vaccines do not cause autism. For example, a Danish study that followed 657,461 children found that the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine did not increase autism risk, even in children with an autistic sibling (Hviid et al., 2019). The American Academy of Pediatrics says decades of large, high-quality studies have found the same thing (AAP, HealthyChildren.org).

There is no single best approach to support. Behavioral, speech-language, and occupational therapies, along with school services, work best when started early. Medicines are not used to change autism itself, but doctors sometimes prescribe them for specific problems that can come with it, such as anxiety, attention difficulties, or irritability.

docs.title: ADHD
docs.text:
Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental condition marked by a lasting pattern of inattention (trouble staying focused, organized, or on task), hyperactivity (restlessness, excessive movement or talking), and impulsivity (acting or interrupting without waiting). Some people have mostly inattentive symptoms, some mostly hyperactive-impulsive symptoms, and some have both. To count as ADHD, symptoms must begin in childhood, show up in more than one setting, and interfere with daily life (NIMH).

ADHD is real and common. An estimated 7 million U.S. children aged 3 to 17 (11.7%) had a current ADHD diagnosis in 2024, according to a national survey of parents (CDC). Studies suggest that genes play a large role, and symptoms usually continue into the teen years and adulthood.

Recall from Chapter 8 that the prefrontal cortex, the brain's planning and self-control center, matures last, and attention and impulse control depend on it. Standard ADHD treatment includes behavioral strategies, parent training, school supports, CBT, and medicine. The most common medicines are stimulants such as methylphenidate and amphetamine. They increase dopamine and norepinephrine signaling, especially in the prefrontal cortex (OpenStax, 14.2). It may seem odd that a stimulant helps a hyperactive person, but boosting prefrontal control can make it easier to filter distractions and hold back impulses.

docs.title: 15.6 Psychiatric Medication: Acting at the Synapse
docs.text:
A psychiatric medication is a medicine used to treat a mental health condition by changing how brain cells signal. Most act at synapses, which you studied in Chapter 3. There are only a few basic moves a drug can make at a synapse:

  • Block reuptake, so a neurotransmitter stays in the synapse longer (like plugging a drain)
  • Block a receptor (an antagonist), so the neurotransmitter can't deliver its message
  • Activate a receptor (an agonist), copying the neurotransmitter's message
  • Boost a receptor's response to its natural messenger
  • Increase release of a neurotransmitter

The table below matches each medication class from this chapter to its main move. These are general mechanisms only; this book never gives doses, and only a licensed clinician can decide whether a medicine is right for someone.

Medication class Main action at the synapse Used for (examples) SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors) Block serotonin reuptake Depression, anxiety disorders Benzodiazepines Boost the response of GABA-A receptors to GABA, the brain's main "brake" Short-term relief of severe anxiety Antipsychotics Block dopamine D2 receptors (newer ones also act on serotonin and other receptors) Schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders Stimulants (methylphenidate, amphetamine) Increase dopamine and norepinephrine signaling ADHD Esketamine nasal spray Acts on the glutamate system Treatment-resistant depression in adults; FDA-approved in 2019 and given only in a certified clinic

Medicines are often combined with therapy, and for many conditions therapy alone works well. Medicines also have real side effects and warnings. For example, the FDA advises that children, teens, and young adults under 25 who start antidepressants be watched closely for new or worsening suicidal thoughts, especially early in treatment or after a dose change (NIMH). Never start, stop, or change a medicine without talking to a doctor.

docs.title: 15.7 The Reward Pathway
docs.text:
Back to Maya's question. First, an analogy. Imagine a teacher with a yellow highlighter. Every time something good or surprising happens (a goal in soccer, a tasty meal, a text from a friend), the teacher highlights it and writes "do this again!" Later, when you see a soccer ball or smell that food, you feel a pull toward it. Your brain has its own highlighter.

That system is the reward pathway, a set of connected brain regions that signal when something is valuable and help you learn to seek it again. Its main messenger is dopamine. The main players are:

  • The ventral tegmental area (VTA), a small cluster of dopamine-making neurons in the midbrain
  • The nucleus accumbens (NAc), a region deep in the front of the brain that is central to motivation and "wanting"
  • The prefrontal cortex (PFC), the front of the brain, which plans, makes decisions, and can say "not now"

Dopamine neurons in the VTA send axons along two main routes. The mesolimbic pathway runs to the nucleus accumbens, and the mesocortical pathway runs to the prefrontal cortex (OpenStax, 14.3). The prefrontal cortex, in turn, sends signals to the nucleus accumbens that help control whether you act on an urge. Memory and emotion regions, such as the hippocampus and amygdala, also connect to this circuit, which is how a place or a song can become linked to a reward.

Scientists still debate exactly what dopamine "means," but it is probably not a simple "pleasure chemical." The leading ideas say dopamine signals surprise and importance: it rises when a reward is better than expected, and it makes reward-linked cues feel worth chasing. That is a form of learning, like the synaptic strengthening in Chapter 9.

Nearly all addictive drugs, though they act on different receptors, end up increasing dopamine signaling in the nucleus accumbens (OpenStax, 14.3). The difference from natural rewards is size and speed: drugs can produce much larger dopamine surges, which powerfully teach the brain to repeat drug use (NIDA).

docs.title: 15.8 Addiction, Tolerance, and Withdrawal
docs.text:
Addiction is a chronic, relapsing disorder in which a person compulsively seeks and uses a drug despite harmful consequences (NIDA). Doctors usually call it a substance use disorder. It involves lasting changes in brain circuits for reward, stress, and self-control. It is not the same as physical dependence: a person taking a prescribed pain medicine can become dependent without being addicted.

Who develops addiction? Genes, including epigenetic effects, account for an estimated 40 to 60 percent of a person's risk. The environment matters too: stress, trauma, family drug use, peers, and drug availability all play roles. Starting young raises risk, because the teenage brain is still building its prefrontal "brakes" (NIDA).

docs.title: Tolerance: the brain turns down the volume
docs.text:
Picture living next to a train track. The first night, every train wakes you up. After a few weeks, you sleep right through it. Tolerance is the brain's version of this. When a drug floods synapses with dopamine again and again, neurons protect themselves by turning down the volume. They can remove receptors from their surface (called downregulation), release less dopamine, and change other signaling steps. The liver can also break the drug down faster (OpenStax, 14.4).

The result is that the same amount of drug gives a smaller effect, so the person needs more to feel the same high, or even just to feel normal. Because the reward circuit has become less responsive, everyday pleasures like food, friends, or music also feel less rewarding (NIDA).

docs.title: Withdrawal: the volume is down and the music stops
docs.text:
Withdrawal is the set of unpleasant symptoms that appear when a person who has developed dependence stops or cuts back on the drug. The brain has adjusted to the drug's constant presence, so taking it away leaves the system below its normal set point. Stress systems, especially in a region called the extended amygdala, become overactive and produce anxiety, irritability, and unease (NIDA). Physical withdrawal often fades over about a week, but psychological symptoms such as low mood and anxiety, and cravings triggered by cues, can last much longer (OpenStax, 14.4).

Researchers describe addiction as a repeating three-stage cycle, each stage linked to different brain regions. The flowchart below summarizes it.

flowchart LR
    A["1. Binge / intoxication<br/>Big dopamine surge in the<br/>reward pathway (basal ganglia, NAc)"] --> B["2. Withdrawal / negative mood<br/>Reward circuit turned down;<br/>stress circuit (extended amygdala) turned up"]
    B --> C["3. Preoccupation / craving<br/>Weaker prefrontal control;<br/>cues and stress trigger craving"]
    C -->|"relapse"| A

This cycle helps explain why "just stop" is hard advice to follow: each stage pushes toward the next. Each stage is also a treatment target. Medicines can blunt a drug's effect, ease withdrawal, or reduce craving, and therapy can strengthen self-control and weaken responses to cues.

Tolerance looks a bit like habituation

In Chapter 9, you saw my gill-withdrawal reflex shrink when I was touched over and over. Tolerance looks similar on the surface, because a repeated stimulus gives a smaller response, but it involves different molecules and much longer-lasting changes in the reward circuit.

docs.title: Diagram: Reward Pathway and Tolerance
docs.text:
Open the Reward Pathway and Tolerance fullscreen

MicroSim specification: Reward Pathway and Tolerance

Type: microsim sim-id: ch15-reward-tolerance Library: p5.js Status: Implemented Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: explain Learning Objective: The learner will explain how repeated drug doses produce tolerance (smaller dopamine responses and a lower baseline from receptor downregulation) and how stopping produces a below-baseline withdrawal dip that recovers over days.

Canvas: drawing area 460 px plus control area 85 px (iframe 547 px); width-responsive.

Controls: Start/Pause, Natural reward, Drug dose, Stop drug, Reset. Starts paused; pressing Natural reward, Drug dose, or Stop drug also starts the clock.

Behavior: Left panel: a side view of the brain with the VTA sending dopamine to the nucleus accumbens (NAc) and prefrontal cortex (PFC), the PFC sending control signals to the NAc, and a row of 10 receptor icons on an NAc neuron. Right panel: dopamine signaling (relative units, original baseline = 1) over a scrolling 20-day window. Natural reward adds a bump of 0.6 times receptor availability; Drug dose adds a faster spike of 2.4 times receptor availability and removes 0.12 of receptor availability (floor 0.35). Stop drug adds a withdrawal dip equal to 0.5 times the receptors lost; the dip fades and receptors recover toward normal over about 20 to 30 simulated days. A message box explains each stage. All values are schematic, not measurements of any real drug.

Try this in order. Press Start, then Natural reward, and watch the small bump. Press Drug dose once and compare the spike. Then give five or six more doses, a second or two apart. Watch three things change at once: each spike gets shorter, the trace between spikes settles below the green "original baseline," and receptor icons disappear. That is tolerance.

Now press Natural reward again. The bump is smaller than before, because fewer receptors receive the signal. Finally, press Stop drug. The signal drops below even the lowered baseline (withdrawal), then climbs back slowly over the following "days" as receptors return. Recovery is real but slow, which is one reason support during early recovery matters. The sim does not show learned, cue-driven craving, which can outlast these receptor changes.

docs.title: 15.9 Nicotine and Vaping in the Teenage Brain
docs.text:
Now we can answer Maya's question. Nicotine is the addictive chemical in tobacco, and most e-cigarettes ("vapes") contain it. Nicotine fits into a type of acetylcholine receptor that is actually named after it, the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor. Activating these receptors leads to dopamine release in the reward pathway (Wikipedia: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor). When nicotine is inhaled in cigarette smoke, levels peak within about 10 seconds (NIDA), and fast arrival plus a dopamine boost is a strong recipe for learning to repeat a behavior.

Vaping has declined in recent years but is still common. In the 2025 National Youth Tobacco Survey, about 1.44 million middle and high school students (5.2%) reported currently using e-cigarettes, down from 5.9% in 2024. That included 7.1% of high school students. Among students who vaped, 89.4% used flavored products and 27.5% vaped every day (FDA).

Why does it matter more for teens? According to the CDC, brain development continues until about age 25, and nicotine during adolescence can harm parts of the brain that control attention, learning, mood, and impulse control. Teens can show signs of nicotine addiction quickly, sometimes before they vape regularly, and adolescents who use nicotine may be at higher risk for addiction to other drugs later (CDC).

When a person dependent on nicotine stops, withdrawal can bring irritability, restlessness, anxiety, low mood, trouble sleeping or concentrating, hunger, and cravings. That matches what Maya saw in Jordan on the weekend trip. These symptoms are temporary and fade as the brain readjusts. Free help designed for teens is available at teen.smokefree.gov, a National Cancer Institute site with a text-message quit program, and the free quitline 1-800-QUIT-NOW offers coaching by phone.

docs.title: How opioids work
docs.text:
Opioids are drugs that act on the body's opioid receptors. Some are prescription pain medicines (such as morphine and oxycodone), some are illegal (heroin), and fentanyl is a synthetic opioid used in medicine but also made illegally. Your body makes its own opioid-like molecules, such as endorphins, that help control pain. Opioid drugs act on the same receptors, especially the mu-opioid receptor.

Opioid receptors sit in pain pathways, the reward pathway, and brainstem regions that control breathing (the medulla and pons). That last location is what makes opioids deadly: too much opioid slows breathing until the brain and heart are starved of oxygen. Fentanyl is especially dangerous. The CDC describes it as up to 50 times stronger than heroin and 100 times stronger than morphine (CDC). Some counterfeit pills made to look like prescription medicines contain fentanyl, and people taking them often don't know it (NIDA).

Overdose deaths have fallen but remain high. In 2024, there were 79,384 drug overdose deaths in the United States, and 54,045 involved an opioid. The overdose death rate fell 26.2% from 2023 to 2024 (CDC NCHS Data Brief 549). Early numbers for 2025 show a third straight year of decline: CDC estimated about 69,973 overdose deaths in 2025, about 44,564 of them involving opioids. These 2025 figures are provisional, which means they may change as more death records come in (CDC NCHS, May 2026).

docs.title: Recognizing an overdose
docs.text:
The CDC lists these signs of an opioid overdose (CDC):

  • Unconsciousness, or the person can't be woken up
  • Slow or shallow breathing, or choking, gurgling, or snoring sounds
  • Discolored skin, especially the lips and nails
  • Small, constricted "pinpoint pupils" that don't react to light

Doctors remember the classic combination of decreased consciousness, pinpoint pupils, and slowed breathing.

docs.title: Naloxone: the antidote
docs.text:
Naloxone is a medicine that rapidly reverses an opioid overdose. It is an opioid antagonist: it attaches to opioid receptors, displaces the opioid, and blocks its effects. Breathing can recover within minutes. It comes as a nasal spray or an injection, and anyone can give it without medical training. In March 2023, the FDA approved Narcan nasal spray for over-the-counter use, making it the first naloxone product available without a prescription (FDA). The FDA has since approved other over-the-counter naloxone nasal sprays, most recently in June 2026 (FDA). A related antidote, nalmefene nasal spray, was approved by prescription later in 2023.

Every reader should know these facts (NIDA):

  1. Naloxone has no effect on a person with no opioids in their body, so giving it when you aren't sure is generally safe.
  2. It does not reverse overdoses from non-opioid drugs such as cocaine or methamphetamine.
  3. It works for only about 30 to 90 minutes, but many opioids last longer. The person can stop breathing again after naloxone wears off, so emergency care is still needed.
  4. Strong opioids like fentanyl may need more than one dose.
  5. A person who is dependent on opioids may go into withdrawal within minutes of naloxone. This is very unpleasant but usually not life-threatening.

Naloxone is not the end of the emergency

If you suspect an overdose, give naloxone if you have it and call 911. Stay with the person, try to keep them breathing, and lay them on their side, because naloxone can wear off before the opioid does.

docs.title: Treating opioid use disorder
docs.text:
Naloxone saves a life in the moment but does not treat addiction. Opioid use disorder is a chronic, treatable condition with effective, FDA-approved medicines (NIDA):

  • Methadone activates mu-opioid receptors slowly and lasts a long time, so it reduces cravings and withdrawal without an intense high. For opioid use disorder, it is given through approved opioid treatment programs.
  • Buprenorphine partly activates mu-opioid receptors and also blocks other opioids from attaching. Since 2023, any clinician whose DEA registration allows prescribing this class of controlled medicine (Schedule III) can prescribe it for opioid use disorder, if state law allows (SAMHSA).
  • Naltrexone only blocks opioid receptors, so opioids can no longer produce a high. It is usually started after a person has fully stopped opioids.

These medicines reduce the risk of overdose death, yet NIDA reports that fewer than 1 in 5 people with opioid use disorder are treated with them. The 2025 national survey agrees: of about 4.0 million people aged 12 or older with opioid use disorder, only 15.7% received one of these medicines in the past year (SAMHSA, 2025 NSDUH). Taking a prescribed medicine for opioid use disorder is treatment, not "trading one addiction for another," much as taking a daily medicine for any other chronic illness is treatment.

docs.title: 15.11 Stigma and Treatment Access
docs.text:
Stigma means negative attitudes, stereotypes, and discrimination aimed at people because of a condition. Treatment access means whether people can actually get care, which depends on cost, insurance, location, wait times, and whether they feel safe asking. The two are linked. NIDA notes that feeling stigmatized can make people with substance use disorders less willing to seek treatment (NIDA). In mental health more broadly, only about half (50.9%) of U.S. adults with a mental illness received mental health treatment in the past year in 2025 (SAMHSA, 2025 NSDUH).

Words matter. Labeling a whole person by their illness can make them sound hopeless or blameworthy. The table below shows swaps recommended by NIDA, plus one for mental illness.

Instead of... Say... Why "addict," "junkie," "abuser" "person with a substance use disorder" Puts the person first, not the condition "clean" / "dirty" (drug test) "tested negative" / "tested positive" Medical terms, no moral judgment "former addict" "person in recovery" Recognizes recovery as ongoing "a habit" "substance use disorder" "Habit" implies a person can simply choose to stop "replacement therapy" "medication for opioid use disorder" Treatment, not a substitute drug "schizophrenic," "crazy," "psycho" "person with schizophrenia" or "person with a mental illness" Avoids slurs and stereotypes

Recovery is common, not a rare miracle. Relapse happens too, as it does in other chronic illnesses. NIDA estimates relapse rates of 40 to 60% for substance use disorders, compared with 50 to 70% for hypertension and asthma. Relapse means treatment may need to be restarted or adjusted, not that it failed (NIDA).

Asking for help is a brain skill

This chapter covers heavy topics, and it's okay if some of it hit close to home. Reaching out to a trusted adult, a doctor, or 988 uses your prefrontal cortex exactly the way it is meant to be used: planning a way forward.

docs.title: At the Bedside: An Overdose at a Dorm Party
docs.text:
Meet the patient

Sam is a 19-year-old college student. At a party, Sam took a pill a friend said was a prescription pain reliever. Later, Sam's roommate found Sam slumped on a couch, unable to be woken, making slow, snoring breaths, with bluish lips. The roommate gave one spray of naloxone from the campus health center and called 911. Within minutes, Sam began breathing faster, woke up confused, and started sweating, shaking, and vomiting.

What the doctor checks: In the emergency department, the doctor checks Sam's airway, breathing rate, and blood oxygen level. The roommate reports that Sam's pupils were tiny before the naloxone. The team checks blood sugar and other causes of unresponsiveness, asks what Sam took, and watches for breathing to slow again as the naloxone wears off. A urine drug screen may be sent, but the standard opiate screen often misses fentanyl unless a fentanyl-specific test is ordered, so the doctor relies mainly on the clinical picture.

Where is the problem? (localization): Slow breathing localizes to the brainstem breathing centers in the medulla and pons, and decreased consciousness reflects depressed brain arousal. Together with pinpoint pupils, these form the classic opioid triad. The fast response to naloxone, an opioid receptor blocker, confirms that opioid receptors were involved.

Diagnosis: Opioid overdose, most likely from a counterfeit pill containing fentanyl.

Why it happens: Fentanyl strongly activates mu-opioid receptors. In the brainstem, this weakens the drive to breathe, so oxygen falls. Naloxone displaced fentanyl from the receptors, so breathing returned. Sam's sweating and vomiting suggest withdrawal, which hints that Sam's brain may already have adapted to regular opioid use (tolerance and dependence, Section 15.8).

Treatment today: Emergency teams support breathing, give more naloxone if needed, and keep watching the patient (NIDA advises monitoring for another 2 hours after the last naloxone dose), because naloxone can wear off before fentanyl does. If the patient has opioid use disorder, the team can start a medication such as buprenorphine and connect the person to ongoing treatment, and can encourage the patient and family to keep naloxone on hand.

What's new in research: Starting treatment in the emergency department works. In a randomized trial of 329 patients with opioid dependence, 78% of those started on buprenorphine in the emergency department were engaged in addiction treatment 30 days later, compared with 37% of those given a referral alone (D'Onofrio et al., JAMA, 2015). Access has also widened. In late 2022, Congress removed the special federal "X-waiver" that clinicians once needed to prescribe buprenorphine for opioid use disorder (SAMHSA), and naloxone nasal spray became available over the counter in 2023.

Your turn: diagnose a variation

Riley is 16. Riley started vaping a year ago "just at parties," but now vapes first thing every morning, can't get through first period without feeling irritable and restless, and has trouble sleeping and concentrating whenever the vape runs out. Riley has tried to stop twice and gave up after a day. Riley is fully awake, breathing normally, and has normal-sized pupils. What is going on, and what would help?

Answer: This is nicotine dependence from vaping, not an overdose. Riley shows tolerance (vaping more often), withdrawal (irritability, restlessness, poor sleep and focus), and failed quit attempts, all signs that the reward pathway has adapted to nicotine. Naloxone would do nothing, because nicotine does not act on opioid receptors. Helpful steps include talking with a doctor or school nurse, counseling, and teen quit programs such as the text program at teen.smokefree.gov. Withdrawal symptoms are temporary.

This is a fictional teaching case. It is not medical advice. If you or someone you know has symptoms like these, talk to a doctor.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
Myth: Addiction is just a lack of willpower. Reality: Addiction involves measurable changes in the brain's reward, stress, and self-control circuits, and genes account for an estimated 40 to 60% of the risk. Repeated drug use weakens the very prefrontal "brakes" a person needs to choose differently, which is why medicines and therapy help.

Myth: Mental illness is rare. Reality: About 20.6% of U.S. adults (one in five) had a mental illness in 2025, and about a third of teens and adults experience an anxiety disorder at some point. You almost certainly know someone affected.

Myth: ADHD isn't real; it's just kids being lazy or hyper. Reality: ADHD is a well-studied neurodevelopmental condition with a strong genetic component. It affects attention, activity, and impulse control in multiple settings and often continues into adulthood. Effective treatments exist.

Myth: Depression is simply a "chemical imbalance" of low serotonin. Reality: Large reviews have not found consistent evidence that low serotonin causes depression. Depression arises from many interacting biological, psychological, and social factors. Antidepressants and therapy still help many people.

Myth: People with schizophrenia have a "split personality" and are dangerous. Reality: Schizophrenia involves psychosis, not multiple personalities. Most people with schizophrenia are not violent, and they are more likely than people without the illness to be harmed by others.

docs.title: Brain Bee Practice
docs.text:
1. Name the midbrain region where the dopamine neurons of the reward pathway begin, and one region they project to.

The ventral tegmental area (VTA). Its dopamine neurons project to the nucleus accumbens (mesolimbic pathway) and to the prefrontal cortex (mesocortical pathway).

2. A patient is unresponsive with pinpoint pupils and a breathing rate of 6 breaths per minute. What drug class is most likely involved, and what is the antidote?

Opioids. The antidote is naloxone, an opioid receptor antagonist that displaces opioids from their receptors and restores breathing.

3. What is the difference between tolerance and withdrawal?

Tolerance is a reduced response to the same amount of a drug after repeated use, for example from receptor downregulation. Withdrawal is the set of symptoms, often opposite to the drug's effects, that appears when a person who has adapted to the drug stops taking it.

4. Which receptor does nicotine activate, and how does that lead to reinforcement?

Nicotine activates nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. This leads to dopamine release in the reward pathway, which reinforces (teaches the brain to repeat) nicotine use.

5. Name the three symptom groups of schizophrenia and give one example of each.

Psychotic or positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions), negative symptoms (reduced motivation or emotional expression), and cognitive symptoms (trouble with attention or memory).

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
1. List the three FDA-approved medications for opioid use disorder discussed in this chapter.
  2. State the two core features of autism spectrum disorder.
Answer
  1. Methadone, buprenorphine, and naltrexone.
  2. Differences in social communication and interaction, and restricted interests and repetitive behaviors.

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
1. Explain why naloxone is generally safe to give to an unresponsive person even when you aren't sure they took opioids.
  2. Explain in your own words why antidepressants taking several weeks to work is evidence against a simple "low serotonin" theory of depression.
Answer
  1. Naloxone only blocks opioid receptors. If no opioids are present, there is nothing for it to reverse, so it has no effect. If opioids are present, it may save the person's life.
  2. Antidepressants raise serotonin at synapses within hours. If low serotonin were the whole cause, mood should improve just as fast. The delay suggests that slower changes in brain circuits, not the serotonin level itself, drive recovery.

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
1. In the Reward Pathway and Tolerance MicroSim, give six drug doses, then press Natural reward. Compare the bump with the one at the start, and use the receptor icons to explain the difference.
  2. A classmate faints at a party but is breathing normally and has normal pupils. Someone wants to give naloxone. What should you do first, and is naloxone likely to help?

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
1. Compare how nicotine and opioids each lead to dopamine release in the reward pathway, and explain why only opioids commonly cause deaths from stopped breathing.
  2. Two students vaped for a year. One quit easily; the other could not. Analyze how genes, environment, and brain development could explain the difference.

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
1. A website claims, "Medications for opioid use disorder just replace one drug with another." Evaluate this claim using evidence from this chapter.
  2. Should your school stock naloxone nasal spray and teach students to use it? Weigh benefits and risks, and recommend a decision.

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
1. Design a 30-second teen public service announcement about vaping that is accurate, avoids scare tactics, and uses two facts from this chapter.
  2. Write a short fictional case of a teen with depression, an anxiety disorder, ADHD, or autism. Include what the family notices, what a doctor would ask, and respectful language throughout.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Mental illnesses are common, real, and treatable; they involve the brain, genes, the body, and life experiences, not personal weakness.
  • Depression, anxiety disorders, and schizophrenia are each more complex than a single "chemical imbalance," and treatment often combines therapy, medicine, and support.
  • Autism and ADHD are neurodevelopmental conditions that begin early in life; a neurodiversity view pairs real supports with respect for different kinds of minds.
  • The reward pathway (VTA to nucleus accumbens and prefrontal cortex) uses dopamine to mark what is worth repeating, and addictive drugs hijack it with unusually large dopamine surges.
  • Repeated drug use causes tolerance (fewer receptors, smaller responses, lower baseline), and stopping causes withdrawal; recovery of these changes takes time.
  • Opioids can stop breathing by acting on the brainstem; naloxone reverses an overdose, but always call 911, and medications for opioid use disorder save lives.
  • Stigma keeps people from care. Use person-first, non-judgmental language, and know the numbers: 988 for crisis support and 1-800-662-4357 for SAMHSA's National Helpline.

You made it through a big one!

You can now trace mood, attention, and addiction back to synapses and circuits, and you know how to help in an overdose. Next, in Chapter 16, we put on the white coat and learn how doctors examine the brain, from the neurological exam to MRI.

docs.title: Quiz: Psychiatric Disorders, Developmental Disorders, and Addiction
Quiz: Psychiatric Disorders, Developmental Disorders, and Addiction
docs.text: Test your understanding of Chapter 15. Choose the best answer, then click Show Answer to check.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
Where are the cell bodies of the dopamine neurons that start the brain's reward pathway?

  1. The nucleus accumbens
  2. The ventral tegmental area (VTA)
  3. The hippocampus
  4. The prefrontal cortex
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Dopamine neurons in the ventral tegmental area, a small midbrain region, send axons to the nucleus accumbens (mesolimbic pathway) and the prefrontal cortex (mesocortical pathway). The nucleus accumbens is a major target of these neurons, not where they begin, which is why A is the most tempting wrong answer.

Concept Tested: Reward Pathway Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
How does naloxone reverse an opioid overdose?

  1. It activates opioid receptors more strongly than the opioid does
  2. It makes the liver break down opioids faster
  3. It attaches to opioid receptors, displaces the opioid, and blocks its effects
  4. It raises dopamine in the brainstem to stimulate breathing
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Naloxone is an opioid receptor antagonist: it occupies opioid receptors without activating them, which removes the opioid's effect on the brainstem breathing centers. It does not activate the receptors (A), which is what opioids themselves do, and it does not work by changing drug breakdown or dopamine.

Concept Tested: Naloxone Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
To be diagnosed with depression (major depressive disorder), how long must symptoms such as a low mood or loss of interest last, for most of the day, nearly every day?

  1. At least 2 weeks
  2. At least 3 days
  3. At least 6 months
  4. At least 1 year
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. NIMH describes the criterion as symptoms most of the day, nearly every day, for at least 2 weeks. Six months (C) is the duration used for generalized anxiety disorder, a different condition covered in the same chapter.

Concept Tested: Depression Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 4
docs.text:
Which statement best explains why scientists describe addiction as a brain disorder rather than simply a bad choice?

  1. Addiction happens only to people who use a drug many times a day
  2. Anyone who takes a drug once becomes addicted
  3. Addiction is caused entirely by genes, so the environment does not matter
  4. Repeated drug use changes reward, stress, and self-control circuits, and genes add substantial risk
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Addiction involves lasting changes in brain circuits for reward, stress, and self-control, and genes account for an estimated 40 to 60 percent of a person's risk. Option C overstates the genetic part: the environment, including stress, peers, and drug availability, also matters.

Concept Tested: Addiction Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 5
docs.text:
Antidepressants raise serotonin at synapses within hours, yet they usually take weeks to improve mood. What does this suggest?

  1. Antidepressants do not work at all
  2. A simple "low serotonin" explanation of depression is incomplete; slower brain changes likely matter
  3. Depression is caused by too much serotonin
  4. The medicine must be taken at a higher dose to work faster
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. If low serotonin were the whole cause, raising it should help right away. The delay points to slower adaptations in brain circuits, which is one reason researchers no longer accept a simple "chemical imbalance" story. Option A is a common overreaction: antidepressants help many people even though the serotonin theory is incomplete.

Concept Tested: Psychiatric Medication Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 6
docs.text:
Why is autism described as a "spectrum"?

  1. Because it is caused by many different vaccines
  2. Because it always gets worse with age
  3. Because autistic people have a wide range of characteristics, needs, strengths, and challenges
  4. Because it only affects the visual system's color processing
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Autistic people share differences in social communication and restricted or repetitive behaviors, but how these show up, and how much support a person needs, varies widely. Option A is false: large studies, including one of 657,461 Danish children, found that vaccines do not cause autism.

Concept Tested: Autism Spectrum Disorder Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 7
docs.text:
At a party, you find a friend who will not wake up, is breathing very slowly with snoring sounds, and has pinpoint pupils. A naloxone nasal spray is in the first-aid kit. What is the best action?

  1. Let the friend sleep it off on the couch and check in the morning
  2. Give the friend coffee to stimulate breathing
  3. Wait to see whether the friend's breathing improves on its own before calling anyone
  4. Give the naloxone, call 911, and stay with the friend, laying them on their side
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Unresponsiveness, slow breathing, and pinpoint pupils are the classic signs of an opioid overdose. Naloxone can restore breathing, but it can wear off before the opioid does, so emergency care is still needed. Letting the person "sleep it off" (A) is dangerous because breathing can stop.

Concept Tested: Opioids Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 8
docs.text:
In the Reward Pathway and Tolerance MicroSim, you give six drug doses, then press Stop drug. What should you predict the dopamine signal will do?

  1. Drop below even the lowered baseline, then climb back slowly over days as receptors return
  2. Jump immediately back to the original baseline
  3. Rise above the original baseline because the drug is gone
  4. Stay exactly where it was, because receptors never recover
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. After repeated doses, receptors are downregulated and the baseline is lower (tolerance). Removing the drug leaves the system below even that level (withdrawal), and it recovers slowly as receptors return. Option B is the common hope that stopping fixes everything instantly, but the brain needs time to readjust.

Concept Tested: Tolerance and Withdrawal Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 9
docs.text:
A 16-year-old vapes every morning. When the vape runs out, they feel irritable, restless, and unable to focus, and they have trouble sleeping. They are fully awake, breathing normally, with normal pupils. Which explanation best fits?

  1. An opioid overdose that needs naloxone
  2. A sudden onset of ADHD caused by vaping
  3. Nicotine withdrawal from dependence on nicotine
  4. Schizophrenia beginning with negative symptoms
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Irritability, restlessness, poor focus, and poor sleep that appear when nicotine runs out are classic withdrawal symptoms, showing that the reward pathway has adapted to nicotine. There are no overdose signs (A), and ADHD (B) begins in childhood and does not appear only when a vape runs out.

Concept Tested: Nicotine and Vaping Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: Question 10
docs.text:
Medications for opioid use disorder reduce the risk of overdose death, yet fewer than 1 in 5 people with opioid use disorder receive them. Which factor best links stigma to this gap?

  1. The medications have been shown not to reduce overdose deaths
  2. Fear of judgment, and the false belief that these medicines just "replace one drug with another," keep people from seeking or offering treatment
  3. Naloxone already treats opioid use disorder, so other medicines are unnecessary
  4. These medications can only be given during an overdose in the emergency department
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Stigma makes people less willing to seek treatment, and medications for opioid use disorder are often wrongly viewed as substitutes for illegal drugs. Option C confuses emergency reversal with long-term treatment: naloxone reverses an overdose but does not treat the disorder.

Concept Tested: Stigma and Treatment Access Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: References: Psychiatric Disorders, Developmental Disorders, and Addiction
References: Psychiatric Disorders, Developmental Disorders, and Addiction
docs.text:
1. Drugs and the Brain (Drugs, Brains, and Behavior: The Science of Addiction) - National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA) - A clear tour of the reward circuit, the extended amygdala, and the prefrontal cortex in addiction, including why drugs cause bigger dopamine surges than natural rewards and how tolerance develops. A good next read after Sections 15.7 and 15.8.
  2. 14.3 Neural Circuitry of Drug Reward - OpenStax, Introduction to Behavioral Neuroscience (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) - A free college-level section on the VTA, nucleus accumbens, and prefrontal cortex, and on competing ideas about what dopamine signals. It shows where this chapter's simplified pathway comes from.
  3. 14.2 Psychotherapeutics - OpenStax, Introduction to Behavioral Neuroscience (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) - Explains how SSRIs, benzodiazepines, antipsychotics, and ADHD stimulants act at synapses, and why the "monoamine" (chemical imbalance) idea of depression is now seen as incomplete.
  4. Medications for Opioid Use Disorder - National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA) - Describes how methadone, buprenorphine, and naltrexone work, where people can get them, and the evidence that they reduce overdose deaths. Useful for understanding the "Treatment today" part of the Bedside case.
  5. FDA Approves First Over-the-Counter Naloxone Nasal Spray - U.S. Food and Drug Administration (March 29, 2023) - The official announcement that Narcan nasal spray could be sold without a prescription. A primary source for a fact many readers will see in pharmacies.
  6. What to Do If You Think Someone Is Overdosing - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) - Lists the signs of an opioid overdose and the steps to take, including giving naloxone and calling 911. Short and practical enough to remember.
  7. Health Effects of Vaping - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) - Explains why nicotine is especially risky for the developing teenage brain and lists common nicotine withdrawal symptoms. Directly answers Maya's question in Section 15.9.
  8. Depression - National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) - A plain-language guide to the symptoms, causes, and treatments of depression, including therapy, medications, and brain stimulation. Includes the 988 Lifeline and safety information about antidepressants in young people.
  9. The serotonin theory of depression: a systematic umbrella review of the evidence - Moncrieff J. et al., Molecular Psychiatry (2022) - The review that found no consistent evidence that low serotonin causes depression. It is advanced reading, and it was debated by other researchers, but it shows how scientists test a popular idea.
  10. Neurobiologic Advances from the Brain Disease Model of Addiction - Volkow N.D., Koob G.F., McLellan A.T., New England Journal of Medicine (2016) - A review by leading addiction researchers on how addiction changes reward, stress, and self-control circuits. Best for ambitious readers and future doctors.

docs.title: Chapter 16: How Doctors Examine the Brain
Chapter 16: How Doctors Examine the Brain
Summary
docs.text: This capstone chapter puts you in the doctor's chair. You'll learn how a neurologist listens to a patient's story, runs the neurological exam from mental status to gait, and uses the findings to answer the most important question in neurology: where is the problem? Then you'll compare the tools that look inside the head (CT, MRI, fMRI, PET, and EEG), learn when a lumbar puncture helps, and see how doctors build a differential diagnosis. Finally, you'll follow one fictional patient from the ambulance to a diagnosis, using ideas from every earlier chapter.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
1. Neurological Exam
  2. Mental Status Exam
  3. Cranial Nerve Exam
  4. Reflex Testing
  5. Lesion Localization
  6. Computed Tomography (CT)
  7. Magnetic Resonance Imaging
  8. Functional MRI
  9. PET Scan
  10. Lumbar Puncture
  11. Differential Diagnosis

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter draws on the whole book. The most important earlier chapters are:

  • Chapter 1: Neurons, Glia, and the Nervous System (myelin, motor neurons, multiple sclerosis)
  • Chapter 4: A Tour of the Brain (lobes, brainstem, spinal cord, cranial nerves, meninges, cerebrospinal fluid)
  • Chapter 6: Hearing, Touch, Taste, Smell, and Pain (dermatomes)
  • Chapter 7: Movement (reflex arcs, the corticospinal tract, upper vs lower motor neurons, the cerebellum)
  • Chapter 10: Sleep and Brain States (the EEG)
  • Chapter 12: Language, Attention, and Decision-Making (aphasia and neglect)
  • Chapter 14: Brain Injury, Stroke, and Epilepsy (stroke, BE-FAST, clot-busting treatment, seizures)

You're the doctor now

I'm Ply, and I've been with you since your first neuron. In this last chapter, everything you've learned turns into a skill: figuring out what's wrong with a real nervous system using your questions, your hands, and a few clever machines. This is how neurologists think, and it's exactly what the patient-diagnosis round of the Brain Bee tests.

docs.title: 16.1 You're the Doctor Now
docs.text:
Maya, 16, has made it to her regional Brain Bee after months of studying between soccer practices. The round she fears most is patient diagnosis. On the screen, a man walks with a stiff, swinging leg, and a short written history sits beside the video. In the International Brain Bee format, students watch patient videos, read a written history, and pick three diagnostic tests before naming a diagnosis (International Brain Bee; rules change, so check your own competition's).

Maya knows dozens of diseases. But the real question isn't "Which disease do I remember?" It's "Where in the nervous system is this coming from?" Now imagine you're a doctor in an emergency room. A patient arrives with weakness on one side of the body. What do you do first? Order a scan? Grab a reflex hammer? This chapter answers that question step by step.

docs.title: 16.2 Where Before What: The Detective's Rule
docs.text:
Before any vocabulary, picture an electrician called to an apartment building with a power problem.

  • If one lamp in one room is dark, the problem is probably that lamp's bulb or cord.
  • If every outlet on the left side of the 5th floor is dead, the problem is in that floor's left-side circuit panel.
  • If every floor below the 3rd floor is dark, the problem is in the main cable that runs down through the building, at about the 3rd floor.

The electrician first asks where the fault must be to explain the pattern of what's broken. Only then does she ask what broke: a blown fuse, a chewed wire, water damage.

Neurologists work the same way. The nervous system is wired in a very orderly way (Chapter 4, Chapter 7), so the pattern of symptoms points to a location. This skill is called lesion localization: using symptoms and exam findings to figure out where in the nervous system the damage (the lesion) must be. A lesion is any area of damaged or abnormal tissue, from a stroke, tumor, infection, or injury. Once the "where" is clear, the doctor asks "what," building a list of possible causes called the differential diagnosis (Section 16.8).

Where, then what

Here's the big idea of this whole chapter: localize first, then name the disease. A blocked artery and a tumor can sit in the same spot and cause the same signs. The pattern tells you where; the timing and tests tell you what.

docs.title: 16.3 The History: Listening to the Patient's Story
docs.text:
The first tool a neurologist uses isn't a machine. It's a conversation. The history is the patient's story: what happened, when it started, how it changed, and what else is going on in their health. The exam begins during the history, because the doctor is already watching how the patient talks, moves, and walks (Merck Manual). A good history answers a few questions:

  • What exactly is the problem? "Weak" might mean loss of strength, clumsiness, numbness, or tiredness.
  • When did it start, and how fast? This is often the best clue to what the lesion is.
  • Is it getting better, worse, or staying the same?
  • What else is going on? Headache, fever, a recent seizure, past strokes, medicines, or family history.

docs.title: Timing tells a story
docs.text:
How fast symptoms appear hints at their cause. The table below summarizes a common rule of thumb. It's a guide, not a law.

How symptoms began Often suggests Example from this book Seconds to minutes A blood vessel problem or a seizure Stroke (Chapter 14) Hours to days Infection or inflammation Meningitis; a multiple sclerosis flare (Chapter 1) Weeks to months Something growing or pressing A tumor pressing on a nerve or the spinal cord Months to years Slow nerve-cell loss (neurodegeneration) Alzheimer's or Parkinson's disease (Chapters 7 and 13)

For a suspected stroke, the key question is when was the patient last known to be normal? Clot-busting treatment only helps within a limited time window, so doctors ask right away (NINDS).

docs.title: 16.4 The Neurological Exam: A Head-to-Toe Tour
docs.text:
The neurological exam is a set of hands-on tests that checks each major part of the nervous system: thinking, cranial nerves, movement, reflexes, feeling, coordination, and walking. Its purpose is to decide whether the nervous system works normally and, if not, to connect each abnormal finding to a structure (Merck Manual). The basics take only a few minutes. Here's a map of the tour; we'll visit each stop below.

Part of the exam What it checks Example test Mental status Alertness, orientation, attention, memory, language "What's today's date? Where are we?" Cranial nerves The 12 nerves of the head and face Follow my finger with your eyes Motor Muscle bulk, tone, strength Push against my hand Reflexes Stretch reflexes and the plantar (sole) response Tap the knee with a reflex hammer Sensation Touch, pain, temperature, vibration, position sense Is this sharp or dull? Coordination Smooth, accurate movement (cerebellum and its connections) Touch your nose, then my finger Gait Walking and balance Walk heel-to-toe in a straight line

docs.title: Mental status: is the "boss" online?
docs.text:
The mental status exam checks the brain's highest functions. The doctor first notes the level of consciousness (alert, drowsy, or hard to wake), then checks (Merck Manual):

  • Orientation: Does the patient know who they are, where they are, and the date?
  • Attention: Can they spell a word forward and backward?
  • Memory: Can they remember three words after a few minutes? Do they recall recent events?
  • Language: Can they speak fluently, understand commands, name objects, and repeat a sentence?
  • Other abilities: calculation, judgment, mood, and copying a drawing.

These findings are powerful localizing clues. Trouble with language or calculation points to the dominant hemisphere, the left one in most people (recall the aphasias from Chapter 12). Ignoring one side of space (neglect) usually points to the right hemisphere. Screening tests such as the Mini-Mental State Examination and the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score these abilities, for example when checking for Alzheimer's disease.

docs.title: The cranial nerve exam: twelve nerves, quick checks
docs.text:
You met the 12 cranial nerves in Chapter 4. They leave the brain and brainstem directly, not through the spinal cord. The cranial nerve exam tests each one with a quick task. Because most of them start in the brainstem, an abnormal finding hints that the problem is in the brainstem or in that nerve. The table summarizes the bedside tests (Merck Manual).

Nerve Main job Quick bedside test I (olfactory) Smell Identify a familiar smell, one nostril at a time II (optic) Vision Read an eye chart; check side vision; shine a light in the pupils III, IV, VI (oculomotor, trochlear, abducens) Eye movements, eyelid, pupil size Follow a finger in all directions; look for a droopy lid V (trigeminal) Feeling in the face; chewing muscles Light touch and pinprick on the face; clench the jaw VII (facial) Facial expression; taste on the front of the tongue Raise eyebrows, close eyes tight, smile VIII (vestibulocochlear) Hearing and balance Whisper a word; look for jerky eye movements (nystagmus) IX, X (glossopharyngeal, vagus) Swallowing, voice, gag Say "ah" and watch the palate rise XI (accessory) Neck and shoulder muscles Shrug the shoulders and turn the head against resistance XII (hypoglossal) Tongue movement Stick out the tongue; a weak side makes it point toward that side

One finding deserves a spotlight: the forehead rule. When a stroke in the cortex weakens the face, the lower face droops but the forehead still wrinkles. When the facial nerve itself (cranial nerve VII) is damaged, the whole half of the face is weak, forehead included (Merck Manual). Why? The nerve cells for the forehead get signals from both hemispheres, while those for the lower face get signals mainly from the opposite one (Wikipedia: Central facial palsy). If one hemisphere is damaged, the other still runs the forehead. If the nerve is cut off, nothing gets through.

Check the forehead

Whenever you see a droopy face, ask the patient to raise their eyebrows. A forehead that still wrinkles points to the brain (a central pattern). A forehead that stays flat points to the facial nerve (a peripheral pattern).

docs.title: The motor exam: strength, bulk, and tone
docs.text:
The motor exam starts by looking. Are any muscles wasted (shrunken)? Are there fasciculations, tiny twitches under the skin? Then the doctor checks tone, the resistance a relaxed limb gives when moved, and tests strength muscle by muscle, comparing sides. Strength is graded 0 to 5 on the UK Medical Research Council scale (Merck Manual):

Grade What the doctor sees 0 No muscle contraction at all 1 A flicker of contraction, but no real movement 2 Movement only when gravity is taken away (for example, sliding the arm across a bed) 3 Movement against gravity, but not against the examiner's push 4 Movement against some resistance 5 Full, normal strength

A sensitive test for mild arm weakness is pronator drift: with both arms held straight out, palms up, eyes closed, a weak arm slowly drifts down and turns inward.

docs.title: Reflex testing: the knee-jerk and its cousins
docs.text:
In Chapter 7 you learned that tapping a tendon stretches the muscle, and a quick loop through the spinal cord makes it contract: the stretch reflex. Reflex testing means triggering these reflexes with a rubber hammer, grading the response, and checking the sole of the foot for an abnormal toe response. Reflexes are graded 0 to 4+ (Wikipedia: Stretch reflex):

Grade Response Meaning 0 No response Always abnormal 1+ Slight but present May or may not be normal 2+ Brisk, ordinary response Normal 3+ Very brisk May or may not be normal 4+ Clonus (repeated rhythmic beats) Always abnormal

Each reflex tests particular spinal cord segments, so reflexes form a built-in map of the cord: biceps (C5 and C6), triceps (C7), knee jerk (mainly L3 and L4), and ankle jerk (S1) (Merck Manual; Wikipedia: Patellar reflex). C, L, and S mean cervical (neck), lumbar (lower back), and sacral (base of the spine).

The most famous reflex test isn't a tendon tap. When the doctor strokes the outer sole, a healthy adult's big toe curls down. If it goes up and the other toes fan out, that's the Babinski sign, described by the French neurologist Joseph Babinski in 1896 (Wikipedia: Babinski sign). In adults, it means damage along the corticospinal tract, the main motor pathway from cortex to spinal cord. In babies, an upgoing toe is normal; it usually switches to downgoing by about 12 months.

Why would damage above the spinal cord make reflexes stronger? The brain normally sends calming signals down to the reflex loops. Cut that brake, and the reflexes run hot. So brisk reflexes, sustained clonus, and a Babinski sign all signal upper motor neuron damage (Merck Manual).

docs.title: The sensory exam: mapping what the patient feels
docs.text:
The sensory exam checks light touch, pinprick (sharp versus dull), temperature, vibration (with a tuning fork), and position sense, the ability to tell which way a toe is being moved with eyes closed. These feelings travel up the cord in different pathways, so the pattern of loss is another clue.

The doctor also maps the edge of any numb area. Recall dermatomes from Chapter 6: each spinal nerve supplies a band of skin. Two landmarks: the nipple line is about T4, and the belly button is about T10 (Wikipedia: Dermatome). Numbness below a horizontal line on both sides is called a sensory level, a classic sign of spinal cord damage at or above that level.

In the Romberg test, the patient stands with feet together, eyes open, then closed. Falling once the eyes close is a positive test: the patient was using vision to make up for lost position sense, often from damage to the spinal cord's dorsal columns or the sensory nerves. It is not a test of the cerebellum (Wikipedia: Romberg's test).

docs.title: Coordination and gait: the cerebellum's report card
docs.text:
In finger-to-nose, the patient touches their nose, then the doctor's finger, back and forth. In heel-to-shin, they slide one heel down the other shin. A side-to-side wobble as the hand moves (an intention tremor) suggests a problem in the cerebellum, which you met in Chapter 7. But weakness can also spoil these tests, so they're read alongside strength (Merck Manual).

Walking tests almost everything at once. A wide, unsteady gait suggests cerebellar trouble. A stiff gait with scraping toes suggests upper motor neuron damage to the legs. Small, shuffling steps suggest Parkinson's disease (NINDS).

So many tests!

That's a lot of hammers and tuning forks, I know. For now, just remember the seven stops from the top down: mental status, cranial nerves, motor, reflexes, sensation, coordination, gait.

docs.title: 16.5 Lesion Localization: Putting the Clues Together
docs.text:
Now comes the detective work. Neurologists localize by asking three questions in order:

  1. Is it the central or the peripheral nervous system? (Upper or lower motor neuron?)
  2. Which side?
  3. What level? (Cortex, brainstem, spinal cord, nerve, or muscle?)

docs.title: Question 1: Upper or lower motor neuron?
docs.text:
Recall from Chapter 7 that movement uses a two-neuron chain. An upper motor neuron runs from the motor cortex down the corticospinal tract. A lower motor neuron runs from the brainstem or spinal cord out through a nerve to the muscle. Damage to each causes weakness with a different signature (Wikipedia: UMN lesion; Wikipedia: LMN lesion; Merck Manual). The table compares the signs you just learned to test.

Finding Upper motor neuron lesion (brain or spinal cord) Lower motor neuron lesion (nerve root or nerve) Tone Increased (spastic) Decreased (floppy, or flaccid) Reflexes Brisk (hyperreflexia), sometimes clonus Reduced or absent Babinski sign Present (big toe goes up) Absent Muscle wasting Little, at least early on Often marked over time Fasciculations Absent Often present Facial weakness Lower face only (forehead spared) Whole half of the face

Real patients don't always match the table. ALS (Chapter 13) damages both kinds of motor neuron and mixes the two sets of signs. So doctors use the whole pattern, never one sign alone.

docs.title: Question 2: Which side?
docs.text:
About 90% of the fibers in the corticospinal tract cross to the other side at the bottom of the medulla, in a spot called the pyramidal decussation (Wikipedia: Pyramidal decussation). This crossing creates the most useful rule in localization:

  • A lesion above the crossing (cortex, deep white matter, most of the brainstem) causes weakness on the opposite side of the body.
  • A lesion below the crossing (spinal cord) causes weakness on the same side, below the level of the lesion.

So right-sided weakness plus language trouble shouts "left hemisphere." Most cranial nerves, though, don't cross before reaching their muscles. That creates a famous brainstem clue, crossed signs: one brainstem lesion damages a cranial nerve on one side and the not-yet-crossed corticospinal tract, causing a cranial nerve problem on one side and arm and leg weakness on the other (Wikipedia: Alternating hemiplegia).

docs.title: Question 3: What level?
docs.text:
Each level of the nervous system leaves its own fingerprint:

  • Cerebral hemisphere: weakness and numbness on the opposite side, plus "cortical" signs such as aphasia, neglect, or loss of half the visual field, which can only come from the brain.
  • Brainstem: crossed signs, double vision, trouble swallowing, slurred speech, or dizziness.
  • Spinal cord: normal face, normal thinking, a sensory level across the trunk, upper motor neuron signs below the lesion, and often bladder problems.
  • Peripheral nerve: weakness and numbness in the territory of a nerve, with reduced reflexes.
  • Muscle: weakness without any numbness, often on both sides and often in the larger muscles close to the trunk, such as those of the hips and shoulders.

The flowchart below turns the three questions into a simplified decision path, the same logic you'll use in the MicroSim.

flowchart TD
    A["Patient with weakness"] --> B{"Brisk reflexes, Babinski sign, spasticity?"}
    B -- "Yes: upper motor neuron" --> C{"Face, language, or vision affected?"}
    B -- "No: reduced reflexes or normal" --> D{"Numbness present?"}
    C -- "Yes, same side as body weakness" --> E["Cerebral hemisphere on the OPPOSITE side"]
    C -- "Cranial nerve on one side, body on the other" --> F["Brainstem"]
    C -- "No, face normal; sensory level on trunk" --> G["Spinal cord"]
    D -- "Yes, in one nerve's territory" --> H["Peripheral nerve"]
    D -- "No numbness at all" --> I["Muscle or neuromuscular junction"]

Notice the last box includes the neuromuscular junction, the synapse between nerve and muscle. Myasthenia gravis from Chapter 3 lives there, which is why it causes weakness without numbness.
