Correct and incorrect answers get case-specific feedback naming the reasoning (or the misconception behind a wrong choice). After two wrong attempts the correct location is revealed. Feedback boxes use both color and a text label.

Try Case 1 first. Before pressing any button, predict which hemisphere is damaged from the summary alone, then watch whether each finding supports your guess. Next, compare Case 1 with Case 2: both patients have a droopy face, but the forehead behaves differently, and that one difference moves the lesion from the brain to a nerve. In Case 3, notice what a head CT can't tell you.

Then try the challenge: can you localize each case with only 3 exam steps? That's the kind of choice the Brain Bee patient-diagnosis round asks you to make.

docs.title: 16.6 Looking Inside: Brain Imaging and Recording
docs.text: Once the exam points to a location, doctors often want to see it. Think of the tools as different cameras: an X-ray camera, a magnetic camera, a "blood flow" camera, a "fuel use" camera, and a microphone for electricity.

docs.title: Computed tomography (CT)
docs.text:
Computed tomography (CT) uses X-rays. An X-ray source spins around the head, detectors measure how much passes through, and a computer builds thin cross-sectional "slices" (NIBIB). Dense bone looks white, and fresh blood shows up bright too, so CT is very good at spotting bleeding in the brain. CT is fast and widely available. Its downsides: it uses ionizing radiation (the cancer risk from one scan is generally small, but exposure adds up over a lifetime), and it shows soft brain tissue in less detail than MRI. Godfrey Hounsfield and Allan Cormack shared the 1979 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for developing it (NobelPrize.org).

Why CT often comes first in a suspected stroke. A stroke is either a blocked artery (ischemic) or a burst one (hemorrhagic), and most are ischemic (Chapter 14; CDC). Clot-busting medicine can save brain tissue in an ischemic stroke but would make a bleed worse, so bleeding must be ruled out first. A plain head CT is the most widely used test for that job, and with an injected dye, CT can also show a blocked artery (CT angiography) (NINDS). Speed matters: one widely cited estimate found that a typical large-vessel ischemic stroke destroys about 1.9 million neurons each minute it goes untreated (Saver, 2006). Doctors sum this up as "time is brain."

A normal CT isn't the all-clear

In the first hours of an ischemic stroke, the CT often looks completely normal. The CT's job in that moment is to look for blood, not to prove there's no stroke. The exam and the history still drive the decision.

docs.title: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
docs.text:
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) uses a powerful magnet and radio waves instead of X-rays. The magnet lines up protons in the body's water; radio pulses knock them out of line, and the scanner detects the energy they release as they realign. Different tissues do this at different speeds, so MRI can tell them apart (NIBIB).

MRI shows the brain and spinal cord in finer detail than CT, clearly separates gray from white matter, and uses no ionizing radiation. A method called diffusion-weighted imaging can show an ischemic stroke earlier than plain CT, especially a small one (NINDS). MRI also reveals the plaques of multiple sclerosis (Chapter 1; NINDS). But it costs more, takes longer, is loud, and means lying still in a narrow tube. Because the magnet pulls on iron-containing metal, some implants, such as certain pacemakers and cochlear implants, can make it unsafe. Paul Lauterbur and Peter Mansfield shared the 2003 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discoveries about MRI (NobelPrize.org).

docs.title: Functional MRI (fMRI)
docs.text: Regular MRI shows structure. Functional MRI (fMRI) shows which areas become more active during a task, but it doesn't record neurons firing. When an area works harder, extra oxygen-rich blood rushes in, more than the area uses. Oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood behave differently in a magnetic field, and fMRI detects the change: the BOLD signal (blood-oxygen-level dependent), discovered by Seiji Ogawa and colleagues in 1990 (Wikipedia: fMRI). Blood flow is slow, so the BOLD response peaks about 4 to 6 seconds after the activity. fMRI shows where (to within millimeters) far better than when, and it is used mostly in research.

docs.title: PET scans
docs.text: A PET scan (positron emission tomography) tracks chemistry. The patient receives a small amount of a radioactive tracer, which gives off particles that produce pairs of gamma rays; detectors map where the tracer collects (NIBIB). The common tracer FDG is a slightly modified glucose molecule, so FDG-PET shows which areas are burning fuel and which have gone quiet. Other tracers bind specific targets: florbetapir, approved in the United States in 2012, binds the beta-amyloid plaques of Alzheimer's disease (Chapter 13; Wikipedia: Florbetapir). PET involves a small radiation dose, and its pictures are less detailed than MRI.

docs.title: EEG: listening to the brain's electricity
docs.text: You met the EEG (electroencephalogram) in Chapter 10: scalp electrodes record the summed electrical activity of many cortical neurons. Hans Berger recorded the first human EEG in 1924 and published in 1929 (Wikipedia: Hans Berger). EEG follows changes millisecond by millisecond but is poor at pinpointing where a signal comes from. Its main clinical job is diagnosing epilepsy (Wikipedia: EEG).

docs.title: Choosing the right tool
docs.text:
The table below compares all five side by side.

Tool What it measures Biggest strength Main limits Typical use CT X-ray density (structure) Fast, widely available, great for blood and bone Radiation; less soft-tissue detail Suspected stroke or head injury in the emergency room MRI Behavior of water protons in a magnet (structure) Fine detail of brain and spinal cord; no radiation Slow, loud, costly; some metal implants unsafe Small strokes, MS, tumors, spinal cord problems fMRI Blood oxygen changes (BOLD) linked to activity Shows where activity happens, to millimeters Indirect; lags by a few seconds Mostly research on brain function PET Where a radioactive tracer collects (chemistry) Shows fuel use or specific molecules like amyloid Radiation; less detailed images Dementia workups, such as amyloid PET EEG Electrical activity at the scalp Millisecond timing; cheap; portable Poor at locating deep sources Seizures and sleep

docs.title: 16.7 Lumbar Puncture: Sampling the Brain's Fluid
docs.text:
Sometimes the answer is floating in the fluid around the brain. Recall from Chapter 4 that cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) bathes the brain and spinal cord inside the meninges. A lumbar puncture (spinal tap) is a procedure in which a doctor inserts a thin needle between two vertebrae in the lower back, usually at the L3-L4 or L4-L5 space, to collect a small sample of CSF (Merck Manual).

A needle near the spine sounds scary, but there's a clever reason this spot is used. In adults, the spinal cord usually ends around the first lumbar vertebra (L1). Below that, the sac holds only loose nerve roots floating in fluid, which tend to slide out of the needle's way (Wikipedia: Lumbar puncture). Heinrich Quincke introduced the needle technique in 1891.

The lab checks the fluid's pressure, cells, protein, and glucose, and looks for germs. This helps diagnose:

  • Meningitis, an infection of the meninges: the fluid may contain white blood cells and bacteria.
  • Bleeding around the brain (subarachnoid hemorrhage): the fluid may be bloody.
  • Multiple sclerosis: special proteins called oligoclonal bands can support the diagnosis.

About 1 in 10 patients gets a headache afterward. More seriously, if a mass in the brain is raising the pressure inside the skull, removing fluid from below could make brain tissue shift dangerously. So when there are warning signs, such as swelling of the optic nerve or new focal deficits, doctors get a CT or MRI first (Merck Manual).

docs.title: 16.8 Differential Diagnosis: Ranking the Suspects
docs.text:
Now you build the differential diagnosis: a ranked list of the conditions that could explain the patient's findings, from most to least likely, keeping dangerous ones in mind even when they're unlikely. Then tests cross suspects off the list. For sudden one-sided weakness, stroke is the top suspect, but several stroke mimics can look like one:

  • Low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) can cause stroke-like symptoms (Wikipedia: Stroke). A finger-stick test takes seconds, so it's checked early.
  • A seizure can leave temporary weakness, called Todd's paresis, that usually fades within 48 hours (Wikipedia: Todd's paresis). Witnesses can say whether the patient shook or stared first.
  • Migraine with aura can cause temporary changes in vision, pins-and-needles feelings, or trouble speaking (NINDS: Migraine).
  • A brain tumor can cause similar signs, but they usually build up over weeks, not seconds.

The pattern narrows the location, and the timing ranks the causes. A sudden left-hemisphere deficit is most likely vascular; the same deficit creeping in over two months points toward something growing. Here's a differential for a 68-year-old with sudden right arm weakness and aphasia that began 50 minutes ago:

Possibility For it Against it Test that decides Ischemic stroke (left hemisphere) Sudden onset; pattern fits one artery None so far CT (no blood), then CT angiography or MRI Hemorrhagic stroke Sudden onset Can't tell without a scan CT shows bright blood Hypoglycemia Can mimic anything Patient isn't diabetic Finger-stick blood sugar Todd's paresis after a seizure Causes one-sided weakness No shaking or staring seen History from witnesses; EEG if unclear Brain tumor Can cause the same signs Onset was sudden, not gradual MRI

That one table uses the crossing motor pathway (Chapter 7), aphasia (Chapter 12), and seizures and stroke (Chapter 14). A differential diagnosis is where everything you've learned works together.

docs.title: At the Bedside: Sudden Weakness on One Side
docs.text:
Meet the patient

Mr. Harold Jensen, 71, was watching TV when his wife saw his left arm slide off the armrest. His speech was slurred, and he didn't seem to notice anything was wrong. She called 911. He was last seen normal 35 minutes earlier. He has high blood pressure and an irregular heartbeat. (Mr. Jensen is a fictional composite.)

What the doctor checks: His finger-stick blood sugar is normal. A focused neurological exam, scored with the NIH Stroke Scale (NINDS), finds:

  • Mental status: awake, but he ignores people on his left and insists his arm is fine (left-sided neglect). Speech is slurred, but language is normal: he names objects and follows commands.
  • Cranial nerves: eyes prefer to look right; left lower face droops, but the forehead wrinkles evenly; he misses fingers held up on his left.
  • Motor: left arm 1/5, left leg 3/5; right side 5/5.
  • Reflexes: 2+ on both sides at first, with a Babinski sign on the left.
  • Sensation: he barely notices touch on his left arm.
  • Coordination and gait: right side normal; he can't stand safely.

A non-contrast head CT shows no bleeding. CT angiography shows a blocked right middle cerebral artery.

Where is the problem? (localization): (1) A Babinski sign and forehead-sparing facial weakness are upper motor neuron signs: central nervous system. (2) The weakness is on the left, and the motor pathway crosses: right hemisphere. (3) Neglect, eyes deviating toward the lesion side, and loss of the left half of vision are cortical signs, and neglect points to the non-dominant (usually right) hemisphere (Wikipedia: Middle cerebral artery). Face and arm weaker than leg fits the middle cerebral artery territory (RCEMLearning). Normal language fits, since language usually lives on the left.

Diagnosis: Acute ischemic stroke caused by a blockage of the right middle cerebral artery.

Why it happens: His irregular heartbeat (atrial fibrillation) raises stroke risk, because blood clots can form in the heart and travel to the brain (Wikipedia: Atrial fibrillation). When a clot lodges in an artery, the neurons it feeds lose oxygen and glucose. Without fuel, their ion pumps fail (recall the sodium-potassium pump from Chapter 2), and the cells begin to die, including the upper motor neurons and cortical areas for the left side of the body.

Treatment today: With no bleeding and an early arrival, he is a candidate for clot-dissolving medicine (thrombolysis). NINDS notes that t-PA can be effective within three hours of symptom onset and that most clinicians now treat within a four-and-a-half-hour window. Because a large artery is blocked, doctors also consider thrombectomy: a catheter threaded from an artery in the leg up into the brain pulls the clot out. Perfusion imaging can identify some patients who still benefit from clot removal up to 24 hours after symptoms start (NINDS). Afterward, care turns to preventing another stroke and to rehabilitation.

What's new in research: Alteplase, the standard clot-busting drug, is given as an injection followed by an hour-long drip. A large Canadian trial called AcT found that tenecteplase, given as a single quick injection, worked about as well as alteplase for acute ischemic stroke (Menon et al., 2022, The Lancet). Based on that trial, the FDA approved tenecteplase (TNKase) for acute ischemic stroke in adults in early 2025; the drug's maker announced the approval on March 3, 2025 (NeurologyLive). In January 2026, the American Heart Association and American Stroke Association stroke guideline recommended either tenecteplase or alteplase for eligible adults treated within 4.5 hours of symptom onset (Prabhakaran et al., 2026, Stroke). A single injection can save minutes when every minute counts.

Your turn: diagnose a variation

Same patient, same exam, same timing. But this time the non-contrast head CT shows a bright white area deep in the right hemisphere. What changed, and should he get clot-busting medicine?

Answer: The bright area is fresh blood: a hemorrhagic stroke in the right hemisphere. The localization is the same, but the cause is different. Clot-busting medicine must not be given, because it could make the bleeding worse. Care instead focuses on finding and controlling the cause of the bleeding (NINDS). This is exactly why the CT comes first.

This is a fictional teaching case. It is not medical advice. If you or someone you know has symptoms like these, talk to a doctor.

docs.title: Common Misconceptions
docs.text:
Myth: A brain scan can read your thoughts. Reality: Scans measure physical things: X-ray density (CT), water protons (MRI), blood oxygen (fMRI), tracer chemistry (PET), or scalp electricity (EEG). An fMRI can show that a language area got busier, not the sentence you were thinking. Doctors use scans to find damage, not to read minds.

Myth: fMRI shows neurons firing directly. Reality: fMRI detects blood-oxygen changes that follow neural activity by a few seconds, an indirect, delayed signal. EEG records electrical activity far more directly and quickly, but it's poor at locating sources.

Myth: If the CT scan is normal, it can't be a stroke. Reality: In the first hours of an ischemic stroke, the CT is often normal. In an emergency, the CT's main job is to rule out bleeding. MRI with diffusion imaging can show a fresh ischemic stroke earlier.

Myth: Damage to the left side of the brain weakens the left side of the body. Reality: Most motor fibers cross at the bottom of the medulla, so a lesion in the left hemisphere weakens the right side. Only below the crossing, in the spinal cord, does weakness appear on the same side as the lesion.

Myth: Any drooping face means a stroke. Reality: A stroke usually spares the forehead, but facial nerve damage, as in Bell's palsy, weakens the whole half of the face (NINDS: Bell's Palsy). Any sudden face droop still needs an urgent medical check, because only a doctor can safely tell the difference.

docs.title: Brain Bee Practice
docs.text:
1. What is the Babinski sign, and what does it mean in an adult?

When the outer sole of the foot is stroked, the big toe goes up and the other toes fan out. In an adult, it indicates damage to the corticospinal tract (an upper motor neuron lesion). It's normal in infants up to about 12 months.

2. A patient's left lower face droops, but she can wrinkle her forehead normally. Is the lesion more likely in the brain or in the facial nerve?

In the brain (a central lesion), most likely in the right hemisphere. The forehead gets signals from both hemispheres, so it is spared when only one hemisphere is damaged. Facial nerve damage would weaken the whole half of the face, forehead included.

3. Why is a non-contrast CT usually done first when a stroke is suspected?

It's fast and widely available, and it's very good at showing fresh blood. Doctors must rule out bleeding before giving clot-busting medicine, which would make a hemorrhage worse.

4. What does fMRI actually measure?

The BOLD (blood-oxygen-level dependent) signal: changes in blood oxygen that follow increases in neural activity. It measures activity indirectly and with a delay of a few seconds.

5. Why is a lumbar puncture done below the second lumbar vertebra?

In adults, the spinal cord usually ends around L1. Below that, only loose nerve roots float in the fluid, so the needle can collect CSF without hitting the cord.

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
1. List the seven main parts of the neurological exam in the order used in this chapter.
  2. Name the imaging tool that uses X-rays and the one that uses a strong magnet and radio waves.
Answer
  1. Mental status, cranial nerves, motor (strength), reflexes, sensation, coordination, gait.
  2. CT uses X-rays; MRI uses a magnet and radio waves.

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
1. Explain why damage to upper motor neurons makes reflexes brisker instead of weaker.
  2. Explain why a lesion in the spinal cord causes weakness on the same side, while a lesion in the cortex causes weakness on the opposite side.
Answer
  1. The brain normally sends signals that calm the reflex loops in the spinal cord. Upper motor neuron damage removes that brake, so the reflexes become exaggerated.
  2. Most corticospinal fibers cross at the bottom of the medulla. A cortical lesion is above the crossing, so it affects the opposite side. A spinal cord lesion is below it, so the fibers there already serve the same side.

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
1. A 30-year-old has weakness and numbness in both legs, brisk knee and ankle reflexes, upgoing toes, normal arms, and numbness from the nipple line down. Where is the lesion, and about what level? Which imaging test would you order?
  2. A patient arrives 40 minutes after sudden right arm weakness and trouble finding words. Put these steps in a sensible order and explain why: MRI of the brain, finger-stick blood sugar, non-contrast head CT, history from the family.

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
1. Compare a patient with an upper motor neuron lesion to one with a lower motor neuron lesion in the same leg. Make a table of at least four exam findings that would differ.
  2. A patient has a weak, droopy left eyelid and an eye that can't move inward on the left, plus weakness of the right arm and leg. Using the idea of crossed signs, localize the lesion as precisely as you can.

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
1. A hospital can buy either a second CT scanner or a second MRI scanner for its emergency department. Using the strengths and limits of each tool, argue which would help stroke patients more, and why.
  2. A website claims that a company can use fMRI to tell whether someone is lying. Using what you know about how fMRI works, evaluate this claim.

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
1. Write your own fictional patient case for a classmate to localize. Include a short history, findings from at least five parts of the neurological exam, and an imaging result. Make sure every finding fits one lesion location, and write an answer key.
  2. Design a one-page "pocket card" for a Brain Bee competitor that summarizes how to tell cortex, brainstem, spinal cord, nerve, and muscle lesions apart.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Neurologists localize first ("where?") and name the disease second ("what?"). The timing of symptoms is one of the best clues to the cause.
  • The neurological exam checks mental status, cranial nerves, strength, reflexes, sensation, coordination, and gait, and connects each abnormal finding to a part of the nervous system.
  • Upper motor neuron lesions cause spasticity, brisk reflexes, and a Babinski sign. Lower motor neuron lesions cause floppy weakness, reduced reflexes, wasting, and fasciculations.
  • Because most motor fibers cross at the bottom of the medulla, brain lesions weaken the opposite side, while spinal cord lesions weaken the same side. A forehead-sparing face droop points to the brain; whole-face weakness points to the facial nerve.
  • CT is fast and good at finding blood, so it usually comes first in a suspected stroke. MRI shows more detail without radiation. fMRI tracks blood oxygen, PET tracks chemistry, and EEG tracks electricity in real time.
  • A lumbar puncture samples cerebrospinal fluid below the end of the spinal cord to help diagnose infections, bleeding, and multiple sclerosis.
  • A differential diagnosis ranks every condition that could explain the findings, including stroke mimics such as low blood sugar and seizures, and uses tests to narrow the list.

From neuron to bedside!

You did it: you started with a single neuron and finished at the bedside, reasoning like a neurologist. Every big idea really does start at a single synapse! Next, the appendices will help you plan for the Brain Bee and explore careers in neuroscience and medicine.

docs.title: Quiz: How Doctors Examine the Brain
Quiz: How Doctors Examine the Brain
docs.text: Test your understanding of Chapter 16. Choose the best answer, then click Show Answer to check.

docs.title: Question 1
docs.text:
A doctor strokes the outer edge of an adult patient's sole. Which response is the Babinski sign?

  1. The big toe curls down and the other toes curl in
  2. The big toe goes up and the other toes fan out
  3. The foot pulls away quickly because the stroke tickles
  4. The knee straightens with a brisk kick
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. An upgoing big toe with fanning of the other toes is the Babinski sign, which in adults points to damage along the corticospinal tract. A downgoing toe (A) is the normal adult response, and a knee kick (D) is the knee-jerk stretch reflex, a different test.

Concept Tested: Reflex Testing Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 2
docs.text:
Which imaging method builds cross-sectional pictures from X-rays passed through the head?

  1. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
  2. Positron emission tomography (PET)
  3. Electroencephalography (EEG)
  4. Computed tomography (CT)
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. CT spins an X-ray source around the head, and a computer turns the measurements into slices. MRI (A) is a common mix-up, but it uses a strong magnet and radio waves, not X-rays.

Concept Tested: Computed Tomography (CT) Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 3
docs.text:
Where is the needle usually placed for a lumbar puncture in an adult?

  1. Between the L3 and L4 (or L4 and L5) vertebrae in the lower back
  2. Between the C1 and C2 vertebrae in the neck
  3. Between the T4 and T5 vertebrae at the level of the nipples
  4. Directly into the spinal cord at the L1 vertebra
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. In adults, the spinal cord usually ends around L1, so a needle at L3-L4 or L4-L5 reaches cerebrospinal fluid among loose nerve roots without hitting the cord. Option D is the mistake the procedure is designed to avoid: the needle never goes into the cord.

Concept Tested: Lumbar Puncture Bloom's Level: Remember

docs.title: Question 4
docs.text:
What does functional MRI (fMRI) actually detect when a brain area becomes more active?

  1. The electrical spikes of individual neurons, millisecond by millisecond
  2. A radioactive sugar tracer building up in busy cells
  3. Changes in blood oxygen that follow the activity by a few seconds
  4. Changes in bone density around the active area
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. fMRI measures the BOLD (blood-oxygen-level dependent) signal: active areas receive extra oxygen-rich blood, and the response peaks a few seconds later. Option A describes what many people assume fMRI does, but recording fast electrical activity is closer to what EEG does. Option B describes FDG-PET.

Concept Tested: Functional MRI Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 5
docs.text:
Why does a stroke in one cerebral hemisphere usually leave the forehead able to wrinkle on both sides?

  1. The nerve cells controlling the forehead receive signals from both hemispheres
  2. The forehead muscles are controlled by the trigeminal nerve, not the facial nerve
  3. Strokes never affect the face, only the arms and legs
  4. The forehead is controlled by the spinal cord, which strokes don't reach
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The forehead's nerve cells get input from both hemispheres, so the healthy hemisphere keeps the forehead working. The lower face gets input mainly from the opposite hemisphere, so it droops. Option B confuses the trigeminal nerve (facial feeling and chewing) with the facial nerve (facial expression).

Concept Tested: Cranial Nerve Exam Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 6
docs.text:
An FDG-PET scan of the brain is mainly useful because it shows:

  1. The fine structure of gray and white matter, without radiation
  2. Fresh bleeding, faster than any other test
  3. The brain's electrical rhythms during sleep
  4. Which brain areas are taking up a glucose-like tracer, a sign of how much fuel they use
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. FDG is a slightly modified glucose molecule, so FDG-PET shows which areas are using fuel and which have gone quiet. Option A describes MRI (and PET does involve a small radiation dose), and option B describes a strength of CT.

Concept Tested: PET Scan Bloom's Level: Understand

docs.title: Question 7
docs.text:
A 60-year-old man arrives with sudden weakness of his right arm. Before any scan, the nurse's finger-stick test shows a very low blood sugar. What is the best interpretation?

  1. Low blood sugar proves he is not having a stroke, so no further workup is needed
  2. Low blood sugar is a known stroke mimic, so it should be treated and the patient reassessed
  3. Low blood sugar means the stroke must be hemorrhagic
  4. Blood sugar is unrelated to neurological symptoms and can be ignored
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Hypoglycemia can cause stroke-like symptoms, so it belongs on the differential diagnosis and is checked early because it's quick to test and fix. Option A goes too far: finding a mimic doesn't automatically rule out a stroke, so the doctor reassesses after correcting the sugar.

Concept Tested: Differential Diagnosis Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 8
docs.text:
During the mental status exam, a patient is alert and follows commands but speaks haltingly and can't name a pen or a watch. Which part of the brain is most likely affected?

  1. The cerebellum
  2. The right (usually non-dominant) hemisphere
  3. The left (usually dominant) hemisphere
  4. The lumbar spinal cord
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Trouble with language (aphasia) points to the dominant hemisphere, which is the left one in most people. The right hemisphere (B) is a tempting choice, but right-hemisphere damage more typically causes neglect of the left side of space, not aphasia.

Concept Tested: Mental Status Exam Bloom's Level: Apply

docs.title: Question 9
docs.text:
A patient has normal thinking, a normal face, and normal arms. Both legs are weak and stiff, the knee and ankle reflexes are brisk, both big toes go up, and pinprick feels dull from the belly button down on both sides. Where is the lesion?

  1. The left cerebral hemisphere
  2. The peripheral nerves of both legs
  3. The brainstem
  4. The thoracic spinal cord
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Upper motor neuron signs in both legs (brisk reflexes, Babinski signs), normal arms and face, and a sensory level near the T10 dermatome all point to the thoracic spinal cord. Peripheral nerve damage (B) would reduce reflexes, not make them brisk.

Concept Tested: Lesion Localization Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: Question 10
docs.text:
A patient has sudden numbness and mild weakness of one hand that is still present. In the emergency room, the non-contrast CT is normal. The team suspects a small ischemic stroke. Which test is most likely to show it?

  1. MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging
  2. A repeat non-contrast CT ten minutes later
  3. An EEG
  4. A lumbar puncture
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Diffusion-weighted MRI can show an ischemic stroke earlier than plain CT and is especially good for small strokes. A repeat CT minutes later (B) is unlikely to help, because early ischemic strokes often look normal on CT; the CT's main early job is to rule out bleeding.

Concept Tested: Magnetic Resonance Imaging Bloom's Level: Analyze

docs.title: References: How Doctors Examine the Brain
References: How Doctors Examine the Brain
docs.text:
1. Introduction to the Neurologic Examination - Merck Manual Professional Edition - A clear overview of every part of the neurological exam, with linked pages on mental status, cranial nerves, strength, reflexes, sensation, and coordination. Written for clinicians, but readable for a motivated high school student who wants to see how real doctors do it.

  2. Stroke: Assess and Treat - National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NIH) - Explains how stroke is diagnosed (NIH Stroke Scale, CT, MRI) and treated (t-PA, clot removal). The best single source for why CT comes first and why "time is brain."

  3. Bell's Palsy - National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NIH) - Describes the symptoms, diagnosis, treatment, and recovery of Bell's palsy, the facial nerve disorder in the MicroSim's second case. Useful for contrasting peripheral facial weakness with stroke.

  4. Computed Tomography (CT) - National Institute of Biomedical Imaging and Bioengineering (NIH) - A plain-language explanation of how CT scanners build images from X-rays, what they're good for, and what to know about radiation.

  5. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) - National Institute of Biomedical Imaging and Bioengineering (NIH) - Explains how magnets and radio waves create MRI images, why MRI shows soft tissue so well, its safety concerns, and a short note on fMRI.

  6. Nuclear Medicine - National Institute of Biomedical Imaging and Bioengineering (NIH) - Covers PET scans and radioactive tracers such as FDG, including how they reveal the body's chemistry rather than its structure.

  7. Appendix A: Methods - OpenStax, Introduction to Behavioral Neuroscience (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) - A free, open textbook section on research methods, including fMRI and EEG. Good for seeing how these tools are used in research as well as in the clinic.

  8. Time is brain—quantified - Saver JL, Stroke, 2006 (PubMed) - The paper behind the estimate that a typical large-vessel ischemic stroke destroys about 1.9 million neurons per minute without treatment. A short read that shows why stroke teams move so fast.

  9. Intravenous tenecteplase compared with alteplase for acute ischaemic stroke in Canada (AcT) - Menon BK et al., The Lancet, 2022 (PubMed) - The randomized trial that found tenecteplase worked about as well as alteplase, supporting its 2025 FDA approval for acute ischemic stroke. A real example of how clinical trials change treatment.

  10. Competition - International Brain Bee - Describes the parts of the international competition, including the patient diagnosis section where students watch patient videos and choose diagnostic tests. Check your own regional or national rules, which may differ.

docs.title: Learning Graph for From Neuron to Bedside
docs.text:
Open the Learning Graph Viewer Fullscreen

This section contains the learning graph for From Neuron to Bedside. A learning graph is a map of the concepts taught in this textbook. Each concept is a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by arrows (directed edges) that show which concepts you need to understand first. For example, the arrow from Action Potential points to Threshold, Voltage-Gated Channel, and Depolarization, because you need those ideas before an action potential makes sense.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for an intelligent textbook. It works like a roadmap: it shows the paths a student can take from basic ideas, like Cell Membrane and Ion, all the way to the bedside, like diagnosing Parkinson's Disease or treating a Stroke.

The foundational concepts sit at the start of the graph. They have no prerequisites of their own. Only arrows from other concepts point into them. The most advanced concepts, such as Differential Diagnosis and Lesion Localization, sit at the far end. To master them you need every concept along the paths they point to.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: The concepts come from the course description for From Neuron to Bedside, which follows the topics tested in the Brain Bee and adds a clinical case to every chapter. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom's Taxonomy (Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, Create) to order its learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text: The course description was turned into a Concept List of 253 concepts, grouped by chapter. Each concept has a short Title Case label of at most 32 characters, so it fits on a node in the graph.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text:
Next, the dependencies between concepts were mapped as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). A DAG has no cycles, so no concept ever ends up depending on itself. Every prerequisite comes from the same chapter or an earlier one, so reading the book in order never asks you to use an idea before it has been taught.

The graph is available in two formats:

  • A CSV file with the columns ConceptID, ConceptLabel, Dependencies, and TaxonomyID.
  • A JSON file in the vis-network format, with metadata, groups, nodes, and edges sections. Each edge has a from concept and the to concept it depends on.

docs.title: Learning Graph Quality Validation
docs.text:
This report checks the overall quality of the learning graph using graph algorithms.

  • Graph structure validation: every concept is connected
  • DAG validation: no cycles
  • Foundational concepts: 5 entry points
  • Indegree analysis: which concepts the most other concepts depend on
  • Longest dependency chains

View the Learning Graph Quality Validation

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy
docs.text:
To see patterns in the graph, each concept is assigned to one of 12 categories, such as Neuroanatomy, Sensory Systems and Pain, or Disorders and Diseases. Each category has its own color in the graph viewer.

  • 12 categories with short codes (for example SIG for Electrical and Chemical Signaling)
  • Categories ordered from foundational biology to clinical practice and research
  • No category holds more than 30% of the concepts

docs.text:
Every concept in the learning graph belongs to exactly one of these 12 categories. The category sets the color of the concept's node in the learning graph viewer. The categories run roughly in the order the book teaches them, from basic biology to the clinic.

Code Category Description Concepts Color FOUND Foundational Biology and Chemistry Basic biology and chemistry needed before anything else: cell membranes, ions, proteins, and concentration gradients. 4 SteelBlue CELL Neurons and Glia The cells of the nervous system (neurons and glia), their parts, and how the nervous system is organized. 19 DarkGreen SIG Electrical and Chemical Signaling How neurons send signals: membrane potentials, the action potential, synapses, receptors, and neurotransmitters. 36 Gold ANAT Neuroanatomy The structures of the brain, spinal cord, and nerves, and how they are named, protected, and supplied with blood. 23 Teal SENS Sensory Systems and Pain How the body turns light, sound, touch, taste, smell, and tissue damage into neural signals, and where those signals go. 26 Orange MOTOR Movement and Motor Control Muscles, reflexes, the motor cortex, the basal ganglia, and the cerebellum. 12 DarkSlateBlue DEV Development and Aging How the brain is built before birth, how it changes in childhood and the teenage years, and how it ages. 14 LimeGreen COG Learning, Memory, and Cognition Learning, memory, neuroplasticity, language, attention, and decision-making. 21 DarkOrchid STATE Sleep, Emotion, and Stress Consciousness, sleep and circadian rhythms, emotion, stress, and reward. 23 LightSkyBlue DIS Disorders and Diseases Neurological, psychiatric, and developmental disorders, injuries, and addiction. 39 Crimson CLIN Clinical Exam, Imaging, and Treatment How doctors examine, image, diagnose, and treat the nervous system, including drugs and procedures. 25 HotPink RES Research Methods and Careers How neuroscience is done: classic cases and model organisms, research methods and ethics, new technology, and careers. 11 SaddleBrown

Total: 253 concepts.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Foundational Biology and Chemistry (FOUND) is small on purpose. It holds only the few ideas from general biology and chemistry that the rest of the book builds on. Nervous System is also a starting point of the graph, but it is filed under Neurons and Glia (CELL).
  • Disorders and Diseases (DIS) and Clinical Exam, Imaging, and Treatment (CLIN) appear in almost every chapter, because each chapter ends with a clinical case.
  • See the Taxonomy Distribution Report for the full list of concepts in each category.

Each question was assigned the level of thinking a full answer asks of the reader. These are judgment calls, not measurements.

Level Count Share Examples Remember 21 28% "How many neurons does the human brain have?", "What is the Brain Bee?" Understand 24 32% "How do neurons talk to each other across a synapse?", "What happens in the brain while I sleep?" Apply 9 12% "What should I do if someone has a seizure?", "What is the best way to study, according to brain science?" Analyze 7 9% "Why does the left side of the brain control the right side of the body?", "What's the difference between a CT scan and an MRI?" docs.title: ISO 11179 self-assessment
docs.text: Criterion Score (out of 25) Notes Precision 23 Each definition is written for the way the term is used in this course. Clinical terms were checked against standard references. Approval dates for drugs and therapies were confirmed by web search on 2026-10-12. Conciseness 23 Every definition is one or two sentences (average 22 words). Terms that pair two ideas, such as "Rods and Cones", "Agonist and Antagonist" and "Ventral and Dorsal Streams", run longer (30 to 37 words) because they define both halves. Distinctiveness 24 Close pairs say how they differ. Examples are short-term vs working memory, learning vs memory, stroke vs ischemic vs hemorrhagic stroke, and nociception vs pain pathway. The text is original and not copied from Brain Facts or any other source. Non-circularity 24 No definition uses its own term to define itself. The two-part entries define each half in independent terms. Sympathetic vs Parasympathetic does not rely on "fight or flight". Free of business rules 22 Definitions describe what things are, not policies. A few entries are guidance or criteria by nature, such as Seizure First Aid, BE-FAST, Return-to-Learn and Play, Teen Sleep Needs (8 to 10 hours) and Depression (at least two weeks). Their definitions keep the factual or diagnostic core, and advice such as "call 911 after 5 minutes" sits only in the examples. Overall ~93/100 Above the skill's 85-point target.

docs.text:
• Estimated Flesch-Kincaid grade: about 10.1 for examples, 12.8 for definitions and 11.5 overall. These come from a rough syllable-count script.

docs.title: Terms and facts I was less sure of
docs.text:
• Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy: The glossary says CTE "can currently be confirmed only after death." This is still the standard view, and research criteria for diagnosing it in living people exist. Re-check before publishing.
  • Anti-Amyloid Antibody: Lecanemab got traditional FDA approval in July 2023 (after accelerated approval in January 2023). Donanemab was approved in July 2024. Both are for early Alzheimer's disease (MCI or mild dementia with confirmed amyloid). The glossary says they "modestly slow decline" and need MRI monitoring for ARIA.
  • Antisense Oligonucleotide: Tofersen (Qalsody) received FDA accelerated approval on April 25, 2023, for SOD1-ALS.
  • Gene Therapy: Zolgensma was FDA-approved in 2019 for children under 2 with spinal muscular atrophy. The glossary says "young children".
  • Clot-Busting Treatment: Names alteplase and tenecteplase. Tenecteplase (TNKase) was FDA-approved for acute ischemic stroke in March 2025.
  • Naloxone: Says the nasal spray has been sold without a prescription in the US "since 2023". The FDA approved it for over-the-counter sale in March 2023, and it reached stores later that year.

  • Numbers used: Only well-established figures appear:

    • resting potential about −70 mV and threshold about −55 mV ("often around")
    • 3 Na⁺ out / 2 K⁺ in
    • action potential 1 to 2 ms
    • sleep cycle about 90 minutes
    • teen sleep 8 to 10 hours (AASM recommendation for ages 13 to 18)
    • Huntington's inheritance 50%
    • seizure first aid 5 minutes (CDC guidance)
    • H.M. surgery 1953, Phineas Gage 1848, Kandel's Nobel Prize 2000

    None has a linked source inside the glossary. The chapters that teach these terms should carry the citations. - Teen Sleep Needs: The definition includes "sleep experts recommend 8 to 10 hours," which is close to a recommendation rather than a definition. Keep it or move it into the example. - Deep Brain Stimulation: I avoided listing the exact FDA indications and said only that it can help some people with Parkinson's disease. - Brain-Computer Interface: Described as being in clinical trials. Update this if a BCI device gets FDA market authorization.

  • Maya appears only in examples that match her canon details (she is 16 and plays soccer).

docs.title: MicroSims
docs.text:
MicroSims are small interactive simulations. Each one focuses on a single idea. Click a card to open it. Teachers: every MicroSim page has an embed code you can paste into your own site.

  • Neuron Explorer

    Explore the parts of a neuron and two glial cells, then send a signal down the axon with and without myelin to see why multiple sclerosis slows or blocks signals.

    Chapter 1

  • Action Potential Simulator

    Interactive membrane-voltage plot showing threshold, the all-or-none spike, refractory periods, firing rate coding, lidocaine block, and the effect of outside potassium.

    Chapter 2

  • Synapse Simulator

    A close-up of a chemical synapse. Fire the presynaptic neuron and see how a reuptake blocker, a receptor antagonist, or fewer receptors change cleft transmitter and the postsynaptic potential.

    Chapter 3

  • Clickable Brain Atlas

    A clickable lateral and midsagittal brain atlas with region info panels and a quiz mode for learning neuroanatomy.

    Chapter 4

  • Visual Pathway Lesion Simulator

    Place a lesion along the visual pathway, from optic nerve to occipital cortex, and see the matching visual field loss in each eye.

    Chapter 5

  • Homunculus and Dermatome Map

    Click a body region to see where it lands on the opposite primary somatosensory cortex and which spinal level (dermatome) or cranial nerve carries it.

    Chapter 6

  • Basal Ganglia Gas and Brake

    A simplified basal ganglia circuit. Slide dopamine from low to high and watch the direct (GO) and indirect (NO-GO) pathways change movement output.

    Chapter 7

  • Synaptic Pruning Over a Lifetime

    An age slider from birth to 30 shows synapses being overproduced and then pruned, earlier in sensory cortex and later in prefrontal cortex, while white matter keeps growing.

    Chapter 8

  • Aplysia Habituation and Sensitization

    Touch a simplified sea slug's siphon and shock its tail to see how one synapse weakens with habituation and strengthens with sensitization.

    Chapter 9

  • Hypnogram Builder

    An interactive hypnogram of an illustrative 9-hour teen night with schematic EEG waves for each sleep stage and a slider that shows which stages are lost when sleep is cut short.

    Chapter 10

  • HPA Axis Feedback Loop

    Trigger a stressor and watch cortisol rise and fall through the HPA axis, then weaken its negative feedback or repeat the stress to see cortisol stay high.

    Chapter 11

  • Aphasia Sorter

    A classification game: read short original speech samples with a clue, then sort each as Broca's, Wernicke's, conduction aphasia, or normal speech.

    Chapter 12

  • Amyloid and Tau Cascade

    A schematic timeline of Alzheimer's disease showing amyloid, tau, neuron loss, and symptoms rising in order, with an illustrative anti-amyloid treatment.

    Chapter 13

  • Stroke Territory Map

    Block the anterior, middle, or posterior cerebral artery on either side and see which side of the body and which functions are typically affected.

    Chapter 14

  • Reward Pathway and Tolerance

    A schematic MicroSim of the dopamine reward pathway showing natural rewards, drug spikes, tolerance from receptor downregulation, and withdrawal.

    Chapter 15

  • Neuro Exam Decision Tree

    Interactive case-based MicroSim: run neurological exam steps on three fictional patients, collect findings, and localize the lesion.

    Chapter 16

  • Learning Graph Viewer

    Explore all 253 concepts in this book and how they depend on each other.

docs.title: Neuron Explorer
docs.text: Run the Neuron Explorer MicroSim fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Neuron Explorer shows a labeled neuron (dendrites, cell body, axon hillock, axon, myelin sheath, nodes of Ranvier, and axon terminals) next to two kinds of glial cells: an oligodendrocyte that wraps myelin around the axon and an astrocyte whose "end-foot" touches a blood vessel. Hover over, click, or choose any part to read its job in the info panel.

The Send signal button fires a signal at the start of the axon. With healthy myelin, the signal races along and is renewed at each node of Ranvier. Check Remove myelin (MS) to strip myelin from 1 to 4 segments, as happens in multiple sclerosis. In the bare stretch, the signal leaks charge, slows to a crawl, and fades. One or two damaged segments make it arrive late. Three or four damaged segments make it fade out before it reaches a healthy node, so the message is blocked.

The signal model is simplified and illustrative. The speeds and fading rate are chosen to show the pattern, not measured from a real nerve. Real conduction speeds are given in the chapter.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Hover over (or click) each labeled part. Read its job in the info panel at the bottom. You can also pick a part from the Explore a part menu.
  2. Press Send signal with healthy myelin. Watch the signal flash at each node and reach the axon terminals.
  3. Check Remove myelin (MS) and leave Damaged segments at 2. Send the signal again. Compare its speed and strength with step 2.
  4. Move the slider to 3 or 4 damaged segments and send another signal. What happens this time?
  5. Use Pause / Resume to freeze the signal and read the strength value in the status line.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Bloom level: Understand (explain). Students will be able to explain the job of each part of a neuron and its nearby glial cells, and explain why losing myelin (as in multiple sclerosis) makes a signal slower and can stop it completely.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9 to 12 (biology, anatomy and physiology, or a neuroscience club)

Duration: 15 to 20 minutes

Prerequisites: Basic cell structure (nucleus, cell membrane, proteins). Students should have read Sections 1.4 to 1.7 of Chapter 1.

Activity:

  1. Label race (5 min). In pairs, one student names a part's job out loud ("collects incoming messages") and the partner finds the part in the sim and checks the info panel.
  2. Predict, then test (5 min). Before removing any myelin, students write a prediction: "If myelin is removed from two segments, the signal will..." Then they test it and record what happened.
  3. Find the breaking point (5 min). Students raise the number of damaged segments one at a time and record the first setting where the signal is blocked.
  4. Connect to medicine (5 min). Students explain in two sentences how this links to the blurry vision and tingling in the chapter's multiple sclerosis case.

Assessment questions:

  1. Which glial cell in the sim makes myelin in the brain and spinal cord? What makes myelin in the rest of the body?
  2. Why does the signal get renewed at nodes of Ranvier but fade in a bare stretch of axon?
  3. In the sim, removing myelin from two segments slows the signal, but removing it from three segments blocks it. Explain this difference in your own words.
  4. MS symptoms can come and go. Using the sim, explain how a small amount of damage might cause a slowed signal while a larger patch causes a lost signal.

docs.title: Action Potential Simulator
docs.text: Run the Action Potential Simulator fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This simulator plots a neuron's membrane voltage (in millivolts) against time (in milliseconds), like a recording from an electrode inside a cell. You can deliver one stimulus or two stimuli in a row, hold a steady stimulus on, block sodium channels with the local anesthetic lidocaine, and change the potassium concentration outside the cell. Dashed and dotted lines mark the threshold (about −55 mV) and the current resting potential (about −70 mV at the normal outside potassium of 4 mM). A side panel shows what fraction of voltage-gated sodium channels are open, inactivated, closed and ready, or blocked, and what fraction of voltage-gated potassium channels are open.

The sim uses a simplified teaching model, not the full Hodgkin-Huxley equations. Below threshold, the membrane behaves like a leaky capacitor that relaxes back to rest. The resting potential comes from the Goldman equation, so it shifts when you change outside potassium. When the voltage reaches threshold and enough sodium channels are ready, a spike with a fixed shape fires: a rise to about +35 mV, a fall, and an undershoot near −80 mV. Sodium channel inactivation drops during each spike and recovers over a few milliseconds, which creates the absolute and relative refractory periods. Time is slowed down a lot so you can watch each phase.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Press Stimulate at the default strength of 3. The voltage bumps up and fades without crossing threshold.
  2. Raise Stimulus strength one step at a time and press Stimulate after each change. Find the weakest strength that fires a spike (6 in this model). Try 8 and 10 and watch the "Last spike peak" readout: it stays at +35 mV.
  3. Check Hold stimulus and try strengths 6, 8, and 10. Count the spikes in each 50 ms sweep. Stronger stimuli give more spikes per second, not bigger spikes. Uncheck it when you are done.
  4. Use Stimulate twice. At strength 10, set the Gap between 2 stimuli to 3 ms (the second stimulus fails), then 4 ms (both fire). Repeat at strengths 8 and 6 and find the shortest gap that works.
  5. Check Block Na+ channels (lidocaine) and stimulate at strength 10. No spike appears, only a passive bump.
  6. Uncheck lidocaine and move Outside K+ to 8, 10, and 12 mM. Watch the resting line rise and the spikes shrink, then fail.
  7. Press Reset at any time to clear the trace. Start/Pause freezes and resumes the clock.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Bloom level: Apply. The learner will predict whether a stimulus produces an action potential, given its strength, its timing after a previous spike, the outside K⁺ concentration, and whether Na⁺ channels are blocked by lidocaine.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9 to 12 (biology, AP Biology, AP Psychology, or a neuroscience elective)

Duration: 25 to 35 minutes

Prerequisites: Ions and concentration gradients, the parts of a neuron, and the vocabulary from Chapter 2 (resting potential, threshold, depolarization, repolarization, hyperpolarization).

Activity: Predict, then test

  1. Warm-up (5 min). Students sketch what they think a spike looks like on a voltage-vs-time graph and label rest, threshold, and peak.
  2. Threshold hunt (5 min). In pairs, students predict the weakest strength that will fire, then test it. They record the peak voltage at strengths 6, 8, and 10.
  3. Refractory challenge (10 min). For strengths 10, 8, and 6, students first predict and then measure the shortest gap that gives two spikes. They explain the trend using the channel panel (inactivated sodium channels versus the undershoot).
  4. Rate coding (5 min). With "Hold stimulus" on, students record spikes per 50 ms sweep at strengths 6, 8, and 10 and convert to spikes per second.
  5. Clinical connection (5 to 10 min). Students test lidocaine and high outside potassium, then write two sentences linking each result to a real situation (a dental numbing shot; high blood potassium).

Assessment questions:

  1. Why does the peak stay at about +35 mV when you raise the stimulus from 6 to 10?
  2. At strength 10, why does a second stimulus fail at a 3 ms gap but succeed at 4 ms?
  3. Why does a strength-6 second stimulus need a much longer gap than a strength-10 one?
  4. With lidocaine on, the voltage bump can rise above the threshold line without a spike. Explain why.
  5. Raising outside K⁺ to 8 mM makes the neuron easier to fire, but 12 mM makes it impossible. Explain both results.

docs.title: Synapse Simulator
docs.text: Run the Synapse Simulator fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This simulator zooms in on one chemical synapse, in slow motion. The presynaptic terminal at the top holds vesicles full of neurotransmitter. When the neuron fires, vesicles release transmitter particles (red dots) into the synaptic cleft. The particles drift across, bind receptors on the postsynaptic cell (green cups that turn bright green while bound), let go, and are pumped back into the terminal by reuptake transporters (blue blocks).

Two graphs show what matters. The top graph tracks how much transmitter is in the cleft. The bottom graph tracks the postsynaptic membrane potential in millivolts, starting from a resting potential of −70 mV. The dashed line marks threshold at −55 mV. When the potential reaches threshold, the postsynaptic cell fires an action potential (up to about +30 mV), and the counter records how many releases succeeded.

A menu switches between four conditions:

  • Normal: transporters clear the cleft quickly, and almost every release reaches threshold. This is because the simulator is modeled on a strong synapse with a large safety margin, like the junction between a motor neuron and a muscle fiber. Most synapses in the brain are weaker: one release makes an EPSP too small to reach threshold, and the cell fires only when many EPSPs add up (summation, Chapter 3, Section 3.5).
  • Reuptake blocker (like an SSRI): transporters are blocked, so transmitter lingers and the response lasts longer.
  • Receptor antagonist: a drug occupies 8 of the 12 receptors without activating them, so the cleft looks normal but the response is small.
  • Fewer receptors (myasthenia-like): 6 of the 12 receptors are gone, as when antibodies remove acetylcholine receptors in myasthenia gravis. The response is smaller and fails more often at high firing rates.

The model is qualitative, and it represents one strong excitatory synapse, not a typical synapse in the brain. Particle numbers, receptor numbers, and timing are chosen to show the correct direction of each change, not real measurements. The resting potential, threshold, and spike peak match the values in Chapter 2. Release gets smaller when the neuron fires rapidly, because the store of ready vesicles takes time to refill. At a real neuromuscular junction, an enzyme (acetylcholinesterase) clears acetylcholine instead of reuptake. The simulator keeps one cleanup method in every condition so that only one thing changes at a time.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Press Fire once to send a single action potential into the terminal. Watch the particles cross the cleft, bind receptors, and disappear into the transporters.
  2. Press Start to let the neuron fire on its own at the rate set by the Firing rate slider (0 to 5 per second, in slow motion). Press Pause to freeze the scene at any moment.
  3. Use the Condition menu to switch conditions. Switching resets the graphs so you can compare fairly.
  4. For each condition, predict what will happen to both graphs before you press Start, then check.
  5. In the "Fewer receptors" condition, compare the success counter at 1 per second and at 5 per second.
  6. Press Reset to clear the graphs and counters.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Bloom level: Apply. Students will predict how a reuptake blocker, a receptor antagonist, and a loss of receptors each change the amount of neurotransmitter in the synaptic cleft and the size and duration of the postsynaptic potential, and then test those predictions.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9 to 12

Duration: 20 to 25 minutes

Prerequisites: resting potential, threshold, and action potentials (Chapter 2); the basic steps of chemical synaptic transmission (Chapter 3, Sections 3.3 to 3.6).

Activity:

  1. Warm-up (3 minutes). Ask: "If a drug made neurotransmitter stay in the cleft longer, what would happen to the next cell?" Have students write a one-sentence prediction.
  2. Normal baseline (4 minutes). Students press Fire once several times and sketch the shape of both graphs.
  3. Predict, then test (10 minutes). For each of the other three conditions, students fill in a table with columns "Cleft graph: higher, lower, or the same?", "Response: bigger, smaller, or longer?", and "Did the cell reach threshold?" They fill in the prediction column first, then run the condition and fill in the observation column.
  4. Myasthenia gravis connection (4 minutes). In the Fewer receptors condition, students record the success counter after about 10 releases at 1 per second and at 5 per second. Discuss why weakness in myasthenia gravis gets worse with use.
  5. Wrap-up (3 minutes). Students sort the drugs from Section 3.8 into "changes the cleft graph" and "changes only the response."

Assessment questions:

  1. In which condition does the cleft graph look normal while the response shrinks? What does that tell you about where the drug acts?
  2. Why does blocking reuptake make the postsynaptic response last longer?
  3. Why do failures in the Fewer receptors condition become more common at a higher firing rate?
  4. Pyridostigmine slows the breakdown of acetylcholine. Which part of the simulator would it change, and how might that help a person with myasthenia gravis?

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim is a stylized, procedurally drawn human brain that you can explore by hovering and clicking. It has two views:

  • Lateral view (side): the left side of the brain, front facing left. It shows the prefrontal cortex and the motor areas of the frontal lobe, the parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes, the cerebellum, the brainstem, the spinal cord, and two landmark grooves, the central sulcus and the lateral sulcus.
  • Midsagittal view (cut down the middle): the brain sliced along the midline. It shows the inner surface of the cerebrum, the corpus callosum, thalamus, hypothalamus, pituitary gland, midbrain, pons, medulla oblongata, cerebellum, fourth ventricle, and spinal cord.

Clicking a region opens an info panel with its name, its main jobs, what happens if it is damaged, and a Brain Bee fact. The shapes are simplified, but every structure is drawn in its correct anatomical position. A Quiz me mode hides the labels, names a structure, and checks whether you click the right one.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Choose a view from the View menu.
  2. Move the mouse over the brain. The region under the pointer turns gold and its name appears.
  3. Click a region (or a black groove line in the side view) to read its info panel.
  4. Uncheck Show labels to test yourself without the name tags.
  5. Press Quiz me. Read the structure named in the panel and click it. You get one try per question. A wrong answer tells you what you clicked, gives a location hint, and highlights the correct structure in gold.
  6. Press Next question to continue. Your score is shown next to the buttons. Press Stop quiz to return to exploring.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Bloom level: Remember (identify). Students will identify 19 major brain structures and landmarks in a lateral view and a midsagittal view, scoring at least 80% in quiz mode in each view.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9 to 12

Duration: 25 to 30 minutes

Prerequisites: Students know what neurons, axons, and myelin are (Chapter 1) and have read the sections of Chapter 4 on the lobes, deep structures, brainstem, and ventricles.

Activity:

  1. Predict (5 minutes). Before opening the sim, students sketch a side view of the brain from memory and label as many structures as they can.
  2. Explore (10 minutes). In pairs, students click every region in both views. For each one, they record one main job and one "if damaged" effect in a two-column table.
  3. Localize (5 minutes). The teacher reads three short symptom stories (for example, "clumsy left arm with normal strength," "trouble understanding speech," "personality change after a forehead injury"). Students click the region they think is damaged and justify their choice using the info panel.
  4. Quiz (5 to 10 minutes). Each student completes the quiz in both views and records their scores. Students below 80% repeat the quiz after reviewing the regions they missed.

Assessment questions:

  1. Which groove separates the frontal lobe from the parietal lobe, and which kinds of cortex lie just in front of it and just behind it?
  2. In the midsagittal view, which structure arches above the thalamus, and what does it connect?
  3. Name the three parts of the brainstem in order from top to bottom.
  4. A patient has unsteady walking and a clumsy right arm but normal strength. Which structure in the atlas is most likely damaged, and on which side?
  5. Why does the atlas accept a click on the prefrontal cortex as a correct answer for "Frontal lobe"?

docs.title: Visual Pathway Lesion Simulator
docs.text: Run the Visual Pathway Lesion Simulator Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim is a top-down (bird's-eye) map of the human visual pathway. Light from the left visual field lands on the nasal (inner) retina of the left eye and the temporal (outer) retina of the right eye. Those fibers are drawn in blue, and they all end up in the right hemisphere. Information about the right visual field is drawn in orange and ends up in the left hemisphere.

The key rule is that fibers from the nasal half of each retina cross at the optic chiasm, and fibers from the temporal half stay on the same side. After the chiasm, each optic tract, lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN), optic radiation, and primary visual cortex (V1) carries the opposite half of the visual world from both eyes.

When you place a lesion, the cut fibers turn gray and dashed. Two circular maps show what each eye can still see, drawn the way the patient sees it (left side of the circle = the patient's left). Dark gray means vision is lost.

The maps are idealized. Real lesions are often partial, and a defect can be uneven between the two eyes.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Start with None (healthy) and trace the blue fibers from both eyes to the right side of the brain.
  2. Check Hide result so you can predict before you look.
  3. Pick a lesion from the Lesion site menu, or click one of the red dots on the diagram.
  4. Sketch what you think each eye will lose. Then uncheck Hide result and compare.
  5. Repeat for all five lesion sites. For each one, explain your answer using the words nasal, temporal, crossing, and same side.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Bloom level: Analyze. Given a lesion site anywhere from the optic nerve to the occipital cortex, the student will predict the visual field defect in each eye and, working backward, localize a lesion from a described field defect.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9 to 12 (also useful for Brain Bee and pre-med review)

Duration: 20 to 25 minutes

Prerequisites: Chapter 4 (occipital, temporal, and parietal lobes; thalamus) and Chapter 5 sections on the retina, optic chiasm, and visual fields.

Activity (predict, test, explain):

  1. Warm-up (3 min). Students cover one eye and notice that each eye alone still sees both the left and right sides of the world.
  2. Prediction round (10 min). In pairs, students turn on Hide result, choose each lesion, and draw two circles per lesion on paper, shading what they predict is lost. Then they reveal the answer and score themselves.
  3. Reverse round (7 min). The teacher describes a field defect ("both eyes lose the upper-right quarter"). Students find the lesion site that produces it.
  4. Wrap-up (5 min). Each pair writes one sentence explaining why a lesion in front of the chiasm affects one eye, but a lesion behind the chiasm affects both eyes.

Assessment questions:

  1. Which single lesion makes each eye lose its outer half of vision? Why does that location cause that pattern?
  2. A patient loses the left half of the visual field in both eyes, but the very center is spared. Where is the lesion most likely to be?
  3. Why does a lesion of the left optic nerve not cause any loss in the right eye?
  4. Damage to Meyer's loop in the left temporal lobe causes loss in which quarter of the visual field? Explain using the fact that the image on the retina is upside down.

Answers: (1) The center of the optic chiasm, because the crossing fibers there come from both nasal retinas, which see the temporal fields. (2) The right occipital cortex (V1), often from a stroke. (3) The left optic nerve carries fibers only from the left eye. (4) The upper-right quarter ("pie in the sky"). Meyer's loop carries fibers from the lower retina, which sees the upper visual field, and the left hemisphere handles the right visual field.

docs.title: Homunculus and Dermatome Map
docs.text: Run the Homunculus and Dermatome Map MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim links two body maps that doctors use every day. The left panel is a front view of a person with clickable dots on 11 body regions. The right panel is a front-view (coronal) slice of one brain hemisphere. Its outer edge shows the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) on the postcentral gyrus as a strip of body-part segments, running from the toes and foot on the inner (medial) wall, over the top of the brain, and down the side to the face, lips, tongue, and throat. Segment sizes are exaggerated for the hands and lips, like the classic sensory homunculus.

When you pick a region, the sim highlights its segment on the opposite hemisphere and gives the spinal level that carries touch from that spot, using the standard ISNCSCI key sensory points (for example C6 for the thumb and T10 for the belly button). The lips have no spinal dermatome; they are supplied by the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V).

Two honest caveats are built in. Dermatome maps differ between textbooks and between people, so the levels are standard test spots, not exact borders. The cortex segment sizes are illustrative, not measurements.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Click any blue dot on the body, or choose a region and side from the dropdown menus.
  2. Look at the right panel. The title tells you which hemisphere you are seeing, and the orange segment shows where that body region is represented.
  3. Read the box at the bottom for the cortex location, the dermatome level (or nerve), and the key test spot.
  4. Switch between the person's right and left side and watch the brain slice flip to the other hemisphere.
  5. Press Quiz me. A gold dot marks a body region. Click the matching segment of the cortex strip. You get two tries, and your first-try score is shown at the bottom right.
  6. Uncheck Show labels to quiz yourself without the segment names.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will be able to locate where a touched body region is represented on the opposite primary somatosensory cortex and name the spinal level (dermatome) or cranial nerve that carries it.

docs.text:
Grade level: 9 to 12 (also suitable for Brain Bee preparation)

Duration: 20 to 25 minutes

Prerequisites: basic brain anatomy (lobes, central sulcus, postcentral gyrus) and the idea that sensory pathways cross to the opposite side.

Activity:

  1. Predict (3 min). Before opening the sim, students sketch where they think the thumb, lips, and foot are represented on the postcentral gyrus, and guess which body part gets the most cortex.
  2. Explore (8 min). In pairs, students click all 11 regions on one side and record each region's cortex segment and dermatome level in a table. They then click the same regions on the other side and note what changes and what stays the same.
  3. Explain (5 min). Pairs answer: Why do the lips and thumb get large segments? Why does the slice flip when you switch sides? Why do the lips have no spinal level?
  4. Quiz (5 min). Each student uses Quiz me with labels turned off and reports a first-try score out of 10.

Assessment questions:

  1. A patient feels numbness on the back of the little finger only. Which spinal level is most likely involved, and which hemisphere would receive touch from that finger if it were on the patient's right hand?
  2. The foot area is on the inner (medial) wall of the hemisphere. Predict what kind of sensory loss a small injury to the top of the brain near the midline might cause.
  3. Two textbooks put the front of the knee in different dermatomes. Explain why this does not make dermatome testing useless.

docs.title: Basal Ganglia Gas and Brake
docs.text: Run the Basal Ganglia Gas and Brake MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim shows the classic, simplified textbook model of the basal ganglia motor loop. The motor cortex excites the striatum. From there, two pathways lead to the GPi/SNr, the output nuclei that act as a brake on the thalamus:

  • The direct pathway (striatal neurons with D1 dopamine receptors) inhibits GPi/SNr. Inhibiting the brake releases the thalamus, so this pathway works like a gas pedal ("GO").
  • The indirect pathway (striatal neurons with D2 receptors, then GPe, then the subthalamic nucleus) ends by exciting GPi/SNr. That presses the brake harder ("NO-GO").

Dopamine from the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) excites D1 neurons and inhibits D2 neurons. Both effects favor movement. When you lower dopamine, the brake gets stronger and the movement meter drops into the "too little" (hypokinetic, Parkinson-like) zone. When you raise dopamine far above normal, the brake gets weaker and the meter moves into the "too much" (hyperkinetic) zone.

Arrows with a pointed head and a + sign are excitatory (the transmitter is glutamate). Lines that end in a flat bar with a − sign are inhibitory (the transmitter is GABA). Thicker, brighter lines mean that connection is more active.

This is a simplified model. The activity numbers are illustrative, not measured. Real basal ganglia have more connections (for example, a "hyperdirect" pathway from cortex straight to the subthalamic nucleus), and scientists still debate how cleanly the two pathways separate.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Start at the default, 100% of normal dopamine. Notice that every pathway has medium thickness and the meter reads "Normal."
  2. Before you move anything, predict: if dopamine falls, which pathway gets weaker, and which gets stronger?
  3. Drag the dopamine slider down to 30%. Check your prediction. The direct pathway (D1 to GPi/SNr) thins, the indirect pathway thickens, the brake (GPi/SNr) gets stronger, and the thalamus goes quiet.
  4. Drag the slider up to 170%. Now the direct pathway dominates, the brake weakens, and the meter enters "Too much."
  5. Find the dopamine levels where the meter switches zones. Press Reset to return to normal.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Bloom Level: Understand (explain)

The learner will explain how a change in dopamine shifts the balance between the direct and indirect pathways and predict whether movement output will be too little, normal, or too much.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9 to 12 (also useful for Brain Bee preparation)

Duration: 15 to 20 minutes

Prerequisites: neurons, synapses, excitatory versus inhibitory transmitters, dopamine, and the location of the basal ganglia and thalamus (Chapters 1 to 4 and Chapter 7 of From Neuron to Bedside).

Activity:

  1. (3 min) Warm-up: ask students what happens to a car that is parked with the brake on, and what happens if you press the gas without releasing the brake.
  2. (5 min) In pairs, students trace the circuit on the screen at 100% dopamine and label each connection as "excites" or "inhibits." They should find the "double negative": the direct pathway inhibits an inhibitor, which releases the thalamus.
  3. (5 min) Students write a prediction for 30% dopamine, then test it. Repeat for 170%.
  4. (5 min) Class discussion: connect 30% to Parkinson's disease (loss of dopamine neurons in the SNc) and 170% to the extra movements (dyskinesia) that some people develop after years of levodopa treatment.

Assessment questions:

  1. Which nucleus in this model acts as the "brake" on the thalamus? (GPi/SNr)
  2. Dopamine excites D1 neurons but inhibits D2 neurons. Why do both effects lead to more movement? (Exciting the direct pathway releases the brake; inhibiting the indirect pathway stops it from pressing the brake harder.)
  3. Predict the meter reading when dopamine is 40% of normal, and explain your answer using the words "direct," "indirect," and "thalamus."
  4. Name one way this model is simpler than the real brain. (It leaves out the hyperdirect pathway and many other connections, and it uses made-up activity numbers.)

docs.title: Synaptic Pruning Over a Lifetime
docs.text: Run the Synaptic Pruning Over a Lifetime MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The developing brain builds far more synapses than it keeps. Then, over years, it removes the least-used ones (synaptic pruning) and wraps long-distance axons in more myelin. These changes do not happen everywhere at once. Sensory areas, such as the cortex that handles hearing, reach their peak synapse density within months of birth and finish pruning in childhood. The prefrontal cortex, which helps with planning and self-control, peaks later and keeps pruning through adolescence and into the twenties.

The MicroSim has two parts:

  • Top: two small patches of neurons, one from sensory cortex (blue) and one from prefrontal cortex (orange). Solid lines are working synapses. Dashed gray lines are synapses that have been pruned. The tan "sleeves" around three long axons get thicker as myelin is added.
  • Bottom: a graph of relative synapse density for each region and relative white matter volume, with a red marker at the age you choose.

All curves are approximate, schematic trends based on research. They are drawn in relative units, not measured numbers, and real people vary a lot. The shapes follow three published findings:

  • Synapse density in human auditory (hearing) cortex peaks around 3 months after birth, while prefrontal cortex peaks after 15 months. Net synapse loss ends by about age 12 in auditory cortex but continues to mid-adolescence in prefrontal cortex (Huttenlocher and Dabholkar, 1997).
  • Pruning of dendritic spines in human prefrontal cortex continues into the third decade of life, the twenties (Petanjek and colleagues, 2011).
  • Total white matter volume keeps rising slowly after childhood and peaks at about 29 years (Bethlehem and colleagues, 2022).

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Start with the age slider at 0 (birth). Notice that both patches have few synapses and almost no myelin.
  2. Drag the slider slowly to age 3. Watch both regions fill with synapses. Which one peaks first?
  3. Keep going to age 12. Watch the dashed "pruned" lines appear in the sensory patch while the prefrontal patch stays crowded.
  4. Move to age 16, Maya's age. Read the note above the graph. Which region is still pruning?
  5. Continue to age 30. Notice that the white matter curve is still creeping upward in the twenties.
  6. Press Start to watch the whole lifetime play out automatically. Press Pause to stop.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Bloom Level: Understand (compare)

Students will compare the timing of synapse overproduction, synaptic pruning, and myelination in sensory cortex versus prefrontal cortex from birth to age 30, and explain why this timing means brain development continues through the teenage years and into the twenties.
