docs.text: <iframe src="https://aaryavvatts-lab.github.io/neuroscience-textbook/sims/ch08-synaptic-pruning/main.html" height="642px" width="100%" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9 to 12

Duration: 15 to 20 minutes

Prerequisites: neurons and synapses (Chapter 1 and Chapter 3), myelin (Chapter 1), and the location of the prefrontal cortex (Chapter 4).

Activity:

  1. Predict (3 minutes). Before opening the sim, students sketch on paper how they think the number of synapses changes from birth to age 30. Most will draw a line that only goes up.
  2. Explore (7 minutes). In pairs, students follow the How to Use steps. They record the age at which each curve peaks and the age at which each one levels off.
  3. Explain (5 minutes). Each pair writes two sentences: one explaining why losing synapses can make the brain work better, and one explaining why "brain development finishes at exactly 25" is too simple.

Assessment questions:

  1. Which region reaches its peak synapse density first, sensory cortex or prefrontal cortex?
  2. At age 16, which region is still pruning?
  3. White matter volume is still rising in the mid-twenties. What does that tell you about the claim that the brain "finishes" at a single age?
  4. Why does the sim label its curves as "schematic" instead of giving exact synapse counts?

Answers: (1) Sensory cortex, within months of birth. (2) Prefrontal cortex. (3) Some kinds of development, like myelination of long connections, keep going gradually into the late twenties, so there is no single finish line. (4) The exact counts come from small numbers of brain samples and vary between people; the sim shows the general pattern, not precise measurements.

docs.title: Aplysia Habituation and Sensitization
docs.text: Run the Aplysia Habituation and Sensitization MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The sea slug Aplysia pulls its gill in when its siphon is touched. Eric Kandel and his colleagues used this simple defensive reflex to show that learning changes the strength of synapses. In the reflex circuit, a siphon sensory neuron connects directly to a gill motor neuron. A tail shock activates facilitating interneurons that release serotonin (5-HT) onto the sensory neuron's terminal.

This MicroSim is a simplified, qualitative model of that circuit:

  • Each siphon touch makes the sensory neuron release a little less transmitter next time, so the gill-withdrawal response shrinks. This is habituation.
  • A tail shock adds serotonin, which makes the sensory neuron release more transmitter, so later touches produce a bigger response. This is sensitization (called dishabituation when it restores a habituated response).
  • Resting lets habituation partly recover and lets short-term sensitization fade.

The numbers on the vertical axis are arbitrary units. They show the direction of each change, not real measurements.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Press Touch siphon once. Note the height of the first blue bar (about 100, the baseline).
  2. Press Touch siphon five or six more times. Watch the bars get shorter and the synapse-strength meter fall below 1.0.
  3. Press Shock tail. An orange "S" line marks the shock, and orange dots show serotonin reaching the sensory neuron's terminal.
  4. Press Touch siphon again. The orange bar is taller than the last blue bar.
  5. Press Rest, then touch again. Compare the response with the habituated bars.
  6. Press Reset, then shock the tail before any touches. Compare the first response with the baseline of 100.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Bloom Level: Understand (explain)

The learner will explain how repeated siphon touches and a tail shock change the strength of the sensory-to-motor synapse, and how that change produces habituation or sensitization of the gill-withdrawal reflex.

docs.text: <iframe src="https://aaryavvatts-lab.github.io/neuroscience-textbook/sims/ch09-aplysia-learning/main.html" height="532px" width="100%" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9 to 12

Duration: 20 minutes

Prerequisites: sensory and motor neurons, synapses, neurotransmitters, excitatory postsynaptic potentials (Chapters 1 to 3)

docs.title: Activity
docs.text:
1. Predict (3 min): Before using the sim, students write down what they think will happen to the gill-withdrawal response if the siphon is touched ten times in a row.
  2. Habituation (5 min): Students touch the siphon at least six times and sketch the bar pattern. They answer: Did the touch change, or did the synapse change?
  3. Sensitization (5 min): Students shock the tail, touch again, and describe the role of the interneuron and serotonin.
  4. Recovery (3 min): Students rest the animal and test again, then compare with their prediction.
  5. Connect (4 min): In pairs, students give one human example of habituation (ignoring a ticking clock) and one of sensitization (jumping at small noises after a scare).

docs.title: Assessment Questions
docs.text:
1. Which synapse weakens during habituation in this model, and what happens to transmitter release?
  2. Which neurotransmitter does the facilitating interneuron release, and where does it act?
  3. Why does a tail shock make the response to a siphon touch bigger, even though the siphon touch itself did not change?
  4. Kandel found that long-term memory in Aplysia needs new proteins and can involve growth of new synaptic connections. How is that different from what this short-term model shows?

docs.title: Hypnogram Builder
docs.text: Run the Hypnogram Builder MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A hypnogram is a graph of sleep stages across a night. This MicroSim shows an illustrative (made-up but typical) night for a healthy teenager who sleeps 9 hours. The night is built from cycles of about 90 minutes. Deep N3 sleep is packed into the first half of the night, and REM periods (red bars) get longer toward morning.

Click any stage name, or hover over the night, to see a schematic EEG trace for that stage: alpha waves for relaxed waking, theta waves for N1, a sleep spindle and K-complex for N2, tall slow delta waves for N3, and low-voltage mixed waves with sawtooth waves for REM. The traces are simplified drawings, not real recordings, but their frequencies and relative sizes follow standard sleep-scoring descriptions.

The Hours of sleep slider moves an "alarm" line earlier in the night. A readout shows how many minutes of REM, N2, and N3 are kept and lost compared with the full 9-hour night.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Click each stage label (Wake, REM, N1, N2, N3) on the left, or choose a stage from the Show EEG for menu. Compare the speed and height of the waves.
  2. Move your mouse across the hypnogram from left to right. The label shows the time and stage under the cursor, and the EEG panel switches to that stage.
  3. Drag the Hours of sleep slider from 9.0 down to 6.0 hours. Watch the gray "lost" region grow and read the minutes lost for each stage.
  4. Try 7.5 hours and 4.5 hours. Which stage is the last to be affected? Which is hit first?
  5. Click Reset to 9 h to restore the full night.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Students will be able to interpret a hypnogram to identify each sleep stage by its EEG signature and explain why shortening sleep removes mostly REM and N2 sleep rather than deep N3 sleep.

Bloom's Taxonomy level: Analyze (interpret)

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9 to 12

Duration: 20 to 25 minutes

Prerequisites: Students should know what an EEG measures, the meaning of frequency and amplitude, and the four sleep stages (N1, N2, N3, REM) from Chapter 10.

Activity:

  1. Predict (3 minutes). Before opening the sim, ask students: "If you sleep 6 hours instead of 9, which sleep stage do you think you lose the most of?" Have them write down a prediction.
  2. Explore the stages (7 minutes). In pairs, students click through all five stages and sketch each EEG trace in their notebooks with a one-word label (for example, "spindles" for N2).
  3. Cut the night short (7 minutes). Students set the slider to 7.5, 6.0, and 4.5 hours and record minutes kept for REM, N2, and N3 in a table.
  4. Explain (5 minutes). Students compare their prediction with the data and write two sentences explaining the pattern using the words "early night," "late night," "N3," and "REM."

Assessment questions:

  1. Which stage has the tallest, slowest EEG waves, and when in the night does most of it occur?
  2. At 6.0 hours, about what fraction of the night's REM is lost in this model, and why?
  3. A classmate says, "Short sleep only costs you deep sleep." Use the sim's numbers to correct this claim.
  4. Name the two EEG features that identify N2 sleep.

docs.title: HPA Axis Feedback Loop
docs.text: Run the HPA Axis Feedback Loop MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Your body answers a stressor with two systems working at two speeds. The fast path runs through sympathetic nerves to the adrenal medulla, which releases adrenaline within seconds. The slow path is the hormone chain called the HPA axis: the hypothalamus releases CRH, the anterior pituitary releases ACTH, and the adrenal cortex releases cortisol. Cortisol raises blood glucose and helps the body cope, and it also travels back to the brain and shuts its own production down. That brake is called negative feedback.

The top half of the MicroSim is a causal-loop diagram. Plus signs (+) mean "increases the next step." Minus signs (−) on the dashed red arrows mean "slows the earlier step," which is cortisol's negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary. Boxes glow more strongly as their hormone rises above its resting level. The bottom half plots cortisol (thick red line) and adrenaline (thin orange line) over time.

This is a simplified teaching model in relative units (1.0 = resting baseline). It is not fitted to patient data. It leaves out the daily cortisol rhythm, vasopressin, the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex, and differences between people.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Leave Feedback strength at 1.0 and press Stressor! The clock starts. Notice that adrenaline jumps within a few simulated minutes, while cortisol rises more slowly and peaks later.
  2. Watch cortisol return to the dashed baseline line. With intact feedback, that takes about an hour in this model.
  3. Before the next step, predict: if the brake is weaker, will the cortisol peak be higher, lower, or the same? Then drag Feedback strength down to 0.3 and press Stressor! again. Compare the two peaks.
  4. Press Reset, set the slider back to 1.0, and check Chronic stress. A new stressor now arrives every 30 simulated minutes. Notice that cortisol never gets back to baseline.
  5. Finally, keep Chronic stress checked and slide Feedback strength to 0. Cortisol climbs far higher and stays there. This is the model's picture of a stress system that cannot switch off.
  6. Use Start/Pause to freeze the graph at any moment and read the values in the boxes and the legend.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Bloom Level: Analyze

Bloom Verb: differentiate

Students will differentiate a healthy, self-limiting acute stress response from a sustained cortisol elevation. They do this by predicting, and then observing, how the cortisol curve changes when negative feedback is weakened or when stressors repeat.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9 to 12 (biology, AP Psychology, anatomy and physiology, or a neuroscience club)

Duration: 20 to 25 minutes

Prerequisites: hormones travel in the blood; the hypothalamus and pituitary sit at the base of the brain; the meaning of "negative feedback" (a thermostat is a good analogy).

Activity:

  1. Warm-up (3 min). Ask: "What does a thermostat do when the room gets too hot?" Connect it to negative feedback.
  2. Predict (3 min). Students sketch what they think cortisol will do after one stressor, and write one sentence about how a broken "thermostat" would change their sketch.
  3. Explore (10 min). In pairs, students run the four scenarios: (a) one stressor with feedback 1.0, (b) one stressor with feedback 0.3, (c) chronic stress with feedback 1.0, (d) chronic stress with feedback 0. For each one, they record the highest cortisol value and whether cortisol returned to baseline.
  4. Explain (5 min). Students compare their data with their predictions and explain each difference using the words CRH, ACTH, cortisol, and negative feedback.
  5. Connect (3 min). Discuss: Why do adrenaline and cortisol peak at different times? Why might a stress system that stays switched on for weeks affect sleep, mood, and memory?

Assessment questions:

  1. Which hormone does the pituitary release in response to CRH, and which gland does that hormone act on?
  2. In the model, why does adrenaline peak before cortisol?
  3. A student says, "Negative feedback means stress is bad for you." Use the simulation to correct this statement.
  4. Describe two different ways cortisol can end up staying high in the model, and explain how they differ.
  5. What is one thing this simple model leaves out that real bodies have?

docs.title: Aphasia Sorter
docs.text: Run the Aphasia Sorter MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Aphasia is a language disorder caused by damage to the brain's language network, most often from a stroke. Doctors and speech-language pathologists tell the main types apart by listening for three things: whether speech is fluent, whether the person understands what is said to them, and whether they can repeat a sentence.

This MicroSim turns that bedside skill into a sorting game. Each round shows one short speech sample and a one-line clue about comprehension or repetition. You decide whether it is Broca's aphasia, Wernicke's aphasia, conduction aphasia, or normal speech. There are 10 items (3 Broca's, 3 Wernicke's, 2 conduction, 2 normal), shown in a new random order each round.

All speech samples were written for this book. They are simplified teaching examples, not recordings of real patients, and real people with aphasia vary a lot. The game uses only three aphasia types plus normal speech. Real clinics also see other types, such as global, anomic, and transcortical aphasia, and many patients have mixed patterns that don't fit one box.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the speech sample in the white box. Ask: is it fluent, or slow and broken? Does it make sense?
  2. Read the clue in the yellow box. It tells you about comprehension or repetition.
  3. Click one category button: Broca's, Wernicke's, Conduction, or Normal. You get one answer per item.
  4. Read the feedback. It tells you whether you were right, names the correct category, and explains which clue decides it.
  5. Click Next for the next item. After item 10 you'll see your final score.
  6. Click Restart at any time to reshuffle and start a new round.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Bloom's level: Analyze (classify). The learner will classify short speech samples as Broca's aphasia, Wernicke's aphasia, conduction aphasia, or normal speech by analyzing fluency, comprehension, and repetition, scoring at least 8 of 10 correct.

docs.text: <iframe src="https://aaryavvatts-lab.github.io/neuroscience-textbook/sims/ch12-aphasia-sorter/main.html" height="647px" width="100%" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9 to 12 (also suitable for Brain Bee preparation and introductory pre-med courses)

Duration: 20 to 25 minutes

Prerequisites: Students should know the four lobes of the brain, that each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body, and the terms fluency, telegraphic speech, paraphasia, neologism, comprehension, and repetition (Section 12.4 of Chapter 12).

Activity:

  1. Warm-up (5 min): Ask students to describe a time they couldn't find a word ("tip of the tongue"). Explain that aphasia is a much more severe and lasting language problem after brain injury, and that it does not affect intelligence.
  2. Play (10 min): Students play one full round alone, then a second round with a partner. Partners must say out loud which clue (fluency, comprehension, or repetition) decided each answer before clicking.
  3. Discuss (5 to 10 min): Which items were hardest? Why are the "normal" samples tricky? Why can a fluent speaker still have a serious language disorder?

Assessment questions:

  1. A patient speaks in long, smooth sentences full of made-up words and cannot follow "Close your eyes." Which type of aphasia is this, and which lobe is most likely damaged?
  2. Two patients both have poor repetition. One is nonfluent, the other fluent with good comprehension. Name each type of aphasia.
  3. Why does Broca's aphasia often come with weakness of the right arm, while Wernicke's aphasia usually does not?
  4. Write one original speech sample for each of the four categories, with a clue, that a classmate could sort correctly.

docs.title: Amyloid and Tau Cascade
docs.text: Run the Amyloid and Tau Cascade MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Alzheimer's disease doesn't start when memory problems start. Brain changes begin a decade or more before symptoms appear. This MicroSim draws a schematic timeline from age 40 to 90 with four curves:

  1. Amyloid plaques (orange): clumps of beta-amyloid protein that build up between neurons.
  2. Tau tangles (blue): twisted threads of tau protein inside neurons.
  3. Neuron loss and brain shrinkage (gray).
  4. Memory and thinking problems (red).

The order of the curves follows the widely cited hypothetical biomarker model of Jack and colleagues (Lancet Neurology, 2010), in which amyloid becomes abnormal first and symptoms come last. The exact ages and curve shapes are illustrative. In this model, amyloid crosses the dashed "abnormal on tests" line at about age 50, tau at about 60, neuron loss at about 65, and symptoms at about 73. The clinical stage changes from preclinical to mild cognitive impairment at about age 72 and to dementia at about age 78. Real people vary a lot. Jack and colleagues noted that roughly 20 to 40 percent of older adults with normal thinking already have significant amyloid in their brains, and the delay between amyloid and symptoms differs from person to person.

The checkbox starts an illustrative anti-amyloid treatment at the chosen age. The amyloid curve falls, but the other curves stay the same, because the model makes no claim about how much treatment changes them. The message under the panels summarizes what real trials have shown.

Schematic model, not real patient data.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Start at age 50. Notice that the orange amyloid curve has already reached the "abnormal on tests" line, yet the clinical stage says there are no symptoms.
  2. Drag the age slider slowly to the right. Watch the order in which each curve crosses the dashed line.
  3. Watch the tissue cartoon: orange plaques appear between cells first, then blue tangles appear inside cells, then neurons fade away.
  4. Find the age where the stage changes to mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and then to dementia.
  5. Set the age to 74 (MCI) and check the treatment box. Move the slider forward and read the message.
  6. Uncheck the box, set the age to 86, and check it again. Read how the message changes.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Bloom Level: Understand (verb: explain)

The learner will explain why Alzheimer's brain changes are best detected and treated early, using the order in which amyloid, tau, neuron loss, and symptoms rise.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9 to 12

Duration: 20 minutes

Activity:

  1. (3 min) Ask: "If your grandparent started forgetting names last year, when do you think the brain changes started?" Collect guesses.
  2. (7 min) In pairs, students drag the slider from 40 to 90 and record the age at which each curve crosses the "abnormal on tests" line. They write the four curves in order.
  3. (5 min) Students start treatment once at age 74 and once at age 86, and copy the message they see each time.
  4. (5 min) Class discussion: Why do doctors want blood tests and PET scans that detect amyloid before symptoms? Why aren't anti-amyloid drugs a cure?

Assessment questions:

  1. In the model, which change appears first, and about how many years pass before the stage changes to mild cognitive impairment? (Amyloid, at about age 50; roughly 20 years pass before MCI at about age 72.)
  2. Why does removing amyloid late in the disease not bring back memory? (Tau tangles have spread and many neurons are already lost; dead neurons are not replaced.)
  3. A 55-year-old has a positive amyloid scan but a normal memory test. Which stage is that in the model? (Preclinical Alzheimer's disease.)

docs.title: Stroke Territory Map
docs.text: Run the Stroke Territory Map MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
A stroke's symptoms depend on which artery is blocked and on which side of the brain. This MicroSim links two pictures:

  • A brain slice drawn like a CT scan. The front of the brain is at the top, and the person's right hemisphere is on your left, the convention doctors use when reading scans. Each hemisphere is divided into the territories of the anterior cerebral artery (ACA), middle cerebral artery (MCA), and posterior cerebral artery (PCA).
  • A body figure facing you. Its right side is also on your left. A small "Vision" circle shows what the person sees, with their left half of vision on the left.

When you block an artery, its territory darkens, the face, arm, and leg on the opposite side of the body light up (dark red for the main problem, light red for milder or possible problems), the mouth droops for MCA strokes, and the lost half of vision is shaded for PCA (and possibly MCA) strokes. An info panel lists the typical deficits.

The patterns follow the "Selected Stroke Syndromes" table in the Merck Manual Professional Version (Overview of Stroke). They are typical patterns only; real strokes vary in size and location, and the territory shapes are simplified wedges, not an exact anatomical atlas.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the starting panel. Notice the R and L markers: both pictures face you, so the person's right is on your left.
  2. Check Predict first to hide the body.
  3. Choose an artery (ACA, MCA, or PCA) and a hemisphere (Left or Right), or click a colored region of the brain slice.
  4. Predict which side of the body will be affected and whether the face, arm, leg, vision, language, or attention will be involved.
  5. Uncheck Predict first to reveal the answer and read the info panel.
  6. Repeat for all six combinations and look for the rule that never changes.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Bloom level: Apply. Given which cerebral artery (ACA, MCA, or PCA) is blocked and in which hemisphere, students will predict which side of the body and which functions are typically affected.

docs.text: <iframe src="https://aaryavvatts-lab.github.io/neuroscience-textbook/sims/ch14-stroke-territories/main.html" height="702px" width="100%" scrolling="no"></iframe>

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9 to 12

Duration: 15 to 20 minutes

Prerequisites: the motor and touch body maps (Chapter 6), crossing motor pathways (Chapter 7), visual fields (Chapter 5), and language areas (Chapter 12)

Activity: Stroke detective

  1. (3 min) Review: each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body, and the leg area of the motor strip sits near the midline and the face and arm areas sit on the outer side.
  2. (8 min) In pairs, students turn on Predict first and work through all six artery-and-side combinations. For each, one partner predicts and the other checks the sim. Record results in a table: artery, side, body parts affected, special signs (aphasia, neglect, vision loss).
  3. (5 min) Give three short patient descriptions and ask students to name the most likely blocked artery and side:
    • Left leg much weaker than the left arm, face normal (right ACA)
    • Right face and arm weakness with trouble speaking (left MCA)
    • Cannot see the left half of the world, no weakness (right PCA)
  4. (3 min) Discuss why real strokes might not match these patterns exactly.

Assessment questions

  1. A right MCA stroke usually affects which side of the body, and what attention problem may appear?
  2. Why does an ACA stroke affect the leg more than the arm?
  3. A patient has no weakness but has lost the right half of vision in both eyes. Which artery and which side are most likely involved?
  4. Why does language trouble usually go with left MCA strokes rather than right MCA strokes?

docs.title: Reward Pathway and Tolerance
docs.text: Run the Reward Pathway and Tolerance MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This MicroSim is a schematic (simplified) model of how the brain's reward pathway responds to natural rewards and to an addictive drug. The left panel shows a side view of the brain. Dopamine neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) send signals to the nucleus accumbens (NAc) and the prefrontal cortex (PFC), and the PFC sends control signals back to the NAc. Below the brain, a row of 10 receptor icons stands for the dopamine receptors on a nucleus accumbens neuron.

The right panel plots dopamine signaling over time in relative units, where the original baseline equals 1. A natural reward produces a moderate, brief bump. A drug dose produces a much larger, faster spike. With repeated doses, receptors are removed (downregulation), so each spike shrinks and the baseline sinks below normal: this is tolerance. Pressing Stop drug causes a dip below even the lowered baseline (withdrawal), which slowly recovers over simulated days as receptors return.

All numbers are illustrative. The model shows the direction of the changes described by NIDA and OpenStax, not measurements of any real drug. It does not show learned, cue-triggered craving, which can last much longer than the receptor changes.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Press Start to run the clock (about 1 simulated day per second). The sim begins paused.
  2. Press Natural reward. Watch the small bump on the plot (marked N) and the glow along the VTA pathways.
  3. Press Drug dose once (marked D). Compare the spike height with the natural reward.
  4. Press Drug dose five or six more times, a second or two apart. Watch the spikes shrink, the trace settle below the green "original baseline," and receptor icons disappear.
  5. Press Natural reward again and compare its bump with step 2.
  6. Press Stop drug (marked S). Watch the withdrawal dip and the slow recovery of the signal and the receptors over the next 20 to 30 days.
  7. Press Reset to start over. Use Pause at any time to study the plot.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Bloom level: Understand. Students will explain how repeated drug doses produce tolerance (smaller dopamine responses and a lower baseline caused by receptor downregulation) and how stopping the drug produces a below-baseline withdrawal state that recovers slowly.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9 to 12

Duration: 20 to 25 minutes

Prerequisites: neurons and synapses, neurotransmitters and receptors, dopamine, and the idea that synapses can change with experience (Chapters 3 and 9).

Activity:

  1. Predict (3 min). Before using the sim, students write a prediction: "If someone takes the same drug every day, will each dose feel the same? Why or why not?"
  2. Explore (10 min). In pairs, students follow the How to Use steps. One partner runs the sim while the other records: the height of the first drug spike, the height of the sixth spike, the number of receptor icons after six doses, and the lowest point of the signal after Stop drug.
  3. Explain (5 min). Pairs write two to three sentences that use the words receptor, tolerance, and withdrawal to explain their data.
  4. Connect (5 min). Class discussion: Why might everyday activities feel less enjoyable to someone with tolerance? Why does recovery take time and support, and not just willpower?

Assessment questions:

  1. Why does the sixth drug dose produce a smaller spike than the first?
  2. After several doses, why is a natural reward's bump smaller than it was at the start?
  3. What happens to the signal right after Stop drug, and what has to change for it to recover?
  4. Name one thing this schematic model leaves out about real addiction.

docs.text: Run the Neuro Exam Decision Tree MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Doctors don't start a neurological workup by ordering a scan. They take a history, examine the patient step by step, and then ask one question: where in the nervous system is the problem? This MicroSim lets you practice that reasoning on three fictional patients:

  1. Right-sided weakness: sudden weakness and trouble speaking (a left-hemisphere pattern)
  2. Face droop on waking: weakness of one whole side of the face (a peripheral facial nerve pattern)
  3. Stiff, weak legs: weeks of leg stiffness with a numb band below the belly button (a spinal cord pattern)

Each exam button reveals one finding. You decide which findings matter, then commit to a location: left cerebral hemisphere, right cerebral hemisphere, brainstem, spinal cord, peripheral nerve, or muscle. The feedback explains why your answer does or doesn't fit.

All three patients are fictional teaching composites. The findings follow standard textbook patterns, such as upper versus lower motor neuron signs and forehead-sparing versus whole-face weakness. Real patients are often less tidy.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Choose a case from the Case menu and read the patient summary.
  2. Press exam buttons (Mental status, Cranial nerves, Strength, Reflexes, Sensation, Coordination, Gait) and scan buttons (Order CT, Order MRI). Each one adds a short finding to the Findings list and shows a longer explanation below it. Buttons you've used turn blue.
  3. After at least 3 steps, choose a location from the Location menu and press Check.
  4. Read the feedback. If you're wrong, try again. After two wrong tries, the sim tells you the answer so you can choose it and read the reasoning.
  5. Press Reset to start the same case over, or choose a new case.

Challenge: Can you localize each case correctly using only 3 steps? Which 3 steps are most useful for each case?

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Bloom Level: Analyze

Students will be able to localize a lesion to the left or right cerebral hemisphere, brainstem, spinal cord, peripheral nerve, or muscle by analyzing a pattern of exam findings (upper versus lower motor neuron signs, side of the body, and level of sensory loss).

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text:
Grade level: 9 to 12 (also useful for Brain Bee patient-diagnosis practice)

Duration: 20 to 25 minutes

Prerequisites: The motor pathway crosses to the opposite side (Chapter 7), the parts of the brain (Chapter 4), cranial nerves, and the idea of upper versus lower motor neurons (Chapters 7 and 16).

Activity:

  1. Warm-up (5 min): Ask the class, "If the left side of the brain is damaged, which side of the body gets weak? Why?"
  2. Pairs (12 min): Partners work through all three cases. Before pressing Check, each pair writes down their localization and the two findings that convinced them most.
  3. The 3-step challenge (5 min): Pairs restart one case and try to localize it with only 3 exam steps. Which steps did they pick, and why?
  4. Debrief (3 min): Compare the facial findings in Case 1 and Case 2. Why does one spare the forehead and the other doesn't?

Assessment questions:

  1. In Case 1, which two findings best show that the problem is in the brain, not the spinal cord?
  2. Why is weakness of the whole half of the face, forehead included, a sign of facial nerve damage rather than a stroke in the cortex?
  3. In Case 3, what is a "sensory level," and why does it point to the spinal cord?
  4. Brisk reflexes and a Babinski sign are upper motor neuron signs. Name two lower motor neuron signs.
  5. Why is a head CT not enough to find the problem in Case 3?

docs.title: Learning Graph Viewer
docs.text:
Open Learning Graph Viewer Fullscreen (recommended)

This interactive viewer lets you explore the learning graph for From Neuron to Bedside: 253 concepts, from the cell membrane to the neurological exam, and the prerequisite arrows that connect them.

docs.title: Categories
docs.text:
Each node is colored by its category in the concept taxonomy:

Color Category Code Steel blue Foundational Biology and Chemistry FOUND Dark green Neurons and Glia CELL Gold Electrical and Chemical Signaling SIG Teal Neuroanatomy ANAT Orange Sensory Systems and Pain SENS Dark slate blue Movement and Motor Control MOTOR Lime green Development and Aging DEV Dark orchid Learning, Memory, and Cognition COG Light sky blue Sleep, Emotion, and Stress STATE Crimson Disorders and Diseases DIS Hot pink Clinical Exam, Imaging, and Treatment CLIN Saddle brown Research Methods and Careers RES

Larger boxes are concepts that more of the book builds on (a higher Concept Impact Score). Foundational concepts are the ones with no outgoing arrows.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Search: Type in the search box to find specific concepts
  • Category Filtering: Use checkboxes to show/hide concept categories
  • Interactive Navigation: Click and drag to explore, scroll to zoom
  • Statistics: View real-time counts of visible nodes and edges

docs.title: Using the Viewer
docs.text:
1. Search for Concepts: Start typing in the search box to find concepts. Click on a result to focus on that node.

  2. Filter by Category: Use the category checkboxes in the sidebar to show or hide groups of related concepts. Use "Check All" or "Uncheck All" for bulk operations.

  3. Navigate the Graph:

    • Drag to pan around the graph
    • Scroll to zoom in and out
    • Click on a node to select it and highlight its connections
    • Click the hamburger menu to collapse or expand the sidebar

  4. View Statistics: The sidebar shows counts of visible nodes, edges, and foundational concepts.

docs.title: Graph Structure
docs.text:
• Foundational Concepts: Prerequisites with no dependencies
  • Advanced Concepts: Topics that build on multiple prerequisites
  • Edges: Arrows point from a concept to its prerequisites

The graph uses a force-directed layout that positions related concepts near each other.
